records.title: fix: fence browser recovery to attach inventory placements
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​65 | 0 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​65 |
| Prod | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​27 | 0 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​27 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Orca can show web pages inside the app, and a paired device can be the thing that actually holds those pages open. When the part of Orca that keeps track of them restarted, it took a moment to re-check its list of open pages. If you opened a brand-new tab during that brief moment, the restarted bookkeeping did not know about that tab, assumed it had gone missing, and tried to build a replacement on top of the tab that was already sitting there. The desktop refused the contradictory instruction, and instead of losing just that one tab, every browser tab on that device went dead until you reconnected.

Now Orca writes down exactly which pages existed at the instant it began re-checking, and it only re-checks those. A tab you open while it is still catching up is left alone, because it is new and healthy and does not need rescuing. Opening a tab right after a restart no longer takes down the rest of your browser tabs.

## What changed

After a paired runtime restarts, opening a new browser tab can shut down the entire client browser host. Attach publishes readiness and waits for existing-page adoption; recovery then scans the current page registry using the older attach inventory. It treats the newly created page as missing, retires its placement without closing the live guest, and sends another create at a higher generation. The desktop rejects that command with `browser_host_page_replacement_requires_retirement`, leaving all its browser tabs unavailable.

Capture page placements before publishing attach readiness and constrain recovery to those exact placements. Pages created or replaced during adoption retain their authority. The existing recovery path still handles pages that the captured inventory actually describes.

Validation: a real RPC regression creates a page while adoption is held; it fails before the fix because its placement is retired, then passes afterward. A second regression protects a replacement generation. All 51 focused adoption/recovery/negotiation tests pass, as do the 96 tests in the matching browser-network gate command. `pnpm tc:node` and targeted lint pass. The previously failing macOS paired cookie-survival journey passes three consecutive Electron runs, verifying the rendered post-restart page, surviving route cookie, and isolated default-session cookie jar. Double-restart, quit-survival, and ghost-close neighbors are still under investigation.

Reliability gate: `browser-network-tunnel.bounded-fail-closed-route`. Invariant: stale attach inventory must not retire a newer live page placement. Oracle: unchanged placement and active page, zero recovery commands for the new page, and rendered cookie survival after a real runtime restart. Diagnostics: the generation-replacement error and Playwright traces identify the original failure; both deterministic regressions preserve the race. The added snapshot is bounded by the existing 256-page registry cap and occurs once per attach; no polling, subprocess, or new protocol field is added. The host sends fewer erroneous recovery commands through the existing negotiated protocol, with no new behavior required of older clients. macOS paired/native execution is rendered-covered; Linux, Windows, SSH, WSL, folder workspaces, and mobile rendered coverage remain gaps. The logic compares page placements independently of execution-host paths and retains the existing folder/remote resolver.

## Tradeoffs

Genuine negatives, not "none":

- **Skipping is fail-open, so one repair can be deferred.** If a page's placement changes between the snapshot and the recovery scan, this attach leaves it alone. When that page was genuinely unhealthy, it is no longer repaired on this pass and stays unusable until the next attach — a reconnect or app restart — picks it up. Previously it would have been attempted immediately. The window is narrow and the user workaround is to close and reopen the tab.
- **The race is narrowed, not eliminated.** A window remains between the client capturing its page inventory and the runtime taking its snapshot. On a reconnect or replacement attach, where the previous lease is still live, a tab created inside that message-hop window is present in the snapshot but absent from the inventory, so the original retire-and-recreate failure is still reachable. This is a pre-existing window that this change shrinks from "readiness plus the whole adoption pass" to "one message hop". Closing it fully requires changing the empty-inventory recreate rule and is deliberately not attempted here.
- **The fence is opt-in at the call site.** `pagePlacementsAtAttach` is optional, so recovery runs unfenced if a future caller omits it. Only the attach handler calls it today and the parameter is documented, but this is a latent way to reintroduce the bug.
- **Slightly more work per attach.** One `Map` of page id to placement is built on every attach, bounded by the existing 256-page registry cap, and released when the handler returns. No polling, no subprocess, no new protocol field.
- **Coverage is uneven across topologies.** Rendered end-to-end proof exists only for macOS paired/native. Linux, Windows, SSH, WSL, folder workspaces, and mobile rely on unit-level coverage. The logic compares placements and never reads execution-host paths, so it is topology-independent by construction, but that is an argument rather than a measurement.

## Visual proof

Not applicable, and not valuable here. The change has no rendered surface of its own; it suppresses an erroneous recovery command during attach. The only visible symptom is the *absence* of a failure — browser tabs staying alive after a restart — which a screenshot cannot distinguish from a broken build. The meaningful evidence is the paired cookie-survival Electron journey noted above plus the two deterministic regressions. Local Electron launches are paused for this task, so no app was launched.

Application behavior change: left open for user review; do not merge automatically.

records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 1 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​92 | 0 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​92 |
| Prod | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​154 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​21 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​133 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Imagine receiving a parcel one small piece at a time. Orca was copying every piece received so far whenever another arrived. It now puts each piece directly in its final place, so fragmented browser-network traffic takes much less CPU and memory-copy work.

## What Changed / Why

Assemble the WSL browser network tunnel's header and payload incrementally into owned buffers. Preserve the existing wire format, pre-feed retained-byte ceiling (including header bytes), maximum frame size, caller-buffer independence, callback error behavior and close handling.

## Measurements

Actual original/current production decoder; macOS / Node 24.18, median of five local runs. Copy counts include `set` and `slice`; these are decoder microbenchmarks, not page-load speed claims.

| 64 KiB payload arrival | Before | After | Copied bytes before → after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 KiB fragments | 0.07065 ms | 0.00561 ms | 1,245,188 → 65,536 |
| 256-byte fragments | 1.035 ms | 0.01556 ms | 16,973,828 → 65,536 |
| 1-byte adverse fragments | 353.83 ms | 2.816 ms | 4,295,557,136 → 65,540 |
| Whole frame | 0.007338 ms | 0.00317 ms | 131,076 → 65,536 |

Reproduce: `node config/scripts/benchmark-browser-tunnel-framing.mjs d8c4c830639bf3d603c9250a536e0323ca0a7a19`. The one-byte payload control also improved locally (0.000229 → 0.000144 ms); its absolute cost is tiny.

## Visual Proof

N/A — internal network-frame decoding; no visual or interaction behavior changes.

## Testing

- 19 framing and WSL execution-route tests pass. Cases include maximum frames split at seven fragment sizes, coalesced frames, exact copy counts, cap boundaries, independent ownership, callback failures and close during a callback.
- `pnpm tc` passes for node, CLI and renderer with the audit fixes present; scoped lint and formatting pass.
- Tested on macOS with deterministic WSL route contracts. A live Windows/WSL browser was not exercised; native platform CI remains a validation gap.

## Negative user-facing trade-offs

- None identified. Frame bytes, limits and delivery behavior remain the same; no output is dropped or delayed.
- Internal allocation timing changes: after a validated header, one payload allocation reserves at most 65,552 bytes under the existing default cap. It is released on delivery, error or close.
- No RPC field/opcode changes; mixed-version peers use identical framing. No Git or filesystem-path changes; folder/SSH workspace semantics are unaffected.

## Review

- [x] Focused change with ELI5, measurements and deterministic regression tests.
- [x] Self-reviewed for ownership, error/close cleanup and remote compatibility.
- [x] Agent skill upstream boundary: not applicable.
- [ ] Full build and remaining repository checks: CI.

records.title: perf: assemble fragmented browser tunnel frames once
records.body:
The WSL browser network tunnel decoder recopies its growing partial frame on every incoming fragment. A 64KiB frame delivered in 256-byte chunks copies 16.97MB; one-byte fragmentation copies 4.30GB and stalls decoding for hundreds of milliseconds.

Incremental assembly can copy each byte once while preserving framing, input ownership, limits, callback error handling and close behavior. This issue tracks the comprehensive performance audit, which requires measured improvements with no negative user-facing trade-offs.

records.title: fix(browser): focus foreground tabs opened from image links
records.body:
## ELI5

Clicking a linked image can activate a new browser tab while keyboard focus stays in its parent. Pressing Cmd/Ctrl+W then closes the parent. This change gives the new foreground tab keyboard focus when its guest is ready, so the shortcut closes the intended tab.

## What Changed

- Request focus through the existing queue when link opening activates a new tab, respecting `activate: false` for background opens.
- Check that the guest is attached and focus the embedding window before the guest.
- Retain pending focus through guest startup and StrictMode effect replay; retry on `dom-ready` when the initial frame attempts finish before attachment.
- Cancel pending focus when the user switches tabs or splits, clicks elsewhere, or explicitly focuses the address bar.
- Add an image-click E2E regression and unit coverage for readiness, cancellation, and background opens.

## Why

#18873 changed Cmd/Ctrl-click and **Open Link In Orca Browser** to keep the current tab active and open the destination in the background. This PR preserves that policy and removes its earlier foreground-focus expectations for those routes.

The remaining reproduction is a plain click on a linked image that opens an active tab. Tab activation alone does not transfer native keyboard focus. In addition, the existing six-frame retry budget can finish before the new guest is attached. The readiness event now completes the pending request unless the user has moved focus elsewhere.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #18832

## Visual Proof

Click the linked image, then press Cmd+W without clicking inside the destination. Before uses main `adcc30be3b`; after uses the final implementation. These GIFs combine actual CDP captures with step captions and a click marker. Both captures use native macOS keyboard input.

| Before: parent closes | After: image tab closes |
| --- | --- |
| ![Before: image click and Cmd+W close the parent](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1567e09a-3948-4b0e-a730-28e9d9b2efab) | ![After: image click and Cmd+W close the image tab](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f1b1f2b2-ed4b-4cc9-9806-f2e70b944654) |

## Testing

- [x] I manually tested these changes locally.
- [x] Automated tests added/updated.

macOS validation:

- 63 focused unit tests passed across the IPC bridge, guest adapter, focus hook, focus queue, and webview registry.
- 21 existing remote/client-hosted browser focus tests passed.
- Image-click E2E passed: destination DOM focus, close-key forwarding to the focused guest, and opener preservation.

records.title: [Bug]: [Browser] Cmd+W closes the opener instead of a newly opened link tab
records.body: ### Operating system macOS ### Orca version v1.4.197 ### Details ## Summary A link can open and visually activate a new Orca browser tab while keyboard focus remains with the original tab. Pressing `Cmd+W` then closes the opener instead of the newly opened tab. The problem was observed after directly opening a link in a new tab and after choosing **Open Link In Orca Browser** from a link's context menu. An image link was the initial example, but the issue concerns new-tab focus rather than image rendering. ## Repro ### A. Direct link opening 1. Open a page in an Orca browser tab containing a link with `target="_blank"`. 2. Click the link so it opens in a new Orca browser tab. 3. Without clicking inside the destination page, press `Cmd+W`. ### B. Context-menu link opening 1. Open a page containing a link in an Orca browser tab. 2. Right-click the link. 3. Choose **Open Link In Orca Browser**. 4. Without clicking inside the destination page, press `Cmd+W`. ### C. Command-click link opening 1. Open a page containing a link in an Orca browser tab. 2. Hold **Command (⌘)** and click the link to open it in a new Orca browser tab. 3. Release Command. Without clicking inside the destination page, press `Cmd+W`. **Actual:** The original tab closes, while the newly opened tab remains open. **Expected:** Keyboard focus follows the newly activated tab. `Cmd+W` closes that tab and leaves the opener open. ## Workaround Use the destination tab's close button instead of the keyboard shortcut.

records.title: perf(persistence): skip rewriting unchanged terminal scrollback snapshots
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​178 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​29 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​149 |
| Prod | 3 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​51 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​110 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​59 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Every time you click from one terminal split pane to another, Orca saves your session. As part of that save it **rewrote your terminal scrollback files to disk** — all of them, every time — even though not a single byte had changed. At 8 sleeping terminals that's 4 MB of synchronous disk writes per pane click, on the main thread.

This PR makes the writer remember what it last put at each path and skip the write when the content is identical. Same files on disk, just without rewriting them.

Split out of #18739 because this is the one change in that series that keeps state between calls (a small digest map), so it deserves its own review and its own revert button.

## What Changed

- **`terminal-scrollback-snapshot-write-memory.ts`** (new) — a per-process map from snapshot path to `{ digest, size, mtimeMs, ino }` of the file the last rename produced (stat taken on the temp file before the rename, which preserves inode and mtime). Capped at 256 entries, evicting the least recently republished path.
- **`terminal-scrollback-snapshots.ts`** — both writers (`writeTerminalScrollbackSnapshotSync` and the async variant) compute a SHA-256 of the buffer; on a digest match they `stat` the path and return the existing ref **only if size, mtime and inode still match the file this process wrote**. Anything else — file missing, replaced, or modified in place — drops the entry and writes. The entry is also dropped by both delete helpers and on write failure. A fresh process always writes at least once.
- **`config/scripts/scrollback-snapshot-write-skip-benchmark.mjs`** (`pnpm bench:scrollback-snapshot-write-skip`) — runs the production writer in both modes: with the memory reset each round (every leaf reaches disk, the pre-change behaviour) and with it retained.

The memory is a hint, not the source of truth. The on-disk check is what makes the skip safe; the map only decides whether the check is worth running.

## Why

The main thread is what serves file-explorer, editor and git IPC, so this is disk time those requests spent queued behind a pane click.

## Measurements

`pnpm bench:scrollback-snapshot-write-skip`, 8 retained scrollback leaves at the 512 KB cap, median of 9 rounds, M4 Max, 5 runs each. The baseline is disk-bound and noisy run to run (4–10 ms); the after number is stable.

| Per session write | Before | After (digest only) | After (digest + stat check) | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| scrollback snapshot republish (8 unchanged leaves) | 4.2–10.0 ms | 1.52–1.55 ms | 1.50–1.55 ms | **3–6x** |
| **synchronous disk writes** | **4.00 MB** | **0 MB** | **0 MB** | |

The 8 `stat` calls on a hit are lost in the SHA-256 cost of hashing 4 MB; the remaining 1.5 ms is the hash, not disk.

## Linked Issue

N/A — perf follow-up found while profiling the session write path.

## Visual Proof

N/A — no UI or interaction change; the bytes on disk are identical.

## Negative user-facing trade-offs

**None identified.** Specifically:

- No staleness. The digest guard skips a write only when the bytes are byte-identical to what this process already wrote at that path. Different content always writes.
- No lost scrollback. A skip requires the file at the path to still have the size, mtime and inode this process gave it. A file that is missing (deleted by us, by a racing async delete, or by anything external), replaced, or modified in place fails that check and is rewritten. Delete paths and write failures drop the entry as well, and the memory is per-process, so a restart always writes at least once.

Two things worth stating explicitly rather than hiding:

- **Cold writes cost ~0.19 ms more per leaf.** The SHA-256 is computed on every call, so a first write or a content change pays the digest on top of the encode it already did (measured: 188 µs for a 512 KB string). An actively printing terminal whose buffer changes between session writes pays this each time; eight such leaves add ~1.5 ms to a write that previously cost ~4–10 ms in disk I/O for the same leaves.
- **Memory:** the map holds at most 256 entries (digest + three numbers, ~15 KB) and lives for the process. Eviction is least-recently-republished, so a hot pane is never evicted ahead of a cold one.

The earlier "external writers" caveat is gone: the on-disk check closes it by construction rather than by audit. The only way to get a stale skip is a writer that replaces the file with the same size, same inode and same mtime to the millisecond, which is not something a file replace produces.

## Testing

- `pnpm tc` ✅
- `pnpm test src/main/terminal-scrollback-snapshot-write-skip.test.ts src/main/persistence` — 901 passed ✅
- `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed` ✅
- New: `src/main/terminal-scrollback-snapshot-write-skip.test.ts` (10 tests): republish is a no-op on the same inode and mtime for both the sync and async writer, and the memory is shared between them; content change rewrites; sync delete and async delete (with a legacy fallback root, which the write never targets) then republish rewrites; the file vanishing, being replaced, or being modified in place with the same size and inode behind the memory all rewrite; the 256 cap holds and evicts the least recently republished path, never a hot one.

records.body:

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## Summary

Cloudflare Turnstile fails inside Orca's embedded browser ("Verification failed" / error 600010) while the same sites pass in Chrome. The cause is Orca's own user-agent rewrite: stripping the `Electron/x` and `orca/x` tokens to present a plain-Chrome UA is what Cloudflare rejects, because a Chrome UA that ships no client hints reads as a spoof. The same Electron binary, machine and IP clears every challenge with its stock UA.

PR #885 introduced that rewrite specifically to fix 600010, so it was treating a symptom it created. Issue #11518 later found the same rewrite is what broke Google sign-in.

### Changes

- **Keep Electron's stock UA on every partition.** The `webRequest` handler now only owns the host-scoped Google auth Firefox switch, which is unchanged.
- **Delete the anti-detection script.** Measured on Electron 43: plugins are already a real 5-entry `PluginArray`, `window.chrome` exists, and `navigator.webdriver` is `false` with the debugger attached. Three of its four premises were false, and the overrides it installed (instance-level `webdriver`, non-native `Permissions.prototype.query`, stubbed `chrome.csi`/`loadTimes`) are themselves published bot signatures.
- **Stop attaching a CDP debugger to every browsing guest.** Only a detach listener remains, because a detach clears Chromium's standing auth-UA override.
- **Stop sending `Runtime.enable` into cross-origin iframes** when the agent bridge auto-attaches. The Turnstile widget is one, nothing reads iframe Runtime events, and that domain's serialization side-effect is the documented Cloudflare CDP tell.
- **Add a real-Electron test** (`browser-session-ua-wire-identity.electron.test.ts`) that captures headers as they leave the network stack: stock UA to ordinary hosts, Firefox with zero client hints to `accounts.google.com`. Reintroducing the rewrite turns it red.

### Evidence

Deterministic A/B, same binary, fresh partition per run, interleaved:

| Variant | dash.cloudflare.com/login | scrapingcourse.com/cloudflare-challenge |
|---|---|---|
| As shipped (rewrite + script + debugger) | 600010 | stuck on "Just a moment" |
| Empty script | 600010 | stuck |
| No debugger | 600010 | stuck |
| Rewrite + `sec-ch-ua` headers added | 600010 | stuck |
| Rewrite + CDP `userAgentMetadata` matching headers | 600010 | stuck |
| **Stock Electron UA** | **clean form** | **cleared** |

TLS (JA4) and HTTP/2 fingerprints are byte-identical to real Chromium, so the network layer is not involved. Verified in the dev build after the change: the dashboard login form renders with no verification error and Sign in enabled, and the managed challenge reports bypassed.

### Regression considerations

- **Google sign-in** improves: #12608 already measured that the cleaned UA hit `/v3/signin/rejected` while the stock UA completed and stayed usable. The Firefox auth-host switch is kept as-is.
- **Native-UA profiles** (`--no-ua-spoof`) now behave like every other profile except that they also skip the Google switch. The setting is retained for wire compatibility.
- **Sites that gate on the `Electron/` token** will now see it. That is the trade every comparable embedded-browser app makes; a per-host allowlist can be added if a specific site turns up.
- Follow-up worth doing separately: align session permission states with Chrome defaults in `setPermissionCheckHandler` (geolocation/midi currently report `denied`), which the deleted script tried and failed to paper over from the page side.

## ELI5

The ports UI was asking the app store for a runtime target object. Even when the target had not changed, that lookup created a new object, so React thought the store changed continuously and eventually stopped the render loop with error #185. This change subscribes to the stable host ID first and derives the target afterward.

records.title: [Bug]: Agent Dashboard preview terminal shows xterm's "potentially dangerous" confirm dialog for links and never opens the browser
records.body:
## Summary

Clicking a hyperlink in the Agent Dashboard's preview terminal (both the in-window drawer and the pop-out window) shows xterm.js's built-in confirm dialog — `Do you want to navigate to <url>? WARNING: This link could potentially be dangerous` — and confirming never opens the link in the system browser.

## Repro

1. Open the Agent Dashboard (pop-out window or in-window drawer) on a card whose agent printed a URL. Claude Code and Codex emit URLs as OSC 8 hyperlinks, so almost any agent output with a link reproduces this.
2. Click the link in the preview terminal.
3. A native confirm dialog appears: `Do you want to navigate to …? WARNING: This link could potentially be dangerous`.
4. Confirm — nothing opens in the browser. The renderer console logs `Opening link blocked as opener could not be cleared`.

## Expected

Links open in the system browser under the same Mod+click gesture the preview already uses for plain-text URLs, with no confirm dialog.

## Root cause

The preview terminal (`AgentTerminalPreview` → `installPreviewTerminalCompatibility` → `installPreviewTerminalLinks`, `src/renderer/src/components/dashboard-popout/preview-terminal-links.ts`) only loads `WebLinksAddon`, which covers plain-text URLs. It never sets `terminal.options.linkHandler`, so **OSC 8 hyperlinks** — which bypass `WebLinksAddon` and are handled by xterm core's `OscLinkProvider` — fall through to its `defaultActivate`: a `confirm()` dialog followed by `window.open()`, which is a dead end in Electron (`window.open` never reaches the OS browser).

Regular terminal panes don't have this bug: `installTerminalPaneLinkHandling` sets `pane.terminal.options.linkHandler` (`src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/terminal-pane-pane-links.ts:171`), routing OSC 8 links through Orca's own `handleOscLink`.

## Fix

Set `terminal.options.linkHandler` in `installPreviewTerminalLinks`, routing activation through the existing `window.api.shell.openUrl` path under the same Mod+click gesture, with `allowNonHttpProtocols: false` so non-http(s) OSC 8 links stay inert instead of confirming. PR to follow.

records.title: docs(daemon): correct stale per-5s full-checkpoint claims in snapshot bench
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 1 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​17 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​9 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​8 |
| Prod | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## Context

Investigating #18489 ("Daemon re-serializes full scrollback synchronously every 5s, stalling the PTY pump").

**The reported mechanism does not exist on current `main`.** It was removed in #5292 (`fix: replace per-5s full-buffer terminal checkpoints with an incremental log`, 2026-06-12), ~5,200 commits before HEAD and well before the reporter's v1.4.196.

What the 5s tick actually does today (`daemon-pty-checkpoint-persistence.ts:41`, protocol >= 13; current `PROTOCOL_VERSION` is 36):

- calls `takePendingOutput` — drains queued records, `snapshot: null` (`session-output-plane.ts:241`), no buffer serialization
- appends those records to the incremental log

A full `getSnapshot()` serialize happens only on: clean disconnect / final checkpoint, pending-buffer overflow (2MB), or the 5MB log cap (`TERMINAL_HISTORY_LOG_MAX_BYTES`) — and is additionally bounded by `FULL_CHECKPOINT_COOLDOWN_MS = 45_000` per session.

This is already covered by a regression test: *"appends increments for only dirty sessions on the periodic timer"* asserts `checkpoint()` is never called on the tick (`daemon-pty-adapter-history-checkpoints.test.ts:117`).

## The actual defect

`headless-emulator-snapshot-cost.bench.test.ts` was **added by** #5292 to justify that change, but its header comment still describes the pre-fix design in the present tense. #18489 quotes exactly those lines as "already known internally" — the stale comment is what produced the false report.

This PR corrects the stale comments and the emitted `interpretation` strings so the harness states which design its numbers describe. No behavior change.

## Test plan

- `pnpm test src/main/daemon/daemon-pty-adapter-history-checkpoints.test.ts` — 20 passed

records.body:
## Summary

The WSL CLI reaches a Windows Orca host through the local runtime RPC transport (a Windows named pipe). `browser.snapshot`, `browser.screenshot`, and `browser.wait` can block in agent-browser startup/paint/condition waits, but the runtime long-poll classifier treated them as short RPCs. The 30s socket/named-pipe idle timer could therefore close a healthy request before the browser helper replied; the CLI surfaced `runtime_unavailable`. `eval`, `click`, and tab commands remain on the short path.

This patch classifies those three browser methods as the existing `wait` long-poll class. That enables the existing keepalive frames and abort/slot accounting for both Unix sockets and Windows named pipes. No new wire fields, opcodes, retries, polling, or fallback routing are introduced.

## Deterministic evidence

- Oracle: `src/main/runtime/runtime-rpc-long-poll-transport.test.ts`
- Classifier assertions cover the affected methods (`browser.snapshot`, `browser.screenshot`, `browser.wait`) and controls (`browser.eval`, `browser.click`, `browser.tabSwitch`). On the base revision those new assertions are red because the methods classify as short RPCs.
- A real newline-framed local RPC session delays `browser.snapshot` for 120ms, observes >=2 keepalives, and receives exactly one terminal response on the candidate.
- Focused result: `pnpm test src/main/runtime/runtime-rpc-long-poll-transport.test.ts src/cli/browser.test.ts` — 57 passed.
- Additional result: 49 tests passed across local long-poll, WebSocket long-poll, remote client, and envelope suites; 38 browser bridge/lifecycle tests passed.
- `pnpm tc:node` passed.
- `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed` passed with 0 new findings.

## Compatibility and limits

The keepalive frame is already part of the existing RPC envelope and is understood by current/legacy clients; this changes only host-side classification. The existing long-poll cap still bounds concurrency and returns `runtime_busy` under saturation.

This workspace is macOS. Windows 2, WSL2, ConPTY, and the physical Windows named-pipe path were not available, so no physical Windows/WSL reproduction is claimed. The oracle exercises the same classifier and real local framed transport used by that path, but it does not prove WSL interop, PowerShell argv forwarding, or Windows kernel named-pipe behavior. A >30s end-to-end timeout was not run in CI because it would make the regression suite unnecessarily slow; the causal boundary is the host idle timer plus the missing classifier entry.

Linear was not mutated; the session's `orca-ide` Linear CLI was unavailable.

records.title: fix(terminal): make wrapped-line search rewind iterative and bound its scans

| Prod | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​543 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​8 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​535 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## What

> **Upstream:** submitted as [xtermjs/xterm.js#6149](https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js/pull/6149) (issue [#6148](https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js/issues/6148), Node-only repro attached there). The patch applies cleanly to upstream master; `config/patches/xterm-upstream.json` carries a `$upstream` note so the entry can be dropped once a release ships it.


Terminal search could kill the whole terminal surface when a pane held one very long un-newlined line — base64, a minified bundle, a single huge log record.

`@xterm/addon-search`'s `SearchEngine._findInLine` rewound to the first row of a wrapped line by **calling itself once per wrapped row**, so recursion depth equalled the number of screen rows the logical line occupies. Orca's scrollback default is 5,000 rows and the max is 50,000 (`src/shared/terminal-scrollback-policy.ts:1`, `:3`). The `RangeError` is thrown synchronously inside `findNext`, escapes `safeFind` (which deliberately rethrows anything that is not the known decoration error — `src/renderer/src/components/terminal-search-safe-find.ts:32`) out of `TerminalSearch`'s effect (`src/renderer/src/components/TerminalSearch.tsx:105`), and trips the `terminal.workbench` error boundary.

**Two failure modes, with different reach — be precise about which is which** (round 4 corrected an earlier overclaim here):

- **The `RangeError` crash needs a deep line, not just the default scrollback.** In this repo's harness a 5,000-row wrapped line does *not* overflow — it takes ~16 s (see RED below). The committed crash test uses 12,000 rows deliberately. So the crash half most plausibly needs a raised scrollback (the 10k/25k/50k presets), a narrower terminal, or a deeper ambient renderer stack than happy-dom/Node gives the tests. The field report below is a real, correctly-attributed `_findInLine` recursion crash, so the shape is reachable in production — but "every user" is not what the evidence supports for the *crash*.
- **The multi-second freeze does hit the 5,000-row default**, unconditionally, on the renderer main thread.

**Field crashes addressed** — cluster `xterm-search-recursion`, **1 report**:

| Report | Orca version | OS | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `012eb5be-ffb3-4a5c-b095-ce839410c161` | 1.4.194 | Windows 10.0.26200 (x64, win32) | `terminal.workbench` |

The crash is not Windows-specific — nothing in the mechanism is platform-dependent; win32 is simply the one OS that reported it.

The fix lands through the repo's existing xterm patch harness (source patch under `config/patches/xterm-src/` plus the generated dist patch, both emitted by `config/scripts/regenerate-xterm-patches.mjs` from the pinned upstream commit `d3e32b3`). `@xterm/addon-search` is added to `config/patches/xterm-upstream.json` and `pnpm-workspace.yaml:47` alongside the packages already patched. No new mechanism.

Six commits (the sixth is the takeover pass, see below):

1. **`8d5d1d548b7` — the crash.** `_findInLine`'s rewind becomes a loop instead of self-recursion. Reverse search keeps its single-step-and-return behaviour (see the disclosed limitation in **Trade-offs**).
2. **`6fddfd04e5b` — the sibling freeze.** The forward scans walk every buffer row and `_findInLine` rewinds each wrapped row to its line start, so one long line costs O(rows²) on the renderer main thread — re-run on every find-bar keystroke and again 200 ms after every `onWriteParsed`. A wrapped row whose line was already scanned from its first row is now skipped (`_isRowCoveredByEarlierSearch`).
3. **`dfc50830319` — soundness of that skip, forward direction.** A logical line whose first row was evicted from the scrollback has no line start left in the buffer, so nothing covered its rows and the wrap-around loop skipped straight past them. Row 0 is now never skipped **in the forward loop**.
4. **`8a28de5255a` — bounding every scan.** Removing the recursion also removed the only thing that *stopped* an unbounded scan, so above the old stack-overflow depth the failure mode flipped from a bounded crash to a blocked main thread. Three unbounded scans are now bounded: the rewind stops at row 0 (after a reflow the buffer's ring holds negative indices, so `getLine(-1)` answers with a stale wrapped line and the walk ran backwards forever); `translateBufferLineToStringWithWrap` stops at `buffer.active.length` (a line longer than the whole scrollback leaves every row wrapped and the ring cycles back to row 0); and `wholeWord`/forward-regex now scan on within a line instead of giving up at the first rejected hit, which makes the matcher monotone in its start offset and lets the skip apply to every search mode.
5. **`ed19fbc0244` — bounding the many-matches shape.** `SearchAddon._highlightAllMatches` calls `SearchEngine.find` once per match, up to the addon's 1,000-decoration limit, and every call resumes deep inside the logical line. Three things in that path were O(line) per call — the rewind to the line start, `stringLine.toLowerCase()`, and `_bufferColsToStringOffset` summing the cells of every row before the resume column — so a line with many matches stayed quadratic after commit 4 bounded the no-match scan. `_bufferColsToStringOffset` now reads whole rows out of the cached `lineOffsets`; `SearchLineCache` gains `lineStartRow` (remembers the wrapped span it last resolved, keeping the row-0 bound) and `caseFoldLine` (memoizes the folded line per row). Both memos sit beside `_linesCache` and are dropped by `_destroyLinesCache`, so they inherit its invalidation exactly.
   *Correction to that commit message:* it says "Three things in that path were O(line) per call". A **fourth** O(rows)-per-match walk survives — see **Trade-offs**.
6. **`ddf8eb13da4` — takeover: measured each memo in commit 5 and dropped the two that were dead weight; fixed reverse search on a trimmed head.** Overriding each memo with its naive version on the committed 30 000-row / 750-match shape: the `lineOffsets`-based `_bufferColsToStringOffset` is the whole win (10.9 s → 74 ms). `lineStartRow`'s span memo and `caseFoldLine` were worth under 200 ms combined and nothing on the no-match scan, so both are gone: the rewind is a plain bounded loop in `_findInLine`, the case fold is the original `toLowerCase()`, and `SearchLineCache` keeps only the buffer-length bound. Net −126 lines of patched addon source and the retention cost noted under Trade-offs disappears. Reverse search now searches row 0 when it is wrapped, mirroring commit 3, so the disclosed reverse trimmed-head limitation is fixed and the regression test drives both directions (fails red on the previous build for `findPrevious`).

### Explicitly NOT proven here

- **No live-app reproduction.** The fix is inside a library the tests drive directly; there is no `$electron` / real-window capture of the crash or of the fix. The field crash report above is the only real-world evidence.
- **No Windows measurement.** The field crash is win32; every timing above is macOS/Node v24 under happy-dom. The mechanism is platform-independent, but the numbers are not Windows numbers.
- **The stack-overflow crash is not reproduced at Orca's default scrollback**, only at 12,000 wrapped rows. See **What**.
- **Differential-fuzz harnesses are not committed.** The 300-scenario fuzz cited in commit `8a28de5255a` and the 400-scenario oracle run cited for `ed19fbc0244` come from the commit messages. Round 4 ran its *own* independent 600-cell and 1,500-cell fuzzes against a hand-written oracle and corroborated the central soundness claim (below), but none of these harnesses ship — see follow-up 5.
- **`pnpm test` (full suite), `pnpm lint` (aggregate with ratchets), `tc:node`, `tc:cli`** were not run. The change touches no main/CLI code.

## ELI5

Type something into a terminal's find bar and the terminal has to figure out where each line really starts. Lines that are too long to fit the window get folded onto several rows, so the search walks backwards row by row until it finds the beginning. It did that walk by having a function call itself once for every folded row — and a computer can only nest calls a few thousand deep before it gives up. One gigantic line with no line breaks in it (a chunk of base64, a minified JavaScript bundle, one enormous log entry) is easily tens of thousands of rows tall, so the search ran out of room and threw an error. That error escaped, React's safety net caught it, and the entire terminal area of the app vanished — every pane, not just the one being searched.

The fix rewrites that backwards walk as a plain loop, which has no depth limit. While doing that we found the same long line also made searching absurdly slow — the search re-walked the whole line once for every row of it, so a single find took ~17 seconds and the app was frozen the entire time — and that a few of those walks had no stopping condition at all in unusual buffer states. So the loop now knows when to stop, and it skips folded rows it has already covered. Searching a pane full of one huge line now takes about 14 milliseconds instead of 17 seconds, and it does not crash.

One case is knowingly left imperfect: searching **backwards** through a giant line whose very beginning has already scrolled off the top of the buffer finds nothing. It found nothing before this PR too (it used to point at a row that does not exist), so nobody is worse off — but it is not fixed here.

## Trade-offs

**Behaviour deliberately differs from upstream `@xterm/addon-search`.** This is a patched dependency, so that is the point, but it is a real difference and the diff is not a pure bug fix:

- **Whole-word search now finds more matches than before.** Upstream gave up at the first `indexOf` hit that was not on a word boundary, so searching `needle` with whole-word enabled in `aneedlea needle done` found *nothing*. It now finds the real match. Orca's find bar does not expose whole-word (`TerminalSearch.tsx` wires only `caseSensitive` and `regex`), so this reaches no user today.
- **Forward regex is now anchored to the logical line, not to the wrapped row.** Upstream ran `exec` over `slice(offset)`, which silently re-anchors `^` and `\b` at whatever column the row happened to wrap at. A regex like `^foo` could previously match in the middle of a wrapped line; it no longer does. **This is the one user-visible semantic change Orca's UI can reach.** Regex users may see fewer or different matches — correctly, but differently.
- **A line longer than the whole scrollback used to be searched wrong.** Upstream either found nothing or over-counted matches by walking the buffer's ring twice. Result counts on that shape will change.
- **A match next to a wide character that wrapped is no longer skipped.** `_bufferColsToStringOffset` summed the cells of the rows before the resume point, counting the trailing null placeholder of a wide character that wrapped to the next row — a cell `translateBufferLineToStringWithWrap` had already dropped from the joined string, and which the reverse map (`lineOffsets`) therefore does not count either. Commit 5 reads the same `lineOffsets` the reverse map uses, so the two now agree. Result counts on buffers with CJK or emoji at a wrap boundary go **up**.

**~~DISCLOSED LIMITATION — reverse search still cannot reach a trimmed-head wrapped line.~~ Fixed in `ddf8eb13da4`; the paragraph below is kept for history.** Commit 3 fixed the forward direction only. The mirrored reverse path is left as upstream: `_findInLine` returns unconditionally for *any* `isWrapped` row, including row 0 (patched `src/SearchEngine.ts:281-286`), so a logical line whose first row was evicted from the scrollback has no line start left and is never searched in reverse at all.

- **What happens:** on that buffer shape, `findPrevious` returns `false` and `_selectResult(undefined)` calls `terminal.clearSelection()`. Round 4 measured it on the HEAD build (cols 22 reflowed to 19, rows 6, scrollback 2, buffer length 8, `getLine(0).isWrapped === true`, 27 real occurrences verified against an independent oracle): `findNext` walks the matches correctly; three successive `findPrevious` calls all return false and clear the selection.
- **Not a regression.** Pristine upstream "succeeds" on the same input by selecting rows 9, 8, 8 of an 8-row buffer — a phantom out-of-range selection. HEAD trades that for a clean miss. Across round 4's 600-cell ground-truth fuzz exactly 3 cells regress this way (all with `row0Wrapped=true`) and 0 regress the other way.
- **Residual risk, and who it reaches.** `SearchAddon._updateMatches` fires `findPrevious` 200 ms after every `onWriteParsed`, and a `false` result clears the selection — so on exactly the buffer shape this PR targets (one huge line, head trimmed), a pane that is still producing output drops the find bar's active match on every output tick. That is a real, if narrow, find-bar annoyance for a user searching a still-streaming pane full of one giant line. It is **not** a crash and not a data-loss risk.
- **The committed guard test does not cover it.** `terminal-search-long-wrapped-line.test.ts:215` is named `keeps reaching matches in a wrapped line whose first row was trimmed away` but drives only `search.findNext` — verified: the file contains no `findPrevious` call at all. The name reads as bidirectional coverage that does not exist. Not renamed in this PR; see follow-up 7.

**Performance costs.** Two, both small and both new information relative to earlier revisions of this description, which claimed "none found":

- **A fourth O(rows)-per-match walk survives** in the path commit `ed19fbc0244` claims to have bounded. The match-index-to-row mapping (patched `src/SearchEngine.ts:362-369`) restarts from index 0 of `lineOffsets` on every match, and `lineOffsets` has one entry per wrapped row, so the highlight-all pass over one N-row line is O(N × matches) — roughly 5×10⁷ array comparisons at the 50,000-row max against the 1,000-decoration limit. It is bounded and cheap in practice: it sits inside the committed 30,000-row/750-match budgeted test, measured at 73/80/162 ms on HEAD. Accuracy note on the commit message and a hint for whoever revisits the highlight pass, not a defect.
- **~~New steady-state retention.~~ Gone in `ddf8eb13da4`: `caseFoldLine` was removed.** `caseFoldLine` (patched `src/SearchLineCache.ts:124-129`) keeps a second full copy of the largest logical line's text alive beside `_linesCache`'s copy for the cache's 15 s TTL — roughly 4–8 MB extra retained on a 50,000-row × 80-col scrollback holding one un-newlined line, where the pre-branch `stringLine.toLowerCase()` produced a collectable temporary. Correctly dropped by `_destroyLinesCache` (line feed, cursor move, resize, TTL) and small next to `_linesCache`'s own per-line string plus its 50,000-entry `lineOffsets` array. A disclosure gap, not a leak.

The wrapped-row skip itself only removes work; the boundary checks are one comparison each.

**No newly-swallowed errors.** Nothing is added to `safeFind`'s catch; the bounded loops return normally where the unbounded ones previously crashed or hung, which is the intended change.

**Maintenance cost.** `@xterm/addon-search` becomes a fourth patched xterm package, so it joins the `xterm_patch_sync` CI lane and every future xterm version bump. That lane is green (output above); `config/scripts/pr-code-change-scope.mjs` emits `xterm_patch_sync=true` for this PR's changed paths.

**Cross-cutting concerns: none engaged.** Pure renderer-side JS in a bundled dependency — no path handling, no child processes, no platform branches, so macOS/Linux/Windows behave identically (the win32 field report is where it was seen, not a platform dependency). Nothing touches the execution host, so SSH and folder-workspace cases are unaffected. No wire change: the host still publishes the same terminal bytes; only the client's local search over its own xterm buffer changed, so nothing is owed to capability negotiation.

**Who is affected:** every Orca user who searches a terminal pane holding a very long un-newlined line gets the freeze fix. The crash fix reaches those same users at deeper line lengths than the tests reproduce at the default scrollback (see **What**). Regex users may see different match sets. The reverse-search limitation above reaches only users searching a still-streaming pane whose giant line has been trimmed at the head.

## Adversarial review

**4 rounds. Converged clean: round 4 returned no blocking findings.** Every blocking finding raised in rounds 1–3 was fixed in code. Two round-2 points were **rebutted** rather than fixed; one round-3 point was **accepted as-is**; five round-4 points are **accepted as disclosed limitations** and are all written into **What**, **Fix evidence** and **Trade-offs** above rather than deferred.

**Round 1 — 1 blocking, FIXED (`dfc50830319`).** The reviewer reproduced the crash fix as correct, then found the wrapped-row skip added in commit 2 unsound for the exact buffer shape this PR is about: a wrapped row whose logical line's *first row* has been evicted from the scrollback. The skip returned true for any `isWrapped` row, but a trimmed line has no line start left in the buffer to cover it, so the wrap-around loop skipped straight past it. Reproduced at the 5,000-row default: repeated find-next permanently stranded the user on two out-of-range phantom rows while the find bar still reported 4 matches. The reviewer's mechanism was right and the implementer's original tradeoff note was empirically wrong — with a *full* scrollback ring, `getLine(-1)` returns a stale line rather than `undefined`. Fixed by never skipping row 0 in the forward loop. (The mirrored reverse path was **not** fixed; round 4 found that gap — see below.)

**Round 2 — 1 blocking, FIXED (`8a28de5255a`); 2 points REBUTTED.** The reviewer found that removing the recursion also removed the only thing that aborted an unbounded scan: below the old stack-overflow depth the patch was neutral-to-better, but *above* it the failure mode flipped from a bounded crash to an unbounded synchronous freeze — 48 s to a `RangeError` became 5.4 minutes of blocked renderer main thread, reachable with one click on the find bar's regex toggle. The reviewer also reported that whole-word search silently misses matches upstream, independent of this branch. Both confirmed and fixed: the root cause was `_findInLine`'s non-monotone matcher (`wholeWord` returning at the first non-boundary hit; forward regex bailing on a zero-length match), so both now scan on within the line, the skip applies to every option, and the mode exclusion list is gone. Investigating that turned up two further non-terminating walks (the post-reflow negative-index rewind, and `translateBufferLineToStringWithWrap` on a line longer than the scrollback), both bounded in the same commit.

Two round-2 claims were **REBUTTED with evidence, not fixed**:
- *"Swapping a bounded recursion for an unbounded loop does not happen."* Rebutted because it **does**: after `resize()` the buffer's backing array carries negative keys (204 of them in the regression test's buffer), so `getLine(-1)` answers with a stale wrapped line instead of `undefined`. This rebuttal argued the reviewer had been too *generous*, and produced an extra fix (the row-0 rewind bound).
- *"The reflow fuzz is inconclusive rather than failing"* — both attempts had blown past 40-minute and 15-minute caps, which the reviewer attributed to happy-dom being slow. Rebutted: that was the negative-index infinite loop, not slowness. The same 300-scenario corpus now completes in 34 s.

Doc drift the reviewers flagged (`.github/workflows/pr.yml` and `docs/reference/xterm-patch-regeneration.md` both still describing the old package list) was fixed.

**Round 3 — 1 blocking, FIXED (`ed19fbc0244`); 1 point ACCEPTED AS-IS.** Round 3 confirmed the crash fix, reproduced the RED/GREEN split independently, and ran its own 700-scenario differential fuzz against a skip-disabled build of the same source with 0 divergences. Its blocking finding: commits 1–4 bounded the rewind, the wrapped-row rescan and the forward line walk, but left `_highlightAllMatches` → `_findInLine` → `_bufferColsToStringOffset` unbounded, so above the default scrollback the branch converted a ~0.4 s `RangeError` that the `terminal.workbench` boundary recovers from into a multi-second hard freeze of the renderer main thread — re-fired by every find-bar keystroke and every 200 ms of streaming output. The reviewer measured 15.1 s at 30,000 rows and attributed 95 % of it to `_bufferColsToStringOffset`; that attribution was right, and profiling the remainder found two further O(line)-per-match costs (the per-match rewind and the per-match `toLowerCase`). All three are now memoized against the line cache's existing lifetime, with a committed 5,000 ms-budgeted regression test in all three search modes.

Round 3's non-blocking points:
- *The claim/evidence block handed to review was stale* (described 2 commits against a 4-commit branch; asserted a `regex`/`wholeWord` exclusion commit `8a28de5255a` had removed). A handoff artefact. Acknowledged; this description is rewritten against HEAD each round, and round 4 found further staleness in it, now also corrected (see **Fix evidence**).
- *Scope: the branch changes upstream matcher semantics, not just termination.* **Accepted and documented** — that is the **Trade-offs** section. The reviewer's own fuzz put the user-visible surface at regex anchoring.
- *Invariant asymmetry: the wrap-around loop guards the skip with `y > 0`; the two forward loops do not.* **ACCEPTED AS-IS, not fixed.** Safe today because both `SearchEngine.find` call sites pass `startRow >= 0`, so `y >= 1`. The precondition lives in `_isRowCoveredByEarlierSearch`'s doc comment. **Residual risk:** a future caller passing `startRow = -1` would silently skip row 0 — a latent correctness trap for a maintainer, not reachable by any code that exists today.

**Round 4 — no blocking findings; 5 non-blocking, ALL ACCEPTED AS DISCLOSED LIMITATIONS.** Round 4 re-ran every load-bearing command rather than trusting this description: it reverse-applied the dist patch to restore pristine upstream and got 14 failed / 3 passed of 17; it rebuilt the intermediate four-commit tree and produced an independent RED for commit 5 specifically (35.4 / 32.1 / 31.5 s vs 73 / 80 / 162 ms on HEAD); it verified the source and dist patch hunks are byte-identical and `regenerate-xterm-patches.mjs --check` is in sync from pinned upstream `d3e32b3`. It then attacked the fix's own failure class — "bounded crash traded for an unbounded hang" — hypothesising that the reverse-regex `searchStringLine.slice(0, offset)` inside the `exec` loop was newly reachable now that the forward crash no longer preempts `findPreviousWithSelection`. **Hypothesis refuted by measurement**: at 1,000 / 2,000 / 4,000 / 5,000 rows, four successive `findPrevious` calls each, timings are flat (regex `[18,3,3,3]` → `[20,13,11,10]` ms; plain `[12,0,0,0]` → `[10,0,0,0]` ms) — V8 returns the receiver for a whole-string slice. It also ran its own 600-cell ground-truth fuzz against an independent oracle: HEAD's `resultCount` matches the oracle in 600/600 with 0 out-of-range selections, while pristine upstream over-counts in 23 and produces 22 out-of-range selections — independently corroborating that the wrapped-row skip loses nothing and that the divergences from upstream are upstream defects being fixed.

The five findings, and where each now lives:
1. **Reverse-direction trimmed-head hole, and a guard test whose name hides it.** The strongest finding. Accepted as a disclosed limitation — see **Trade-offs** for the mechanism, the `_updateMatches` interaction, why it is not a regression, and who it reaches. Follow-ups 7 and 8 track the fix and the test rename. **This is the one item a human reviewer must weigh.**
2. **PR-body overclaim on who the crash reaches.** Confirmed against this PR's own RED evidence and **corrected in the text** — the **What** section now separates the crash (needs a deeper line than the default reproduces) from the freeze (hits the default), and "every Orca user who searches a terminal pane" is gone.
3. **A fourth O(rows)-per-match walk survives** the path commit `ed19fbc0244` claims to have bounded. Confirmed by reading the code; bounded and cheap in practice. **Disclosed under Performance costs** and tracked as follow-up 9.
4. **New steady-state retention from `caseFoldLine`** not mentioned under the old "Performance costs. None found." **Disclosed under Performance costs.**
5. **Stale numbers in the evidence block** (61 tests, 382519 bytes). **Fixed** — the whole **Fix evidence** section was re-run against HEAD, with the superseded numbers called out inline.

Round 4 also re-confirmed the scope/maintenance note from round 3 (fourth patched xterm package, regex re-anchoring as the only user-reachable semantic change) and verified `pr-code-change-scope.mjs` emits `xterm_patch_sync=true`. It left the worktree clean and byte-verified `node_modules` back to its as-installed patched state.

**Post-round-4 re-verification** (this description's own run, on `ed19fbc0244`): 17/17 green, five sibling test files 64/64, `pnpm tc:web` exit 0, oxlint exit 0, `check:code-quality:changed` 0 new findings, `regenerate-xterm-patches.mjs --check` in sync, exit 0. RED re-run and replaced (14 failed / 3 passed of 17). No code changed; only this description.

## Follow-ups

1. **Upstream all four hunks to xterm.js.** The recursion is still present in `@xterm/addon-search` 0.17.0-beta.301. The whole-word bail (`aneedlea needle done` finds nothing) and the regex `slice(offset)` re-anchoring are plain upstream defects worth filing on their own, independent of the crash. Every hunk carried here is maintenance cost until upstream takes them.
2. **`SearchAddon._updateMatches` still re-runs the entire highlight scan 200 ms after every `onWriteParsed`.** The scan is now cheap, so this is no longer a freeze, but a busy pane still redoes the full-buffer scan several times a second for no reason. Debounce or invalidate incrementally. (This is also the mechanism that makes the reverse-search limitation above visible on a streaming pane.)
3. **`SearchLineCache` remembers exactly one wrapped span and one folded line.** That is all the highlight-all pass over a single long line needs, and every other caller walks unwrapped rows where the memo is O(1) anyway. A buffer that alternated between two very long lines would thrash it; nothing in Orca drives search that way today.
4. **The find bar re-runs `findNext` synchronously on every keystroke** (`src/renderer/src/components/TerminalSearch.tsx:105`) with no debounce — only a length cap on the query. Cheap now, but it is still full-buffer work on the renderer main thread per keypress.
5. **No committed differential fuzz for the search path.** Three separate fuzz harnesses (commit `8a28de5255a`'s, commit `ed19fbc0244`'s, and round 4's independent oracle) all pass, and none of them ship. A committed, seeded, bounded version would guard the skip's soundness against future edits.
6. **No Windows CI measurement of terminal-search cost.** The one field report is win32 and all timings here are macOS.
7. **Fix reverse search on a trimmed-head wrapped line** — mirror commit `dfc50830319`'s row-0 exemption into the `isReverseSearch` branch of `_findInLine`. Disclosed limitation, not a regression; see **Trade-offs**.
8. **Rename or extend `terminal-search-long-wrapped-line.test.ts:215`.** It is named `keeps reaching matches in a wrapped line whose first row was trimmed away` and drives only `findNext`. Either say `findNext` in the name or drive both directions (which will fail until follow-up 7 lands).
9. **The match-index-to-row mapping restarts from `lineOffsets[0]` per match** (`src/SearchEngine.ts:362-369`). Bounded and inside the budgeted test, but it is the one remaining O(rows)-per-match walk in the highlight path.

| Prod | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​79 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​28 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​51 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Orca was doing homework it immediately threw away: building big temporary lists just to answer yes/no questions, copying every network message twice, and re-reading entire files to check one number. This PR deletes that throwaway work. Same answers, less CPU, less garbage for the collector.

## Merge Risk

**LOW.** No correctness regression in any hunk; the one hunk whose justification did not hold has been reverted.

- All remaining hunks verified semantically identical to the code they replace — including the Windows `\`→`/` case in `FileExplorerVirtualRows.tsx` (`TreeNode.relativePath` is normalized at both construction sites, `file-explorer-directory-listing.ts:30` and `file-explorer-name-filter-projection.ts:144`), and the `undefined`-vs-`[]` divergence from `?? []` in `project-host-compatibility.ts` (unreachable — `mergeProjectHostSetupCompatibilityState` always returns real arrays).
- **Reverted — the `unix-socket-transport.ts` chunk-carry rewrite.** Its comment claimed it avoided O(n²) rescans, but `chunks` is reset to `[remainder]` on every `data` event, so the join plus the tail `Buffer.byteLength` is two passes where the old code did one; isolated benchmarks (900 KB frame, 4 KB chunks) showed no win. It also moved consumed-frame bookkeeping out of the closure, so a synchronous throw from the handler would have re-dispatched already-dispatched frames.
- **Cleaned up:** the two byte-identical array comparators in `project-host-compatibility.ts` folded into one generic `arraysEqualByJson`; the dead `if (byTab.size === 0) return byTab` branch removed from `smart-attention.ts`.
- Suites green across the touched areas (509 files / 4337 tests); `oxlint` clean.

## What changed (6 files, all deletions of redundant work)

- `use-sort-order.ts`: cold-start probe no longer `flat()`s all tabs into a throwaway array — nested `some()` short-circuits.
- `smart-attention.ts`: no more `[...a, ...b.flatMap()]` temp arrays or `flatMap(map)` just to build a Set — direct loops.
- `FileExplorerVirtualRows.tsx`: drop per-row `normalizeRelativePath` (2 regexes) — paths are already normalized at construction.
- `use-monaco-editor-decorations.ts`: single `buildGitConflictDecorations` pass instead of `has*` scan + `build` re-parse.
- `project-host-compatibility.ts`: reference-equality + length fast-path before per-row stringify; identical refs skip stringify entirely.
- `structured-tui-process-identity.ts`: `push` instead of spread-copy index builds; `Set` instead of `rows.some` scans in the 50ms poll loop.

## Measurements

Microbenchmarks (node, local):

| Fix | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| project compat, identical refs, 1000x | ~1012ms (full stringify) | ~0ms (ref-equal skip) |
| project compat, equal content 20x | ~13.7ms | ~14.2ms (no regression) |
| `ps` index build, 1500 rows, 20x | ~4.1ms spread-copy | ~1.6ms push (2.5x) |
| sidebar `flat().some` 500x @400 workspaces | ~25.3ms + 1200-elem throwaway | ~13.9ms, zero alloc (45% less) |

Tests: `structured-tui-process-identity`, `project-host-compatibility`, `remote-workspace-snapshot-cache`, `monaco-conflict-decorations` — 22 passed. `ws/relay/unix/smart-attention` suites — 78 passed. Changed-code quality gate: 0 new findings.

## Negative user-facing trade-offs

None. Every change returns bit-identical values:

- Sort probe: identical boolean, earlier short-circuit only.
- Attention index: identical map contents/membership, same malformed-key skips.
- Explorer: `normalize(normalized) === normalized` — same lookup keys.
- Monaco: `build → []` iff `has* → false` (same line predicates) — existing test pins the empty case.
- Project compat: same equality verdicts, per-row stringify fallback preserved.
- Snapshot cache: same token reuse/echo suppression; revision is the host monotonic version.
- Unix-socket: same 1MB cap, framing, oversized path.
- TUI identity: identical children maps, first-match-wins preserved, same exclusion sets.

records.title: [Other]: Does macOS computer-use run silently in the background, or does it require/steal foreground focus?
records.body:
## Question

Both Codex (OpenAI) and Claude Code (Anthropic) now implement **background / silent computer-use on macOS** — the agent can drive the UI (clicks, typing, screenshots) without stealing foreground window focus, so the user can keep working in another app while the agent operates.

**Does Orca's macOS computer-use (`orca computer …`) also operate silently / in the background, or does it require (and grab) foreground focus?**

If it does grab focus today: is silent background computer-use on macOS on the roadmap, and is the focus-stealing considered expected behavior or a bug to fix?

## What I observed

On my machine, during computer-use operations Orca appears to **grab / steal the foreground window** (the target app, or sometimes Orca itself, jumps to the front), which is exactly the behavior Codex and Claude Code have moved away from. I want to confirm whether this is intended or a known limitation before reporting it as a pure bug.

## Environment

- Orca: 1.4.194 (build 1.4.194)
- OS: macOS 15.7.7 (Build 24G720), Apple Silicon (arm64)
- Computer-use provider: default (whatever `orca computer capabilities` advertises on this install)

## Related issues

- #16674 — Windows browser automation stealing foreground focus (no flag to disable). Same class of problem, but Windows + browser only.
- #15954 — Feature request for a `cua-driver` computer-use provider with background input. Suggests background input is not yet generally available.
- #12592 — macOS `orca computer click --x/--y` no-op (closed). Hints the macOS computer-use path has had focus/activation gaps before.

## Ask

1. Is silent / background computer-use on macOS supported today (or planned)?
2. If not, is the foreground-focus grabbing I'm seeing expected, and is there a setting/flag to suppress it?

Happy to turn this into a proper `[Bug]:` report with repro steps if the focus-stealing is unintended.

records.title: fix(computer-use): prefer RemoteSigned over Bypass on Windows
records.body:
## ELI5

Windows Computer Use used to start PowerShell with "ignore the script policy" (`-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`) on every click. That flag is an EDR-shaped command line. Now the first launch asks for the milder `RemoteSigned` policy. Bypass is used only if that first start is blocked by execution policy, and only once.

## What Changed

- Added `src/main/computer/windows-powershell-execution-policy.ts` (the file `docs/reference/windows-edr-posture.md` already cited) to build `-File` argv and classify policy-blocked stderr.
- `execBridge` on Windows now starts `powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -File <script> <operation>`.
- If that spawn fails with a policy-block (`execution policy` / `running scripts is disabled`) and was not killed by timeout, it retries **once** with `Bypass` and the same `-File` operands.
- Success, non-policy errors, and non-Windows `python3` launches do not retry. No `-EncodedCommand`, no `cmd.exe /c`.
- Tests spy `execFile` for first-argv RemoteSigned, policy-block Bypass retry, success-no-retry, and non-policy no-retry.

## Why

The EDR posture doc already described RemoteSigned-first with a one-shot Bypass fallback, but the helper file was missing and live argv was always Bypass. Unconditional Bypass is a scored command-line signal; AGENTS.md / CONTRIBUTING say not to add it as the first flag. Restricted / AllSigned hosts still need a fallback so packaged `runtime.ps1` can run.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #18281

## Visual Proof

N/A — no visual or interaction change. This is main-process Computer Use PowerShell argv only.

## Testing

- [ ] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below

Plan 014 verification (macOS):

- `pnpm test src/main/computer/desktop-script-provider-bridge.test.ts src/main/computer/windows-powershell-execution-policy.test.ts` — 12 passed
- `pnpm tc:node` — exit 0
- `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed` — exit 0
- `test -f src/main/computer/windows-powershell-execution-policy.ts` — helper exists; EDR doc citation is now true

No live Windows Restricted-policy host was run. Full `pnpm lint` / `pnpm build` left to CI per the plan.

The plan's `pnpm test src/main/computer/desktop-script-provider-bridge.ts` filter does not match Vitest's `*.test.ts` include; the colocated `.test.ts` files were run instead.

## Review

- **Cross-platform**: Windows argv only. macOS/Linux still use `python3` + script (tested). No path separators hardcoded into construction (`path.join` N/A — script/operation paths are passed through). No `metaKey` / shortcut changes.
- **SSH/remote**: Computer Use desktop-script launch is local to the execution host's main process. No RPC / stream / opcode change (`docs/reference/remote-wire-compatibility.md`). No process-liveness verdict change (`docs/reference/ssh-execution-boundary.md`). A Windows execution host gets the same RemoteSigned-then-Bypass argv; SSH Linux is unchanged.
- **Security**: first argv no longer spells Bypass. Retry Bypass is once, only after a policy-blocked `-File` start, never `-EncodedCommand` or `cmd.exe /c`. `windowsHide` stays as already shipped. Classifier is conservative (`execution policy` / `running scripts is disabled`) so unrelated bridge errors do not Bypass.
- **Performance**: one extra PowerShell start only on policy-blocked hosts; success path is a single spawn.
- **GitLab**: N/A (no provider-specific git/review behavior).
- **STOP check**: did not need `cmd.exe /c` or `-EncodedCommand`. Packaged `-File` plus policy-block classification is the documented fallback, not Bypass-only argv.

## Agent skill upstream boundary

- [x] Not applicable, or this change follows `docs/reference/agent-skill-sharing-upstream-boundary.md` and copies or mechanically translates no upstream skill-installer source, tests, fixtures, registry entries, path tables, comments, or documentation.

## Notes

Ensure no issues in: Security, Cross-platoform support (Linux, Windows, Mac), Remote SSH, Mobile, general backwards compatibility, performance

## Checklist

- [x] This PR is small and focused
- [x] I explained what changed and why (including ELI5)
- [x] Before/after screenshots or videos attached for UI changes, or `N/A` with reason
- [x] Self-reviewed for correctness, security, and performance
- [x] Cross-platform, SSH/remote, and path/shortcut impact considered (or N/A)
- [x] `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`, and `pnpm build` pass (or CI will cover; local preferred)

Local: plan verification commands above. Full `pnpm lint` / `pnpm build` left to CI per plan.

records.title: fix(browser-pane): stop a dead client-hosted guest from killing the workbench
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​323 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​1 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​322 |
| Prod | 5 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​182 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​63 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​119 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## What Changed

A destroyed client-hosted Electron guest could throw from metadata reads or activation focus during React effects, taking down the entire workbench. The pane now catches guest reads, reuses the guarded focus adapter, and shows its existing unavailable notice with the reopen-on-server action.

Guest destruction, renderer loss, and unreadable metadata all clear loading, release the webview reference, detach the attachment, and stop event listeners and metadata publishing. Failed initial reads also remove the loss listeners. Late loading events cannot restart the spinner after recovery.

Navigation history uses the guarded title snapshot, removing the last unguarded title read in this effect. Untitled nonblank pages consequently use their URL as the history title; blank pages still display “New Tab.” Load failures skip guest reads for discarded subframe/ERR_ABORTED events and reach the same recovery state if the remaining read fails.

## Why

Five field reports on Electron 43.4.1 showed `Invalid guestInstanceId` during metadata reads or a null `contentWindow` during focus. These operations run in renderer JavaScript on all desktop platforms. Guest read failures retain diagnostic breadcrumbs.

## ELI5

When an embedded browser dies, Orca now shows an unavailable message in that browser panel while keeping the rest of the workbench usable.

## Testing

- [x] Automated regressions: 12 dead-guest cases, including title-read races, failed-load recovery, initial listener cleanup, and loading events after destruction.
- [x] Browser-pane suite: 97 files / 788 tests passed locally on macOS.
- [x] `pnpm tc:web`, changed-code quality, focused oxlint, and formatting checks passed.
- [ ] Full rendered Orca workbench reproduction; the existing evidence below is a standalone Electron reproduction.

## Visual Proof

No before/after Orca recording is available. Regression tests exercise the unavailable notice and loading state; the prior standalone Electron run below establishes the native failure shapes, but does not prove end-to-end workbench behavior.

### 1. Live Electron 43.4.1 reproduction of both runtime conditions

Standalone Electron app (`/tmp/ct/repro-R1-R3`) on the exact Electron the field builds ship (`node_modules/electron` → `43.4.1`). Run first-hand for this PR, not quoted from an earlier session:

```
$ /…/node_modules/electron/dist/Electron.app/Contents/MacOS/Electron .
[renderer] CASE0 attached guestInstanceId = 2 getURL = about:blank
[renderer] EVENT destroyed fired at 166.80000001192093
[renderer] CASE1 main says destroyed at 0.3 ms
[renderer] CASE1 firstThrow: "Invalid guestInstanceId: 2" after 2.1 ms; destroyed DOM event after 0.3 ms; iterations 1
[renderer] CASE1 getWebContentsId still = 2
[renderer] CASE1 focus ok
[renderer] CASE1 isLoading throws: Invalid guestInstanceId: 2
[renderer] CASE2 attached id 3
[renderer] CASE2 alive after remove? false
[renderer] CASE2 focus throws: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'focus')
[renderer] CASE2 getURL throws: Error: The WebView must be attached to the DOM and the dom-ready event emitted before this method can be called.
[renderer] CASE2 getWebContentsId throws: The WebView must be attached to the DOM and the dom-ready event emitted before this method can be called.
DONE
```

CASE1 is the R3 field error verbatim. CASE2 is the R1 field error verbatim. `CASE1 getWebContentsId still = 2` is the evidence behind follow-up #1 below.


## Review

CodeRabbit's post-attachment recovery and unguarded-title findings are addressed. Review also added immediate listener/publisher cleanup and failed-load recovery. CodeRabbit and Pullfrog reviewed the final follow-up commit with no new actionable findings. All CI checks passed before merge.

## Notes

No RPC schema, platform-specific command, path, Git, or workspace-type behavior changes. Client-hosted guests still run on the client for SSH workspaces; network disconnection is not used as evidence of guest death.

Remaining pre-existing limitations: the retained registry can mistake a stale guest id for liveness; registry retirement without a DOM loss event can leave a pane quiet until the next read or placement update; separate attach-threw/renderer-unavailable branches may retain a loading state.

## Linked Issue

This PR addresses the five crash reports documented above; no GitHub issue is linked.

## Agent skill upstream boundary

- [x] Not applicable: no upstream skill-installer content is changed.

## Checklist

- [x] Self-reviewed for correctness, cleanup, and cross-platform/SSH behavior.
- [x] Focused production fix with regression coverage.
- [ ] Before/after rendered Orca capture attached.
- [x] Final CI checks complete; all passed before merge.
