| Prod | 4 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​83 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​13 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​70 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Every time you opened a browser tab inside Orca, it started its own little timer that asked the app "where is this pane on screen?" sixty times a second, forever. Open eight browser tabs and you got eight separate timers all asking the same question at the same moment. This change replaces all of those with one timer that asks on behalf of every tab at once. The overlays still follow their panes exactly as before, in every window state — the app just stops running eight schedulers where one will do.

An earlier revision of this PR also switched the timer off while the window was hidden. That has been removed: measurement showed Chromium already does exactly that, so the gate saved nothing real and could only misfire (details below).

## What was happening

`src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane/browser-client-page-visible-attachment.ts:111-118` (pre-change) started a permanent `requestAnimationFrame` loop **per shown client-hosted page**:

```ts
let positionFrame: number | null = null
const trackPosition = (): void => {
  syncViewport()
  positionFrame = requestAnimationFrame(trackPosition)
}
if (typeof requestAnimationFrame === 'function') {
  positionFrame = requestAnimationFrame(trackPosition)
}
```

`syncViewport` (same file, line 92) calls `container.getBoundingClientRect()`, which forces a synchronous layout flush. The loop was **not shared** — N shown hosts meant N independent loops and N rAF callbacks per frame — and **never idle**: there is no "nothing moved, stop asking" exit; it self-reschedules unconditionally until detach.

The loop's *reason* is legitimate and unchanged: a pane can MOVE without resizing (tab dragged across an even split, sidebar toggled), which fires neither `resize` nor `scroll`, so the body-level fixed overlay would keep painting at the old rect.

The fix adds `src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane/browser-client-page-position-driver.ts`: a module-scoped set of per-host sync callbacks driven by **one** rAF loop. `showRetainedHost` registers `syncViewport` with the driver and releases it on teardown. The loop starts on the first registration and stops on the last.

## Measurement

Harness: a Node script simulating 10 seconds of 60 fps frames against a stubbed `requestAnimationFrame`/`cancelAnimationFrame`, mounting N fake hosts under the old per-host-loop code and the new shared-driver code, counting rAF callbacks scheduled and `getBoundingClientRect()` calls, minus the one-time attach-path work, divided by simulated seconds.

| hosts | rAF callbacks/s before | after | `getBoundingClientRect()`/s before | after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 60 | 60 | 60 | 60 |
| 8 | 480 | **60** | 480 | 480 |

rAF callback scheduling drops from N per frame to 1 per frame — 8 hosts go from 480 to 60 scheduled callbacks per second (−87.5%). Rect reads stay at 60×N because each host genuinely needs its own container rect; they are now batched into a single callback rather than N scheduler entries.

**Correction to an earlier revision of this PR.** It also claimed a "hidden document: 60×N → 0" win from gating the loop on `document.visibilityState`. That row was an artifact of the stub: the harness's fake `requestAnimationFrame` keeps firing while hidden, and real Chromium does not. Measured against the real runtime (Electron 43.4.1, macOS 15, no `backgroundThrottling` override and no visibility-related Chromium switch in `src/main/startup/configure-process.ts` or `src/main/startup/disabled-chromium-features.ts`), counting rAF callbacks in a live `BrowserWindow`:

| window state | `document.visibilityState` | rAF callbacks/s |
| --- | --- | --- |
| shown, unfocused | `visible` | 60 |
| `hide()` | `hidden` | **0** |
| `minimize()` | `hidden` | **0** |
| fully occluded by another window | `hidden` | **0** |
| uncovered again | `visible` | 60 |

So the pre-change per-host loops were **already** costing 0 while hidden. The gate's measured saving in the real app is zero, and it has been removed.

## Negative user-facing trade-offs

**None.** Each preserved behavior:

- **Pane-move tracking (the reason the poll exists):** unchanged, in every window state. Every registered host's `syncViewport` still runs once per frame; the driver's callback iterates all of them. Covered by the test "tracks a pane that moves with no resize or scroll event" and by the two-host test asserting both overlays reposition from the single shared callback.
- **Hidden / occluded windows:** behavior is now identical to pre-change — the loop is never paused by this code, so whatever Chromium schedules is what runs. Pinned by the test "keeps tracking pane moves while the document reports hidden", which fires a `visibilitychange` to `hidden` and asserts both hosts still track a pane move on the next frame with no frame cancelled.
- **`ResizeObserver`, `resize`, capture-phase `scroll` listeners and the `appliedBounds` early-return:** untouched.
- **Cleanup:** every teardown path (detach, hide, error, last unregister) goes through the same release closure, which is now idempotent. The last host cancels the pending frame.
- **A host that throws does not take the others down:** each sync is isolated and the reschedule is unconditional, so the worst case is one overlay stalling, not all of them. See *Failure isolation* under Risk & verification.
- **No new failure mode when `requestAnimationFrame` is absent:** the same `typeof requestAnimationFrame === 'function'` guard is preserved (moved into the driver), and `cancelAnimationFrame` is guarded too.

### Why the visibility gate was removed rather than kept

Three findings, in order of weight:

1. **It saves nothing.** In every window state reproducible on macOS — hidden, minimized, fully occluded — `visibilityState` is `hidden` *and* Chromium is already running 0 rAF callbacks/s (table above). Windows behaves the same via `CalculateNativeWinOcclusion`; Linux has no occlusion tracking at all, so a covered window there stays `visible` and the gate would never engage.
2. **Its only live effect is a known-bad state.** `src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/stale-document-visibility.ts:1-9` documents a field-reported Chromium/macOS bug where the occlusion tracker wedges `visibilityState` at `hidden` after display sleep and never fires another `visibilitychange`, on a window the user is looking at and typing into. That is the one state where a gate would engage while frames still flow — and because no further `visibilitychange` arrives, a gated loop would never resume. The overlay would stop following pane moves permanently. Orca has already been bitten by this gate shape twice (terminal byte delivery, emulator streaming); both had to adopt `getWindowParkVisible()` from `src/renderer/src/lib/window-park-visibility.ts:10`, which layers a stale-input latch on top of `visibilityState`. Reaching for the raw signal here would have reintroduced the bug the latch exists to fix.
3. **The N→1 half is unconditionally safe and is where the win is.** Keeping only that half loses nothing measurable.

The test "keeps tracking pane moves while the document reports hidden" exists to stop the gate being reintroduced.

## Risk & verification

Verified:

- `pnpm tc` — clean.
- `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed` — 0 new findings across 5 changed files (oxlint, type-aware, React Doctor).
- `pnpm run check:react-doctor:changed` — 5 files scanned, 0 issues. Run **after committing on a clean tree**, since `lint:react-doctor:changed` only inspects uncommitted files and goes silent post-commit.
- Full `src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane` suite: 97 files / 781 tests passing.
- Unit test `src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane/browser-client-page-position-driver.test.ts`, 6 cases. It drives the **real** shipping path through `createRetainedHostFixture` (real registry, real body-level host, real visible attachment) with a hand-driven rAF stub, asserting: (a) two attached hosts share one rAF registration, not two; (b) a pane that moves with no resize/scroll event gets its rect updated on the next frame; (c) the loop keeps tracking both hosts across a `visibilitychange` to `hidden`, cancelling nothing; (d) the shared frame is cancelled only when the last host detaches; (e) `BrowserClientPageRetainedRegistry.dispose()` releases its host from the loop without the pane detaching; (f) when one host's sync throws, the other host still syncs on that same frame and the loop is still running on the next one. Case (f) was confirmed to fail against the driver without the isolation fix (the throw propagated out of `runFrame`), so it pins the guarantee rather than merely passing.
- Real-runtime rAF-vs-visibility measurement (table above) run against Electron 43.4.1 on macOS with a scratch `BrowserWindow`.
- **CLI/agent browser automation does not read this overlay rect.** Traced end to end: `orca browser screenshot` → `src/cli/handlers/browser-nav.ts:34` → RPC `browser.screenshot` (`src/main/runtime/rpc/methods/browser-core.ts:84`) → `src/main/runtime/runtime-browser-commands-browser-click.ts:130` → `AgentBrowserBridge` → `src/main/browser/cdp-screenshot.ts:180`, which issues CDP `Page.captureScreenshot` on the **guest** `webContents` (fallback `webContents.capturePage()` at line 261 is also the guest's own surface, never a window composite). Coordinate input takes the same shape: `orca mouse click` → `src/main/browser/agent-browser-bridge-mouse-commands.ts:36-88` resolves the guest `webContents` and dispatches CDP `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` in guest-local coordinates. The renderer-side host `left/top` written by `syncViewport` is never consulted on either path, so a stale overlay rect could not have produced a wrong-region screenshot or a mis-landed automated click. This PR therefore never carried an automation-correctness risk; the risk it did carry was to what a human sees.

**Failure isolation (the guarantee the N→1 change made load-bearing).** Sharing one loop changed the blast radius of a throwing host from 1 overlay to N. In the first revision `runFrame` called `startFrame()` *after* the sync loop with no `try`, so a single host's `syncViewport` throwing would escape before the reschedule and stop **every** overlay on the window tracking its pane — permanently, because the only things that call `startFrame()` again are a new `register` or a `ResizeObserver`/`resize`/`scroll` event, and none of those fire for a pane that merely moves. Low probability (`getBoundingClientRect()` on a detached node returns zeros rather than throwing, and `container`/`host` are non-null at registration) but unrecoverable and window-wide — the same "low probability, unrecoverable, affects everything" shape that argued the visibility gate out above. It is now fixed: each `sync()` runs inside its own `try`/`catch` so a failing host is skipped rather than fatal, the reschedule happens from a `finally` so it is unconditional, and each failing sync is reported once via a `WeakSet` rather than 60 times a second. A throwing host therefore degrades only itself, and only until whatever made it throw clears.

Also fixed here (flagged on the original revision): `BrowserClientPageRetainedRegistry` tore pages down — `dispose()`, `releasePage()`, `disconnectPage()` — without ever releasing the visible attachment's viewport tracking, so a torn-down page's `syncViewport` stayed registered and kept re-reading a container whose host had left the document. The attachment now carries its own idempotent `stopTrackingViewport`, and the registry runs it on both teardown paths.

Not verified:

- No manual run in the packaged Electron app; the overlay-follows-pane behavior was exercised in happy-dom, not against a real compositor.
- The rAF-vs-visibility table was measured on macOS only. Windows and Linux behavior is stated from Chromium's documented occlusion handling, not measured here.
- The wedged-occlusion state itself (display-sleep `visibilityState` wedge) could not be reproduced on demand, so whether frames keep flowing in it is inferred from the field report in `stale-document-visibility.ts`, not directly observed. The change is safe either way: without the gate this code behaves exactly as it did before the PR in that state.
- The driver is module-scoped renderer state shared across every retained registry in the renderer. That is intentional (one document, one rAF clock).
- No change to SSH/remote, main-process, or wire-format code paths; this is renderer-local overlay positioning only.

records.title: fix(worktrees): stop a resolved-worktree snapshot answering for repos it never saw
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 3 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​160 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​153 |
| Prod | 3 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​47 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​9 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​38 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## The red

`tests/e2e/ssh-skill-installation.spec.ts:108` — the worktree-scope case — fails on `origin/main` with `skill-install-workspace-not-found`. Reproduced at `7c94d1219` (detached-equivalent, clean tree): **1 pass then 3 straight failures**, so it is a race that the Docker SSH lane loses reliably, not a rotted spec.

This is a **product bug**, not a test bug. Evidence below.

## Root cause

`OrcaRuntimeService.listResolvedWorktrees()` caches one fleet-wide snapshot for `RESOLVED_WORKTREE_CACHE_TTL_MS` (1s) and reuses it on **time alone**. Nothing invalidates it when a repo is registered. For up to a second after a repo row lands, every caller reads a snapshot computed before that repo existed.

Instrumented run (timestamps ms, trimmed):

```
290736 LIST_CALL  cachedExpires=281560  nrepos=1     <- fleet snapshot recomputed
290736 COMPUTE    repos=[ local test repo only ]     <- SSH repo not registered yet
290765 ROWS       repo=<local> host=local ok=true n=2  ... snapshot valid until 291773
290898 LIST_CALL  cachedExpires=291773  nrepos=2     <- SSH repo now registered; served from cache
291615 SSHTARGET  want=<repoId>::/tmp/orca-docker-relay-perf-repo
                  repos=[ local, {id, /tmp/orca-docker-relay-perf-repo,
                                  connectionId: ssh-…, executionHostId: ssh:ssh-… } ]
291619 LIST_CALL  cachedExpires=291773  nrepos=2     <- STALE snapshot, no SSH rows
       -> throw skill-install-workspace-not-found
```

The repo row is present and correctly stamped `ssh:<target>`. `resolveSkillSshTarget` resolves the workspace-scope destination through the fleet snapshot (`src/main/runtime/runtime-skill-install-authority.ts:52-63`), gets zero rows because the snapshot predates the repo, and mints `skill-install-workspace-not-found`.

That is the shape [`docs/reference/ssh-execution-boundary.md`](../blob/main/docs/reference/ssh-execution-boundary.md) rules out: *"Absence from a client-side set … none of these observe the process. They are `unverifiable` by construction."* The client asserted a remote workspace was absent on the strength of bookkeeping that had never looked at the host.

**Why the lane fails deterministically and other scopes pass:** the spec connects the SSH target and installs immediately, so the install always lands inside the one-second window. Global scope never resolves a workspace (`destination.executionTarget` names the connection directly), and the folder case at line 111 runs later, after the window has closed. The asymmetry is timing, not scope-specific path computation.

## The fix

The snapshot now carries the repo-registration revision it was computed under, and is reused only while that revision still holds. The counter is the one `bumpLocalWorktreeScanGeneration` already advances on every repo add, removal and update, so the check is O(1) and cannot drift from the mutation sites — no second counter to keep in sync, no `getRepos()` hydration on the cached path.

Scope: a snapshot that never scanned a repo no longer answers for it. Everything reading `listResolvedWorktrees` benefits; skills is just where it hard-failed instead of self-correcting on the next poll.

## Not #18273

[#18273](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/18273) is a real and separate security finding — the *relay* trusting client-supplied `workspace.path`. It is not this failure:

- The error is thrown **client-side, before any RPC reaches the relay** (`runtime-skill-install-authority.ts:61`, inside `skillInstallDestinationUsesSsh`), so the relay's `authority()` never runs.
- #18273's Step 2 would *introduce* a `skill-install-workspace-not-found` on the relay; it does not explain one on `074a2366bf`/`7c94d1219` today.
- Nothing here resolves a remote path from the client filesystem. The path comes from a remote `git worktree list` over the relay; the bug is a cache that had not run that scan yet.

#18273 should still be implemented on its own merits. Same for #18280 / #18277 — no shared machinery with this.

## Not a merged-PR regression

The stale-snapshot behaviour predates today's SSH work. `resolveSkillSshTarget`'s use of the fleet inventory and `RuntimeResolvedWorktreeCache`'s time-only reuse both arrive with #17605 (the `OrcaRuntimeService` split) and are unchanged by any of today's 28 SSH merges. #18257's class (a call site missing `testInfo`) is also unrelated — `startDockerSshRelayTarget(testInfo)` is already correct in this spec.

## Verification

Before (at `7c94d1219`, clean tree):

```
✘ ssh-skill-installation.spec.ts:54 (22.2s)
Error: page.evaluate: Error: Error invoking remote method
  'skills:installPackageVersion': Error: skill-install-workspace-not-found
    at installAndVerify (tests/e2e/ssh-skill-installation.spec.ts:152:32)
    at tests/e2e/ssh-skill-installation.spec.ts:108:13
1 failed
```

After — 3 consecutive runs:

```
=== RUN 1 ===  ✓ … through the real relay (22.5s)   1 passed (32.4s)
=== RUN 2 ===  ✓ … through the real relay (21.5s)   1 passed (22.2s)
=== RUN 3 ===  ✓ … through the real relay (21.6s)   1 passed (22.4s)
```

- `pnpm tc` — exit 0
- `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed` — 0 new findings across 5 files
- `pnpm test src` — 69127 passed. Two failures in `src/main/native-chat/agent-session-wire/structured-tui-transcript-catchup.test.ts` (a `vi.waitFor` deadline plus a worker fork exit) touch no repo/worktree state and pass in isolation; load-sensitive flake, unrelated.
- New `src/main/runtime/runtime-resolved-worktree-cache.test.ts` (4 cases) and a runtime-level regression in `worktree-scan-cache-ttl.spec.ts`. Negative control: with the fix reverted and the tests kept, the runtime-level case fails (`1 failed | 1230 passed`); with the fix, `1231 passed`.

## Follow-up, not fixed here

The same call site still reports `skill-install-workspace-not-found` when the SSH scan itself is *unavailable* — `listRepoWorktreesForResolutionUncached` returns `{ ok: false, worktrees: [] }` for a missing provider or a thrown scan, and `resolveSkillSshTarget` cannot tell that from a real absence. Distinguishing them needs scan availability plumbed through `listResolvedWorktrees`, which is a larger change than this red warrants. Worth its own issue.

records.title: Align computer-use PowerShell with the EDR posture doc
records.body:
Defensive maintenance finding from an internal audit of `074a2366bf`. No exploit steps or payloads. Implement by following this plan exactly. Do not commit files under `plans/` in the implementation PR.

---

# Plan 014: Align computer-use PowerShell with the EDR posture doc

> **Executor instructions**: Follow this plan step by step. Run every
> verification command and confirm the expected result before moving to the
> next step. If anything in the "STOP conditions" section occurs, stop and
> report — do not improvise. When done, update the status row for this plan
> in `plans/README.md` — unless a reviewer dispatched you and told you they
> maintain the index.
>
> **Drift check (run first)**: `git diff --stat 074a2366bf..HEAD -- src/main/computer/desktop-script-provider-bridge.ts docs/reference/windows-edr-posture.md`
> If any in-scope file changed since this plan was written, compare the
> "Current state" excerpts against the live code before proceeding; on a
> mismatch, treat it as a STOP condition.

## Status

- **Priority**: P1
- **Effort**: S
- **Risk**: MED
- **Depends on**: none
- **Category**: security
- **Planned at**: commit `074a2366bf`, 2026-09-03

## Why this matters

`docs/reference/windows-edr-posture.md` says computer-use launches PowerShell with `-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned` and falls back to Bypass only after a policy-blocked start, via `src/main/computer/windows-powershell-execution-policy.ts`. That helper file is **absent**. Live argv is always Bypass:

`src/main/computer/desktop-script-provider-bridge.ts:14-24`:

```ts
platform === 'windows'
  ? [
      '-NoProfile',
      '-NonInteractive',
      '-ExecutionPolicy',
      'Bypass',
      '-File',
      scriptPath,
      operationPath
    ]
```

The doc at lines 248-251 even quotes `RemoteSigned` on this same file. Distinct from Claude hook `-EncodedCommand` tickets (#17876, #17977, #16629) — do not change hook launchers.

AGENTS.md / CONTRIBUTING: do not add `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` as the unconditional flag; do not add `-EncodedCommand`.

## Current state

- `execBridge` in `desktop-script-provider-bridge.ts` uses `execFile` from `node:child_process` (not `runProcess`). Do not switch to `shell: true`.
- Non-Windows branch is `python3` + script — leave it.
- `windowsHide` is not set here; do not add `cmd.exe /c`.

## Commands you will need

| Purpose | Command | Expected on success |
|---------|---------|---------------------|
| Typecheck | `pnpm tc:node` | exit 0 |
| Tests | `pnpm test src/main/computer/desktop-script-provider-bridge.ts` | all pass (create test file if missing) |
| Lint changed | `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed` | exit 0 |

## Scope

**In scope**:
- `src/main/computer/desktop-script-provider-bridge.ts`
- New `src/main/computer/windows-powershell-execution-policy.ts` (the path the doc already names) **or** inline RemoteSigned-first in the bridge if a separate file is overkill — prefer the named file so the doc is true
- Tests for argv
- `docs/reference/windows-edr-posture.md` only if the implemented fallback classification differs; keep it accurate

**Out of scope**:
- Hook wrappers / `wsl-cli-scripts.ts`
- Changing computer-use Python/macOS paths
- Kaspersky EncodedCommand (#17876)

## Git workflow

- Branch: `fix/computer-use-execution-policy`
- Commit: `fix(computer-use): prefer RemoteSigned over Bypass on Windows`
- Do NOT push or open a PR unless the operator instructed it.

## Steps

### Step 1: RemoteSigned first

Windows argv must start:

`-NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -File <scriptPath> <operationPath>`

(`-NoLogo` only if the doc requires it and tests for the current argv already expect it — match current flags except Bypass → RemoteSigned.)

If the process exits with a policy-block (classify from stderr/exit the same way hook-launcher does if such a helper exists in `src/main`; otherwise match strings `disabled` / `execution policy` conservatively). Retry **once** with Bypass, same `-File` args. Never Bypass on the first spawn.

Do not use `-EncodedCommand`.

**Verify**: unit test spies `execFile` (or the bridge’s spawn) and asserts first argv contains `RemoteSigned` not `Bypass`.

### Step 2: Policy-block retry test

Simulate first spawn failing with a policy error → second spawn uses Bypass. First spawn success → no second spawn.

**Verify**: `pnpm test` on the new/updated test file.

### Step 3: Doc

If `windows-powershell-execution-policy.ts` now exists, the EDR doc citation is true. If you inlined, update the doc path to `desktop-script-provider-bridge.ts` so it does not point at a missing file.

**Verify**: `test -f src/main/computer/windows-powershell-execution-policy.ts` **or** `rg windows-powershell-execution-policy docs/reference/windows-edr-posture.md` is gone.

## Test plan

- First argv is RemoteSigned.
- Policy-block → one Bypass retry.
- Success → no Bypass.
- Model after other `execFile` mock tests in `src/main/computer/` if any; else `src/main/rate-limits/gemini-cli-oauth-extractor.ts` comment style (execFile not exec).

## Done criteria

- [ ] `pnpm tc:node` exits 0
- [ ] Unconditional Bypass is gone from the first Windows argv
- [ ] Tests exist and pass
- [ ] EDR doc does not reference a missing file
- [ ] No files outside the in-scope list
- [ ] `plans/README.md` status row updated

## STOP conditions

- Restricted hosts cannot run `-File` of a packaged script even with RemoteSigned, and classifying policy-block is unreliable — report; do not leave Bypass as the only argv.
- You would need `cmd.exe /c` or `-EncodedCommand`.

## Maintenance notes

- Reviewer: `rg ExecutionPolicy src/main/computer` should not show Bypass except the retry path.
- Do not “fix” EDR by disabling computer-use on Windows.

records.title: refactor(process-table): split the snapshot module along the capture/index seam
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​7 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​5 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​2 |
| Prod | 6 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​134 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​137 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​3 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## Why

**`main`'s `static analysis` lane is currently red, and it fails on every PR — including PRs that do not touch the offending file.** This PR unblocks it.

```
src/shared/process-table-snapshot.ts:463:2: error eslint(max-lines): File has too many lines (308). help: Maximum allowed is 300.
```

`.oxlintrc.json` caps `src/**/*.ts` at 300 counted lines (`skipBlankLines`, `skipComments`). `origin/main`'s copy of `src/shared/process-table-snapshot.ts` counts **308**, so `pnpm exec oxlint` fails on a clean checkout of `main` with no local changes. #17831 and #17871 are both red on this lane, and #17871 does not touch the file at all.

Verified on `main` (`c2fce8028962`):

```
$ pnpm exec oxlint
src/shared/process-table-snapshot.ts:463:2: error eslint(max-lines): File has too many lines (308). help: Maximum allowed is 300.
```

## The seam

The file already held two clusters with genuinely different reasons to change:

1. **The POSIX `ps` capture layer** — `PS_ARGS`, the 32MB buffer ceiling, the lenient and strict parsers, `ProcessTableCaptureError`, the truncation guard, and the in-flight + TTL snapshot reader that collapses concurrent scans (issue #6288).
2. **The derived correlation indexes** — `buildProcessTableIndex`, `collectDescendantsFromIndex`, `lookupProcessTableIndex`, `getProcessTableIndex`, `scoreForegroundCandidateRow`.

Cluster 2 is generic over `ProcessIdentityRow` and is *not* `ps`-specific: `src/main/providers/windows-foreground-process-rows.ts` runs the same index pass over the Windows process table, which never forks `ps`. That is the seam.

Cluster 2 moves to **`src/shared/process-table-index.ts`**, verbatim, along with the types it exclusively owns (`ProcessTableIndexStats`, `ProcessIdentityRow`, `ProcessTableIndexOf`, `ProcessTableIndex`). Import direction is one-way: the index module takes a type-only `ProcessTableRow`; the capture module imports nothing back.

`getStrictProcessTableSnapshot` and friends stay at `src/shared/process-table-snapshot.ts`, so the `vi.mock('../shared/process-table-snapshot', ...)` in `src/relay/pty-handler-inventory-process-evidence.test.ts` and the relay pty handler's import are untouched.

### Counted lines (non-blank, non-comment)

| File | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `src/shared/process-table-snapshot.ts` | **308** ❌ | **232** ✅ |
| `src/shared/process-table-index.ts` | — | **77** ✅ |

Both halves sit well under the 300 cap, so the next small change to either one does not re-break `main`.

## Pure refactor

No behavior change. Same exports, same semantics. records.title: perf(windows): drop the unread Memory flag and share one process-table projection per snapshot
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​169 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​10 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​159 |
| Prod | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​177 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​117 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​60 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

On Windows, twice a second Orca asks the operating system for a **memory reading on every single running program** — about 1,050 of them — and then throws every one of those readings away without looking at it. Nothing in the app reads that field.

And separately: those 1,050 processes get looked up once per open terminal. With 11 terminals open, Orca builds the *same* index of the *same* 1,050 processes 11 times over, a fraction of a second apart, instead of building it once and sharing it. The snapshot itself was already shared; only the work done on top of it was not.

This PR stops asking for the memory field, and shares the index.

---

## What was wrong, and what I found when I checked

Three fixes. I verified each against the code and the vendored addon source rather than taking the brief at face value; **two details in the brief were wrong** and are corrected below.

### Fix 1 — the snapshot requested a `Memory` field with zero consumers

`src/main/windows/windows-process-table.ts` set `ProcessDataFlag.Memory | CommandLine | CreationTime` and surfaced the result as `WindowsProcessRow.memoryBytes`.

A full `rg memoryBytes src/` finds **no reader.** The only other hits are an unrelated local variable in `src/main/memory/collector.ts` / `memory-snapshot-buckets.ts` (the Resource Manager's own CIM sweep, which needs `PageFileUsage` and CPU counters in one pass and cannot use this table), plus the module's own test and a comment in `windows-process-table-cim-scan.ts` saying the CIM fallback deliberately leaves it undefined. Nothing consumed it, so `memoryBytes` is removed along with the flag.

**Cost, read out of the vendored addon source** (`@vscode/windows-process-tree@0.8.0`, as patched by `config/patches/`):

```c
// src/process.cc:47-63  -- GetProcessMemoryUsage, called per row when MEMORY is set
hProcess = OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ, false, pid);
if (GetProcessMemoryInfo(hProcess, &pmc, sizeof(pmc))) { ... }
```

So `Memory` costs one `OpenProcess` **plus** one `GetProcessMemoryInfo` per process, per snapshot, and the handle it takes carries `PROCESS_VM_READ`.

> **Correction to the brief.** The brief said "`process.cc:52` and `:84` each do `OpenProcess(...)` plus `GetProcessMemoryInfo` per process." Line 52 is right. Line 84 is **`GetCpuUsage`**, which calls `GetProcessTimes`, not `GetProcessMemoryInfo` — and Orca never calls it (`getProcessCpuUsage` is explicitly rejected in `windows-process-enumeration.md` for its blocking `Sleep(1000)`). So the `Memory` flag costs **one** extra handle per process, not two. The "roughly 2100 `OpenProcess`/sec, of which the Memory half is dead work" figure still holds: it was 2 handles per process (Memory + CommandLine) and is now 1.

### Fix 2 — every pane re-projected and re-indexed the whole snapshot

`src/main/providers/windows-foreground-process-rows.ts`, per inspection:

- `native.map(toProcessRow)` — a fresh ~1050-object array;
- `rows.some(row => row.pid === rootPid)` — linear scan;
- `collectDescendants(rows, rootPid)` — a whole-table `Map` plus ~1050 child arrays, rebuilt from scratch;
- `rows.find(row => row.pid === anchorPid)` — a second linear scan.

POSIX already had the fix: `getProcessTableIndex()` in `src/shared/process-table-snapshot.ts` memoizes `byPid` / `childrenByPpid` per snapshot identity in a `WeakMap`. The brief's diagnosis here is exactly right, including the subtle part — **the `.map()` defeated any such memo by construction**, because it returns a new array identity on every call, so even wiring `getProcessTableIndex` in directly would have missed every time.

Now: a `WeakMap` caches the `toProcessRow` projection keyed by the native rows array, and the projected array (now stable) feeds the existing `getProcessTableIndex`. Both lookups become `byPid` hits and the descendant walk reads the shared `childrenByPpid`.

Rather than adding a parallel Windows index, `buildProcessTableIndex` / `getProcessTableIndex` / `lookupProcessTableIndex` are now generic over the row shape (`ProcessIdentityRow = { pid; ppid }`), and the descendant walk moved into a shared `collectDescendantsFromIndex`. `ProcessTableIndex` stays as an alias, so no POSIX caller changed shape.

The "related and smaller" item was clean, so it is included: `src/main/providers/agent-foreground-process.ts` had a byte-identical duplicate `collectDescendants` with the same per-call Map rebuild on POSIX. It now uses the shared index too — `getFreshProcessTableSnapshot()`/`getProcessTableSnapshot()` already return a per-capture-memoized array, so the identity the memo needs is there.

### Fix 3 — `docs/reference/windows-edr-posture.md` was wrong in three places

I checked all three against the vendored source. **All three claims were false at the base commit.**

| Claim in the doc | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| (a) "`Memory` is retired" | It was **not**. `windows-process-table.ts` set it on every snapshot. It *is* retired now — by this PR. |
| (b) "one cache per flag set… 6.3 ms p50 / 12.3 ms p50 at 492 processes" | There is **no** flag-set split and never was. One TTL cache serves everyone, deliberately (the code comment says a split "would restore exactly the fan-out it exists to prevent"). Those two p50 figures describe no code path in the tree. |
| (c) "the command line now comes from the kernel through `NtQueryInformationProcess`'s `ProcessCommandLineInformation`… `ReadProcessMemory` is absent from the compiled addon, asserted against the binary's import table" | **False.** `process_commandline.cc:32` opens `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION \| PROCESS_VM_READ`; `:38` queries `ProcessBasicInformation` (to find the PEB, not the command line); `:41`, `:43`, `:47` are three `ReadProcessMemory` calls walking PEB → `RTL_USER_PROCESS_PARAMETERS` → command-line buffer. No import-table assertion exists anywhere in the repo, and none would pass. |

(c) is the one that mattered beyond tidiness: the doc told future contributors that the MDE **"suspicious memory activity"** signal — the thing Incident D fired on — had been removed. It had not. Both docs are now rewritten to describe what the code actually does, and to state precisely what this PR changed (`Memory`'s second handle: gone) versus what remains (one `PROCESS_VM_READ` handle and a PEB read per process, from `CommandLine`). Moving to `ProcessCommandLineInformation` would genuinely retire the remote read; the doc now labels that as unwritten work rather than shipped.

---

## Measurements

### Measured here — unit-level counters (`src/main/providers/windows-foreground-process-inspection-cost.test.ts`)

Simulated 1,050-process table, 11 panes inspecting inside one 500 ms TTL window. Counters are `Map.prototype.set` calls (scoped patch, restored in `finally`) and distinct projected-row object identities. **Fail-first confirmed** by reverting `src/` and re-running.

| Counter, per 11-pane sweep on one snapshot | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Snapshot projections (`native.map(toProcessRow)` passes) | **11** | **1** |
| Row objects allocated by projection (11 × 1050 vs 1 × 1050) | **11,550** | **1,050** |
| `Map` insertions during the sweep | **11,550** | **0** |
| `Map` insertions, one-time index build (amortised over all 11 panes) | — | **2,100** |
| Whole-table linear scans (`.some` + `.find`) | **22** | **0** |
| Flag bitfield sent to the addon | **7** (`Memory\|CommandLine\|CreationTime`) | **6** (`CommandLine\|CreationTime`) |
| `OpenProcess` calls the addon makes per snapshot | **2 × N** | **1 × N** |

Net per snapshot window: **11,550 → 2,100** Map insertions and **11,550 → 1,050** row objects, and the index cost is now paid once no matter how many panes share the window (it stops scaling with pane count entirely).

The after-numbers are exact, not bounded: 0 Map insertions across the sweep, 1 distinct projection. The committed assertions are the tight ones (`=== 1`, `< TABLE_SIZE`).

### Not measured here — the module's published figures

The flag-cost claim rests on `@vscode/windows-process-tree`'s own published numbers, reproduced in `docs/reference/windows-process-enumeration.md`, measured on Windows 11 at 1,050 processes:

- pid + ppid + name: **15.9 ms p50** / 17.5 ms p95
- **+ memory + command line**: **30.6 ms p50** / 33.7 ms p95
- `Get-CimInstance` via PowerShell: 706 ms p50

Those are **the module's figures for both extra fields together**. This PR removes one of the two. I have not measured where `CommandLine` alone lands between 15.9 and 30.6 ms and I am not claiming a number — the doc now says so explicitly instead of implying a split.

### Needs a real Windows box — with the exact command

Nothing here was run on Windows; all profiling of this app to date was on macOS. What would settle it:

| Question | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Handle churn from the flag change | `Get-Counter '\Process(Orca)\Handle Count' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 60`, with 11 panes inspecting, before vs after |
| Snapshot wall time for `CommandLine`-only vs both flags | `Measure-Command` around a loop calling `getProcessList` at each bitfield, on a ≥1000-process host |
| Main-process CPU attributable to inspection | `Get-Counter '\Process(Orca)\% Processor Time' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 120` at 11 panes, idle |
| Whether MDE stops scoring "suspicious memory activity" | It will not — `CommandLine` still does the PEB read. Only an addon patch to `ProcessCommandLineInformation` would test that. |

---

## Negative user-facing trade-offs

**None.** Specifically:

- **Detection results are unchanged.** Same rows in, same rows out. `byPid` is built first-wins on duplicate pids, which is exactly `rows.find()` semantics; `childrenByPpid` is built in capture order and the walk pops last-pushed-first, so `collectDescendantsFromIndex` emits descendants in the identical order to the old per-call walk, and the subsequent `.sort()` is stable in V8. Agent foreground-process detection and has-children answers are byte-identical — asserted by a dedicated case in the new test file, and the pre-existing `windows-agent-foreground-process-scan-volume.test.ts`, `windows-foreground-process-rows.test.ts`, `agent-foreground-process*.test.ts` and `structured-tui-process-identity.test.ts` all pass unchanged.
- **Removing `Memory` has no reader.** Full-repo grep above; the only other `memoryBytes` identifiers belong to the Resource Manager's independent CIM sweep. If a future caller wants a working set off this table it should not use this field anyway: `process.cc:59` stores `pmc.WorkingSetSize` into a `DWORD`, so anything above 4 GB wraps — already documented, and now cross-referenced from the flag comment.
- **Rows are shared, not copied.** The projected array is handed to multiple readers, so `queryWindowsProcessRowsFresh` now returns `readonly WindowsProcessRow[]`. I checked both callers (`windows-pty-root-identity.ts`, `structured-tui-process-identity.ts`) — one reads, one `.map()`s; neither mutates. Descendant candidates are still `{ ...row, depth }` copies, and `anchorRow` is read-only at every use site.
- **Caches are correctly bounded.** Both memos are `WeakMap`s keyed by the snapshot array identity, so an entry dies with its snapshot — no new retention, no cross-snapshot staleness, and `resetWindowsProcessTableForTests()` still invalidates everything by producing a new array.
- **No EDR posture regression.** Strictly fewer handles opened per process, no new interpreter hop, no PowerShell, no `child_process`. Enumeration still goes solely through `windows-process-table.ts`.

## Verification

- `pnpm tc` — clean (run once, at the end)
- `npx oxlint <changed files>` — clean; `npx oxfmt --check` — clean
- `npx vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/main/windows src/main/providers src/shared` — **690 files / 7,457 tests pass.** The 11 failures are all `*.node-pty.test.ts` real-PTY tests, which need node-pty built from source; they fail identically on a pristine `main` in this sandbox and touch none of this code.

records.title: fix(terminal): replay paired-runtime snapshots at the host's grid
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 4 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​395 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​4 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​391 |
| Prod | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​121 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​114 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## The bug

Opening a workspace on a paired Windows runtime (`awin`) from a Mac client shows a near-empty terminal pane, while the same pane on the Windows host renders the full Claude Code frame. It never heals, because the agent is idle and emits nothing.

## Root cause

A paired remote pane parses the host's authoritative terminal image at **whatever grid its own xterm currently has**.

The host dimensions every snapshot it publishes (`cols`/`rows` in the `SnapshotStart` frame), and `decodeSnapshotInfo` already parses them — but only the **requested**-snapshot path read them back. Both **push** paths (initial subscribe, server-pushed recovery) in `remote-runtime-terminal-binary-snapshots.ts` called `onSnapshot(...)` without the grid, so `remote-runtime-pty-transport.ts` handed the drain an image with no geometry and `replay-data-drain.ts` wrote it at the pane's grid.

Serialized frames are grid-relative: rows are newline-fed and the frame ends in an absolute CUP. Parsed at a different grid they re-wrap and clip, and since an alternate-screen TUI has no scrollback the rows scrolled off the top are gone for good.

This is asymmetric with every other restore path in the codebase — `applyMainBufferSnapshot` (hidden restore) and `applyReattachPayload` (SSH/cold restore) both resize to the source grid, replay, then fit back.

Grid divergence is the *normal* state here, not an edge case: while investigating I measured the live session with the host PTY at **143×43** and the Mac client's xterm at **154×68** at the same moment (the host also displays the pane and owns the viewport, so the client's claim is not applied).

## Evidence

I pulled the **real** snapshot bytes off the running host (`serializeBuffer`, 7,191 chars, host grid 154x68) and replayed them into scratch xterm instances at a range of client grids:

| client grid at replay | rows painted | first visible row |
|---|---|---|
| 154x68 (matches host) | **47** | `. Five are fully green. Let me see what's failing...` |
| 143x43 | 35 | `| #17894 | Lint gate fixed on Node 24 ...` (top of frame lost) |
| 120x68 | 55 | `. The failure is src/main/cursor/hook-service.test.ts...` (re-wrapped, wrong rows) |
| 80x24 (xterm's pre-fit default) | 22 | `exists. Nothing in the release workflow creates it...` |

**The mismatch only damages the frame when the destination is narrower or shorter than the source.** A destination that is wider *and* taller is unaffected, because no row exceeds the destination width and the extra rows are simply blank. A follow-up review confirmed this with a synthetic full-width frame: replaying a 143x43 frame into a 154x68 pane is byte-identical before and after this change, while replaying it into a 120x43 pane goes from 21 mangled rows (first row `row23`, zero right edges intact) to 43 correct rows.

That damaging direction is reachable in normal operation, not just in theory:

- Grid divergence between host and client is the steady state on a paired runtime that the host also displays. While investigating I measured the host PTY at **143x43** while the client's xterm was at **154x68** at the same moment, because the host owns the viewport and the client's claim is not applied.
- A freshly mounted remote pane sits at xterm's **80x24** default until its first fit. In the same live session I found a mounted, subscribed remote pane still at 80x24 while its sibling was at 154x68 - so a snapshot pushed on subscribe can land narrower *and* shorter than the host before the pane has ever been fitted.

**Scope of the claim:** this PR demonstrably fixes grid-mismatch mangling, which is severe in the narrower/shorter direction. It has *not* been demonstrated that the specific blank pane in the original report was produced by this path rather than by another cause, since the pane's grid at replay time was not captured before the app moved on. That investigation stays open.

## The fix

Carry the grid the host **already publishes** through the multiplexer and transport, then reuse the existing choreography:

1. `onSnapshot` meta gains `cols`/`rows`; both push paths forward `info.cols` / `info.rows`.
2. The transport forwards them as `snapshotCols` / `snapshotRows` on the replay meta.
3. `replay-data-drain.ts` resizes xterm to the source grid (with `suppressStructuralReplayPtyResize`, so the layout step never reaches the PTY), replays, then runs `safeFitAndThen` + `createReattachGridPush` — the same helper `applyReattachPayload` uses — to fit back and push the pane's real grid to the PTY.

**Wire compatibility:** no new field, no new opcode, no capability negotiation. `cols`/`rows` have always been on `SnapshotStart`; a host that omits them reads as *unknown* and the pane keeps today's behaviour (covered by a test).

**Scope:** only payloads that carry proven dimensions take the new path, so local, SSH and cold-restore replays are untouched.

**Known trade:** when the pane is *shorter* than the host, replay-then-shrink still drops rows the pane cannot display — the same trade `applyReattachPayload` already makes. Today those rows are wrong rather than missing; after this they are the host's true image, and the post-fit PTY grid push gives the TUI the geometry to repaint.

## Related

- #12768 (`fix(terminal): restore paired snapshots at the source grid`, open since Aug 5, last touched Aug 7) diagnosed the same root cause. It is a much wider change — it also removes a client-side viewport cache and reworks shutdown rollback — and has been stale for four weeks against a main that has moved a long way. This PR is the minimal grid fix on current main; happy to close it in favour of a rebased #12768 if its author wants to revive that instead.
- Adjacent but distinct: #15997 (cold-parked reveal repaints at the wrong pane height), #12349 (stale rows composited over the current frame).

## Testing

- `src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/remote-runtime-pty-snapshot-source-grid.test.ts` — new. Drives **real binary frames** through the **real** multiplexer into the **real** transport: initial push carries the grid, recovery push carries the grid alongside its clearing prologue, and an undimensioned host reads as unknown.
- `src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/pty-connection-remote-snapshot-source-grid.test.ts` — new. Asserts the drain resizes to the source grid *before* writing the frame, pushes the pane grid (not the host grid) to the PTY afterwards, leaves the grid alone when no dimensions were published, and demonstrates on `@xterm/headless` that the frame only survives at the source grid.
- Both new tests were confirmed to **fail** on the unpatched tree and pass with the fix.
- `pnpm test src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/ src/renderer/src/runtime/` — 582 files / 5379 tests pass. Two existing snapshot-meta assertions were updated for the new fields.
- `pnpm tc` clean; `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed` — 0 new findings across 11 files; `oxlint` clean; max-lines ratchet OK.

records.title: [Bug]: Built-in browser `snapshot` / `screenshot` / `wait` intermittently fail with `runtime_unavailable` while `eval` / `click` / `tab *` keep working (Windows host, CLI from WSL2)
records.body:
Operating system: Windows
Orca version: 1.4.194

Short summary:
When driving Orca's built-in browser from the CLI (`orca-ide` wrapper inside WSL2 Ubuntu, `ORCA_ORCHESTRATION_COMPATIBILITY_HOST_KIND=wsl`), the read-only inspection commands `snapshot`, `screenshot` and `wait` fail most of the time with `runtime_unavailable` ("The Orca runtime closed the connection before responding. Restart Orca and try again."), `runtime_timeout`, or `browser_error`, even though `orca status --json` reports `runtime.state = "ready"` and `reachable = true` immediately before and after. During the same session `eval`, `click`, `tab list/create/switch/close` succeeded on every call, so the browser page itself is alive and responsive.

What happened?
- `orca tab list --json` → ok (2 tabs)
- `orca snapshot --page <id-of-a-NON-active-tab> --json` → `runtime_unavailable` (reproducible every time)
- `orca tab switch --page <id> --json` → ok, then immediately `orca snapshot --json` → ok (works right after a switch)
- a few commands later, same active tab, `orca snapshot --json` → `runtime_unavailable` again, while `orca eval --expression "document.title" --json` in between → ok
- `orca screenshot --json` → ok once right after `tab switch`; later calls on the same active tab → `runtime_unavailable`, then `browser_error` after another `tab switch`
- `orca wait --page <id> --timeout 10000 --json` → `runtime_timeout`; `orca wait --selector ".copy-chat-key" --json` → `runtime_unavailable` (page had the selector, `eval` confirmed `querySelectorAll(...).length === 5`)
- `orca status --json` between failures → `"state": "ready", "reachable": true` every time; Orca never actually restarted.

How can we reproduce it?
1. Windows 11 host running Orca 1.4.194, terminal is a WSL2 Ubuntu shell opened by Orca (`orca-ide` on PATH).
2. `orca-ide tab create --url <any page with a large DOM, e.g. an AdminLTE admin page> --json`
3. `orca-ide tab create --url <second page> --json` (second tab becomes active)
4. `orca-ide snapshot --page <first tab's browserPageId> --json` → `runtime_unavailable`
5. `orca-ide tab switch --page <first tab> --json`, then `orca-ide snapshot --json` → ok
6. Run `orca-ide eval --expression "document.title" --json` 2–3 times, then `orca-ide snapshot --json` again → `runtime_unavailable` (intermittent, but happened in most of ~8 attempts)

Anything else that might help:
- Pages were normal HTTPS sites (a Bootstrap/AdminLTE admin page and a small chat page), default profile.
- Running two CLI commands concurrently (e.g. `snapshot` and `tab close` from two shells) also produced `runtime_unavailable` for one of them; the failures above were with strictly sequential commands.
- The CLI wrapper in WSL is `orca-ide` → `.../Programs/orca/resources/bin/orca.exe`.
- Workaround that worked for us: use `eval` for DOM inspection/actions instead of `snapshot`, and only call `snapshot`/`screenshot` immediately after `tab switch`.

records.body:
### Operating system

macOS

1.4.193

### Details

Short summary:

On macOS, `orca computer type-text` duplicates the supplied text in an Electron/React contentEditable composer. The visible and accessibility read-back becomes:

`<input text><placeholder><input text>`

No message was sent during testing.

Environment:

- Orca Computer Use provider version: 1.0
- Provider SHA-256: ee86ac05cd488ff8819c606d49f5378e5d6c77daf2c271e1f9cc9c794771ccdb
- Target application: Hermes Desktop v0.20.6 (+957)
- Target bundle ID: com.nousresearch.hermes
- Target control: Electron/React contentEditable composer

What happened?

A fresh Hermes session was prepared manually. The composer was empty and no active transcript was present.

After confirming the exact application, window, and focused composer receiver, I ran a non-sensitive single-line probe:

```
orca computer type-text --app com.nousresearch.hermes --window-id <WINDOW_ID> --text HERMES_INPUT_PROBE_20260901_A --json
```

The action returned:

- path: synthetic
- verification.state: unverified
- verification.reason: synthetic_input

The visible composer and accessibility snapshot contained:

```
HERMES_INPUT_PROBE_20260901_AGive Hermes a taskHERMES_INPUT_PROBE_20260901_A
```

The same duplication occurred with a multiline payload supplied through `--text-stdin`, so the problem is not limited to multiline input or stdin handling.

I also tested `set-value` once on a fresh empty composer:

```
orca computer set-value --app com.nousresearch.hermes --window-id <WINDOW_ID> --element-index <COMPOSER_ELEMENT_INDEX> --value "<TEST_TEXT>" --json
```

The result was:

- verification.state: unverified
- verification.reason: value_mismatch
- actualPreview: Give Hermes a task

The text appeared visually, but the React input state was not updated and the semantic Send button did not appear.

Expected behavior:

1. The supplied text should appear exactly once.
2. The placeholder should not become part of the composer value.
3. React input state should be updated.
4. The Send button should appear.
5. The provider should return verified only after exact same-receiver read-back.

Code-level observation:

The signed macOS computer-use provider binary applies `CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString` to both the keyDown and keyUp CGEvents and posts both events. This matches the observed two-copy insertion in the contentEditable receiver.

Suggested minimal fix:

- Attach the Unicode payload only to the keyDown event.
- Post a keyUp event without a Unicode payload.
- Reconfirm the target PID, window, and focused receiver immediately before posting.
- Read back the exact composer value after input and return verified only when it matches.

No Hermes application source was modified. No test message was sent.

How can we reproduce it?

1. Open an Electron application with a React contentEditable composer and a visible placeholder.
2. Focus the empty composer.
3. Confirm the focused receiver with `orca computer get-app-state`.
4. Run `orca computer type-text` with a short single-line probe.
5. Compare the visible composer and accessibility read-back with the supplied text.

The supplied payload is inserted twice with the placeholder between the two copies.

records.title: fix(computer-use): run the Windows runtime as one persistent helper
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 6 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1362 | 0 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1362 |
| Prod | 16 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1113 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​34 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1079 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## What MDE flagged

Incidents E and F: multi-stage Defender for Endpoint incidents mapped to ATT&CK **Execution + Collection**, described as "Screenshots were taken unexpectedly on this device… Screen capture code was found in a script launched by powershell.exe", with the contributing factor "Executes suspicious MSIL code".

The cause was the shape of the computer-use provider, not the feature itself. `desktop-script-provider-client.ts` created a fresh temp dir per operation, wrote `operation.json`, and `desktop-script-provider-bridge.ts` spawned:

```
powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File <runtime.ps1> <operation.json>
```

One PowerShell process per click, per keystroke batch, per screenshot — roughly ten short-lived `powershell.exe` PIDs in a burst. Because the process was new every time, `runtime.ps1`'s `Add-Type -TypeDefinition @"…"` (inline C# P/Invoke into user32.dll: `SendInput`, `mouse_event`, `SetCursorPos`) **re-emitted MSIL on every single operation**, which is what the "suspicious MSIL" factor was scoring.

## Behaviour change

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `powershell.exe` processes per session | ~10 per burst, one per operation | 1, reused |
| MSIL emission | once per click | once per session |
| Execution policy flag | `Bypass` | `RemoteSigned`, `Bypass` only as a logged one-time fallback |
| Request transport | a temp `operation.json` per operation | NDJSON over stdin/stdout |

### Persistent runtime host

`runtime.ps1` gains a `-Serve` switch. In serve mode it performs all `Add-Type` / assembly loading once, writes one `{"ready":true}` line, then loops on `[Console]::In.ReadLine()`, answering one compact JSON object per line on stdout until stdin closes. `-OperationPath` one-shot mode is untouched — `runtime-render.test.ps1`, `verify-computer-native.mjs` and the existing bridge tests all still drive it, and it remains the fallback path.

`src/main/computer/desktop-script-runtime-host.ts` owns exactly one child: lazy spawn via `spawnProcess` (never `node:child_process`; the ratchet allowlist is unchanged), strict serialization, a 30s per-request timeout, restart on crash, 120s idle shutdown, and `dispose()` reached from `DesktopScriptProviderClient.shutdown()`. It is split into `desktop-script-serve-channel.ts` (one child, NDJSON framing) and `desktop-script-runtime-availability.ts` (failure counting, cooldown, policy escalation) to stay under `max-lines` without a disable.

The client-facing contract is the existing `BridgeRequest`/`BridgeResponse`; the only wire addition is an optional `requestId`. Linux stays on the existing one-shot `python3 runtime.py` path, unchanged.

### Request correlation

Each request carries an id the helper echoes. Serialization alone would let a single stray stdout line answer every later request with the previous response — **silently acting on stale element indexes, with no error raised**. A mismatched or unsolicited reply is fatal to the child rather than merely logged. Non-JSON noise (a banner, a stray write) is *ignored* rather than fatal: with the id doing the real correlation, aborting on a banner would make a chatty host permanently unusable.

### `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` → `RemoteSigned`

Measured on Windows 11: `-File <unsigned local .ps1>` fails under `Restricted` but runs under `RemoteSigned`, and the installed packaged script carries **no Mark-of-the-Web** (NSIS extraction writes no `Zone.Identifier`), so `RemoteSigned` is sufficient in the shipping configuration.

`Restricted` is still the Windows *client* default, so both Windows spawn sites fall back **once** to `Bypass` on a policy-blocked start, and log it. The retry requires **empty stdout** as well as a matching stderr: operations are not idempotent and responses embed window titles, so matching the policy pattern against a snapshot containing the words "SecurityError" or "UnauthorizedAccess" would have replayed the operation — a second click, keystroke or paste. `runBridgeProcess` rejects with a `BridgeProcessFailure` carrying the raw streams so that decision can never read a mapped message.

**Proper long-term fix, not in this PR:** Authenticode-sign `runtime.ps1` in the inner-binary signing pass in `.github/workflows/release-cut.yml`. That pass currently stages only `.exe`/`.dll`/`.node`; adding `.ps1` would let the flag drop entirely.

## Degrading without silently undoing the fix

The failure handling is the part most worth reviewing, because every mistake in it is invisible: computer use keeps working while the process burst and per-operation MSIL emission come straight back. Three rules earn their complexity.

**1. No permanent latch.** A helper that dies before answering is retried, then cools down for 60s, then is **re-probed**. The client falls back per operation and keeps the host, so one bad spawn cannot strand a session on one `powershell.exe` per click. Every plausible cause is transient — a Defender scan touching the script mid-launch, a locked CSC temp directory failing one `Add-Type`, memory pressure.

**2. A replay must be provable, never inferred.** `-Serve` announces `{"ready":true}` *after* its `Add-Type` work and *before* its first read, and a request is replayed only when the helper died **before announcing**. "No reply came back" is not "the operation did not run": `runtime.ps1` synthesizes the input and only then builds the snapshot, allocating a full-window bitmap and walking the UIA tree — the heaviest, most fault-prone part, where a native GDI+/UIA fault is uncatchable by `$ErrorActionPreference` and leaves the click already delivered. Inferring "never started" from a missing response turned one requested click into three from the host plus a fourth from the one-shot bridge, reported as a single failed operation. A `runtime.ps1` predating the announcement — reachable via `ORCA_COMPUTER_DESKTOP_SCRIPT_PROVIDER_PATH` — is covered by an observation-tool allowlist until a ready line proves otherwise.

**3. A single success must not excuse a helper that keeps dying.** `recordSuccess()` clears the failure count only after a **clean run of three** operations, not on any one reply. Resetting on a single success reads like the obvious simplification and is the bug: a helper that answers one operation and dies on the next would reset the count forever and be respawned once per operation — precisely the pattern this PR removes, reintroduced through its own recovery path. Relatedly, `enterCooldown()` resets the counters: the wait is the penalty, and leaving the count at the limit would let the first death after recovery re-enter a full cooldown, stranding an interleaved workload on the one-shot bridge.

Host-detected aborts (timeout, desynchronised reply, oversized line) suppress the exit handler, so they are counted and logged explicitly — otherwise they bypassed the accounting entirely and a helper failing that way was respawned once per operation forever.

## Other fixes from review

- **Diagnostics escape the sidecar.** The provider runs inside a fork whose stdio is piped and never read, so `console.warn` was discarded — including the only signal that a machine had fallen back to `Bypass`. Warnings now travel over the sidecar's existing IPC channel and are printed by the main process.
- `close` rather than `exit`, so stderr is drained before a failure is classified.
- `dispose()` latches, so a request queued behind teardown cannot respawn a helper.
- `MAX_RESPONSE_CHARS` named for the UTF-16 units it actually counts; per-line `trim()` replaced with an index-based CR strip that does not copy a megabyte payload; `$ProgressPreference = 'SilentlyContinue'` and `-NoLogo` so nothing else can reach the response stream.
- The Windows SIGTERM/`TerminateProcess` teardown gap in `sidecar-entry.ts` is documented where the handlers are registered.

## What this does not fix

The remaining Defender surface is the behaviour itself, not the process shape: `$graphics.CopyFromScreen(...)` for screen capture and `SendInput`/`mouse_event` for synthetic input. The report says that is only reducible via a **signed native helper** owning those calls instead of PowerShell. Separate follow-up.

`config/scripts/verify-computer-native.mjs` still uses `Bypass` for its two dev/CI checks — deliberately left alone, since it runs on CI runners rather than user devices.

## Verification

- `pnpm tc` clean; `oxlint` clean; `check-max-lines-ratchet` clean; `child-process-import-boundary` ratchet clean
- `pnpm test src/main/computer/` — **22 files, 134 tests, all passing**
- `node config/scripts/verify-computer-native.mjs` — PowerShell parse, one-shot handshake and the snapshot renderer tests pass on Windows
- `desktop-script-runtime-host.win32.test.ts` drives the **real** `runtime.ps1 -Serve` on a real Windows box: three operations, one spawn
- Real-hardware protocol checks: a `get_app_state` response arrived as a single intact 484,565-character line with its `requestId` echoed, followed by a correlated second response on the same process
- Every failure-path fix has a regression test that was **confirmed to fail without it**: no replay of a mutating tool after a pre-answer death; no replay once the helper announced readiness; bounded respawn under repeated desync and repeated timeout; one cooldown per outage

records.title: Cold restore drops OSC-8 link ranges when a no-op resize record follows the checkpoint
records.body:
## Summary

On the cold-restore path, a checkpoint's OSC-8 hyperlink ranges are dropped if the post-checkpoint log contains **any** resize record — including a no-op one produced by an ordinary reattach. Restored hyperlinks in scrollback lose clickability.

Cosmetic fidelity loss, not corruption or data loss.

## Mechanism

`HeadlessEmulator.resize()` unconditionally clears `restoredOscLinks`, which is correct when rows actually shift but fires on same-size resizes too:

```ts
resize(cols: number, rows: number): void {
  if (this.disposed) return
  this.restoredOscLinks = []      // cleared even when dims are unchanged
  this.terminal.resize(cols, rows)
}
```
`src/main/daemon/headless-emulator.ts`

The restore path sets the links and then replays records that resize:

- `src/main/daemon/history-reader.ts:298` — `emulator.setRestoredOscLinks(checkpoint.oscLinks)`, then `:313` — `await replay.resize(record.cols, record.rows)`
- `src/main/daemon/daemon-durable-history-snapshot.ts:91` (set) → `:180` (resize, via `replayPendingRecords`)

And no-op resizes genuinely reach the durable log, because `src/main/daemon/session-output-plane.ts:109-111` records every resize with no same-size dedupe, while every attach re-asserts the pane's dimensions.

## Repro sketch

1. Session with OSC-8 links in scrollback; let it checkpoint.
2. Reattach (or otherwise cause a same-size resize record after the checkpoint).
3. Cold-restore the session.
4. Links present at checkpoint time are no longer clickable in restored scrollback.

## Notes

Long-standing — it predates and is independent of #17667. That PR incidentally narrowed it by gating no-op resizes to protect a snapshot cache; #17752 removed the cache and with it the gate, restoring the emulator to its prior behavior byte-for-byte. So this is not a regression from either PR, just a latent bug that became visible during their review.

Two plausible fixes, either sufficient:
- clear `restoredOscLinks` only when `cols`/`rows` actually change; or
- dedupe same-size resize records at `session-output-plane.ts:109` so they never enter the durable log.

Found during adversarial review of #17752.

records.title: perf(terminal): drop the headless snapshot cache, keep the spawn lock
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 1 | 0 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​230 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​230 |
| Prod | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​38 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​202 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​164 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Orca got two speed fixes in #17667. One of them turned out not to earn its keep, and it was the one that cost memory — so this removes it and leaves the other alone.

The removed one remembered a picture of each terminal's contents so it wouldn't have to redraw it. Sensible idea, except reconnecting to a terminal only ever asks for the last 1000 lines, and redrawing 1000 lines is already cheap. So the remembering saved almost nothing while holding onto several megabytes per terminal, forever, for as long as that terminal existed.

The fix that's staying is the one that actually made switching worktrees faster: terminals used to reconnect one at a time, each waiting for the one before it. Now they go together. That costs no memory at all.

## What this removes

The snapshot memoization from #17667 and everything serving it: the mutation epoch, `markMutated`/`markWritten`, the no-op resize gate, and the `HeadlessSnapshotCache` module. `headless-emulator.ts` returns to its pre-#17667 shape.

**The shared/exclusive spawn lock from #17667 stays.** It is the half carrying the measured win.

## Perf differential — what is kept vs given up

### Kept: the spawn lock (no memory cost)

The `options` phase is pure lock queueing, so it isolates the lock exactly. 4-tab worktree activation, per tab:

| | before #17667 | after, and still true here |
|---|---|---|
| `options` | 0 / 125 / 212 / 291ms | **1 / 1 / 1 / 1ms** |
| total per tab | 493 / 566 / 647 / 677ms | **226 / 253 / 282 / 309ms** |

Unaffected by this PR.

### Given up: nothing measurable

Controlled A/B on merged main — same worktree, same sessions, same machine — reattach `stable_adoption` per session:

| config | per-session |
|---|---|
| cache + resize gate (as merged) | 16 / 67 / 78 / 87ms |
| cache off, gate on | 17 / 55 / 68 / 80ms |
| cache off, gate off | 13 / 62 / 73 / 83ms |

Indistinguishable; the spread between repeat samples of the same config exceeded the spread between configs. Cold 4-tab activation was likewise unchanged: **217–296ms without the cache vs 226–309ms with** — expected, since a first attach is always a miss.

### Why it under-delivered

The serialize is bounded by what the session **retains**, not by what a client asks for. A live daemon session is constructed with `scrollback: resolveDaemonSessionScrollbackRows()` (`terminal-host-session-create.ts:126`), which `headless-emulator.ts:87` hands to xterm as the retained buffer capacity — `DAEMON_SESSION_SCROLLBACK_ROWS = 1000`, override bounded 100–5000 (`daemon-session-scrollback-window.ts:8`). The cap exists because unbounded retention once OOM-killed a host owning 100+ terminals.

A client may request far more — the snapshot RPC clamps `requestedRows` to `[0, 50_000]` (`daemon-request-router.ts:222-225`) — but it still gets only the ~1000 rows the buffer holds. So the serialize the cache was built to avoid is cheap on every live-session path.

Worse, the cache keyed on the **requested** value. A client asking 50,000 and one asking 5,000 produced two distinct keys for byte-identical content, thrashing a 2-entry cache (`MAX_CACHED_SNAPSHOT_WINDOWS = 2`). The one genuinely larger window — durable-history restore at `DAEMON_RESTORE_SCROLLBACK_ROWS = 5000` (`history-reader.ts:284`) — builds a fresh emulator per restore and snapshots it once, which a per-instance cache is structurally incapable of helping.

The original PR optimized a serialize without first measuring how expensive that serialize is *on the paths that call it*.

(Earlier revisions of this description misdescribed the mechanism — first as attach "not requesting the full buffer", then as a 1000-row *request* window. It is a 1000-row *retention* cap. The conclusion was unchanged throughout; the corrected framing is stronger evidence for removal, not weaker.)

## What removing it buys

- **Up to ~8MB per emulator** of steady-state retention returned (4MB/entry × 2 windows), held for the session's lifetime with no aggregate budget across sessions. Sessions with a runtime-side mirror have two emulators.
- **Deletes an invalidation contract** that produced three separate over-invalidation bugs during review — the zero-byte parse fence, `setCwd`/`setLastTitle`, and the no-op resize — each of which silently reduced the cache's own hit rate. That contract was convention-enforced, so every future mutator had to remember it.

## If we want it back

The honest version needs an aggregate byte budget across sessions (`cold-restore-payload-cache.ts` already implements exactly that one directory over) and a workload where the attach-path serialize is actually expensive. Neither exists today.

## Tests / risk

2972 pass across `src/main/daemon` and the runtime suites; `pnpm tc` clean; changed-code quality gate clean. Main-process/daemon only — no renderer, wire, or persisted-format change.

records.title: fix(lint): merge duplicate process-table-snapshot imports
records.body:
## `main` is currently red

`static analysis` fails on `main` and therefore on **every open PR**:

```
src/main/providers/agent-foreground-process-batch.test.ts:5:8:
  Modules should not be imported multiple times in the same file
Found 1 warning and 0 errors.
```

The code-quality pass runs `oxlint --config config/oxlint-code-quality-native-plugins.json src config tests mobile --deny-warnings`, so that single warning fails the job.

The file imports `'../../shared/process-table-snapshot'` twice — once at line 2-5 and again at line 10-13, with `./agent-foreground-process` sandwiched between them. Introduced by #17525.

## Fix
