records.title: Remote browser pages inherit Chromium origin zoom
records.body:
If you zoom a site in Orca's local browser, then open that same site from a paired client, the remote page comes in huge. Cmd/0 on the remote pane does nothing.

## Details

Chromium stores page zoom per origin per partition (`HostZoomMap`). Local panes reassert zoom on every `dom-ready`. Offscreen guests (headless/`orca serve`) and screencast sessions never did, so leftover origin zoom from a local tab leaks into the remote stream.

## Reproduction

1. On the host Mac, open Orca and create a local browser tab for `https://github.com/electron/electron` (any origin works).
2. Focus the page and press Cmd++ a few times until the page is clearly zoomed (about 150–170% is enough).
3. Pair a remote client: another desktop, the web client, or a phone. The host can also be `orca serve`.
4. On the remote client, open a new browser tab to the same URL.
5. The remote page is zoomed in. GitHub's header overflows. You see less of the page. Cmd/0 on the remote pane does not reset it.

Expected: a newly opened remote page starts at 100%, same as a new local tab.

## Platforms

Reproduced on macOS with an isolated Orca profile. Same partition sharing applies to Linux headless serve and SSH/offscreen guests.

records.title: [Bug]: Agent browser automation (orca tab create/switch) forcibly steals Windows foreground focus — no setting or flag to disable
records.body:
## Summary

When a coding agent drives the built-in Orca browser via the CLI (core workflow for browser-automation tasks), **the Orca main window forcibly steals the Windows foreground focus on every tab create/switch**, interrupting whatever the user is typing in other apps. There is currently **no setting or flag to disable this**.

Related but more specific than #13278 (which describes the symptom without a repro or root cause).

## Environment

- Orca: **1.4.188** (Windows installer)
- OS: Windows 10/11 (focus stealing is most aggressive on Windows due to the foreground-lock workaround, see below)
- Workflow: agent sends `orca tab create` / `orca tab switch` / `orca snapshot ...` from an Orca-managed terminal while the user is working in another app (IDE, browser, chat).

## Steps to reproduce

1. Focus any other application (e.g. a text editor) and start typing.
2. From an agent terminal (or any shell), run:
   ```
   orca tab create --url https://example.com --json
   ```
3. The Orca window jumps to the foreground; your keystrokes now land into Orca.
4. Same happens on `orca tab switch --index <n>` while another app is focused.

Commands that do **not** steal focus (good): `orca snapshot`, `orca click`, `orca eval`, `orca navigate` — when targeted at an already-active tab via `--page <browserPageId>`.

## Root cause (from app.asar of 1.4.188)

I dug into the bundled main-process bundle and found three distinct paths that force window activation, none of which are gated by a user setting:

**1. `focusOnCreate` defaults to true when creating browser tabs**

```js
const shouldFocusOnCreate = args.focusOnCreate !== false; // default: focus
```
→ creating a tab focuses the renderer, which raises the main window.

**2. The CDP bridge handles `Page.bringToFront` unconditionally**

```js
if (msg.method === "Page.bringToFront") {
    if (!this.webContents.isDestroyed()) this.webContents.focus();
    ...
}
```
Agent-browser tab activation (what `orca tab switch` drives) always triggers `webContents.focus()` → window raised, no "is the window currently in the background?" check.

**3. `activateWindow()` uses a Windows-specific foreground-lock bypass**

```js
function activateWindow(window, app, platform, setTimer) {
    safelyFocusApp(app);
    safelyRevealWindow(window);
    if (platform === "win32") {
        window.moveTop();
        pulseAlwaysOnTop(window, setTimer); // setAlwaysOnTop(true) … 250ms … false
        retryFocus(window, app, setTimer);  // +100ms retry
    }
}
```
`pulseAlwaysOnTop` is a deliberate workaround for Windows' SetForegroundWindow restrictions — i.e. even when the OS tries to protect the user's foreground, Orca forces itself on top. This is reached via `shouldActivateDesktopForSecondInstance(argv)` → `!argvRequestsServeMode(argv)`, so essentially every second-instance CLI invocation is eligible.

## Impact

Agent-driven browser testing/verification is a headline Orca workflow, but it makes the machine unusable for anything else while the agent runs: every tab operation rips the user out of their current window. Users must either minimize Orca (downgrades to taskbar flash) or move it to another virtual desktop.

## Requested behavior (any of these would fix it)

1. **CLI flag**: `orca tab create --no-focus` / `orca tab switch --no-focus` (and/or a global `ORCA_NO_FOCUS=1` env var) so agent-driven automation can stay fully background.
2. **Setting**: a "Keep Orca in the background when agents use the browser" toggle (Settings → Browser or → General).
3. **Conditional activation**: in the `Page.bringToFront` handler, skip `webContents.focus()` when the Orca window is not the foreground window at that moment (only mark the tab active internally).

Option 3 is the least invasive and keeps interactive use behaving exactly as today.

Happy to provide traces/procmon evidence if useful. Thanks for the great product — the agent browser skill itself works beautifully once focus stealing is out of the way!

records.title: [Bug]: Embedded browser tab can stop scrolling and reload does not recover
records.body:
## What happened

I hit a state where one Orca embedded-browser tab could no longer scroll a long page with the mouse wheel or PageDown. Reloading the tab did not recover it. Opening the same URL in a fresh Orca tab with the same authenticated browser profile fixed it immediately.

I do not have a deterministic trigger yet. The affected tab had been open for a while and had gone through navigation, reloads, and browser automation.

## Environment

- Orca 1.4.188
- macOS 26.5.2 (25F84), Apple Silicon
- Local runtime

## Expected behavior

Wheel and PageDown should move the document while `document.scrollingElement` has remaining vertical scroll range. Reloading should also clear any stale per-tab input state.

## Actual behavior

Wheel events reached the page and were not canceled, but the browser did not apply the default scroll. PageDown also had no effect. Reloading preserved the broken state.

## Diagnostic evidence

On the affected tab:

- `scrollHeight` was approximately 8,580 px, `clientHeight` approximately 1,391 px, and `scrollTop` was `0`.
- `html` and `body` had no overflow lock, fixed positioning, inline lock styles, dialog/overlay, scroll snap, `touch-action`, or overscroll constraint.
- A wheel input with `deltaY = 900` reached capture and bubble listeners, was `cancelable`, and was never `defaultPrevented`; `scrollTop` remained `0`.
- PageDown left `scrollTop` at `0`.
- `orca scroll --direction down --amount 900` moved `scrollTop` from `0` to `900`.
- The same wheel input on another long Orca browser tab moved `scrollTop` from `0` to `900`.

I also isolated the page content in the affected tab:

- Hiding its wide inner scroller did not restore wheel scrolling.
- Replacing the entire body with a plain 5,000 px-tall `div` did not restore wheel scrolling.
- Reloading restored the real page but not wheel scrolling.
- Opening the same URL in a new tab, using the same browser profile, restored wheel scrolling.

That points to stale per-tab input, gesture-latching, or compositor state rather than page content. I cannot tell which internal layer owns the failure from the outside.

## Useful reproduction check

The trigger is intermittent, but once a tab is affected it is easy to distinguish from a page-level scroll lock:

1. Confirm `document.scrollingElement.scrollHeight > document.scrollingElement.clientHeight`.
2. Attach capture and bubble `wheel` listeners and confirm the event arrives without `defaultPrevented` becoming true.
3. Send wheel input and observe that `scrollTop` does not change.
4. Reload the same tab and observe that it remains stuck.
5. Open the same URL in a fresh tab with the same profile and observe that wheel scrolling works.

It may be useful to compare the Chromium target's wheel-routing, gesture-latching, and compositor/input state before and after recreating the tab. A recovery path that recreates or resets that state when wheel events repeatedly produce no scroll progress would also prevent users from being trapped in the broken tab.

records.title: fix(browser): bound the agent-browser daemon's life instead of hoping teardown runs (#16367)
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​531 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​18 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​513 |
| Prod | 5 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​255 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​26 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​229 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

When Orca opens a browser for an agent, it starts a little background helper program that actually drives the browser. Orca was never able to shut those helpers down reliably — they detached from Orca completely, so if Orca quit, crashed, or was force-killed, the helpers just kept running forever, and two of them had grown to about 25 GB and 7 GB of memory, which filled the machine until everything froze. Now every helper turns itself off after ten minutes of doing nothing, Orca actually waits for them to close when you quit, and on start-up Orca cleans up any leftovers from a previous run.

The one helper that runs a remote user's own browser is deliberately left alone. A review round found this PR was doing the opposite in one place: it closed that helper — and the whole browser hanging off it — every single time Orca started, not just after a crash. That is fixed: Orca now looks for a live tab first and, if it finds one, leaves the browser exactly as the user left it.

## What Changed

Original commit (`a12a2fd171f`) plus three review rounds (`294fdeb6d73`, `c9a065be2e1`, `a73395ba43c`) — 13 files, +864/−51.

**1. A self-imposed idle timeout — the only bound that survives SIGKILL.** `agent-browser-process-environment.ts` now sets `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = 10 min` on **every** platform (previously it returned the inherited env untouched on win32 and whenever a caller had already set `AGENT_BROWSER_SOCKET_DIR`, so those paths got nothing). An operator-set value passes through untouched.

**2. The bound is asymmetric, on purpose — and the orcad daemon is now reused, not killed.** The first fix round *removed* the timeout from the orcad external-Chromium daemon (`external-chromium-browser-session.ts`): that daemon owns a remote user's whole Chromium tree, so idling it out would have closed their live browser and every tab in it.

The same round then contradicted that reasoning: `start()` issued a `close` before every `open`, which kills the daemon **and** its Chromium tree — and `start()` runs on every provider start, not only after a crash, so an `orca serve` restart took the remote user's browser and every tab in it. The justification for that `close` was borrowed from the pane bridge, which passes `--cdp` and so genuinely holds a port that dies with its Orca. This session passes only `--session` and `--profile`: nothing binds it to the old process, and the daemon owns its Chromium independently, so a survivor is reusable as-is.

Fixed in `a73395ba43c`: `start()` probes for an active tab and returns it untouched; only a session name that answers nothing is closed and reopened — which is still the killed-orcad case the stable session name exists to recover. This matters more as orcad becomes the backend the remote host runs on: the browser it manages belongs to a user, not to the process driving it this minute.

**3. Quit actually waits.** `destroyAllSessions()` was fire-and-forget and was the only teardown step not in `settleTeardownWithinDeadline`, so `app.quit()` was reached long before any daemon closed. It is now a barrier member (`index.ts:3545`) — and each per-session close runs with an explicit `TEARDOWN_CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000` instead of inheriting `EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS = 90_000`, so the member is individually bounded well inside the 20 s deadline. The loop also walks the **union** of `sessions` / `pendingSessionCreation` / `pendingSessionDestruction`, so a daemon spawned by a session still being created no longer outlives quit.

**4. Headless owner boundary.** In `orca serve`, `OffscreenBrowserBackend.closeTab` destroyed the page without ever retiring its daemon, and it unregistered the guest first — which would have defeated `onTabClosed`'s `webContentsId` lookup even if it had been wired up. The backend now takes a `getAgentBrowserBridge` hook and awaits the new page-id-keyed `AgentBrowserBridge.onPageClosed(browserPageId)` **before** `unregisterGuest`, on both `closeTab` and the unexpected `webContents 'destroyed'` event. `destroyAll` drops each entry before destroying so the destroyed handler cannot queue a second, unawaited retirement outside the quit barrier.

**5. Start-up sweep** for daemons left by a previous run. `closeStaleAgentBrowserSession` only ever reset the one name a new tab was about to reuse, so a crash with 10 open tabs left 9 daemons untouched forever. New `agent-browser-orphan-sweep.ts` uses `session list --json` + `--session X close` — no pid-walking, per the argument in `windows-pty-job.ts:4-24` — filtered to the `orca-tab-` prefix and guarded by `isSessionLive`.

**6. Ownership is proven, not assumed.** The sweep originally ran whenever `AGENT_BROWSER_SOCKET_DIR` was merely *set*, which an inherited value satisfies — two Orca profiles sharing one socket dir would sweep each other's live daemons. `createAgentBrowserProcessEnvironment` now returns `{ env, ownsSocketDirectory }` and the sweep gates on `ownsSocketDirectory`. **Windows deliberately gets no enumeration at all** (named pipes make the directory moot) rather than a machine-wide sweep that could close another process's daemons; it stays bounded by the idle timeout, which needs no ownership proof.

**7. Idle-out is no longer silent.** The bridge tracks `session.lastCommandAt`; when the gap reaches the configured idle timeout it resets `session.initialized` and re-seeds `pendingInterceptRestore`, so configured network routes are replayed onto the replacement daemon instead of requests silently hitting the real network. Detection is skipped entirely when no idle bound is configured.

**8. The sweep has a kill switch (`c9a065be2e1`).** `ORCA_DISABLE_AGENT_BROWSER_SWEEP=1` disables it, matching the existing `ORCA_DISABLE_CODEX_TRUST_RPC` / `ORCA_DISABLE_HTTP2` convention. Of the three new behaviours, the other two were already field-recoverable without a build — the idle bound is an env passthrough an operator can raise (use a large value, not `0`), and the quit close is bounded at `TEARDOWN_CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000` inside the 20 s teardown deadline. The sweep was the only one whose failure modes (closing a daemon it should not, or spawning one process per stale name on a profile holding hundreds) were revert-only. **macOS caveat:** a Finder-launched Orca does not see shell env, so both this flag and an `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` override need `launchctl setenv` or a terminal launch.

Cleanups from the same rounds: dropped the dead `.catch(() => {})` on `sweepOrphanedSessions`, collapsed the two identical sweep timeouts into one `SWEEP_TIMEOUT_MS`, dropped the never-read `success?: unknown` from `SessionListEnvelope`, and deleted two tests that only re-exercised `settleTeardownWithinDeadline` (already pinned in `quit-teardown-deadline.test.ts`).

## Why

`agent-browser` is a client/daemon CLI. Orca only ever spawns the short-lived **client**; the client forks a persistent daemon Orca holds **no handle on**. Reproduced directly against agent-browser 0.27.0: a freshly spawned daemon is **PPID 1 immediately**, with the whole Chrome tree under it. Per its README the daemon self-terminates only when `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` is set — and Orca set it nowhere. So nothing bounded a daemon's life: no idle timeout, no max lifetime, no memory cap, no health check, no reaper.

Evidence for each leak path:

- Idle bound never set: `agent-browser-process-environment.ts` returned `inheritedEnv` untouched on win32 and on the socket-dir-override path.
- Quit leak: `index.ts:3487` (pre-fix) called `destroyAllSessions()` unawaited while every neighbour was a `settleTeardownWithinDeadline` member; `destroySession` spawns a fresh `agent-browser --session X close` child and waits on it (`agent-browser-bridge.ts:2465`), so **every open tab's daemon survived a normal quit**.
- Headless in-run leak: `orca-runtime-browser.ts:2062` takes the offscreen branch and calls only `offscreen.closeTab`, which never reached the bridge. A long-lived `orca serve` opening and closing 50 pages a day leaked all 50 daemons; nothing in the original commit closed them.
- Crash leak: `closeStaleAgentBrowserSession` only reset the single name a new tab was reusing.

Reported impact (#16367): two orphans at ~25.6 GiB and ~7.2 GiB RSS drove a 64 GiB cgroup to its limit until Orca, Claude, Codex and Chrome all entered uninterruptible `D` state under headless `orca serve`.

10 minutes for the idle bound is >6× the bridge's 90 s `EXEC_TIMEOUT_MS`, so it cannot cut a command, a retry chain, or a normal think-gap between two user commands, while capping an abandoned daemon at minutes instead of days.

### Corrections to the earlier analysis

- **The orcad `close`-before-`open` was justified from the wrong path, and is gone.** It was reasoned about as if this session behaved like the pane bridge, which passes `--cdp` and therefore really does hold a port that dies with its Orca. The orcad session passes only `--session` and `--profile`, so a surviving daemon is not bound to the dead process and is reusable as-is. Closing it unconditionally destroyed a live remote browser on every provider start — the exact outcome exempting this path from the idle bound was meant to prevent.
- `getOffscreenBrowserBackend()?.destroyAll?.()` does **not** have the same bug: it is declared `void` and is fully synchronous. No barrier entry needed.
- #10179's queue bounds are **irrelevant** here — they bound Orca's own main-process heap, while the 25.6 GiB was daemon RSS.
- `/tmp/orca-ab-*` does **not** grow unboundedly: the key is `sha256(userDataPath)`, one stable dir per profile.
- HAR capture never auto-stopping remains the prime suspect for *where* the 25 GiB accumulates inside the daemon, but that is inference from code, **not a measurement**.

## Risk & Trade-offs

**Merge risk: Medium-high.** The one change that could destroy a remote user's live browser is fixed and pinned by tests, so what remains is an unexercised Windows path and a headline memory number attributed to HAR capture by reading code rather than by measuring the leaking process. (Was **High**; what moved it: the orcad close-on-every-start bug is fixed in `a73395ba43c`, and the sweep — the only new behaviour whose failure modes were revert-only — now has the `ORCA_DISABLE_AGENT_BROWSER_SWEEP=1` kill switch.)

### What could go wrong

- ~~**The orcad daemon is closed on every provider start, taking a remote user's live browser and every tab with it.**~~ **Fixed and pinned (`a73395ba43c`).** `start()` now probes for an active tab and returns it untouched; only a name that answers nothing is closed and reopened. Both new tests were verified to fail against the old behaviour — one asserts no `close` and no `open` is issued when a session answers, the other that a silent name is still reclaimed.
- **Windows behaves differently from what was tested, because Windows was still not run.** Windows deliberately gets the idle timer and no start-up sweep (named pipes make socket-dir ownership unprovable, and a machine-wide sweep could close another process's daemons). That design is defensible, but zero Windows runs happened, so the idle-env change on win32 — a path that previously returned the inherited env untouched — is unexercised. What would surface it: a Windows user's browser tab failing to start, or daemons surviving a crash for the full 10 minutes. **This is now the largest single unknown in the PR**; the run that would close it is spelled out under Testing.
- **`agent-browser`'s notion of "idle" is not what we think it is, and long sessions get cut.** The 10-minute bound is built on the tool's README plus one manual run against 0.27.0. If the daemon measures from process start rather than last command, any session older than 10 minutes gets its daemon killed and respawned. Bounded and self-healing — `execAgentBrowser` reasserts `--cdp` on every call, so the session comes back — but a user would see a browser tab reset mid-task. No automated test can pin this without the real binary; the Windows run below would settle it as a side effect.
- **A daemon idles out mid-work and the user loses an in-flight HAR capture, silently.** This is not hypothetical — it is a known, accepted gap (see below). Any capture spanning a >10-minute gap between bridge commands is gone, and nothing tells the user. Network intercept routes *are* replayed onto the replacement daemon, so only HAR is affected. Likelihood: low for interactive use (10 min is >6× the 90 s exec timeout), realistic for a long unattended `orca serve`. What would surface it: an empty or truncated HAR with no error.
- **Quit hangs longer than before on a wedged daemon.** `destroyAllSessions()` used to be fire-and-forget; quit now waits on it. Each close is capped at 5 s and the whole thing sits inside the existing 20 s teardown barrier, so the worst case is bounded — but quit is measurably slower when a daemon will not close.
- **The start-up sweep closes a daemon it should not have.** Two narrow paths remain: a TOCTOU window between `isSessionLive()` and the close spawn, and a profile with hundreds of stale `orca-tab-` names producing hundreds of sequential subprocess spawns after launch. Both are low-impact (the session respawns; the sweep is unawaited and off the critical path), and both are now switchable off in the field with `ORCA_DISABLE_AGENT_BROWSER_SWEEP=1` rather than needing a revert — but the spawn count is still uncapped when the sweep is on.
- **A wedged-but-alive orcad session is now reused instead of reclaimed.** The reuse probe treats "an active tab answers" as proof the daemon is healthy. A daemon that lists tabs but cannot drive them would be reused rather than replaced, where the old code would have blown it away. Judged the right trade: a false "healthy" costs a failed command, a false "dead" cost the user their whole browser.

### What a user gets in exchange

The reported failure in #16367 stops happening: two orphaned daemons at ~25.6 GiB and ~7.2 GiB RSS drove a 64 GiB cgroup to its limit until Orca, Claude, Codex and Chrome all went into uninterruptible `D` state. Every orphan class named in that issue is now bounded at 10 minutes, and three of the four are closed deterministically instead — daemons die on quit, on headless page close, and on the next start-up after a crash. Before this, an `orca serve` opening and closing 50 pages a day leaked all 50 daemons, forever, with nothing in the codebase capable of reclaiming them. The idle bound is the only one that survives SIGKILL, which matters precisely because a cgroup at its memory limit kills Orca outright and no teardown code runs at all.

### Trade-offs accepted

- **The orcad external-Chromium daemon is deliberately left unbounded, and now also left running.** It owns a remote user's whole Chromium tree; idling it out — or closing it on start — would close their live browser and every tab in it. It is reclaimed only when its session name answers nothing. This means one daemon class still has no SIGKILL-proof bound, and a genuinely wedged-but-responsive one is not reclaimed.
- **In-flight HAR capture lost to an idle-out fails silently, not loudly.** Only the dropped-network-route half of that review finding was fixed. Reconstructing a capture on a fresh daemon has no existing machinery, and hard-erroring would break callers whose capture was fine. **Not fixed. Owed as a follow-up.**
- **Windows gets no deterministic reclamation at all — only the timer.** Chosen over a machine-wide sweep that could kill another process's daemons. Windows is the weakest-covered platform here by design *and* by testing.
- **#16564's idempotent serve SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers were declined** and belong in their own PR — today's `process.once` means a `beforeunload` veto on the first signal makes a second SIGTERM a no-op. **Real, unfixed, owed as a separate PR.**
- **#16564's concurrency-4 close fanout and 35 s supervisor grace were declined** in favour of the 5 s per-close bound. Our close set is small; #16564's own body concedes >16 retirements can still blow the 20 s barrier.
- **Env snapshot shape changed on two paths.** `createAgentBrowserProcessEnvironment` now returns a shallow copy on win32 and on the mkdir-failure path, where it previously returned the live `process.env` reference. The bridge snapshots once in its constructor, so post-construction PATH/DISPLAY mutations are not picked up on those two paths. Both mutators are macOS/Linux start-up steps, so this is likely inert — **but the ordering was never verified.**
- **The Linux headless `orca serve` topology from the issue was never run against the built app.** The owner-boundary fix that closes that exact leak is covered by unit tests only.

### How to back it out

Clean revert, and the riskiest single behaviour can be disabled without one (`ORCA_DISABLE_AGENT_BROWSER_SWEEP=1`; on macOS via `launchctl setenv` or a terminal launch, since a Finder-launched Orca does not see shell env). No schema, no migration, no persisted state — the only durable artifact is the per-profile socket directory under `/tmp/orca-ab-*`, which is keyed on `sha256(userDataPath)` and was already there before this PR. Reverting restores the previous (leaking) behaviour immediately with no cleanup step.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #16367

This closes the reported failure: every class of orphan named in the issue is now bounded (idle timer), and three of the four are also closed deterministically (quit barrier, headless close, start-up sweep). Two known gaps are documented under Review rather than left implied — Windows has no deterministic reclamation, only the 10-minute timer; and an in-flight HAR capture lost to an idle-out is still lost silently.

## Visual Proof

N/A — every change is in the main process and in a detached CLI daemon's lifetime (process env, quit teardown, page-close wiring, start-up sweep); nothing renders and no user-facing copy, layout, or interaction changes.

## Testing

Real output from the fix rounds (worktree `/tmp/fixwt-16588`, head `a73395ba43c`):

```
$ pnpm tc
> node config/scripts/run-typecheck-projects-in-parallel.mjs
(clean exit, no diagnostics)

$ pnpm test src/main/browser src/main/orcad
 Test Files  171 passed | 1 skipped (172)
      Tests  1530 passed | 1 skipped (1531)
   Duration  18.14s

$ npx vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts \
    src/main/quit-teardown-agent-browser-daemons.test.ts src/main/quit-teardown-deadline.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  5 passed (5)

$ npx oxlint <13 changed files>
(no output — clean)
```

The 1 skip is pre-existing: an integration test that needs a real operator executable.

**Non-vacuity — each new test was re-run against the pre-fix source and fails there:**

```
x replays intercept routes after the daemon idles out
x bounds every teardown close well inside the quit barrier
x closes a session still being created when everything is torn down
x does not enumerate with a socket directory Orca inherited
x never bounds the daemon that owns the Chromium tree
x reuses a surviving session instead of closing the user's browser   (a73395ba43c)
x reclaims a session that answers nothing, then opens                (a73395ba43c)
```

The two `a73395ba43c` tests are the proof for the orcad fix: the first fails against the previous behaviour because `close` and `open` were both issued against a session that already had a live tab; the second pins that a silent name is still reclaimed, so the killed-orcad recovery the stable session name exists for is not lost. The kill switch adds two more (`enumerates nothing when disabled, even when Orca owns the socket directory`, `still sweeps when the flag holds any other value`) — new-code coverage rather than regression proofs, since the flag did not exist before.

The original commit's `it.each` idle-timeout test also fails pre-fix on all three platforms, and the quit-teardown source-shape tests fail pre-fix because `index.ts` had no `agentBrowserShutdown` binding and `destroyAllSessions` was not a barrier member. The sweep, orcad-env and offscreen-retirement tests cover new modules, so they are new-code coverage rather than regression proofs.

**Reviewer re-ran independently** on a clean checkout of the branch: `pnpm tc` clean and `pnpm test src/main/browser src/main/orcad` green.

**Manual verification against the real agent-browser 0.27.0 binary (macOS):**

- Daemon is PPID 1 immediately — the reported orphaning reproduced.
- Idle timeout works: the daemon exited, the Chrome tree died with it, socket sidecars cleaned up.
- **The check that mattered:** a daemon attached over `--cdp` (the bridge's mode) idles out **without closing the attached browser**, so an Orca tab is never killed by its own daemon expiring.
- Sweep primitive end-to-end: `session list --json` → `{"data":{"sessions":["orca-tab-sweepprobe"]}}`; `--session X close` killed the PPID-1 orphan.

**Recommended before merge — still not done.** Launch Orca on **Windows** with `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=20000`, open a browser pane, run a command, idle 30 s, confirm the daemon is gone, then run another command in the same pane and confirm it succeeds with the tab still alive. That single run converts three unknowns at once: that the changed win32 env path actually delivers the variable, that "idle" is measured from last command rather than process start, and that an idled-out daemon does not take the Electron webview with it.

Also not verified end-to-end: the Linux headless `orca serve` topology from the issue (a long-lived serve opening/closing many pages) was never run against the built app — the headless owner-boundary fix is covered by unit tests only.

- [x] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below

## AI Disclosure

<!-- Internal contributor — N/A -->

## Review

### Credit

**Jinwoo Hong (@Jinwoo-H), #16564** identified the headless owner-boundary gap this PR originally missed entirely, and he was first and right on three separate points:

1. **Owner-boundary retirement in the headless path.** In `orca serve`, `OffscreenBrowserBackend.closeTab` destroys the page without ever retiring its `orca-tab-<pageId>` daemon, and it unregisters the guest *first*, which would defeat `onTabClosed`'s `webContentsId` lookup even if it were wired up. Our original commit reclaimed that leak only via the 10-minute idle timer. **The fix here is inherited from @Jinwoo-H's #16564**: the `getAgentBrowserBridge` hook and awaiting the bridge before `unregisterGuest` are his design.
2. **A bounded teardown close.** He bounded `agent-browser close` at 5 s rather than letting it inherit the bridge's 90 s exec timeout inside a 20 s quit barrier. Our original commit moved `destroyAllSessions` into the barrier while leaving the 90 s timeout — a wedged daemon would have hung quit for the whole deadline. **`TEARDOWN_CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000` is taken from #16564.**
3. **`destroyAllSessions` must cover sessions still being created.** The union over `sessions` / `pendingSessionCreation` / `pendingSessionDestruction` is **his fix, adopted here**.

His judgement that a PPID-1 helper is normal, and that cleanup must key on session identity rather than pid or process name, matches the conclusion our sweep reached independently — he did not need our analysis to get there. The two PRs are complementary rather than competing: #16564 is the deterministic in-run retirement; this one adds the bound that survives a SIGKILL (which #16564 explicitly declines: "deliberately adds no … idle reaper"). A cgroup at its memory limit kills Orca outright and no teardown code of either PR runs.

### Fixed this round

- **The orcad `close`-before-`open` destroyed a live remote browser on every provider start.** Not a crash-only path — `start()` runs on every provider start. Fixed in `a73395ba43c` by probing for an active tab and reusing it; only a name that answers nothing is reclaimed. This was the finding that had held the merge risk at High.
- **The sweep had no field remedy short of a revert.** Fixed in `c9a065be2e1` with `ORCA_DISABLE_AGENT_BROWSER_SWEEP=1`.

### Declined, with reasons

- **#16564's idempotent serve SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers (`registerServeSignalHandlers`).** Adjacent and worth taking separately — today's `process.once` means a `beforeunload` veto on the first signal makes a second SIGTERM a no-op. It touches serve process lifecycle rather than the daemon-orphan path, so it belongs in its own PR, not in this diff. **Not fixed by this PR.**
- **#16564's concurrency-4 close fanout and 35 s supervisor grace.** #16564's own body concedes >16 retirements can still exceed the 20 s barrier; the 5 s per-close bound gives the barrier guarantee without the fanout. Our close set is small.
- **Failing loudly when an in-flight HAR capture is lost to an idle-out.** Only the dropped-network-route half of that finding was fixed (routes are replayed). Reconstructing an in-flight HAR capture on a fresh daemon has no existing machinery, and hard-erroring would break callers whose capture was fine. **A HAR capture that spans a >10-minute idle gap is still lost silently.**
- **Keepalive ping / self-heal in `resolveTargetPage` for the orcad path.** Removing the bound from that daemon removes the failure mode outright with strictly less code; a periodic `tab` list would add unbounded subprocess churn per registered page.
- **Reverting `createAgentBrowserProcessEnvironment` to a live `process.env` reference on win32 and the mkdir-failure path.** See residual risk 2 below; reverting would reintroduce cross-platform inconsistency for no observed defect.

### Residual risk

1. **Idle semantics are not proven.** `agent-browser`'s idle definition comes from its README plus one manual run against 0.27.0. If "idle" were measured from daemon start rather than last command, the 10-minute bound would cut long sessions. No automated coverage can pin this without the real binary — the Windows run recommended under Testing would settle it.
2. **Env snapshot shape changed.** The function now returns a shallow copy on win32 and on the mkdir-failure path, where it previously returned the live `process.env` reference. The bridge snapshots it once in its constructor, so post-construction mutations (`hydrate-shell-path.ts:395` sets PATH, `ensure-virtual-display.ts:129/165` sets DISPLAY) are not picked up on those two paths. Both mutators are macOS/Linux start-up steps and the Linux success path already copied, so this is likely inert — **but the ordering was not verified.**
3. **Start-up sweep has no cap on list size.** A profile with hundreds of stale names means hundreds of sequential `agent-browser` spawns after launch. Off the main thread and unawaited, so latency-invisible, but unbounded subprocess churn. Disableable with `ORCA_DISABLE_AGENT_BROWSER_SWEEP=1`; still uncapped when on.
4. **Narrow TOCTOU** between `isSessionLive()` and the close spawn: a tab created in that window could have its brand-new daemon closed. Low impact — `execAgentBrowser` reasserts `--cdp` on every invocation, so the session simply respawns.
5. **Windows is the weakest-covered platform here, by design and by testing.** No sweep, so a Windows crash leaves per-tab daemons for the full idle window with no deterministic reclamation — and the win32 idle-env path itself has still never been run.
6. **Known trade-off:** if a helper daemon idles out while the bridge holds an active HAR capture, that capture is lost on the next command's fresh daemon. Network intercept routes *are* now replayed (see What Changed #7); HAR capture is not.
7. **The orcad reuse probe trusts a tab listing as a health check.** A daemon that answers `tab` but cannot drive its Chromium is reused rather than replaced. Deliberate: a false "dead" verdict costs the user their entire browser, a false "healthy" one costs a failed command.

## Agent skill upstream boundary

- [x] Not applicable, or this change follows `docs/reference/agent-skill-sharing-upstream-boundary.md` and copies or mechanically translates no upstream skill-installer source, tests, fixtures, registry entries, path tables, comments, or documentation.

## Notes

- **Cross-platform:** idle bound applies on all three platforms; sweep is macOS/Linux only, with the reasoning stated above. No new direct `child_process` use — the sweep goes through `runProcess`.
- **Kill switch:** `ORCA_DISABLE_AGENT_BROWSER_SWEEP=1` disables the start-up sweep. On macOS a Finder-launched Orca does not see shell env, so this flag (and any `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` override) needs `launchctl setenv` or a terminal launch. To relax the idle bound rather than remove it, set a large value — not `0`.
- **SSH / remote:** the orcad external-Chromium path is the remote execution host's browser; it is excluded from the idle bound *and*, as of `a73395ba43c`, never closed while it still answers, so a remote user's live browser is not closed by an Orca restart. No wire-format change, so no mixed-version concern.
- **Backwards compatibility:** an operator-set `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` or `AGENT_BROWSER_SOCKET_DIR` is preserved untouched.
- **Performance:** the point of the change. Quit gains up to 5 s per wedged daemon, bounded inside the existing 20 s barrier.

records.title: fix(worktree): stop push-target rollback deleting a sibling's remote
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​101 | 0 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​101 |
| Prod | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​13 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​3 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​10 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

Split out of `616d2a4ec8c`, which also carried the Windows relay fix that shipped as #16550. Original work by @AmethystLiang; I dropped it from that branch so the release cherry-pick stayed minimal, and this is it getting its own PR. Unrelated to Windows.

## The bug

When a push target reuses an existing Orca-created fork remote, it deliberately **inherits ownership** of it, so that the last worktree using it can clean it up:

```ts
// Why: if a later PR worktree reuses an Orca-created fork remote, it
// must inherit ownership so deleting the final user can remove it.
remoteCreated = isRemoteCreatedByKnownWorktree(existingRemote)
```

Rollback then reused that same flag to decide whether to undo its own work:

```ts
} catch (error) {
  if (remoteCreated) {
    await execGit(['remote', 'remove', remoteName], repoPath).catch(() => {})
  }
  throw error
}
```

But `remoteCreated` being true doesn't mean *this call* added the remote — it can equally mean a sibling worktree added it and is still pushing to it. So if the fetch fails while creating a worktree that reused a sibling's fork remote, rollback deletes that remote out from under the sibling.

The two meanings were never separable from one flag: cleanup needs "does anyone own this," rollback needs "did I add this."

## The fix

Track `remoteAddedHere` alongside `remoteCreated`. Ownership semantics are unchanged — cleanup still inherits. Rollback now only removes a remote this call actually ran `remote add` for.

The local path (`worktree-push-target-setup.ts`) and the SSH path (`worktree-remote.ts`) had the same bug independently, so both are fixed.

## Validation

Both regression tests were confirmed to catch the bug — reverting just the production change while keeping the tests fails exactly the two new cases:

```
FAIL  worktree-push-target-setup.test.ts > keeps a reused remote a sibling worktree owns when the fetch fails
  AssertionError: expected [ [ 'remote', 'remove', …(1) ] ] to deeply equal []
FAIL  worktrees-ssh-fork-push-target-remote.test.ts > keeps a reused fork remote a sibling worktree owns when the SSH head fetch fails
  AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to not be called with arguments: [ [ 'remote', 'remove', …(1) ], …(1) ]
```

With the fix: 17/17 pass. `pnpm tc` clean, oxlint clean.

records.title: fix(browser): retire helpers with page owners
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 5 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​504 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​13 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​491 |
| Prod | 10 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​289 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​49 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​240 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

Each Orca browser page owns a named `agent-browser` helper. Headless page close, unexpected renderer destruction, and runtime quit could drop the page without waiting for that exact helper to retire. The helper could then remain detached under PID 1 and retain browser memory indefinitely.

This change makes helper retirement part of the page/runtime ownership contract: close the exact named session when its owner ends, preserve unrelated pages, and stop admitting replacement sessions once shutdown begins.

## What Changed

- Retire `orca-tab-<pageId>` before unregistering or destroying an explicit headless page.
- Run and join the same exact cleanup when offscreen WebContents is unexpectedly destroyed.
- Make offscreen and bridge-wide shutdown terminal, including sessions still being created or retired.
- Bound lifecycle close commands to five seconds and cleanup fanout to four subprocesses.
- Join browser cleanup through Electron's existing 20-second quit barrier.
- Keep headless SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers installed and idempotent so duplicate terminal/supervisor signals cannot bypass teardown.
- Give the serve supervisor 35 seconds before SIGKILL, longer than Electron's committed teardown deadline.
- Register deterministic lifecycle coverage in `agent-browser.owner-boundary-cleanup`.

## Why

Latest main and the reported Orca 1.4.187 lifecycle both allowed an Orca-owned helper to survive its page or runtime. A live `agent-browser` process having PPID 1 is normal, so cleanup is keyed by stable page/session identity rather than PPID or process name.

The invariant is: after a page owner closes or is destroyed and the five-second third-party shutdown grace expires, no live helper session named `orca-tab-<pageId>` remains; unrelated live pages survive, and runtime quit joins the bounded cleanup attempt.

This deliberately adds no startup process sweep, idle reaper, timer-only cleanup, global process-name kill, or wire change. Those approaches cannot safely distinguish an orphan from a legitimate long-lived page without a durable ownership ledger.

## Linked Issue

Addresses #16367 / STA-5400.

Related but not duplicate: #14552 / STA-4341 concerns legitimately open headless tabs retaining Electron renderers. This PR supersedes only the helper-cleanup slice independently identified in #15254; it does not implement renderer parking or an idle-retention policy.

## Visual Proof

N/A — main-process resource lifecycle change with no UI or interaction change.

## Testing

- [x] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated

Deterministic oracle:

```text
pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts \
  src/cli/runtime/serve-signal-exit-diagnostic.test.ts \
  src/main/browser/offscreen-browser-backend-lifecycle.test.ts \
  src/main/browser/agent-browser-bridge-session-lifecycle.test.ts \
  src/main/browser/agent-browser-bridge-tab-routing.test.ts \
  src/main/startup/desktop-startup-ordering.test.ts
```

- Original focused candidate: 5 files / 60 tests passed; final follow-up: 6 files / 63 tests passed.
- Full `src/main/browser`: 162 files / 1,469 tests passed.
- Production-reverted control: 12 of the original 58 lifecycle assertions failed.
- Disabling only the final process-swap timeout and shutdown-admission controls: 3 of 15 bridge lifecycle tests failed.
- `pnpm tc`: passed.
- `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed`: passed, zero new findings.
- `pnpm run check:reliability-gates`: passed.
- `pnpm build:cli` and `pnpm build:electron-vite`: passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

Live macOS headless serve calibration used an isolated profile, folder workspace, port, and agent-browser socket directory. Two concurrent pages created two exact PPID-1 helpers at roughly 10–11 MiB RSS and 16–18 fd rows. Closing one removed only its helper/session within five seconds while the other survived reconnect. With signal cleanup disabled, Ctrl-C left exact helpers alive; the candidate emptied session inventory and removed the app/helper PIDs and port.

Not validated live: physical Linux/cgroup, SSH, WSL, paired-client, or long-soak topologies.

## Review

Three fresh OpenCode adversarial and performance reviews found one valid late-exit supervisor timer race; it was reproduced, fixed, and re-reviewed clean. Known bounded-cleanup gaps are recorded in the reliability gate:

- Four-way five-second batches can exceed the 20-second app barrier above 16 worst-case retirements.
- A third-party close timeout/error remains best-effort; there is no safe owner-PID escalation ledger.
- The 35-second supervisor grace increases worst-case shutdown latency versus the previous five seconds.

records.title: fix(runtime): retire timed-out provider snapshot acquisitions
records.body:
## Description
Visible terminal snapshot reads timed out without retiring the in-flight provider buffer acquisition, so the next read rejoined the same hung promise.
`readVisibleTerminalState` now passes `retireOnTimeout: true` with the existing 750ms bound.

## Focused fix
- In scope: retire the timed-out provider snapshot acquisition used by `readVisibleTerminalState`.
- Out of scope: spawn/listProcesses, snapshot parsing, provider mode tracking.

## Preserves
- Timeout still returns null; healthy in-flight captures still share one acquisition.
- The existing `finally()` identity-delete is unchanged.

## Evidence
- Test: `pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/main/runtime/orca-runtime.test.ts`
- Result: **1207 passed**, 1 skipped
- New case `retires a timed-out visible provider snapshot instead of rejoining it` fails without the one-line change.

## User-regression-tradeoffs
None. A hung provider read already timed out; it can now retry instead of sticking to the dead promise.

Fixes #16531

The cross-version browser placement test used a rolling baseline via `resolveBaselineReleaseRef()`, which could pick up newer stable releases. When the baseline eventually includes the client placement feature, the test fails because it's meant to validate backwards compatibility against older versions.

## Solution

Pin the test to an explicit baseline `v1.4.184` that predates client placement. This ensures consistent wire-compatibility verification against a known legacy version, independent of future stable releases.

## What Changed

Replaced the dynamic `resolveBaselineReleaseRef()` call with explicit constant `LEGACY_BROWSER_PLACEMENT_RELEASE_REF = 'v1.4.184'`. Updated comments to clarify: v1.4.185 moved the tab-create schema and renamed it, so an explicit pin avoids coupling the baseline choice to that unrelated refactor.

## Why

A rolling stable baseline eventually contains every additive feature. For cross-version wire compatibility, the baseline must remain on an old version to validate the contract. An explicit version pin ensures this stability.

records.title: fix(updater): surface and degrade renderer shutdown checkpoint failures (STA-5505)
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​580 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​22 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​558 |
| Prod | 10 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​332 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​57 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​275 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

Fixes the STA-5505 stranding mode: the in-app updater refused to install with `Renderer shutdown checkpoint was not completed.` while the actual error thrown inside the shutdown persist was swallowed by a bare `catch {}` — no log, no dialog detail, no recovery.

## Root-cause findings (full details on STA-5505)

- The only producer of the checkpoint-failed event is the `beforeunload` persist handler; the error fires when `persist()` throws synchronously.
- On the reproducing workspace, main-process traces show the first install attempt (13:30:57, pre-restart process) **passed** the checkpoint and invoked the native installer; every attempt in the freshly restored process (13:36+) died renderer-side before its IPC ever reached main (`updater_quit_and_install_started` never recorded).
- Demonstrated mechanism class (live rig, real 5.8MB profile copy): **synchronous Zustand subscribers throw through `setState`** — `session-write-subscriber` and `use-runtime-graph-sync` (paired-host publication) both run projections inside every `set()`, including the `captureAllSleepingAgentSessions('quit')` call in the shutdown checkpoint. Any state shape one projection chokes on turns into a deterministic, unexplained update refusal.
- The guard's tradeoff (block the update rather than lose the session snapshot) is preserved; this PR makes the failure explained, field-diagnosable, and degradable where a safe tier exists.

## Changes

1. **Surface the cause** — the guard now logs the swallowed error, records a `renderer_shutdown_checkpoint_failed` crash breadcrumb (lands in `main.trace.ndjson`), and publishes the message via a DOM attribute so the context-isolated preload can name it in the thrown error. The Update Error dialog now reads e.g. `Renderer shutdown checkpoint was not completed: entries.map is not a function`.
2. **Stop failing the checkpoint on sleeping-agent quit-capture errors** — the periodic capture refreshes resume records every 60s, so the loss window is bounded; blocking the update on it was strictly worse.
3. **Extend the existing durable-session degradation** (already codified for snapshot-build failures) to full-session staging failures, under the same conditions: intentional restart in progress and no dirty editor buffers. Dirty drafts still hard-block, and a failed durable-only stage still fails the checkpoint.

The persist body moved verbatim from the inline closure in `use-app-session-persistence.ts` to `shutdown-checkpoint-persist.ts` with injected deps so the flow is directly testable.

## Red/green

Tests written against the extracted (behavior-identical) pre-fix logic, then the fix applied:

```
RED (pre-fix):
 ❯ src/renderer/src/app-shell/shutdown-checkpoint-persist.test.ts (8 tests | 2 failed)
     × does not fail the checkpoint when the sleeping-agent quit capture throws (STA-5505)
     × degrades to durable-only staging when full staging throws during an intentional restart (STA-5505)
 ❯ src/renderer/src/lib/shutdown-checkpoint-guard.test.ts — 1 failed | 9 passed
     × publishes the failure cause and records a crash breadcrumb (STA-5505)
 ❯ src/shared/renderer-restart-preparation.test.ts — 1 failed | 7 passed
     × names the published failure cause in the thrown checkpoint error (STA-5505)

GREEN (post-fix):
 shutdown-checkpoint-persist.test.ts   Tests  8 passed (8)
 shutdown-checkpoint-guard.test.ts     Tests  10 passed (10)
 renderer-restart-preparation.test.ts  Tests  8 passed (8)
```

End-to-end proof in an isolated dev rig hydrated from a copy of the reproducing 5.8MB profile (475 sleeping agents): forcing a persist failure with a dirty buffer present makes the real `window.api.app.restart()` reject with `Renderer shutdown checkpoint was not completed: entries.map is not a function` — cause named, restart correctly blocked.

Also verified: `pnpm typecheck:web`, `pnpm tc:node`, both oxlint scans (plain + type-aware) clean; adjacent suites `renderer-shutdown-checkpoint.test.ts` (8), `quit-path-durable-write-blocking.test.ts` (14), `app-startup-routing.test.ts` (23), `session-write-subscriber.test.ts` (24) all pass.

## Not addressed here (separate finding)

The trace also shows the 13:30:57 install **passed** the checkpoint, invoked Squirrel, relaunched — and came back on the old version with `ShipIt` still running 20 minutes later. That is a second, independent stranding cause (native installer hang) and deserves its own ticket.


## Addendum: same root cause as #15352 (macOS quit silently ignored)

Open issue #15352 (quit accepted, nothing happens, renderer healthy, SIGKILL-only, v1.4.184) is the **same defect through the silent door**: `confirmNativeWindowClose` dispatches the same synthetic `beforeunload`; when the checkpoint guard's `persist()` throws, it `preventDefault()`s and the close path hit `if (!accepted) { return }` — quit dropped with no dialog and no log line, exactly matching that issue's evidence (healthy renderer, empty trace). This also dates the defect to at least 1.4.184 (2026-08-18), supporting state-dependence over a fresh code regression.

Second commit completes the quit door:
- the quit checkpoint runs inside a window-close scope, so full-session staging failures degrade to the durable tier for app-level closes too (dirty editor drafts still hard-block, and the dirty-file veto's dialog flow is unchanged — it publishes no failure reason);
- if the checkpoint still vetoes the quit, the published cause is shown in a toast instead of the quit dying silently, and the `renderer_shutdown_checkpoint_failed` breadcrumb lands in `main.trace.ndjson` — directly closing #15352's "nothing is logged" gap.

Additional green: `shutdown-checkpoint-persist.test.ts` (8), `shutdown-checkpoint-guard.test.ts` (11), `window-close-request-coordinator.test.ts` (12), `app-startup-routing.test.ts` (23); `typecheck:web` and both oxlint scans clean.


## Addendum 2: review-pass hardening (commit 15c72d40c7)

An adversarial review of the first pass surfaced three refinements, applied:
- **Retry-then-degrade for staging**: the first full-session staging failure stays a visible, retryable error (naming the cause); only a repeat failure trades the full snapshot for an unblocked shutdown. A transient IPC failure therefore keeps its retry instead of silently costing just-captured scrollback.
- The sleeping-capture continue-on-failure comment now states the real cost (periodic capture skips done panes and never stamps quit origin — the loss is a weaker live-origin resume record, still strictly better than a blocked update or SIGKILL'd quit), and the swallowed failure records a `renderer_shutdown_sleeping_capture_failed` breadcrumb.
- The source-shape test pins the exact degradable-shutdown gate (`isIntentionalAppRestartInProgress() || isWindowCloseCheckpointInProgress()`) so a rewiring cannot arm the degrade tiers on arbitrary unloads while suites stay green.

records.title: [Bug]: agent-browser processes can consume tens of GB and make headless orca serve unresponsive
records.body:
### Operating system

Linux

### Orca version

1.4.187

### Details

# [Bug] `agent-browser` processes can consume tens of GB and make headless `orca serve` unresponsive

## Environment

- Orca: `1.4.187`
- OS: Linux x86_64
- Mode: headless `orca serve`
- Memory cgroup limit: 64 GiB
- Workspace: loop-backed filesystem
- Bundled browser helper: `<orca-install>/resources/agent-browser-linux-x64`

## Summary

After running Orca headlessly for an extended period, I found multiple `agent-browser-linux-x64` processes reparented to PID 1.

Two of them were using approximately:

```text
agent-browser  ~25.6 GiB RSS
agent-browser   ~7.2 GiB RSS
```

Together they pushed the 64 GiB cgroup to its memory limit.

This caused severe memory reclaim and file-cache refaulting, which eventually saturated the workspace loop device. Orca, Claude, Codex, Chrome, and other processes started entering uninterruptible `D` state.

The Orca server was still listening on port 6768, but the application layer no longer responded, so initially this looked like a remote/networking failure.

## Evidence

Memory was essentially at the cgroup limit:

```text
memory.current ≈ 64 GiB
memory.max     = 64 GiB
```

Most memory was anonymous:

```text
anon ≈ 61 GiB
file cache ≈ 0.6 GiB
```

There was also very heavy reclaim/refault activity:

```text
workingset_refault_file ≈ 4.46 billion
pgscan                  ≈ 4.82 billion
pgsteal                 ≈ 4.72 billion
```

The workspace loop device stayed saturated:

```text
READ MB/s   R await ms   inflight   busy%
373.2          50.68        128      100%
345.2          56.65        125       99.6%
361.5          55.99        122      100%
314.4          66.60        125      100%
382.4          46.47        128      100%
```

Typical blocked processes included:

```text
orca-ide     D  wait_on_page_bit_common
orca-ide     D  blk_mq_get_tag
claude       D  blk_mq_get_tag
chrome       D  blk_mq_get_tag
```

During the incident, approximate read I/O attribution was:

```text
orca             145 MB/s
codex             62 MB/s
claude            54 MB/s
agent-browser     51 MB/s
other             44 MB/s
```

## Recovery

I terminated only the two very large `agent-browser-linux-x64` processes.

Immediately afterward:

```text
memory.current:  ~64 GiB → ~35 GiB
file cache:      ~0.6 GiB → ~4 GiB
loop inflight:   128 → 0
D-state count:   ~20+ → 0
```

The existing `orca serve` process recovered without being restarted, and remote access started working again.

## Expected behavior

Orca-managed `agent-browser` processes should have a bounded lifecycle and should eventually be cleaned up when their owning browser/session/runtime is no longer active.

Processes reparented to PID 1 should not remain indefinitely and grow until the runtime reaches its memory limit.

## Suggested investigation

- Track and clean up `agent-browser` sidecars when their owning session/tab/runtime ends.
- Detect stale Orca-owned `agent-browser` processes on startup or reconnect.
- Consider explicitly configuring an idle timeout for Orca-managed browser sessions.
- Add diagnostics or safeguards for unusually high `agent-browser` memory usage.

## Related

- Orca #14552
- Orca #9138 
- `vercel-labs/agent-browser` #1536
- `vercel-labs/agent-browser` #1334

records.title: fix(orcad): close the browser-provider gaps
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 8 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​967 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​6 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​961 |
| Prod | 6 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​210 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​25 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​185 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

Stacked on #16193. Closes the gaps found reviewing it against the handoff.

## The live bug this found

The runtime advertises `browser.tabCreate.known-id.v1` **unconditionally**, so a web client sends a provisional page id for a page that does not exist yet (`web-runtime-session.ts:563`). The Electron sidecar's generic `requestedPageId` branch then ran `tabs.require()` on it first and threw — **every known-id create against the Electron provider failed.**

The adoption logic was already there; only the ordering was wrong. Verified in both directions: reverting the fix fails the test.

This is the advertise-something-you-cannot-do class the design work is about, and it was found only because we went looking for the missing coverage.

## Gaps closed

**1. The integration test skipped in CI forever.** It was gated on `ORCA_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` and nothing ever set it. Now a dedicated `orcad_browser` job resolves the runner's preinstalled Chrome and **fails hard if it is absent** — an unset variable is exactly how this stayed dead, so a future runner image dropping Chrome must break loudly rather than silently reverting to the bug.

Notes: Chrome not the image's chromium, because Ubuntu 24.04's AppArmor only grants `userns` to the Chrome `.deb` and the code path gives no `--no-sandbox` escape hatch. No xvfb (agent-browser is headless by default). No `native-runtime` (the provider drives the prebuilt Rust binary, never node-pty). Wired into `verify`'s `needs` and **both** result loops, or it would report without blocking. ~2 runner-minutes, fully parallel — PR wall-clock unchanged.

**2. The Electron provider had zero tests** — the path anyone with the desktop app hits.

**3. Browser unavailability reported one message for four distinct causes**, including telling an operator to set a variable they had already set. Now a typed cause carried through to `degradations[]`.

## Verification

- Failure injection on the **combined** branch, not just per-agent: dropping `--json` from the agent-browser argv still fails the integration test (`expected undefined to be 'chromium'`) after the new unavailable-cause mechanism landed on the same catch path.
- `pnpm run typecheck`, `pnpm run lint` clean; ratchet 0; `build-orcad` reports zero electron and zero `node:sqlite`; `smoke:orcad-terminal` passes.
- Updated the workflow-parallelism guard, which correctly caught the new job missing from `verify`'s required-check list — and added an assertion that `verify` actually reads it.

## Correction carried in the code

The 120s timeout comment originally said the 30s cold start meant "CI is always that cold case". A Linux run with an empty `~/.agent-browser` was **2.8s**, so that was wrong — the 30s looks like a one-time macOS Gatekeeper cost. Sized for the slow observation anyway, since a timeout here would land as a flaky required check.

## Trade-offs

Zero user-facing, except the `tabCreate` fix, which turns a hard failure into working behaviour.

records.body:

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## Problem

When closing a browser tab, Orca switches to the next tab in visual order (right neighbor, or left if none). This ignores user context — they want to return to what they were working on before, not just the adjacent tab.

## Solution

Changed tab-close behavior to restore the previously-active (MRU) tab instead of picking a visual neighbor. This respects the actual usage pattern and works across content types (browser, terminal, editor tabs tracked together in the unified system).

## What Changed

**browser.ts**: Improved next-tab selection when closing a browser tab. Uses `pickNeighbor()` to find a candidate, but validates it still exists; falls back to the first remaining tab. Fixed global `activeBrowserTabId` to use the pre-computed worktree-specific selection instead of recalculating.

**Terminal.tsx**: Removed the inline tab-switching logic that was picking neighbors. Moved responsibility to the store via MRU tracking. When closing the last browser tab in a worktree, checks if it's wrapped in the unified tab system before falling back to a file tab.

**Tests**: Added 4 new tests for MRU restoration:
- MRU selection when closing active browser tab in active worktree
- Keeping unified MRU target when closing the last browser tab (switches to previous terminal/editor tab)
- Proper selection for inactive worktrees
- Legacy tab handling without unified wrapper

Updated existing test to verify MRU works across content types (terminal → browser → editor), not just visual neighbors.

## Visual Proof

N/A — interaction change verified by unit tests. Manual verification: open 3+ browser tabs, activate tab A, activate tab B, close tab B → should return to tab A (not the visual neighbor).

records.title: feat(orcad): add headless browser providers
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​438 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​11 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​427 |
| Prod | 21 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1953 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​34 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1919 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## ELI5

`orcad` can now own browser automation without pulling Electron-only browser code into its Node 18 bundle. At startup it uses an installed Orca app through the same headless `orca serve` backend when available; otherwise it launches the operator-provided `ORCA_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` and drives it over real CDP. If neither provider is usable, the runtime stays up but reports a structured degradation and every browser RPC fails with the closed `browser_unavailable` code.

## What Changed

- Added startup browser-provider resolution through the existing `setRuntimeBrowserCommandsFactory` seam:
  1. installed Orca Electron launcher on macOS, Linux, or Windows;
  2. `ORCA_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` plus the bundled platform `agent-browser` binary;
  3. no provider, with explicit refusal.
- Added an isolated Electron `orca serve` sidecar that:
  - uses the incumbent offscreen browser backend;
  - communicates over its private local Unix socket / named pipe with pairing disabled;
  - preserves caller-visible page IDs across mixed versions;
  - fences explicit worktree scope and keeps per-worktree tab indices/active pages;
  - removes stale tab mappings, bounds response buffering, and tears down its process/profile on failure or shutdown;
  - removes `browser.headless.v1` from status if the sidecar dies.
- Added the external Chromium provider using the native `agent-browser` CDP client:
  - real Chromium launch from `ORCA_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE`;
  - navigation, evaluation, screenshots, tab lifecycle, input, storage, cookies, capture, and environment commands;
  - target/session/profile/executable override flags stripped from raw `browser.exec` commands;
  - requested page IDs and worktree ownership preserved;
  - bounded subprocess output and close deadlines.
- Added the optional, mixed-version-safe `RuntimeStatus.degradations[]` field and projected it through local and remote CLI status JSON.
- Changed the no-provider factory from a message-only `Error` to `BrowserError('browser_unavailable', ...)`, including screencast unsubscribe.
- Kept screencast separate: neither new `orcad` provider advertises `browser.screencast.v1`.
- Hardened `build-orcad.mjs`:
  - copies the current platform's `agent-browser` binary beside `orcad.js`;
  - fails on any `electron` importer;
  - fails on any `node:sqlite` importer.
- Extended the shared Electron/`orcad` smoke harness with optional browser capability, navigate, evaluate, and screenshot assertions.
- Fixed `orcad` signal/startup cleanup so async runtime and browser-provider teardown completes before exit and startup failures cannot leak providers.

## Why

The two cookie-import modules are the only browser-cluster paths that statically import `node:sqlite`. Re-including that cluster would silently raise `orcad`'s Node floor from 18 to 22.5+, invalidating the deployment model. This keeps that graph boundary intact while preserving headless browser automation, removing the capability trade that previously blocked retiring Electron `orca serve`.

The provider order is deliberate: an installed Electron app reuses the existing, proven `orca serve` behavior; a standalone host can supply any compatible Chromium executable; a future downloaded-Chromium resolver can be inserted as a third startup step without changing the runtime-command seam.

## Linked Issue

N/A — this worktree has no linked Linear issue; this is the reviewed `orcad` viability follow-up requested directly.

## Visual Proof

N/A — no renderer/UI surface changed. Verification drives the public runtime/CLI browser surface against real Electron and Chromium processes.

## Testing

- [x] Automated tests added/updated.

- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check <affected files>` — pass.
- `pnpm exec tsc -p config/tsconfig.node.json --noEmit` — pass.
- `pnpm exec oxlint <affected files>` — pass.
- Browser/runtime/RPC focused suites — 41 passed.
- CLI status + sidecar tab authority suites — 20 passed.
- `ORCA_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE="/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/main/orcad/external-chromium-browser-process.integration.test.ts` — real Chromium navigate/evaluate/screenshot pass.
- `pnpm run build:orcad` — 4.48 MB, 2,048 modules, zero Electron imports, zero `node:sqlite` imports.
- `node config/scripts/runtime-serve-terminal-smoke.mjs --target orcad --browser` — installed Electron provider advertises `browser.headless.v1`; browser navigate/evaluate/screenshot and terminal round trip pass.
- `pnpm run smoke:orcad-terminal` — pass.
- `pnpm run check:runtime-electron-ratchet` — 0 entries, unchanged.
- `pnpm run check:max-lines-ratchet` — no new bypasses.
- Post-smoke process check — no provider processes left behind.

Platforms actually executed: macOS arm64, installed Orca Electron app, Google Chrome arm64. Windows/Linux launcher and native-binary naming contracts have deterministic unit coverage; real Windows/Linux process launch remains CI coverage.

## AI Disclosure


## Review

Readiness checklist verdict: **READY — no proven P0, P1, or P2 findings remain.**

Reviewed explicitly for:

- SSH/remote/network: providers run on the execution host; no client-side fallback; paired-network transport unchanged; sidecar transport is private/local and bounded.
- Crash/retry/growth: startup/command/close deadlines, failed-start cleanup, live health gating, stale-map pruning, bounded buffers/output, no unbounded retries or queues.
- Security/supply chain: no dependency/lockfile changes, downloads, shell execution, embedded credentials, or profile-database imports; explicit executable ownership; raw command target overrides fenced; sidecar pairing disabled and temp root private/randomized.
- Performance/resources: startup polling is bounded and temporary; command subprocess behavior matches the incumbent agent-browser bridge; maps and response buffers are bounded/pruned; provider cleanup verified after repeated smoke runs.

## ELI5

Retire a stalled terminal-screen snapshot before the surrounding readiness wait can finish, so the next terminal read cannot accidentally start the hung request again. Also call the canonical terminal paste sanitizer directly instead of routing through a one-line forwarding function.

## What Changed

- Separated the provider acquisition deadline, detached probe deadline, and caller waiter deadline.
- Preserved the normal 750ms provider acquisition budget; the detached guard settles 10ms later.

Node 26 CI twice reproduced a timeout-ordering race in `OrcaRuntimeService`: the waiter rejected while the visible-only provider acquisition had not yet been marked retired, and the following wider read replaced it, producing a seventh provider call. records.title: fix(runtime): wait for queued writes in park snapshots
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 1 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​98 | 0 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​98 |
| Prod | 1 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​28 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​3 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​25 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

## Problem

When taking park snapshots over SSH, writes to the terminal may be queued and in-flight. The snapshot serialization would drain the current write chain but wouldn't wait for new writes that get queued during that process, resulting in incomplete or stale snapshots for SSH sessions.

## Solution

Added `requireSettled` option to drain the write chain multiple times (up to 64 iterations) until it stabilizes, ensuring all queued SSH output is included. If writes keep queuing indefinitely (never stabilizes), falls back to the provider terminal buffer instead of returning an incomplete snapshot.

This prevents snapshot recovery from losing pending terminal output in SSH scenarios where new writes arrive while serialization is in progress.

## Testing

Added two test cases:
- Verifies queued SSH suffix is included across multiple recovery drains
- Verifies fallback to provider buffer when writes never stabilize

records.title: Fix mobile browser frames after reconnect (STA-4128)
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 3 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​347 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​24 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​323 |
| Prod | 2 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​189 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​88 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​101 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

Author: @BrennanKB5

## ELI5

When mobile reconnects while the next browser screenshot is still loading offscreen, that hidden image can stop reporting that it loaded. Orca now replaces only that stuck hidden image and keeps the last good screenshot visible until a fresh frame is ready.

In plainer words: you have a web page open in a browser tab on Orca Mobile. Your phone drops the
connection for a moment — a lift, a cell handoff, switching between Wi-Fi and data — and comes back.
If the drop lands in the split second a new screenshot of the page is being decoded, that decode
never finishes and never reports back. Every screenshot after it goes into the same dead slot, so the
picture on your screen **freezes on the last frame for the rest of that tab's life**. The page is
still live on the other side; you just never see it change again, and the only way out is closing and
reopening the tab.

Now Orca notices that one stuck slot, replaces just it, and keeps the last good picture on screen
until a fresh one is ready — so there is no blank flash either.

## User-facing before / after

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Your phone reconnects while a browser screenshot is mid-decode | The browser tab freezes on the last picture permanently. Scrolling and clicks still go through, but the view never updates again | The stuck slot is replaced and live updates resume |
| Your phone reconnects with nothing in flight | Worked fine | Unchanged — Orca does nothing at all |
| While the replacement picture loads | — | The last good screenshot stays on screen; no blank flash |
| The connection moves between a relay and a direct link | The same freeze was possible | Handled the same way |

## When it bites

Orca Mobile users with a browser tab open, whenever the connection drops and returns — cellular
handoffs, Wi-Fi/data switches, backgrounding and reopening the app — and only when the drop happens
to land in the moment a screenshot is decoding.


## What Changed

- Track each mobile browser image layer's URI independently so a reconnect render cannot move an unready hidden frame onto the visible layer.
- On an authenticated `connected` boundary, remount only an unresolved hidden decoder and fence late `onLoad`/`onError` callbacks by decoder epoch.
- Keep healthy reconnects inert and retain the existing logical `browser.screencast` subscription.
- Add deterministic pane, physical reconnect, and relay/direct migration coverage plus the `mobile-browser.frame-continuity` reliability gate.

## Why

Current main already replays retained subscriptions after a physical socket reconnect and attaches them to the replacement session during logical relay/direct migration. The remaining freeze is in the React Native double buffer: if the hidden `Image` misses `onLoad`, every later frame continues updating that hidden layer while the last decoded layer remains visible forever.

This supersedes #14115:

1. It leaves transport replay in the transport instead of restarting the pane's logical subscription.
2. It repairs the wedged native decoder while preserving the last decoded frame per layer.
3. It rejects stale callbacks from the discarded decoder and performs zero work when no decode is pending.
4. Its acceptance test reproduces the frozen render surface directly, while separate controls prove physical and both logical migration directions already attach the stream exactly once.

The implementation commit credits @blade035 as co-author for the community contribution that informed this fix.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #14274

Linear: STA-4128

## Visual Proof

Blocked. The iOS simulator loaded this worktree's mobile app, paired to the isolated development runtime, opened the target worktree, and opened a live browser tab; however, the unsigned local runtime exposes no Relay path and there is no safely scoped emulator control for a physical socket drop while preserving the mounted pane. No screenshot is attached because it would not prove the transition, and Android/live-network validation remains uncollected.

## ELI5

When working across multiple workspace folders that run local dev servers (e.g. `localhost:3000`), their cookies, authentication, and localStorage previously collided because all workspaces shared the default browser session. This change adds automatic workspace-scoped browser session profiles derived deterministically from the workspace folder path, giving each project folder its own isolated browser storage partition.

## What Changed

- **Types (`src/shared/browser-workspace-types.ts`)**: Added `'workspace'` scope to `BrowserSessionProfileScope` and optional `folderPath?: string` to `BrowserSessionProfile`.
- **Registry (`src/main/browser/browser-session-registry.ts`)**:
  - Added `resolveOrCreateWorkspaceProfile(folderPath)` to lazily instantiate and register folder-bound sessions.
  - Added `findProfileByFolderPath(folderPath)` for lookup.
  - Derived stable 32-character hex profile IDs using SHA-256 over normalized folder paths, ensuring deterministic partition naming across app restarts.
  - Added `clearProfileStorage(profileId)` to clear cookies and cache for a workspace session without destroying profile metadata.
- **Persisted Profile Validation (`src/main/browser/browser-session-persisted-profile-validation.ts`)**: Added support for validating persisted workspace-scoped profiles and their deterministic hex IDs alongside UUID profiles.
- **IPC & Runtime (`src/main/ipc/browser-session-profile-ipc.ts`, `src/main/runtime/orca-runtime-browser.ts`)**: Added `browser:session:resolveWorkspaceProfile` (with path-traversal validation) and `browser:session:clearProfileStorage` handlers.
