records.title: fix(browser): scope a native cookie import's clear to the domains it imports (STA-4797)
records.body:
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 10 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​884 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​226 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​658 |
| Prod | 7 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​439 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​123 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​316 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

Fixes STA-4797.

## The defect

A native cookie import (**Settings → Browser → Import Cookies → From Google Chrome**) cleared the **entire target partition's cookie jar**, keeping only the non-transplantable `google.com` family. Every unrelated site you were signed into in that partition was silently signed out — no warning before, no disclosure after. Observed in Electron QA on 2026-08-17: a working `the-internet.herokuapp.com` login was destroyed by an import that brought over `github.com`, `nordaccount.com` and `youtube.com`.

The stated rationale — *mixing stale and imported cookies makes sites reject the session* — reaches only as far as the domains being imported. Beyond them a clear has nothing to reconcile. The file/paste path already did the narrow thing through `replaceCookiesForImportedDomains`; the two import paths simply disagreed about scope, and the narrow one is the defensible shape.

## The fix

The native import's clear now covers only the domains it writes, through one shared predicate.

- **`browser-cookie-import-policy.ts`** — `importedDomainScope()` / `domainIsInImportedScope()` are exported as the single scope definition used by all three clears, so they cannot drift apart. (`NON_TRANSPLANTABLE_HOST_KEY_SQL` and `NON_TRANSPLANTABLE_CLEAR_EXCLUDED_ORIGINS` lost their last production callers and are gone.)
- **`browser-cookie-import-clear.ts`** — `removeTransplantableCookies` takes a **required** `importScope`. It is deliberately not defaulted: a default would be the whole jar again. The scope test runs *before* the removal-URL derivation, so an unaddressable cookie parked in an unrelated corner of the jar no longer fails an import that was never going to touch it.
- **The bulk `clearData` shortcut is gone**, and `clearData` leaves `CookieClearSession` for the same structural reason `set` already had. It clears by *exclusion*, so the only scope it can express is "everything except google.com" — the defect itself. An include list is no better: it matches at the registrable-domain boundary, so it would still take host-only siblings the import does not replace, and a partial delete followed by a rejection would destroy them with no identity to restore from (the STA-4090/4170 shape). The frozen per-coordinate plan is now the only removal path, and it covers the imported domains rather than the jar.
- **`browser-cookie-staged-image-clear.ts`** (new) — **this is the half that is easy to miss.** The staged image is a copy of the live jar that replaces it wholesale on the next cold start, so its `DELETE FROM cookies WHERE NOT (<google>)` was a second whole-partition wipe. Narrowing the live clear alone would have re-erased the partition one restart later. It now clears to the identical scope through the identical predicate.

The scope is named from the emitted plan — the same rows the writes come from — so the removal set is the write set. Google stays exempt by policy (STA-3811), unchanged.

## Scope note

The ticket offered a fallback ("at minimum, disclose before destroying"). This PR does the preferred fix instead, which makes the fallback unnecessary: the destroyed scope is now exactly the imported scope, and the summary's existing `domains` field already names it. **No wire or summary-type change**, so nothing here is a mixed-version concern.

## Testing

Fixtures in this module start with an **empty cookie jar**, which is why a full gate stack — review, readiness audit, Electron QA, CI — previously passed a session-erasing defect.

`browser-cookie-import-scope.test.ts` (new) uses a **populated** jar holding a session for a site outside the import set, and reads the **staged file itself** so the restart path is observed rather than assumed:

1. the unrelated site's cookie survives, the stale in-scope cookie is still removed, Google stays exempt, and a blank-domain cookie no longer aborts the import;
2. a subdomain of an imported domain is cleared while a lookalike registrable domain is not;
3. the staged cold-start image keeps the out-of-scope rows.

**All three fail against pre-fix source** (verified by reverting only the fix's source files and re-running): case 3 comes back with 2 staged rows where 3 are expected — the unrelated site's row missing from the restart image.

The real-Electron partition test now seeds **both** an in-scope stale cookie (still removed) and an out-of-scope live one (now survives), so the behaviour is proven against a real Electron cookie jar, not only mocks. That expectation was mutation-checked to confirm the fixture genuinely runs.

Existing tests that only pinned the bulk-`clearData` path were rewritten to pin the per-coordinate removal, and two cases that had become vacuous were re-seeded: one forced its rejection on a domain the import never covered (so nothing entered the removal plan at all). The STA-4170 mid-clear-arrival hooks moved from `clearData` to `snapshotClearIdentities` — the same window — and were mutation-verified to still go red.

`src/main/browser`: **72 files, 773 tests, all passing.** Typecheck and oxlint clean.

---

## Rebased onto #15095

This branch was rebased after #15095 (serialize cookie imports per partition) landed. That PR re-indented the whole native import inside a per-partition lock, so the textual conflict was large and mostly indentation. Rather than resolve it line by line, `browser-cookie-import.ts` was reset to main's version and the five edits above re-applied on top — `git diff origin/main` for that file is now exactly those edits, and `withCookieMutationLock` / `acquireCookieMutationLock` / `mutationLockOwner` are untouched. The scoped staged-image delete sits inside the same `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` it did before.

#15095's new native concurrency detector read *"has the second import started clearing yet?"* off `clearData` call counts. Removing the bulk `clearData` path takes that signal away, so the assertion no longer measured anything. It is re-anchored on the removals themselves — `remove:old-a` present while `remove:old-b` is absent — which distinguishes "the first import cleared" from "the second import cleared" in a way a call count could not, and the completed run pins the exact removal sequence (which incidentally records that each import now clears only its own domain).

Its seeded jar had to move onto the imported domains, for the same reason its own comment already gave for not leaving the jar empty: under a scoped clear, a jar holding only an unrelated site is the empty-jar case in disguise — the clear removes nothing and every assertion passes vacuously.

**Mutation-checked:** with the per-partition lock removed, that detector still fails. #15095's protection is intact.

## ELI5

Last PR put the generated shell-wrapper fixtures in a folder called `__tests__`. That was picked to satisfy the bot that counts test-vs-prod lines, not because it was the right name — this repo already keeps non-TS test data in `__fixtures__`. So: rename the folder to the one we actually use, and fix the bot instead of bending the layout around it.

## What Changed

- `src/main/__tests__/shell-wrapper-snapshots/` → `src/main/__fixtures__/shell-wrapper-snapshots/` (18 pure renames, `src/main/__tests__/` removed)
- `.github/scripts/pr-test-loc-table.mjs`: `isTestPath` now also counts `__fixtures__` and `__snapshots__` path segments
- Test + `.gitattributes` references updated; new classifier cases in `config/scripts/pr-test-loc-summary.test.mjs`

```diff
-const TEST_DIR_SEGMENT = /(?:^|\/)(?:__tests__|e2e|tests)(?:\/|$)/i
+const TEST_DIR_SEGMENT = /(?:^|\/)(?:__tests__|__fixtures__|__snapshots__|e2e|tests)(?:\/|$)/i
```

## Why

`__fixtures__` is this repo's existing convention for non-TS test data — `src/shared/__fixtures__`, `src/main/startup/__fixtures__`, `src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/__fixtures__`. `src/main/providers/__tests__` is the lone `__tests__` dir; everything else co-locates `*.test.ts`. #15363 used `__tests__` purely because it was the only name `isTestPath` matched, which is the layout following the tool rather than the other way round.

Fixing the classifier also corrects **five directories that are misbilled as prod today**, independent of this move:

| Dir | Before | After |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `src/shared/__fixtures__` | `PROD` | `TEST` |
| `src/main/startup/__fixtures__` | `PROD` | `TEST` |
| `src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/__fixtures__` | `PROD` | `TEST` |
| `src/main/runtime/orchestration/__snapshots__` | `PROD` | `TEST` |
| `src/renderer/src/components/settings/__snapshots__` | `PROD` | `TEST` |

### Why only the `__`-wrapped names

Both added names are `__`-wrapped, so a directory cannot carry one by accident. Bare `fixtures/` is deliberately **not** added: it reads as a plausible production module name, and this classifier bills every PR in the repo, so a false positive there is worse than a missed test dir. The two bare `fixtures/` dirs outside `tests/` (`config/scripts/fixtures/`, `src/main/daemon/fixtures/`) stay prod, and there is an explicit test pinning that.

### This PR's own LoC table will be wrong — expected

`pr-test-loc.yml` fetches the classifier from the **default branch**, never `pull/<n>/head`, because the job holds a write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` and may only execute reviewed code. So the table on *this* PR is still computed with the old regex; the fix applies from the next PR onward. Low stakes here — the fixtures move as renames, which carry 0 added/deleted lines either way.

records.title: fix(remote): retire direct-SSH tabs on publisher retraction instead of snapshot absence (STA-4719)
records.body:
## ELI5

Say you have Orca open on your laptop **and** your desktop, both connected to the same server. You close a terminal tab on the laptop. The desktop should notice and close it too — but it didn't. Worse, the desktop would re-upload the tab, making it pop back up on the laptop.

Here's why. The two machines share one list of tabs on the server. The desktop looked at the list, didn't find the tab, and had to decide what that meant. And "not in the list" means two completely different things:

- **"It was closed."** → should disappear here too.
- **"Nobody's told the server about it yet."** → a brand-new tab still uploading. Deleting that would kill a live terminal and the program running in it.

You genuinely cannot tell those apart from absence alone, so the safe guess was always "keep it" — which is why closed tabs came back.

The fix is to stop reading silence and start watching **who wrote the list**. Every update already carries a stamp saying which machine wrote it. So now we remember what each machine has said. If the same machine that previously said *"I have tab X"* later writes a list without X, that's it **taking X back** — a real close, and we act on it. If a machine never mentioned X, its silence tells us nothing and we leave X alone.

Like this: if the friend who told you they're bringing cake later sends a list with no cake, the cake is off. If a stranger sends a list with no cake, you've learned nothing about the cake.

**What you might notice:**
- Closing a tab on one machine now actually closes it on the other, instead of it bouncing back.
- The first close after either machine restarts still won't sync — a fresh machine hasn't told us anything yet, so it gets the benefit of the doubt. It syncs from then on.
- Pinned tabs are left alone on purpose.
- The remote program is never killed. If the other machine's cleanup didn't land, it keeps running on the server rather than being cut off.
- Closing this way is permanent — same as closing it yourself. Scrollback and layout for that tab go with it, and there's no undo.

---
<!-- orca-pr-loc -->
<!-- Programmatic LoC summary. Do not edit by hand; rewritten on every commit. -->

| | Files | Added | Deleted | Net |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 4 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1117 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​17 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​1100 |
| Prod | 9 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​507 | $\color{#cf222e}{\Huge{\mathbf{−}}}$​28 | $\color{#1a7f37}{\Huge{\mathbf{+}}}$​479 |

<!-- /orca-pr-loc -->

Resolves [STA-4719](https://linear.app/stably/issue/STA-4719). Follow-up from #14844.

## Problem

`mergeDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSession` preserves host-unknown local tabs to protect pending uploads. Its own comment names the trade it accepts: *"absence cannot distinguish 'never uploaded' from 'closed by another client on this host'"*, so a tab closed elsewhere survives here until that client's snapshot is applied — and gets re-uploaded, resurrecting it on the host.

## Root cause

Snapshot-absence was overloaded as a proxy for two different facts. The fix is to stop inferring from absence and use a positive signal.

## Fix: retraction, not absence

`workspace.changed` already carries `sourceClientId` (on the wire since #1876). The ledger is now keyed per (target, publisher) and records what each *client* of the host has itself listed. A tab is retired only when **the same publisher that once listed it stops listing it** — a retraction, which is positive evidence that the writer knew the tab and dropped it. Absence from a publisher that never listed the id is structurally inert, however many times it republishes.

Nothing new crosses the wire; the renderer reads a field that has always been there. An old relay yields no publisher and retires nothing. The ledger is memory-only and client-local.

### Why not the alternatives

- **Direct staleness detection is not decidable from the wire.** `RemoteWorkspaceSnapshot` carries only `{namespace, revision, updatedAt, schemaVersion, session}`. The relay CAS rejects unless `baseRevision === current.revision` and publishes `current.revision + 1`, so the base is *always* `revision - 1` and carries zero information — and it is the writer's main-process cache, not the base its renderer built the session from. "Peer closed T" and "peer never knew T" produce byte-identical wire output.
- **"Omission persists across K revisions"** only delays a wrong deletion. A stale peer that publishes twice still retires a live pane. It is a probability knob, not a discriminator.

## Two failure modes this had to survive

Both were found by review and both end in live panes being retired with their remote ptys **not** killed — orphaned processes, the exact invariant the merge's preserve rule exists to protect.

1. **A peer with a narrower repo set.** The namespace is shared by every client of the host, and each client exports only the worktrees whose repo it holds, so a peer deterministically strips whole worktree keys on every push. Closed by a per-worktree-path guard: only retire ids under a path the retiring snapshot still describes, with a per-tab `listed.worktreePath` match. Fails closed on a missing or unparseable path.
2. **The main-cache-ahead-of-renderer race.** `handleRemoteWorkspaceNotification` updates the peer's main cache synchronously while its renderer apply lags, so the peer CAS-es on a revision it never applied and republishes an older tab list at a newer revision. Closed by the retraction rule itself: the peer never *listed* the locally created tab, so it cannot retract it.

## A note on the two rejected guards

Earlier iterations added a local liveness veto. Both settings were wrong, in opposite directions, and both were hidden by an unrealistic fixture:

- keyed on the direct-SSH **retry-lease** ledgers → empty for a tab created while already connected → live panes retired;
- keyed on `terminalTabHasReconnectablePty` → `hydrateTabsSession` + `reconnectPersistedTerminals` stamp it on essentially every host-listed tab → retirement never fired at all.

Both are gone. No local-state predicate participates in the decision, and the selector's docblock says why: the direct-SSH reconnect pass (`retryDirectSshTargetPanes`, run at the end of every snapshot apply) touches every tab of the target, so any veto built on that state is universally satisfied and silently disables the feature. The remaining conditions — publisher identity, target, namespace, strict revision, per-worktree-path — are all statements about the publisher's own evidence, and the retry pass does not write to the ledger.

## Tests

The fixture now routes `finalizeHydratedTerminals` through the real `retryDirectSshTargetPanes`, matching production, so tests exercise the state the app is actually in. Both directions are proven through the real `applyDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSnapshot` path with no `store.setState` seeding of ledgers:

- **fires** — a tab a publisher listed and then dropped is retired;
- **preserves** — rev1 `['agent']`, `setup` created locally while connected via the real create path, stale peer republishing `['agent']` at revs 3–6 ⇒ `setup` survives every time.

Fails closed on unattributed pull, namespace change, non-monotonic revision, missing ledger entry, and stripped path key. Folder workspaces unaffected (scoped to `gitWorktreeIds`, same `splitWorktreeId` the export uses). 3540 tests pass across `src/renderer/src/{hooks,store}`.

## Known residual (documented in the module)

If a peer applies a tab and closes it *without ever publishing a listing containing it*, the retraction is unobservable and the tab is preserved and re-uploaded once, until that peer's next publish makes it retractable. It converges and is never wrong. Closing it needs the closing client to publish the removal — an optional tombstone map on `RemoteWorkspaceSession` (additive-safe, since the relay stores the session blob opaquely) — i.e. a change to what the host holds, not a client-local signal.

records.title: [Bug]: Embedded browser ignores the app-wide HTTP Proxy setting
records.body:
### What happened Settings → HTTP Proxy is set to `socks5://127.0.0.1:1080` (Proxy Bypass Rules empty).
The UI states it "Supports http, https, socks, socks4, and socks5 URLs". The embedded browser does not route through it. Any host that is only reachable
via that proxy fails to load, landing on `chrome-error://chromewebdata/`. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Settings → HTTP Proxy → `socks5://127.0.0.1:1080`, leave Bypass empty 2. `orca tab create --url https://example.com/ --json` # only reachable via the proxy here 3. `orca eval --page --expression "location.href" --json`
→ `chrome-error://chromewebdata/` ### Control results * A directly reachable host loads fine in the same tab, so the browser itself is healthy:
`orca tab create --url https://vivaldi.com/` → loads normally * The same proxy works for another Chromium driven with `--proxy-server=socks5://127.0.0.1:1080`,
so the proxy itself is fine * `orca network --page --limit 5 --json` returns no entries for the failed
navigation, so there is no diagnostic surface for this ### Expected The embedded browser session honours `settings.httpProxyUrl` /
`settings.httpProxyBypassRules`, the same setting other subsystems use. ### Environment * Orca 1.4.184 * macOS 26.5.1, arm64 ### Notes The setting is already validated, persisted and socks5-capable — stablyai/orca#11171 wires it into
git clone and describes it as an existing app-wide setting, which suggests the browser
session simply never applies it (no `session.setProxy` equivalent). Related: stablyai/orca#10665 requests a browser proxy option; this report is narrower — the setting
already exists and is configured, it is just not applied to the browser.
Also related: stablyai/orca#6348 (public CDP attach) would offer a workaround, but is still open.

records.title: Native <select> dropdowns are unusable in the remote browser pane -- the popup renders on the host and is never captured or hit-testable
records.body:
## Summary

When a desktop client is paired to a remote runtime (`orca serve`), clicking a native `<select>` in the browser pane does nothing visible. The popup does open on the host -- the accessibility snapshot reports `combobox [expanded=true]` -- but it's never part of any screencast frame, and clicking where the options should be lands on the page beneath the popup.

The same mechanism makes `window.open()` popups invisible: the page gets a live window handle (so it won't fall back to a redirect flow), but no new tab appears in the pane or in `orca tab list`. The browser's own autofill and password dropdowns are the same class of widget, so sign-in flows get hit twice over.

## Environment

Orca 1.4.183 and current main (the capture and input paths are unchanged). Headless linux runtime (`orca serve`, Xvfb, software GL), desktop client paired over LAN. Reproduces with any native `<select>`.

## Reproduction

1. On the remote host, open a page containing a native `<select>` (putting a custom in-page dropdown and a `<datalist>` beside it makes a useful comparison -- both of those work fine, only the native popup doesn't).
2. From the paired desktop client, click the `<select>` in the browser pane.

Expected: the option list appears and an option can be clicked. Actual: nothing appears. Clicking where the options would be clicks the page under the popup. The value can't be changed by mouse at all.

To rule out a race I forced a page repaint while the popup was confirmed open (`expanded=true` sampled immediately before and after) -- the fresh frame carries the repaint marker and no popup.

## Root cause

The popup is a browser-process widget (`MenuListPopup`), not page content. Two independent consequences of that one fact:

- `Page.startScreencast` captures the page's compositor surface only, so the popup is in no frame
- `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` injects into the page's widget by coordinate, so a click can't reach the popup and lands on the page beneath it

`Input.dispatchKeyEvent` goes to the focused widget, which *is* the popup while it's open -- which is why keyboard (arrows, Enter) works while the mouse doesn't.

An `<option>` also has no layout box in the page (`getClientRects().length === 0`), so the element path fails too: `orca click --element <option-ref>` errors with `CDP error (DOM.getBoxModel): Could not compute box model.` -- and that error is inherent (an `<option>` really has no box in the page), not a bug in the element path. (`orca select --element <select-ref> --value <v>` works and fires `change`, so agents have a working path as long as they never `click` an option.)

## What works today

| Path | Result |
|---|---|
| `orca select --element <select> --value v` | works, fires `change` |
| focus the `<select>`, then `ArrowDown` | works, fires `change` |
| `Alt+ArrowDown` on a focused `<select>` | opens the popup (invisibly) |
| CDP mouse click on the `<select>` itself | toggles the popup open/closed (invisibly) |
| custom in-page dropdown | works |
| `<datalist>` | works |

Only the popup's own option list is unreachable, and only visually and by mouse.

## Suggested directions, roughly in order of generality

1. **Capture the display, not the page surface, for serve-mode streams.** In serve mode every tab is already a real (unmapped) X11 window on the Xvfb display. I prototyped this against 1.4.183 on our own runtime: on screencast start, show + size the tab's BrowserWindow, stream its content region with `ffmpeg -f x11grab` through the existing frame pipeline (wire-unchanged -- the client needs no modification), and inject mouse down/up for the streamed tab as real X events via XTEST so native widgets hit-test correctly. Native `<select>` popups, context menus and `window.open()` windows then render and click exactly as in a local browser, b/c it's literally the same pipeline a local browser uses.

   It works -- select options click and commit end-to-end through the real transport -- but there are real sharp edges (popup-dismissal timing on clicks, wheel has to stay CDP, x11grab has no damage signal so duplicate frames need dropping, dpr>1 clients get 1x frames upscaled), and it's linux/Xvfb-serve-specific by construction. I have the full write-up with measurements and would happily turn it into a PR if this direction is wanted -- though given the client-hosted browser work in flight (#14440 series) it may only make sense for the paths that stay host-rendered.
2. **Render the option list client-side.** The pane already receives an accessibility snapshot containing every option and the `expanded` state; drawing the list in the client and sending the chosen index back (`browser.select`) removes the dependency on capturing or hit-testing a native widget, and works on every host OS.
3. **Forward keys while a popup is open.** With a `MenuListPopup` open, translate pane clicks/scrolls into arrow/Enter key sequences. Cheapest, but the list stays invisible.
4. **Fix the agent path regardless.** `getElementCenter` calls `DOM.getBoxModel` with no fallback; when the resolved node is an `<option>`, routing to the existing `select` implementation instead of failing would make `click --element` on an option work.

Related: #12718 (window.open popups aren't addressable through the agent CLI -- the `window.open` half of this issue is the interactive-pane face of the same gap), #8343 (local desktop popups got origin-bar windows; serve mode has no equivalent), #6701.

One smaller adjacent note: the desktop pane requests `everyNthFrame: 2`, which can drop the final compositor update of an in-page menu/popover on an otherwise static page -- mobile's `browser-screencast-request.ts` uses `everyNthFrame: 1` with a comment saying exactly this. A second, independent way dropdown UI looks broken remotely, though cosmetic next to the native-widget gap above.

records.title: fix(browser): press keys through a US-layout CDP key table instead of a subprocess per keystroke
records.body:
## ELI5

Typing in the remote browser pane launches a new process on the host for every keystroke -- about 160ms per character, so clicking a login field, typing a 17-character password and hitting enter takes ~4 seconds end to end -- and some keys arrive half-formed: F-keys and several named keys carry key code 0, and Shift+1 types `1` instead of `!`. Keys now go straight to the page with the exact events a US keyboard would produce.

## What Changed

`keypress` resolves the key name through a new `cdp-keyboard-us-layout.ts` table -- all 95 printable characters, named keys and their aliases, F1-F24, shifted characters, and `Ctrl+`/`Alt+`/`Meta+`/`Shift+` combinations -- and dispatches the `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` pair over the electron debugger. A key name the table can't express falls back in two tiers:

- a single printable character outside the table (accented letters, non-latin scripts) still dispatches in process, as an IME-style event -- keyCode 229 with the character as text, the same shape composed input already has when it reaches pages
- everything else (media keys, surrogate pairs, combining sequences) goes to the agent-browser helper exactly as before

The helper session is only created on that last fallback, so the fast path never pays for it. Note -- the IME tier is the second commit and drops cleanly if review prefers the smaller scope.

## Why

Two things, really:

1. Latency: one `execFile` per keystroke, b/c the helper exists for element-ref automation and `keypress` just inherited its transport. Measured on the same host, same dev build, main vs this branch (loopback, p50, n=25): **160ms -> 0.5ms**. Typing is serialized on both ends, so through the remote pane that's ~160ms per character.
2. Key fidelity. Measured against the shipped agent-browser 0.27 binary (the shared input-fidelity probe suite -- main fails its double-click checks and every key-fidelity check below):
   - `F5` (F1-F24 generally), `Insert` and `ContextMenu` dispatch `windowsVirtualKeyCode: 0` -- no browser default action fires, and page JS reading `keydown.keyCode` sees 0
   - shifted characters are never derived, so `Shift+a` types `a` and `Shift+1` types `1` instead of `!`
   - US punctuation like `&` arrives with `keyCode: 0` metadata (the character itself types, but keyCode-filtering pages misbehave)
   - non-ASCII printables (`é`, `ß`, `漢`) don't type at all: the helper reports success and fires a keyCode-0 keydown, but no text is ever inserted (measured against the shipped binary -- value stays empty). With the IME tier they type correctly and arrive as `key: 'é', keyCode: 229`, the shape real composed input has

## Key-event semantics

- printable keys dispatch `keyDown` with `text`/`unmodifiedText`; no-character keys (arrows, Tab, Escape, F-keys, shortcut chords) dispatch `rawKeyDown` -- the same pairing Puppeteer uses
- virtual key codes come from a US-layout table, deliberately never from the character's own char code: charCodeAt-derived codes put `&` on 38 (VK_UP) and `.` on 46 (VK_DELETE), which Blink executes as caret commands that swallow the character (verified by dispatching exactly those events -- the `.` one also forward-deletes). The table gives `&` shift+`Digit7` (55), `.` `Period` (190), and so on
- `Ctrl+A` reports `key: 'a'` with ctrl held -- a capital letter in a shortcut is how people write the key, not a request for shift (`Ctrl+Shift+A` still reports `'A'` with both modifiers). Matches what a physical keyboard produces
- result shape is unchanged, `{ pressed: <key> }`, byte-identical to the helper's

## Callouts

- no wire, schema or result-shape change; mixed-version client/server pairs see no difference (`docs/reference/remote-wire-compatibility.md` considered)
- pages can observe the fidelity fixes: `Shift+a` now types `A`, `Shift+1` now types `!`, `Alt+<char>` no longer carries text, editing keys arrive as `rawKeyDown` instead of text-less `keyDown`, bare capitals now set the shift modifier. Each matches a real US keyboard; automation that depended on the previous half-formed events would notice
- unknown key names keep the exact old behavior (helper fallback), so nothing that worked before stops working. Keys resolve from the character the client's keyboard actually produced (the table models the US layout only, as Puppeteer's does -- no locale detection); printables outside it take the IME tier, and surrogate pairs / combining sequences / unrecognized names keep the helper

## Linked Issue

Part of #15308 (same input-latency issue as the pointer-input PR).

## Visual Proof

Before/after typing recordings attached here -- the same sentence sent at ~11 keys/sec through the exact RPCs the pane sends, recorded from the screencast frames the pane receives. Before: the field lags seconds behind the typist and the accented characters never appear at all ("crème" arrives as "crm"). After: keeps pace with the typist, every character lands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9690ac3e-996c-46f6-89ca-661be4af861d

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/195a28ff-f200-4313-8aa4-070758cc51c1


## Testing

- `pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/main/browser/` -- the whole directory passes, including new `cdp-keyboard-us-layout.test.ts` (all 95 printable ASCII characters produce themselves, the seven charCodeAt-collision characters get their US-layout codes, shortcut/named-key/F-key/IME-tier/ null-fallback parsing) and `agent-browser-bridge-keypress-input.test.ts` (dispatched CDP payload pairs, rawKeyDown vs keyDown, modifier masks, the IME-tier dispatch, helper fallback with lazy session creation, tab-gone error).
- `pnpm run typecheck`, `pnpm exec oxlint`, `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed`, `pnpm run check:max-lines-ratchet` -- all clean.
- Live verification on a headless linux serve host, source build, through the real E2EE pairing transport: the input-fidelity probe suite (24 checks when the linked issue was measured, plus a 25th non-ASCII check added with this branch) passes 25/25 here -- typing all 95 printable ASCII characters plus é/ß/ñ/ü/ç/漢 into a real input with caret assertions, Ctrl+A-then-type-replaces-field, Shift+Home selection, F5/Insert/ContextMenu arriving with their key codes, Enter-in-textarea, Tab focus traversal, and that an unsupported key name isn't silently invented. Against the helper path the same non-ASCII characters report success and type nothing (measured live, twice). Unknown-key fallback checked end-to-end (`MediaPlayPause` -> helper -> `{pressed}`).
- Platforms actually tested: linux headless serve.

## Relationship to #13231

#13231 (open) also routes `keypress` (and `type`) through CDP, coming at it from
focus correctness (#12912) rather than latency, and I only found it after building this -- so flagging the overlap explicitly. Where the two differ on keypress, measured by dispatching both PRs' events against a live page:

- #13231 derives unknown single-character key codes from `charCodeAt(0)`, which introduces the collision described above: its `&` dispatches VK_UP with text and gets swallowed, its `.` dispatches VK_DELETE and forward-deletes. This branch's table dispatches the US-layout codes and the characters type correctly
- its modifier parsing is case-sensitive (`ctrl+a` -> no modifiers) and names it can't express dispatch with no VK and report success; this branch parses modifiers case-insensitively and falls back to the helper
- it sends `text` on `keyUp` (nonstandard); this branch strips text on keyUp and on ctrl/alt/meta chords, and adds the shifted-character model
- it also converts `type()` to `Input.insertText`, which this branch deliberately doesn't touch

Happy to coordinate either way -- if #13231 lands first this reduces to swapping its resolver for the table + fallback, and if this lands first, #13231's `type` and focus-scoping work is unaffected.
- [x] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below

## AI Disclosure

Built with Claude Code (Fable 5). Ported from a hand-validated patch prototype running against our own remote runtime; the key table was verified character-by-character by a scripted probe asserting what the page actually received, and claims about the current helper's behavior were re-checked by running the pinned agent-browser 0.27 binary directly. I reviewed the diff before submitting.

## Notes

Security: key names are parsed by table lookup, no eval, no new input surface. Cross-platform: the dispatch path is identical on all platforms; the table is layout-(US)-specific, not OS-specific. Remote/SSH: server-side only, no wire change. Performance: hot path loses a subprocess spawn per keystroke.

## Review

Adversarially reviewed with independent agent passes before submission: correctness (races, debugger-lease lifetimes, event ordering, per-tab state isolation), cross-platform (the dispatch path is the one `mouseClick` already uses on macOS/Windows/Linux; no platform-conditional code added), remote/SSH and mixed versions (no wire or schema change; result shapes byte-compared against the shipped helper binary), agent/integration compatibility (element-ref commands untouched; helper fallback preserved), performance (removes a subprocess spawn per event from the hot path), and basic security (no new parsed inputs, no new surface). Findings that survived review are disclosed in Callouts above.

## Agent skill upstream boundary

- [x] Not applicable, or this change follows `docs/reference/agent-skill-sharing-upstream-boundary.md` and copies or mechanically translates no upstream skill-installer source, tests, fixtures, registry entries, path tables, comments, or documentation.

## Checklist

- [x] This PR is small and focused
- [x] I explained what changed and why (including ELI5)
- [x] Before/after screenshots or videos attached for UI changes, or `N/A` with reason
- [x] Self-reviewed for correctness, security, and performance
- [x] Cross-platform, SSH/remote, and path/shortcut impact considered (or N/A)
- [x] `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`, and `pnpm build` pass (or CI will cover; local preferred)

records.title: perf(browser): dispatch coordinate pointer input in process instead of one subprocess per event
records.body:
## ELI5

Moving the mouse in the remote browser pane launches a whole new process on the host for every wiggle, click and scroll tick -- about 160ms each, and a click is four of them. This makes the runtime deliver mouse events the same fast way it already delivers taps from the mobile app: directly, in process. A click drops from ~640ms to ~1.5ms, and double-click works through the pane for the first time.

## What Changed

`mouseMove` / `mouseDown` / `mouseUp` / `mouseWheel` no longer go through `execAgentBrowser` (an `execFile` of the agent-browser helper per event) -- they dispatch `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` over the electron debugger, the way `mouseClick` has done since it was added for mobile. A new `cdp-pointer-input.ts` module tracks per-tab pointer state (position, held-buttons mask, click cadence) in a WeakMap keyed by the WebContents, so state dies with the tab.

Element-ref commands (`click --element`, `snapshot`, ...) are untouched, they genuinely need the helper's snapshot state.

Two deliberate design points worth flagging up front:

- dispatch doesn't await the renderer's ack by default. The ack for mouse events is frame-bound: ~16ms on a tab someone is watching, ~1s per event on a tab whose renderer idles at 1Hz b/c nothing subscribes to its screencast -- and at 1Hz two clicks can never land inside the 500ms double-click interval, so awaiting costs correctness as well as latency. Events are still written to the debugger in call order, a late dispatch failure comes back as a `browser_error` on the caller's next pointer event instead of being swallowed, and the debugger lease is held until the in-flight command settles. `ORCA_BROWSER_INPUT_AWAIT_ACK=1` restores the waiting behavior if you'd rather have the strict semantics.
- clickCount is tracked (1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1 for repeated presses within 500ms / 2px), where the helper hardcoded `clickCount: 1`. Double-click through the remote pane -- select a word, open a file from a list -- was previously impossible to express at all.

## Why

Measured on the same host, same dev build, main vs this branch (loopback, p50, n=25):

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `browser.mouseMove` | 160 ms | 0.5 ms |
| `browser.mouseWheel` | 160 ms | 0.4 ms |
| one scroll notch (move+wheel, serialized) | 320 ms | 0.7 ms |
| one click (move+down+move+up -- what BrowserPane sends) | 637 ms | 1.5 ms |

`browser.eval` measures 0.4-0.5ms on the same socket, so the transport was never the cost. Both ends serialize input (`enqueueRemoteInput` on the client, the per-session command queue on the server), which means the per-event cost multiplies into every gesture -- this is most of "the remote pane feels laggy". The helper was only translating these events into `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` calls of its own, so no behavior actually depended on the subprocess.

## Callouts

Some deltas from the helper path, all deliberate, listed so nothing is surprising in review:

- result shapes are byte-identical to the shipped helper's (checked by running the pinned agent-browser 0.27 binary): `{moved:true}`, `{pressed:true}`, `{released:true}`, `{scrolled:true,deltaX,deltaY}`. No wire or schema change, so mixed-version pairs just get a faster server (checked against `docs/reference/remote-wire-compatibility.md` -- nothing there applies).
- success now means 'dispatched', not 'renderer processed it' (see above). In practice a read through the same pipeline lands after the input -- measured 20/20 clicks and 10/10 typed strings visible to an immediately-following `browser.eval`, no sleep -- but that ordering is measured, not contractual.
- wheel dispatches at the tracked pointer position. The helper dispatched wheel at (0,0) regardless of any preceding `mouse move` (the CLI never passes x/y), so inner scrollables under the cursor never scrolled and whatever sat at the top-left corner did. Both panes (desktop and mobile) send `mouseMove` before every wheel, so interactive scrolling gets strictly better; headless automation that relied on the (0,0) targeting would notice.
- two clicks at the same point within 500ms now produce a real `dblclick` with `detail: 2`, as a physical mouse would. The old path physically couldn't produce sub-500ms pairs (4x160ms per click), so nothing existing can have depended on fast pairs staying `detail: 1` -- but newly-fast CLI scripting that double-invokes a control in <500ms will now look like a double-click to the page, b/c it is one.
- `button: 'back'` / `'forward'` pass through as real X1/X2 presses with the right buttons-mask bits, as the helper dispatched them. (The element-click path's existing left-coercion is untouched.)
- `mouseUp` with no button releases the held button; the helper always released `left`, which left a right-button press stuck forever. Both panes always pass the button, so only CLI/RPC callers see this.
- non-finite coordinates/deltas are rejected up front (`browser_error`) -- an un-awaited dispatch would otherwise report success and park chromium's invalid-params error on a later event.
- `wc.focus()` on mouseDown mirrors what `mouseClick` already does. The helper never focused anything, so relative to the old down/up path this widens the focus surface the same way every mobile tap already does -- flagging for coordination with #10875/#11732 (agent-input focus stealing), which this PR neither fixes nor worsens beyond the established precedent.
- when the automation-visibility feature swaps the pane's guest WebContents, pointer state resets with it -- equivalent to today, where that swap restarted the helper and dropped its mouse state. Both panes send a `mouseMove` before any down/up/wheel in the same serialized queue, which re-establishes position.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #15308

## Visual Proof

Before/after recordings attached here -- the same click / double-click / scroll sequence driven through the exact RPCs the pane sends, at human cadence, recorded from the screencast frames the pane receives. Before is current main, after is this branch: same 1680px scrolled, but before crawls and never fires dblclick; after is instant, fires `dblclick`, and selects the word.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0ef010e0-a41e-47f7-8795-ae6218e1cb39

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3a154b6d-8113-4323-9d0a-b6cc652ce197

## Testing

- `pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/main/browser/` -- the whole directory passes, including the new `agent-browser-bridge-pointer-input.test.ts` (13 tests: CDP payloads for move/down/up/wheel, position tracking, per-tab state isolation, clickCount escalation and reset, back/forward passthrough, non-finite rejection, deferred-failure surfacing, ack-await mode, lease release ordering, queue cleanup).
- `pnpm run typecheck`, `pnpm exec oxlint`, `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed`, `pnpm run check:max-lines-ratchet` -- all clean.
- Live verification on a headless linux serve host (source build of this branch, real E2EE pairing transport): a 24-check input-fidelity suite passes 24/24 -- click, double-click (fires `dblclick` and selects a word), right-click (`contextmenu`), drag-selection across a text span, plus the keyboard checks. The same suite on a main build of the same base fails both double-click checks. Latency numbers above were taken on the same rig, main vs branch.
- Platforms actually tested: linux headless serve. I'd expect macOS/Windows impact to be limited to the dispatch mechanism those platforms already use for `mouseClick` on every mobile tap, but I haven't run them myself.
- [x] I manually tested these changes locally
- [x] Automated tests added/updated, or explained why not below

## AI Disclosure

Built with Claude Code (Fable 5). It started as a hand-validated patch prototype running against a remote runtime I use daily; all the numbers here come from scripted probes against real instances (including the main-branch baseline, same host and build), and claims about the helper's current behavior were re-checked by running the pinned agent-browser 0.27 binary directly. I reviewed the diff before submitting.

## Notes

Security: no new inputs parsed beyond a finiteness check, RPC surface and schemas unchanged. Cross-platform: the electron debugger dispatch path is the same one `mouseClick` uses on all three platforms. Remote/SSH: no wire change, server-side speedup only. Performance: hot path loses a subprocess spawn per event, nothing new beyond a small per-tab state object.

## Review

Adversarially reviewed with independent agent passes before submission: correctness (races, debugger-lease lifetimes, event ordering, per-tab state isolation), cross-platform (the dispatch path is the one `mouseClick` already uses on macOS/Windows/Linux; no platform-conditional code added), remote/SSH and mixed versions (no wire or schema change; result shapes byte-compared against the shipped helper binary), agent/integration compatibility (element-ref commands untouched; helper fallback preserved), performance (removes a subprocess spawn per event from the hot path), and basic security (no new parsed inputs, no new surface). Findings that survived review are disclosed in Callouts above.

## Agent skill upstream boundary

- [x] Not applicable, or this change follows `docs/reference/agent-skill-sharing-upstream-boundary.md` and copies or mechanically translates no upstream skill-installer source, tests, fixtures, registry entries, path tables, comments, or documentation.

## Checklist

- [x] This PR is small and focused
- [x] I explained what changed and why (including ELI5)
- [x] Before/after screenshots or videos attached for UI changes, or `N/A` with reason
- [x] Self-reviewed for correctness, security, and performance
- [x] Cross-platform, SSH/remote, and path/shortcut impact considered (or N/A)
- [x] `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`, and `pnpm build` pass (or CI will cover; local preferred)

records.title: Interactive input in the remote browser pane costs ~160ms per event -- every mouse/key event spawns a subprocess on the host
records.body:
## Summary

Every mouse move, wheel tick and keypress the remote browser pane sends to the runtime spawns one `agent-browser` helper process on the host. Measured on loopback, so no network involved: `browser.eval` round-trips in 0.4-0.5ms, `browser.mouseMove` in ~160ms. Both ends serialize input (`enqueueRemoteInput` on the client, the per-session command queue on the server), so the costs stack rather than overlap -- one scroll notch is ~320ms and one click (`mouseMove`+`mouseDown`+`mouseMove`+ `mouseUp`, what BrowserPane.tsx sends) is ~640ms before a single pixel comes back. Typing is ~160ms per character, so clicking a login field, typing a 17-character password and hitting enter takes ~4 seconds end to end.

As far as I can tell this is most of the "remote pane feels laggy" experience -- the frame path itself is healthy (roughly 40-55ms glass-to-glass in my measurements).

The subprocess path costs some fidelity too, not just time (all measured against the pinned agent-browser 0.27):

- `clickCount` is hardcoded to 1, and the per-event cost keeps any two clicks well outside the 500ms double-click window anyway, so double-click can't be expressed through the pane at all -- no word-selection, no dblclick handlers
- wheel events are dispatched at (0,0) regardless of pointer position, so inner scrollables under the cursor never scroll
- `F5`/F-keys, `Insert`, `ContextMenu` dispatch `windowsVirtualKeyCode: 0` (no default action, and pages reading `keydown.keyCode` see 0), and shifted characters are never derived -- `Shift+1` types `1` instead of `!`

## Environment

Orca 1.4.183 and current main (`AgentBrowserBridge` routes `mouseMove`, `mouseDown`, `mouseUp`, `mouseWheel`, `keypress` through `execAgentBrowser`). Headless linux runtime, desktop client paired over LAN. The cost is host-side, so it should apply to every remote pairing regardless of network.

## Reproduction

Pair a desktop client to a remote runtime, open a browser pane, scroll or click. Or measure directly against the pairing socket with an RPC timing client. To watch the spawns directly: sample `pgrep -f agent-browser` during input -- I observed 181 distinct helper PIDs during ~180 input RPCs.

## Numbers (same host, same dev build of main, loopback, p50 of 25 iterations)

| RPC | main | in-process port (PRs to follow) |
|---|---|---|
| `browser.eval` (baseline) | 0.5 ms | 0.4 ms |
| `browser.mouseMove` | 160 ms | 0.5 ms |
| `browser.mouseWheel` | 160 ms | 0.4 ms |
| `browser.keypress` | 160 ms | 0.5 ms |
| one scroll notch (move+wheel, serialized) | 320 ms | 0.7 ms |
| one click (move+down+move+up, serialized) | 637 ms | 1.5 ms |

`browser.mouseClick` -- which already dispatches in process and is what MobileBrowserPane.tsx uses -- is sub-millisecond on the same tab today, so the fast path already exists in the codebase; the desktop pane's event vocabulary just never got it.

## Cause

`agent-browser-bridge.ts` has two implementation styles: `evaluate`, `goto`, `mouseClick`, `pdf` talk to the electron debugger directly (sub-millisecond), and everything interactive goes through `execAgentBrowser`, i.e. one `execFile` of the `agent-browser` binary per event. The helper exists for the accessibility snapshot and `@e1`-style element refs -- coordinate input needs none of that, the helper just forwards these events to `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`/`dispatchKeyEvent` itself.

## Fix

Dispatch coordinate pointer input and table-resolvable keypresses over the electron debugger in process, the way `mouseClick` already does, keeping the helper for element-ref commands and as the fallback for key names a US-layout table can't express. Two focused PRs incoming (pointer input, then keypress). An input-fidelity probe suite passes clean on both branches; main fails its double-click checks and the F5/Insert/ContextMenu key codes, and types nothing at all for non-ASCII printables.
