records.title: fix(browser): route remote terminal links to owning host
records.body:
## Summary

- Route the terminal-only “Orca Browser” action to the paired runtime that owns the terminal instead of calling `shell.openExternal` on the viewing client.
- Require an exact capability-backed runtime/workspace match and fail closed on unknown, mismatched, or incapable owners.
- Keep direct SSH system-browser-only and preserve existing routing for generic remote Markdown/editor links.
- Add focused routing contracts and a headed paired Electron journey covering creation, identity, rendering, explicit activation, close convergence, and continued PTY liveness.

Slack report: https://stablygroup.slack.com/archives/C0AK2T3JEF4/p1786567689897109

## Root cause

Remote terminal links were deliberately advertised as system-browser-only. `openHttpLink()` also rejected every non-local source from managed-browser routing, so selecting a terminal HTTP link fell through to the viewing Electron client’s `shell.openExternal()` path. That policy predated safe host-owned browser creation.

## Design rationale

The fix is scoped to terminal links through an explicit `allowRuntimeInApp` opt-in. It reuses the existing managed-browser creation path, asserts the terminal’s runtime owner at the creation boundary, and only advertises “Orca Browser” when that exact paired runtime exposes the required capability. No RPC schema, stream opcode, host publication, focus policy, polling, retry, timer, or listener changes are introduced.

Alternatives considered:

- Changing all remote HTTP-link routing was broader and would alter Markdown/editor behavior.
- Falling back to client Chrome after a host creation failure would hide ownership errors and recreate the reported bug.
- Adding a new runtime RPC was unnecessary because the existing owner-aware browser creation path already provides authoritative creation and mirroring.

## Reproduction and red/green evidence

Invariant: selecting “Orca Browser” for an HTTP link in a runtime-owned terminal creates exactly one browser page on the owning runtime, exactly one client mirror with matching page identity, and zero client external-browser calls.

- Affected latest main `e4c278eb523`: focused owner-routing oracle failed 6/25 assertions. Runtime OSC, WebLinksAddon, and click-fallback paths invoked the viewing client’s external browser, and owner assertions were absent.
- Candidate: the expanded focused oracle passed 84/84 across six files.
- Candidate headed Electron journey: passed in 32.9s. It proved one host page, one exact client mirror, rendered fixture DOM, explicit tab activation, zero external opens, exact host/client close convergence, and fresh output on the original remote PTY.
- Fix disabled: replacing only the runtime browser opener registration with `registerRuntimeHttpLinkBrowserOpener(null)` made the byte-identical Electron journey fail at the host/client identity barrier; no host-owned browser appeared within 60 seconds.

## Validation

```text
pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts \
  src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/terminal-runtime-host-link-routing.test.ts \
  src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/terminal-link-action-routing.test.ts \
  src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/terminal-link-open-hints.test.ts \
  src/renderer/src/lib/http-link-routing.test.ts \
  src/renderer/src/lib/http-link-modifier-routing.test.ts \
  src/renderer/src/lib/workspace-browser-tab-open.test.ts
# 84 passed

ORCA_E2E_WEB_CLIENT=1 ORCA_E2E_FORCE_HEADFUL=1 \
  pnpm exec playwright test tests/e2e/paired-remote-terminal-browser-link.spec.ts \
  --config tests/playwright.config.ts --project electron-headless --workers=1
# 1 passed

pnpm run typecheck
pnpm run check:reliability-gates
pnpm run check:max-lines-ratchet
pnpm exec oxlint <changed TypeScript files> --deny-warnings
pnpm exec oxfmt --check <changed TypeScript/JSONC files>
git diff --check
```

Final architecture/security, performance/resource/platform, and UX/readiness reviews were clean.

## Risks and gaps

- Live paired-server E2E currently covers macOS. Linux, physical Windows, headless `orca serve`, and multiple simultaneous viewers remain live-topology gaps.
- Direct SSH intentionally remains system-browser-only because it has no paired Orca browser runtime.
- The change preserves the existing asynchronous focus policy; explicitly clicking the browser tab focuses it.
- Mixed-version behavior fails closed when the owning runtime lacks managed-browser capability.

records.title: fix(mobile): resume browser screencast after transport reconnect
records.body:
## ELI5

On mobile, the in-app browser shows the host's browser as a live picture stream. If the connection blips (network drop or relay switch) and reconnects, the picture used to freeze on the last frame — taps still worked, but the image never updated until the tab was reopened. The pane never restarted the picture stream after reconnecting. This PR makes the pane notice the reconnect and restart the stream, so the browser picture comes back to life.

## What Changed

- Adds `useBrowserScreencastReconnectSignal` — a hook returning a number that increments only on a **re**connect (connected → away → connected), derived from the logical RPC client's existing `onStateChange`. It ignores the very first connect.
- `MobileBrowserPane`'s `browser.screencast` subscribe effect now depends on this signal, so on every reconnect the effect tears down and recreates the stream and resets its double-buffer render state.

One new module + one effect-dependency line. No wire/RPC/stream-opcode changes and no new dependencies.

## Why

`MobileBrowserPane`'s screencast subscribe effect depended only on the stable logical client, so it never re-ran on a relay `migrateTo` / direct-socket reconnect. The host tears down `Page.startScreencast` on reconnect and only restarts it on a fresh `browser.screencast` subscribe — which never came. A single missed offscreen `<Image>` `onLoad` across the blip then left `pendingFrameLayerRef` stuck, so every later frame painted only the hidden layer: the display froze on the last decoded frame while input RPCs kept landing. Driving the effect off a reconnect-derived signal is the minimal fix — it reuses the client's own state events and changes no transport behavior.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #14274

## Visual Proof

No visual change. The change recovers a pane that was already frozen; there is no new UI to screenshot. See **Testing** for how the behavior is verified.

## Testing

- [x] Automated tests added/updated
- [ ] I manually tested these changes locally

- `use-browser-screencast-reconnect-signal.test.tsx` — behavioral test (react-test-renderer + mock RPC client): the signal stays `0` on the first connect and on duplicate `connected` states, and increments once per reconnect — including across a `disconnected → connected → disconnected → connected` sequence from a fresh start and across repeated reconnect cycles.
- `mobile-browser-pane-source.test.ts` — source invariant that `MobileBrowserPane` consumes the reconnect signal in its screencast subscribe-effect dependency array.

Behavioral verification of the freeze→resume path needs a paired host and a live transport reconnect (relay migration or direct-socket drop/recover) on a real device/emulator; the unit tests pin the underlying invariant that drives it. Platforms in scope: mobile (iOS/Android). The hook is RN-agnostic and keys off the shared logical client.

Locally: `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm lint` pass, and the screencast test files pass in isolation. The full `mobile/` suite has a pre-existing, unrelated failure in `src/transport/host-store.test.ts` (a zod schema-resolution error in a different subsystem; this PR does not touch it). CI is the source of truth for the full run.

A bounded pending-frame watchdog (force-swap the visible layer if the offscreen `onLoad` is missed outside a reconnect) is intentionally deferred to a follow-up to keep this change small.

## AI Disclosure

Developed with assistance from Claude (Anthropic). The root-cause analysis, approach, and tests were reviewed by the contributor.

## Review

- **Cross-platform:** uses only the logical client's `onStateChange` / `getState` (RN-agnostic); works for both direct-socket recovery and relay `migrateTo`. No platform-specific code.
- **Wire compatibility:** no RPC params, stream frames, or opcodes changed; host-side emission is unchanged, so paired clients/hosts of mixed versions are unaffected.
- **Performance:** no per-frame work added — the signal changes only on a reconnect.
- **UI quality:** no visual change; recovers an already-frozen pane.
- **Security:** no auth/transport surface changed.
- **SSH / remote / folder workspaces:** the fix keys off the logical client's state transitions, which are identical across local, relay, and SSH transports.

records.title: [Bug]: `orca serve` always dies from SIGTRAP on SIGINT/SIGTERM — FATAL electron_browser_main_parts.cc:527 "Failed to shutdown."
records.body:
### Operating system

Linux — Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, x86_64, glibc 2.43.

### Orca version

v1.4.180 — `orca-linux.AppImage` from the GitHub release, extracted with `--appimage-extract` and started through `squashfs-root/AppRun`, the layout `docs/reference/headless-linux-server.md` documents for hosts without FUSE.

### Details

#### Short summary

`orca serve` never exits cleanly. On `SIGINT` — the stop path the CLI help documents ("Runs in the foreground and prints the bound endpoint … Stop it with Ctrl+C") — and equally on `SIGTERM`, the Electron main process aborts with

```
[FATAL:electron/shell/browser/electron_browser_main_parts.cc:527] Failed to shutdown.
```

and dies from `SIGTRAP`: wait status 133, core dumped. The TCP listener is released and the child processes (including the auto-started `Xvfb :99`) are reaped, so at first glance this is only an unclean exit — but on a service-managed headless host it is not cosmetic. Details below.

#### Reproduction

Plain foreground run, no service manager involved. `--no-sandbox` is required because an extracted AppImage has no setuid `chrome-sandbox` and this kernel sets `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`.

```sh
env -u DISPLAY LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 \
  ~/.local/orca/current/AppRun --no-sandbox serve --port 6768 \
  --pairing-address 192.168.1.20 --json &
pid=$!
# wait until {"type":"orca_server_ready", ...} appears
kill -INT "$pid"
wait "$pid"; echo "status: $?"
```

Result, on every attempt:

```
ready ok
--- sending SIGINT ---
Trace/breakpoint trap  (core dumped)
status: 133                      # 128 + SIGTRAP
[FATAL:electron/shell/browser/electron_browser_main_parts.cc:527] Failed to shutdown.
```

`kill -TERM` behaves identically: status 133, same FATAL line.

#### Why this matters beyond an unclean exit

The headless guide's own unit uses `ExecStart=/opt/orca/orca-linux.AppImage serve …`, so every service-managed host meets this on each stop and each restart:

* `systemctl stop` leaves the unit in `Result=core-dump` with `status=5/TRAP`, so a genuine crash is indistinguishable from a normal stop.
* With the guide's `StartLimitIntervalSec=300` / `StartLimitBurst=5`, five ordinary restarts — an updater applying new builds, for instance — trip the start limiter and the server stays down until `systemctl reset-failed`.
* Every stop writes a core dump of a \~200 MB Electron process wherever `kernel.core_pattern` points.
* `RestartPreventExitStatus=3`, documented for the duplicate-profile case, is the only exit status the unit can act on; the shutdown status carries no information.

Workarounds currently in my unit: `Restart=always` rather than `on-failure`, `StartLimitIntervalSec=0`, `LimitCORE=0`, and `systemctl reset-failed` before each restart.

#### Expected behaviour

`orca serve` completes its own shutdown and exits 0 after `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`.

#### Relation to existing issues

This is not stablyai/orca#14067 / stablyai/orca#14071. There the packaged `orca-ide` launcher shell was a signal boundary: the signal never reached the supervisor and the listener stayed alive. Here `AppRun` is executed directly with no launcher shell in front, the signal does reach the Electron process, and the listener is released — the process then fails its own shutdown sequence and traps. Both can be true at once, and fixing the launcher boundary would not change this trap.

records.title: fix(terminal): never wipe a painted pane for a snapshot that carries no image
records.body:
## ELI5

When the app asks the host "give me this terminal's contents" and the host answers with nothing, we used to erase the pane and paint nothing in its place. Now we keep what's on screen.

## What Changed

One guard in the hidden-output restore path (`pty-connection.ts`): skip the replay writes when the snapshot carries no image at all — normal buffer, empty `data`, no `scrollbackAnsi`.

Retry and banner behavior are untouched. An empty image still counts as a successful, non-bannered recovery; this only stops the destructive paint.

## Why

`buildMainModelSnapshotReplayWrites` opens the normal-buffer branch with `ESC[2J ESC[3J ESC[H`. The `ESC[3J` wipes xterm **scrollback**, not just the screen. That is correct when the snapshot carries history to paint in its place. It is destructive when the image is empty: the pane loses everything and gets nothing back.

An empty image reaches that code because `outcome.snapshot` is an object, so it is truthy even when `data === ''`. The nearby "no answer" cases are already handled correctly — a null snapshot becomes `retry-worthy`, and a host-reported `no-serializable-buffer` is classified `retry-worthy` — so this is the one shape of "the host had nothing" that fell through to a wipe.

An empty image is the absence of an answer, not proof the pane is empty. Existing coverage pinned that this case must not banner and must not retry, but nothing pinned what it paints, which is how the wipe survived.

Scoped deliberately to the restore path. The two reattach call sites of the same builder are left alone — they paint into a pane that is being rebuilt anyway, and widening this would make the change harder to reason about.

## Linked Issue

No existing issue — found while reviewing the restore path for #14095 (the two interact; see below). Happy to file one if preferred.

## Visual Proof

`N/A` — no intentional repaint. The change is the absence of a destructive replay; a deterministic headless-terminal oracle verifies the retained screen and scrollback exactly.

## Testing

Added `preserves the painted normal buffer when a successful hidden restore has no image` to `pty-connection.test.ts`. It seeds a real headless normal buffer with eight painted lines and four scrollback rows, drives the production hidden-output restore with empty `data` and `scrollbackAnsi`, then compares all lines, visible lines, and `baseY` with the control path.

Verified red with the guard bypassed: the buffer collapsed to four blank rows with `baseY: 0`. Verified green with the guard restored.

```
pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/remote-hidden-output-restore-outcomes.test.ts src/renderer/src/components/terminal-pane/pty-connection.test.ts --reporter=dot
-> 577 passed

pnpm exec tsc --noEmit -p config/tsconfig.tc.web.json
pnpm exec oxlint <three focused files>
pnpm exec oxfmt --check <three focused files>
-> clean
```

- [x] Automated tests added/updated
- [ ] I manually tested these changes locally — reproducing in-app needs a host that reports a successful empty-image snapshot; the deterministic provider/terminal test is the primary oracle.

## Reliability Contract

- **Invariant (`terminal-output.scrollback-restore`):** a successful normal-buffer hidden restore with no image preserves the already-painted screen and scrollback, while success classification remains non-retrying and non-bannered.
- **Failure source:** a truthy snapshot object with empty `data` reached the normal-buffer replay builder and emitted screen/scrollback clears.
- **Oracle:** exact headless-terminal normal-buffer equality after the production restore path; the existing outcome suite separately pins one request, no legacy fallback, and no loss banner.
- **Gate:** `config/reliability-gates.jsonc` entry `terminal-output.scrollback-restore` (experimental/partial); its focused `pty-connection.test.ts` command and the adjacent outcome suite pass.
- **Provider/platform coverage:** the decision runs after local/daemon/SSH/remote-runtime snapshot normalization and contains no provider, filesystem, shell, path, or platform branch. The modern remote-runtime outcome is covered directly; macOS/Linux/Windows, WSL, SSH, folders, worktrees, and relay wire shapes are unaffected.
- **Performance budget:** three scalar checks on an already-bounded restore path; the empty-image case skips replay construction, two xterm writes, and parsing. No polling, retry, subprocess, allocation-growth, or wake-loop change.
- **Diagnostics:** exact `allLines`, `visibleLines`, and `baseY` diffs identify any future destructive replay; existing lifecycle diagnostics remain unchanged.
- **Residual gap:** no packaged Electron fault-injection journey produces this uncommon host response. The deterministic lower-layer oracle proves the ANSI/buffer behavior without a broad UI flow.

## Relationship to #14095

Independent and reviewable alone, but they interact and **this one should land first or together**. #14095 makes a recovery re-subscribe re-request the retained buffer, so it drives this path far more often than a visibility flip does. Without this guard, a recovery whose snapshot came back empty would wipe the pane — producing the exact blank pane #14095 exists to fix.

Branched off `main`, not off #14095, so the two can merge in either order.

## Review

- **Cross-platform:** renderer-only, no platform-specific code.
- **SSH/remote:** applies to any transport reaching the hidden-output restore; strictly reduces destructive writes.
- **Backwards compatibility:** no wire or IPC change.
- **Performance:** one boolean decision on a rare path; skips work rather than adding it.

records.title: fix(browser): preserve partitioned Google cookies on import
records.body:
## Summary

- replace native Chromium bulk cookie clearing with bounded selective removal
- skip Google-family destination cookies before any destructive operation, so excluded cookies are never cleared or reconstructed
- preserve file, Firefox, Safari, Google exclusion/accounting, and toast behavior

## Electron coverage

A real Electron 43 process creates a partitioned accounts.google.com cookie through Chromium CDP, runs the production selective-removal implementation, and verifies the complete CDP cookie remains unchanged while a stale non-Google cookie is removed. The test also pins the public API gap: Electron Cookies.get exposes the cookie but omits partitionKey, so snapshot/restore cannot preserve partition identity. Linux runs the same fixture through Xvfb with the required sandbox override.

## Performance

This intentionally restores the O(N) bounded-concurrency removal path. The real-Electron measurements recorded for #13966 were 3.6 ms at 100 cookies, 195.2 ms at 1,000, and 2,226.6 ms at 3,300 versus 1.0 ms, 8.8 ms, and 35.8 ms for bulk clear (3.5x to 62.1x slower); correctness takes priority because the bulk path can invalidate active Google sessions.

## Validation

- 60 focused tests across five files, including the real Electron partition test

records.title: [Feature]: Allow closing browser tabs by page ID from the CLI
records.body:
### Problem or use case

External integrations can create an Orca browser tab with `orca tab create --json` and retain its stable `browserPageId`, but `orca tab close` only accepts an index.  Resolving the page to an index before closing introduces a race if the tab list changes.

### Proposed solution

Allow `orca tab close --page <browserPageId>`, matching `orca tab switch --page <browserPageId>` and the existing page-targeting support in the close handler

### Alternatives or additional context

Specifically, this will allow a nice Pi extension, that I recently added Orca support to ( https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-interview-tool/ ), to close the exact Orca tab it created after a form is submitted successfully.  Closing by index isn't safe because tab indexes can change between lookup and close.

records.title: [Feature]: Add Cloudflare Tunnel as a pairing target for the browser access link
records.body:
### Problem or use case

Orca can already serve its full web client to a browser: **Settings → Remote Orca Servers → Share this host** mints an access link, and the runtime serves the bundle itself at `/web-index.html`. But the addresses that link can advertise all assume the browser can already reach the machine — a LAN IP, a Tailscale address, or a tunnel the user wired up by hand.

There is no supported path for "open Orca in a browser from outside my network" without either a VPN or hand-rolled infrastructure.

A Cloudflare Tunnel is the obvious fit — one command, no inbound firewall change, TLS terminated at the edge — but the **Custom address** field cannot actually accept one today:

1. `parseServerShareAddress` rejects `http(s)://` outright, so pasting the URL `cloudflared` prints fails validation with no hint that `wss://` is required instead.
2. Typing the bare hostname is worse, because it silently produces a broken link. A scheme-less address takes the `parseHostOverride` path in `resolveAdvertisedPairingEndpoint` and **inherits the bound local port**, so `foo.trycloudflare.com` gets advertised as `ws://foo.trycloudflare.com:6768` — against a tunnel edge that only answers on 443. The link looks fine and never connects.

So the capability is not merely undiscoverable, it is unreachable through the existing field unless the user happens to know to type `wss://host` by hand.

### Proposed solution

Add **Cloudflare Tunnel** as a first-class choice in "Where will this link be opened?", alongside Another device / This computer only / Custom address:

- Show the exact command to run, using the runtime's real bound port: `cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, with a copy button.
- Accept the `https://….trycloudflare.com` URL `cloudflared` actually prints, normalizing it to `wss://` internally so the port-inheritance trap above cannot happen.
- Reject loopback, tailnet, and LAN hostnames in that field, since a tunnel fronting those produces a link the outside world cannot open.
- Warn when the hostname is a quick tunnel, because those are regenerated on every `cloudflared` restart and silently invalidate a previously generated link.
- Reuse the existing device pairing, E2EE, and revocable access grants unchanged.

This also makes the browser client usable remotely for the first time: the tunnel terminates TLS, so the page is `https://` and the socket is `wss://`, which avoids the mixed-content rejection in `isMixedContentWebSocket` that blocks the plain-LAN `http://` + `ws://` pairing.

### Alternatives or additional context

- Relaxing `parseServerShareAddress` to accept `https://` would fix (1) but not (2), and would leave the user to work out that a tunnel needs a scheme at all.
- #12535 asks for the same thing on the **Orca Mobile** pairing surface (Orca Relay / LAN). This issue is the desktop **Share this host** surface, which that one does not cover. Worth deciding whether they should be tracked together.
- No native Cloudflare integration or automatic provisioning is needed. The user runs `cloudflared` themselves; Orca only needs to accept the URL it prints and advertise it correctly.

records.title: fix(browser): disable unsupported FedCM
records.body:
## ELI5

Orca's embedded browser claimed it could use Google's newer FedCM sign-in even though Electron could not finish that flow. Google therefore skipped the working popup route; Orca now truthfully hides that unsupported capability so Google uses its popup fallback.

## What Changed

- Disable Chromium's `FedCm` feature process-wide before sessions or WebContents are created.
- Preserve and deduplicate existing `disable-features` values, including the existing `IntensiveWakeUpThrottling` opt-out.
- Add focused unit coverage for switch composition and a real Electron webview E2E oracle for capability exposure, popup creation, opener connectivity, and messaging.

## Why

Electron exposed `IdentityCredential` and `IdentityProvider`, so legacy Google `gapi.auth2` selected FedCM; the token request then failed and no popup was attempted. Capability exposure is Chromium-owned process state, so early main-process configuration is the authoritative boundary.

A renderer property-deletion shim was rejected because it is frame- and timing-dependent and cannot cover every guest, popup, or offscreen page authoritatively. Permission/session blocking was rejected because it still advertises FedCM, which is the signal that diverts gapi into the broken path.

## Linked Issue

Fixes #12854

## Visual Proof

Candidate full Orca view showing both FedCM capability flags false and the popup fallback path:

![Orca FedCM fallback oracle](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bb655bda-c4bd-4732-adfc-2c7687708f0b)

Visible popup fallback:

![Popup fallback](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2843c17f-8e5c-40df-8fc4-a7d372e648a2)

The production UI is unchanged; these images show the preserved popup interaction and backing oracle state.

## Testing

Final merge base: `09ec516ae50b7b83fa65343d9ad96159e3fe71fc`

Exact oracle command, unchanged across runs:

```bash
pnpm exec electron-vite build --mode e2e
SKIP_BUILD=1 pnpm exec playwright test tests/e2e/browser-fedcm-fallback.spec.ts \
  --config tests/playwright.config.ts --project electron-headless --workers=1
```

- Affected final main / candidate with the startup call disabled: **RED**. Both constructors were present, the page selected `fedcm-selected`, and no popup WebContents appeared; three independent assertions failed.
- Candidate `6422233186`: **GREEN**, `1 passed`. Both constructors were absent, the page selected `popup-live`, the popup URL/title and live `window.opener` were verified, and the popup delivered `postMessage` to its opener.
- Candidate with only `disableUnsupportedChromiumFeatures()` reverted/disabled on the final merge base: **RED** with the same failures; restoring the exact reviewed source returned **GREEN**, `1 passed`.

Local validation on macOS:

- `pnpm run typecheck:node`
- `pnpm exec vitest run src/main/startup/configure-process.test.ts src/main/browser/browser-manager.test.ts src/main/browser/popup-origin-bar-window.test.ts` — 121 passed

The full view and popup were visibly checked; CDP independently verified URL/title, `window.opener !== null`, and opener `postMessage`. Only worker-launched processes were cleaned up. A live Google credential/client-ID exchange was not run because no credential was available.

## AI Disclosure

OpenAI Codex assisted with reproduction, implementation, testing, and review under human-directed issue ownership.

## Review

Fresh architecture/platform/readiness and performance/resource/test-reliability review rounds were clean. Security/UX validation was proportional because there is no UI source change; existing popup security suites and the real popup/opener oracle passed. Elegance review found each hunk necessary and the centralized switch-merging helper the smallest durable implementation.

The switch is startup-only and applies consistently to macOS, Linux, and Windows. It changes no RPC/wire format, Git/provider behavior, SSH, WSL, folder-workspace, worktree, mobile, or paired-runtime contract. Linux E2E GPU fallback remains intact, and the implementation adds no renderer hot path, timers, listeners, polling, or persistent resources.

records.title: Fix paired remote HTML browser ownership and focus
records.body:
## Summary

- Route paired HTML browser creation to the runtime that owns the worktree, preventing a competing local browser identity.
- Preserve the requesting client's right-side preview placement while mirroring the host-authoritative browser page.
- Open the HTML eye-button preview in the background: the editor remains active until the user explicitly clicks the browser.
- Keep ordinary New Browser Tab creation focused with its existing bounded focus guard.

## Issue

https://linear.app/stably/issue/STA-3872/unable-to-open-html-files-in-remote-server

## Reproduction and authority

**Invariant:** one paired-client HTML preview creates one browser page on the worktree-owning runtime and one client mirror. It remains in the requested split without taking editor focus; an explicit browser click activates it on client and host; closing it preserves the editor and terminal.

**Observed failure:** the split appeared briefly and collapsed, two blank browser tabs could appear, and clicking them could return to the Claude/terminal tab.

**Authority:** the worktree-owning runtime owns browser creation and page identity. The requesting client owns only its local split placement and focus choice.

Current byte-identical Electron oracle: `tests/e2e/paired-remote-html-browser-focus.spec.ts` (SHA-256 `2ec1dcf101f922c86a9e1e20c5a0cb785e478fd2c1fe0c6c9d89b43dd4048dd1`).

- Latest main `346e59c879`: **red** in 11.8s; two client HTML browser workspaces appeared.
- Candidate: **green**; one host page, one client workspace/tab, stable split, rendered DOM, editor retained focus after creation, explicit click focused the browser, and browser-only close converged.
- Candidate with only `focusOnCreate: false` disabled: **red** in 12.3s; preview creation activated the browser instead of retaining editor focus.

The earlier byte-identical oracle (`5806b23f…`) separately proved the owning-runtime seam: affected main was red, the candidate was green, and disabling only owning-runtime routing was red with duplicate client workspaces.

## Root cause and design

The paired client previously opened/staged browser state locally even though the remote runtime owned the worktree and browser page. Host publication then introduced a second identity and host group placement, allowing reconciliation to duplicate, collapse, or refocus the client surface.

The fix follows ownership:

1. Paired HTML opens execute `browser.tabCreate` on the worktree owner.
2. A bounded client placement record maps that host page into the viewer's requested split.
3. Side previews pass `focusOnCreate: false`, so the host creates them inactive and the client records no focus intent or temporary listener.
4. Exact-snapshot replay handles publication arriving before the create response reveals the canonical page ID.
5. An explicit browser click uses the existing activation path and becomes authoritative on client and host.

Ordinary New Browser Tab actions retain their existing focused-create behavior and bounded listener. No new wire field, opcode, RPC method, retry protocol, deterministic page ID, receipt ledger, TTL, timer, or polling loop is introduced.

## Alternatives considered

- Keep provisional local creation and deduplicate after host adoption: rejected because two authorities still exist during the race.
- Auto-focus side previews and guard every intervening navigation: rejected for this path because background creation is simpler and matches the approved UX.
- Add durable create receipts/retries or deterministic requested page IDs: rejected as broader protocol machinery with ambiguous-success and collision risks.
- Remove focus from every browser creation: rejected because normal New Browser Tab should remain focused; the option is scoped to the eye-button preview.

## Risks and compatibility

- Behavior change: paired remote eye-button previews no longer auto-focus. Users must click the preview to interact with it; this is intentional.
- Local HTML previews retain their existing auto-focus behavior; this PR scopes the UX change to the reported paired-remote path.
- Placement state is capped at 128 and cleared on adoption, failure, worktree teardown, or environment teardown.
- No OS path/shell behavior or wire shape changes. macOS, Linux, Windows, folder workspaces, Git worktrees, SSH, WSL, and mixed client/host versions keep their existing protocol surface.
- Live paired validation covers macOS. Linux, physical Windows, and rendererless `orca serve` remain explicit topology gaps; no Windows-specific primitive is causal here.

records.title: perf(renderer): keep remote snapshot batches linear
records.body:
## The one-sentence version

When a remote host sends updates for 1,200 workspaces at once, Orca used to photocopy the entire filing cabinet 1,200 times — once per workspace. Now it photocopies it once, writes all 1,200 updates into that copy, and files it. **52× faster at 1,200 workspaces.**

---

## Start here: what is actually happening

A remote Orca host tells your client about its workspaces through `session.tabs` snapshots — one per workspace, describing that workspace's terminals, browser pages, editors, and agent panes.

On reconnect or replay, the host does not send these one at a time. It sends a **batch**: every workspace at once.

The renderer stores these in maps keyed by workspace. Those maps are immutable — the standard React/Zustand rule that you never edit state in place, you make a modified copy. Reconciling one snapshot means copying the map, changing one entry, and swapping the copy in.

That rule is correct. Applying it **once per workspace inside a batch** is what was expensive.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph BEFORE["Before — one full copy per workspace"]
        direction TB
        B1["Snapshot 1 arrives"] --> B2["Copy ALL maps (1,200 entries)"] --> B3["Edit entry 1"] --> B4["Swap in"]
        B4 --> B5["Snapshot 2 arrives"] --> B6["Copy ALL maps again"] --> B7["Edit entry 2"] --> B8["Swap in"]
        B8 --> B9["... ×1,200"]
    end

    subgraph AFTER["After — one copy for the whole batch"]
        direction TB
        A1["Batch of 1,200 arrives"] --> A2["Copy ALL maps ONCE (a draft)"]
        A2 --> A3["Edit entry 1 in the draft"] --> A4["Edit entry 2 in the draft"] --> A5["... edit entry 1,200"]
        A5 --> A6["Swap the finished draft in ONCE"]
    end
```

The cost of the old shape is quadratic: copying an N-entry map N times is N² work. That is why the numbers get dramatically worse as workspace count grows rather than just proportionally worse.

## Measured

Synthetic reconnect fixture, one ready remote terminal and one working agent per workspace, prior sequential reducer vs. the batch path on the same machine:

| Workspaces | Before | After | Speedup |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 400 | 86.5 ms | 6.8 ms | **12.8×** |
| 800 | 338.5 ms | 10.6 ms | **31.8×** |
| 1,200 | 811.1 ms | 15.5 ms | **52.5×** |

Note the shape: workspaces triple, old cost grows ~9×, new cost grows ~2×. Quadratic became linear.

811 ms is a visibly frozen window. That is a single reconnect to one busy host.

The second change is related: looking up "which agent panes belong to this tab?" used to scan every agent pane in the app, once per workspace. Those are now indexed by owner, so an agent-heavy batch stops re-scanning globally.

## Where this runs in production

- The initial `session.tabs.listAll` when you connect to a remote host.
- The batched `snapshots` stream event — i.e. **every remote reconnect and replay**, for every paired runtime environment.

Reconnects are exactly when a user is already waiting.

---

## The behavior change you should actually review

Everything above is a pure speedup. This part is not, and it deserves a decision.

`updateHostSessionTabIdMappings` runs on **every** snapshot apply. It clears the local→host tab id mappings belonging to a worktree. Previously it did that by **string prefix match**:

```
delete every key starting with `${environmentId}:${worktreeId}:`
```

Worktree ids are built as `${repoId}::${absolutePath}` (`src/shared/pty-session-id-format.ts:15`). On POSIX, **absolute paths may legally contain a colon.**

So consider two sibling worktrees:

| Worktree | Its id | Its mapping keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | `repo::/w` | `env:repo::/w:<tabId>` |
| B | `repo::/w:2` | `env:repo::/w:2:<tabId>` |

Every key belonging to **B** also starts with the prefix computed for **A**. So whenever worktree A published a snapshot, it silently wiped worktree B's tab mappings.

**What that looked like to a user:** a wiped mapping makes tab close fall back to `toHostSessionTabId(terminalTabId)`. The comment already in `terminal-tab-actions.ts:136` describes the symptom — close "silently fell back to a local-only prune and the host's next snapshot re-added the tab." In other words: *you close a tab, and it comes back.* Reordering and moving tabs hit the same fallback (`web-runtime-session.ts:768`).

This PR replaces the prefix scan with an exact `(environmentId, worktreeId)` index, so **only** the worktree that actually published gets cleared.

**This is a bug fix, not a regression** — but it is a real behavior change and it should be merged as one, not waved through as "pure perf." Less reachable on Windows, where colons are not legal inside path components.

## Compatibility

- **Renderer-only.** Two files, both under `src/renderer/src/runtime/`.
- **No wire involvement whatsoever**: no RPC, no stream opcode, no protocol version, no persisted schema. `hostSessionTabIdByLocalKey` is purely client-side bookkeeping.
- **Old and new remote hosts are unaffected.** They send byte-identical snapshots either way; only how the client indexes them locally changed. A client on this build talking to a host on any older build behaves exactly as a client without it, minus the sibling-wipe bug.

## Correctness argument for the batch rewrite

The risk in a copy-on-write draft is a read seeing a value that a *later* write in the same batch was supposed to produce, or vice versa. This was checked explicitly:

- Every read of the 20 draft-owned record fields happens **before** that record's first write within a snapshot pass.
- `writableWebSessionTabsRecord(state, k, undefined)` returns `{...(state[k] ?? {})}` — identical to the inline spreads it replaces, so the single-snapshot path is provably unchanged.
- The `agentPaneKeysByTabId` index is built before the first mutation of `agentStatusByPaneKey`, and is kept in sync on every add and delete.
- Key insertion order of the resulting records is unchanged.
- Per-snapshot reducer order, scalar/array semantics, and focus/close/handoff side effects are preserved.

One invariant is load-bearing and worth naming: `writableWebSessionTabsRecord` mutates its `state` argument when a batch context is present. That is safe **only** because `applyWebSessionTabsSnapshots` hands it a shallow copy `{ ...state }` and every read precedes its write. If someone later passes the real store state, this breaks quietly. A guard test for that invariant would be a reasonable follow-up.

`activeGroupIdByWorktree` now routes through a value-equality gate, so a patch that changed identity but not value is no longer emitted. Content is the same; one redundant notification disappears.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`
- [x] `ORCA_CROSS_VERSION_BASELINE_REF=v1.4.177 pnpm test` — 4,603 files passed, 15 skipped; 49,334 tests passed, 97 skipped
- [x] `pnpm build`
- [x] Renderer runtime suite — 67 files, 634 tests passed

The regression test compares the final batch result against repeated immutable single-snapshot reconciliation across terminal, agent-status, browser, editor, removal/replacement, and provisional-handoff cases — i.e. it asserts the fast path and the slow path agree, rather than asserting the fast path's own output. Also covered: input immutability, empty-batch identity, and selective same-environment mapping teardown.

The baseline ref is pinned because an unrelated repository tag named `v799` currently outranks the intended release tag during automatic baseline selection.

The temporary benchmark harness used for the table above was removed from the diff.

records.title: fix(browser): exclude Google cookies from imports - direct sign-in is the only Google path (STA-3811)
records.body:
## Summary

STA-3811: cookie imports never touch the Google cookie family. Unconditional, on every import path (native Chromium, file, Firefox, Safari) — an import writes no google.com-family cookie and removes none, regardless of what is already in the jar.

Why the general rule instead of a provenance check: an in-app Google sign-in is the only Google session that survives, because transplanted cookies get flagged by anti-fraud and expire within ~1h. So there is never a case where importing Google cookies beats what is already there — a live in-app session is more valuable, and an older *imported* session is worthless either way. Distinguishing the two only justified machinery (a cookies-changed provenance observer, an import-suppression window, provenance-conditional staged-DB handling) that the general policy makes unnecessary.

The exclusion is a named list, not new machinery:

```ts
// browser-cookie-import-policy.ts
const NON_TRANSPLANTABLE_DOMAINS = ['google.com'] as const
```

Criterion: sites with server-side device-bound sessions that reject transplanted cookies. A future site is one entry, not a new code path. `isNonTransplantableCookieDomain()` matches the registrable family (`google.com` and `*.google.com`, not `withgoogle.com` / `google.com.evil.example`); `NON_TRANSPLANTABLE_HOST_KEY_SQL` is derived from the same list for the Chromium `host_key` column.

Where it applies:

- **Incoming snapshot** — Google rows are dropped before anything is written, on both the native decrypt loop and the validated-cookie path. Counted in `skippedCookies`.
- **Clear/replace step** — the native path swaps `clearStorageData({storages:['cookies']})` for `removeAllCookiesExcept(...)`; the `replace-imported-domains` path never sees Google in its scope because the exclusion runs before the scope is computed. The staged restart-fallback DB uses `DELETE FROM cookies WHERE NOT (<google>)` so a cold-restart replay does not undo the exemption — it is the same clear step, just deferred.

`isGoogleSourceBoundCookie` (SIDCC / STRP / AEC) is kept but is now subsumed for google.com by the broader exclusion; it stays as the general rotation-only rule for any family added without a full exclusion, and is still directly unit-tested.

**Disclosure (same PR — it discloses the policy).** Both cookie-import menus carry a one-line muted caption so the exclusion is visible at the moment of decision: the browser toolbar Import Cookies submenu and the Settings browser-profile import dropdown. Copy: *Google requires signing in directly - imports skip it.* Rendered with `DropdownMenuLabel` (`text-[11px] text-muted-foreground`, `font-normal`) per `docs/STYLEGUIDE.md`, added through the localization catalog like neighboring strings. No confirmation dialog.

## Screenshots

Text-only addition; caption appears at the top of both import menus.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint` (full gate: oxlint, native + type-aware code quality, reliability gates, max-lines ratchet, localization catalog/extraction/coverage)
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`
- [x] Changed-code quality gate: `0 new findings` across 9 changed files (code quality, type-aware, React Doctor)
- [x] `pnpm test` — `vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/main/browser/` (34 files, 598 passed), plus `src/renderer/src/i18n src/renderer/src/components/settings/browser` (21 files, 159 passed) and the new disclosure suite
- [ ] `pnpm build`
- [x] Mutation-resistant: emptying `NON_TRANSPLANTABLE_DOMAINS` flips **9** tests red across the predicate, the SQL, the file path, and the native path. Deleting the caption JSX flips the render test red.

Coverage added:

- `browser-cookie-import-google-exclusion.test.ts` — file path: import with Google cookies present writes none and removes none, whether the existing Google cookies came from an in-app sign-in or an older import; native path: no wholesale `clearStorageData`, live Google cookies survive, live Google rows stay in the staged restart DB.
- `browser-cookie-import-policy.test.ts` — registrable-family matching incl. lookalikes, the `host_key` SQL run against a real SQLite table, the deliberate youtube.com exemption, `removeAllCookiesExcept` semantics and failure aggregation.
- `browser-cookie-import-google-disclosure.test.tsx` — both menus render the caption; catalog entries match the copy on both surfaces.

## AI Review Report

Reviewed both import pipelines end to end for the new invariant (never write, never remove). Risks checked: (1) suffix confusion — the predicate normalizes and requires the registrable family, asserted at both the TS and SQL layers against `withgoogle.com` and `google.com.evil.example`; (2) the replace-scope path — the exclusion must run *before* `replaceCookiesForImportedDomains` computes its scope, or Google would be cleared and not repopulated, so the ordering is asserted by a test that fails if the filter moves; (3) the deferred clear — the staged DB replaces the whole live DB at cold start, so leaving `DELETE FROM cookies` unqualified would silently reintroduce the wipe one restart later; covered by a staged-rows assertion; (4) `skippedCookies` accounting stays exact on both paths so the existing toast copy remains truthful. Cross-platform: main-process only, no shortcuts or labels, no new paths; the predicates and SQL are platform-independent; existing per-platform decryption is untouched. Session mocks in three suites gained `cookies.get` because the clear step now enumerates the jar instead of calling `clearStorageData`.

## Security Audit

No new IPC surface, no command execution, no new file reads. The SQL predicate is built from a module-level literal list, never from user or cookie data. The selective clear reads only cookie name/domain/path/secure and reuses the existing removal-URL construction, so it cannot widen removal scope beyond what `clearStorageData` already did. Fail-closed behavior preserved: removal failures aggregate and abort the import through the existing error path. Net effect is strictly less destructive than before — one fewer domain family is ever deleted.

## Notes

- **Behavior change:** imports no longer carry Google cookies at all. Users who want Google in Orca sign in directly in the browser pane; the caption says so in both import menus. Clearing cookies (Settings → trash icon) is unchanged and still removes Google state.
- **Scope:** the `google.com` registrable family only. `youtube.com` (incl. `accounts.youtube.com`) is deliberately **not** excluded — YouTube accepts a transplanted session and re-issues its cookies via the sign-in relay, so excluding it would silently drop imports users asked for. Documented at the list and locked in by a test.
- **Dropped from the earlier revision:** the Google-provenance state machine on `browserSessionRegistry` (persisted `in-app` / `imported` marker in `browser-session-meta.json`), its `cookies` `changed` sign-in observer, the `beginCookieImport`/`endCookieImport` suppression window, and `browser-google-session-protection.ts`. None of it is needed once imports never touch Google.
- Toast copy from #13666 is untouched and still reads correctly under this policy; the two PRs' files are disjoint.

records.title: fix(browser): offer one-click recovery from Google CookieMismatch (STA-3811)
records.body:
## Summary

STA-3811 fix 3/4: after a cookie import, navigating Google sign-in can land on `accounts.google.com/CookieMismatch` — Google's dead-end page telling the user to clear cookies manually, which they can't easily do from inside the embedded browser. Orca now detects a committed main-frame navigation onto that page and **offers** the fix instead of performing it: a toast says sign-in hit a stale-cookie error and carries a **Reset Google cookies** action. Nothing is cleared until the user clicks it.

- On the click (and only then): clear the partition's **google.com-family cookies only** (every other site's session survives), then navigate the tab back into the flow — the flow's `continue` URL when it stays on Google over https, else `https://accounts.google.com/`.
- Detection at `did-navigate` (commit), not `did-start-navigation` — a sign-in nav that 302s into CookieMismatch never re-fires `did-start-navigation` with the mismatch URL.
- Prompt throttle: at most one toast per partition per 2-minute window (session-keyed WeakMap), plus a per-tab toast id, so a recurring mismatch or several tabs in one partition can't stack toasts. The destructive step needs no loop guard now that it is user-initiated.
- The navigation target comes from the mismatch URL stashed in main, never from renderer input; the IPC handler only accepts a `browserPageId` string from the trusted renderer.
- Applies in every UA mode (clean-Firefox and native alike) — the mismatch is about the cookie jar, not the presented identity.
- Cookie import code untouched.

## Screenshots

No new surface: a standard sonner warning toast using the existing action-toast idiom ("Google sign-in hit a stale-cookie error" / "Reset Orca's Google cookies to sign in again — other sites are unaffected." / action **Reset Google cookies**), single-line description (sonner collapses newlines), `duration: Infinity` like Orca's other actionable toasts so the offer waits for the user.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint` (oxlint clean; `audit:code-quality:native`, `audit:code-quality:type-aware`, and all three localization verifies pass) plus `check:code-quality:changed` — 0 new native / type-aware / React Doctor findings across the 10 changed files
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` (non-incremental `typecheck:tsc` — node, cli, and web projects clean)
- [x] `pnpm test` — targeted with explicit `--config config/vitest.config.ts`: `browser-google-cookie-mismatch-recovery.test.ts`, the new `browser-manager-google-cookie-mismatch.test.ts` and `browser-google-cookie-mismatch-handler.test.ts`, `browser-manager.test.ts`, `browser-manager-grab.test.ts`, `ipc/browser.test.ts` (151 tests), and all 42 browser-pane renderer suites (332 tests)
- [ ] `pnpm build` — left to CI; change is plain TS modules with no packaging impact
- [x] Tests cover: the detection predicate (host/path/scheme edges incl. `accounts.google.com.evil.example`), the recovery-target rules, the scoped clear (Google cookies removed with correct removal URLs, github/example cookies retained, per-cookie failure tolerated), detection prompting the renderer **without** clearing or navigating, one prompt per partition across repeats and tabs, independent partitions prompting separately, the user-action path clearing only Google cookies and navigating to the continue target, and refusal to clear for a tab with no pending detection (incl. a repeated accept)

## AI Review Report

Self-reviewed the diff for: silent destructive behavior (removed — clearing is now reachable only through `recoverFromGoogleCookieMismatch`, called by one IPC handler behind `isTrustedBrowserRenderer`), redirect-vs-start-navigation detection gap (detection stays at commit), open-redirect via the `continue` param (only https Google-family targets honored, and the URL comes from main's own stash), suffix-confusion domains (`normalizeCookieDomain` + exact/`.google.com`-suffix match, covered by tests), replayed accepts (the stash is consumed, so a second click is a no-op), and destroyed-guest races (checked before and after the clear). Per-guest state is dropped in `cleanupGuestPolicyAttachment` and `unregisterAll`, so nothing leaks past a process swap or teardown. Cross-platform: no platform-dependent code — URL parsing, Electron cookies API, and IPC behave identically on macOS/Linux/Windows; no shortcuts, labels, paths, or shell usage touched.

## Security Audit

The renderer can now ask main to clear cookies, so the handler validates the sender (`isTrustedBrowserRenderer`) and the argument shape, and takes only a `browserPageId` — no URL, domain, or cookie name crosses the boundary. Main refuses unless that tab has a mismatch it detected itself, and derives the navigation target from the stashed mismatch URL restricted to https Google-family hosts. Cookie deletion is scoped by normalized domain (rejects `user@google.com`, `google.com.evil.example`, etc. via the existing hardened `normalizeCookieDomain`) and only ever *removes* cookies in the guest's own partition — no values are read out or transmitted. The main→renderer notification is a `browserPageId` payload only.

## Notes

Offscreen/remote-driven guests with no attached renderer simply get no prompt (and no clear) — the page behaves exactly as it does today. If the clear partially fails, the navigation still runs; a persisting mismatch then shows Google's page again with the offer available after the throttle window, so behavior degrades to the status quo, never worse.

records.title: fix(browser): keep one identity across hosts during Google sign-in (STA-3811)
records.body:
## Summary

Direct in-app Google sign-in (the #12884 Firefox-UA-on-auth-hosts fix) reaches the genuine password page but, for some accounts, greys out with a frozen progress bar after clicking **Next** and never advances (STA-3811). Root cause: a **cross-host identity inconsistency**. While the auth document is on screen, `applyGoogleAuthUserAgent` sets the WebContents UA to Firefox — so `navigator.userAgent` **and the default request `User-Agent` header for every subresource/XHR** become Firefox, including requests to non-auth Google hosts (`www.gstatic.com`, `play.google.com`, the sign-in challenge endpoints). The header layer (`setupClientHintsOverride`) only Firefox-izes requests whose **URL** is an auth host; for every other request it rewrote `sec-ch-ua` to Chrome brands. The result on the wire: **Firefox UA paired with Chrome client hints** on each cross-host request — a sharper bot tell than either signal alone, and a plausible cause of Google's anti-abuse flow stalling the challenge (a hang) rather than issuing a clean rejection.

This is fix **1/4** for STA-3811 (the correctness prerequisite). It does **not** touch cookie-import code (owned by other workers).

### Fix
In `setupClientHintsOverride`, when a request already carries the Firefox auth UA (regardless of destination host), **strip all client hints** (real Firefox sends none) instead of rewriting them to Chrome. The UA and hint surfaces then tell one consistent Firefox story for the whole sign-in flow. Gated on the same `googleAuthOverride` flag as the auth-host switch, so:
- **Imported-native profiles** never install the Firefox switch → branch stays inert.
- **Non-Google sites** carry the cleaned-Chrome UA, not Firefox → they still get Chrome hints, so the Cloudflare/Turnstile default is untouched.

### Evidence
Extended `tests/tools/google-signin-ua-probe.cjs` with `app-current` / `app-fixed` modes that mirror the shipped code exactly and log per-request identity (incoming vs outgoing UA + hints) for **all** requests. On the real `accounts.google.com` load:

| mode | cross-host `firefox-ua-with-chrome-hints` mismatches |
| --- | --- |
| `app-current` (shipped) | **18** (www.gstatic.com, fonts.gstatic.com, play.google.com) |
| `app-fixed` (this PR) | **0** — cross-host requests present a clean Firefox identity, no client hints |

## Screenshots

No visual change.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm typecheck` (tsconfig.node) — clean
- [x] `pnpm oxlint` (changed files) — clean
- [x] Changed-file vitest: `src/main/browser/` — 33 files / 591 tests pass, incl. 3 new cases (strip-on-Firefox-cross-host, keep-Chrome-on-non-Google, inert-when-googleAuthOverride-false)
- [x] `oxfmt --check` — clean
- [ ] `pnpm build` (not run in this worker)

## AI Review Report

Reviewed the request-header override path for scope creep and layer disagreement. Confirmed the new branch keys off the outgoing `User-Agent` header value (case-insensitive), which faithfully reflects the WebContents UA override for subresources — verified empirically via the probe (incoming UA = Firefox on gstatic/play.google.com requests). Cross-platform: the Firefox UA's platform token is chosen by `process.platform` (unchanged); the fix itself is a platform-agnostic string comparison, so macOS/Linux/Windows behave identically. No shortcuts, paths, or shell behavior touched.

## Security Audit

No command execution, path handling, secrets, or IPC changes. Input handling is limited to reading one request header and comparing it to a fixed UA constant, then conditionally deleting `sec-ch-ua*` headers. The change only ever **removes** headers on the Firefox-auth path — it cannot widen what a non-Google site sees. No follow-up needed.

## Notes

Fix 1/4 for STA-3811. Remaining follow-ups (separate tickets/PRs, not this change): in-app sign-in ordering vs cookie imports, and the import-preserves-in-app-Google-session product change. A residual JS-layer inconsistency (`navigator.userAgentData` still reports Chromium brands under the Firefox UA) is out of scope here; Google's initial checks tolerate it (the QA reaches the real password page), and the header-layer wire identity is the surface implicated in the submit hang.

records.title: Avoid synchronous webview URL IPC during browser pane render
records.body:
## Summary
- derive browser toolbar, external-open, and artifact URLs from the per-page live URL cache instead of synchronous webview getters during React render
- seed the cache from the initial persisted URL without overwriting later committed navigation, while retaining existing navigation, reload, failure, popup isolation, and explicit-destroy cleanup behavior
- add an architectural render boundary regression and lifecycle cache coverage

## Performance
- before: the supplied renderer profile attributed 2,135.361 ms of sampled synchronous URL IPC to the browser render path (2,092.265 ms in external URL resolution and 43.096 ms in current URL resolution), with two synchronous guest queries per render
- after: an Electron CDP benchmark forced 30 browser-page renders over 334.4 ms and instrumented 0 webview URL getter calls (0 per render)

## Validation
- 340 browser-pane and BrowserTab tests passed across 44 files
- renderer typecheck and max-lines ratchet passed
- native and type-aware changed-file lint passed; the aggregate changed-code wrapper itself could not parse the Node 26 engine warning because this checkout requires Node 24
- Electron CDP validation attached to the exact child checkout identity, loaded Example Domain visibly, preserved the URL and enabled external-open across reload, and rendered the local connection failure with the attempted URL and recovery actions

## Residual risk
The original concurrent main-process persistence workload is not deterministic to replay, but the synchronous guest call is structurally absent from the guarded render slice and runtime instrumentation observed zero calls across forced renders.

records.title: perf(runtime): hydrate lineage snapshot once
records.body:
## Summary

- hydrate inferred worktree lineage once when serving `worktree.lineageList`
- read both lineage maps from the same hydrated snapshot
- preserve the standalone lineage methods and the existing RPC contract

## ELI5

The remote Orca server keeps two views of the same workspace family tree. Previously, one request effectively said: update the family tree, return view one, update it again, then return view two.

Now it updates the family tree once and returns both views from that snapshot. Callers receive the same answer, but the server avoids a redundant lineage pass on every request. The old second pass usually reused the short-lived worktree cache, so this PR does not claim that it removes a second Git scan.

## Screenshots

No visual change.

## Compatibility

- no RPC names, parameters, response shapes, or stream content changed
- mixed client and remote-server versions remain supported
- standalone lineage callers keep their existing behavior
- SSH hosts and folder workspaces use the same hydration path as before

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`

records.title: [perf-remote] perf(renderer): park hidden remote browser screencasts
records.body:
## Summary

Parks remote-browser screencasts when the Orca window stays hidden:

- shares the emulator stream's reactive window-visibility gate with remote browser panes
- waits 500ms before parking so a quick app switch does not reconnect the stream
- unsubscribes the existing screencast while preserving the remote page, last frame, and page handle
- resumes immediately when the window becomes visible or real input proves macOS visibility is stale
- preserves the existing active/inactive-pane gate, explicit reconnect behavior, retry cancellation, and lifecycle-generation fencing

### ELI5

A remote browser is a little like a video call with a browser running on another computer. Before, Orca kept asking that computer to take, compress, send, and decode new pictures even while the Orca window was minimized or covered up. Now Orca hangs up only the video feed after half a second. It leaves the browser page and its last picture in place, then reconnects the feed when you come back instead of creating a new browser page.

This is structural hardening for the observed remote-host slowdown. It is not presented as a confirmed root-cause fix for the v1.4.177 to v1.4.178 regression.

## Screenshots

No visual change.

## Work bounds

| Scenario | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active remote browser while Orca stays hidden | Screencast remains subscribed indefinitely | Unsubscribe is requested after the 500ms grace |
| Each delivered frame | Host capture/JPEG work, network transfer, renderer buffer copy + Blob/object URL + image decode + three React state-write calls | No new delivered-frame work after renderer teardown |
| Quick hide/show under 500ms | Stream remains live | Unchanged; the timer is canceled and no reconnect occurs |
| Return after parking an established page | N/A | Reuses the stored remote page handle and starts one replacement stream; no `browser.tabCreate` |
| Retained hidden state | Live stream plus current frame | One last-frame object URL and the existing remote page |

The parked request is the existing JPEG-quality-70 `browser.screencast`, capped at 3840x2160 and configured for every second compositor frame. The bound applies per mounted active remote-browser pane. It does not park the remote page's JavaScript, session-tab mirrors, native-chat streams, file watchers, or other runtime subscriptions.

Revealing an established pane performs the existing two `browser.tabShow` calls, one `status.get`, and one new screencast subscription. It does not create another page.

The 500ms value is the requested grace. Chromium may schedule a hidden renderer timer later because background throttling remains enabled. Once cleanup runs, renderer callbacks and tokens are retired immediately; the host's existing `Page.stopScreencast` command retains its bounded 8-second debugger timeout.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`
- [x] `pnpm test` with `ORCA_CROSS_VERSION_BASELINE_REF=v1.4.177`: 4,596 files / 49,269 tests passed; 16 files / 99 tests skipped
- [ ] `pnpm build` — full native packaging not run; `pnpm build:electron-vite` passed
- [x] Added or updated high-quality tests that would catch regressions

Additional checks:

- focused remote stream + visibility suites: 52/52 tests passed
- deterministic tests cover 499ms quick return, the 500ms park boundary, initial hidden mount, inactive pane, stale macOS visibility recovery after a completed park, cleanup, same-page reopen, one `browser.tabCreate`, and restored `live` status
- `pnpm check:code-quality:changed`
- `pnpm check:react-doctor:changed`
- `pnpm check:max-lines-ratchet`
- `git diff --check`
- production Electron main/preload/renderer build

The unpinned suite can select an unrelated repository-history tag named `v799`, whose tree predates this repository layout. The full run therefore pins the intended release baseline, `v1.4.177`.

## AI Review Report

Three read-only adversarial passes traced the renderer effect, preload/main unsubscribe path, host CDP teardown, page-handle reuse, generation fencing, retry/liveness cancellation, StrictMode replay, and the full readiness checklist.

The review loop specifically caught or closed these risks:

- visibility had to be reactive rather than sampled once when the effect opened
- stale macOS `document.visibilityState` recovery needed coverage after the stream was already parked
- page reuse needed an assertion that reopening produces two streams for the same page with only one creation RPC
- visibility-gating the viewport observer would introduce a late-resize/reopen race without additional cancellation, so that unrelated path stays unchanged
- the hook harness initially recreated its fake lifecycle on render; production uses one stable lifecycle and the corrected test now models it

Final readiness verdict: no P0, P1, or production P2 findings.

The review covered SSH/relay disconnects, late subscription resolution, in-flight page creation, repeated hide/show, stale visibility, cleanup and retry bounds, mixed client/host versions, folder workspaces, macOS/Linux/Windows behavior, and mobile-facing compatibility.

## Security Audit

No dependency, command execution, parser, filesystem, auth, secret, persistence, IPC/RPC method, schema, stream opcode, or remote-wire payload changes. The renderer only changes when it holds an existing validated screencast subscription. Unsubscribe retains the existing ownership checks and dedicated transport cleanup.

## Notes

- Mixed client/server versions remain compatible because no exchanged content or host behavior changes.
- An established remote page is preserved. If its initial creation is still in flight when parking wins, the existing cancellation path closes it and a later reveal may create it again.
- A decode already in flight is invalidated by the stream token and revokes its object URL instead of publishing a hidden frame.
- The viewport observer remains active while hidden; a resize can issue its existing bounded viewport RPCs, but it cannot start a parked stream because restart requires a current subscription.
- The remote page and its JavaScript intentionally remain alive, and one last frame remains retained until replacement or unmount.

records.title: [Perf-SS] Own oversized automation output snapshot tails
records.body:
## Summary

### ELI5

JavaScript can keep an entire large string alive when code stores only a small `slice` of it. A new remote-runtime automation may receive one initial terminal snapshot approaching the 2 MiB transport cap, while Orca retains only its last 256 KiB. Previously that small logical tail could keep the full decoded snapshot backing allocation alive.

This change rebuilds only the rare oversized partial tail from its UTF-16 code units, so the retained 256 KiB owns its storage and the discarded prefix can be collected. Ordinary terminal chunks keep the PSS-013 fast path.

### Production reachability

- Background automation terminals start at 120×40.
- The remote host serializes the initial desktop terminal snapshot without a 256 KiB server trim.
- Snapshot frames are reassembled into one string up to the renderer transport limit of 2 MiB UTF-8.
- The automation watcher receives that initial string as one `append`.
- Orca's production xterm serializer at 120×40 produced a valid 964,878-code-unit / 1,924,878-byte snapshot with `A` plus 200 combining marks per cell. A smaller 55-mark shape already crossed the logical cap at 268,878 code units / 532,878 bytes.

No RPC, stream framing, persistence format, terminal cap, or UI behavior changes.

### Performance proof

Separate-process, actual-module, forced-GC measurement with the 1,924,878-byte production snapshot:

| Implementation | Retained heap |
| --- | ---: |
| Previous `slice` | +1,958,784 bytes |
| Owned UTF-16 tail | +554,520 bytes |
| Improvement | **-1,404,264 bytes / 71.7%** |

A separate 64 MiB backing-store probe retained about 64 MiB externally with `slice`; the owned copy retained approximately zero external backing plus the intended ~256 KiB string.

An independent Electron V8 15.0 audit used a 16 Mi-code-unit two-byte source:

- Previous slice: 33,554,784 retained heap bytes
- Owned copy: 533,080 retained heap bytes
- Copy cost for an 8 Mi-code-unit source, 120 samples: 0.402 ms median / 0.476 ms p95
- Immediate transient heap was bounded at 1,350,328 bytes and released after the copy.

The cost is determined by the retained 256 KiB tail, not the discarded source size. The copy runs only when one partially trimmed source chunk is itself larger than 256 KiB. Ordinary chunks do not enter it, and the ordinary append benchmark showed no measurable median regression.

### Proof of no regression

- The cap remains exactly 256 KiB of JavaScript UTF-16 code units.
- Copying uses `charCodeAt` / `fromCharCode`, preserving every code unit, including split and lone surrogates.
- Raw output is still capped before ANSI/control stripping.
- Sticky truncation, later appends, repeated oversized appends, transcript precedence, and snapshot persistence are unchanged.
- A differential oracle compares the candidate against the previous shift/slice algorithm across seeded chunk, control-sequence, surrogate, oversized, and subsequent-append boundaries.
- The helper copies in bounded 4,096-code-unit blocks; it has no timers, listeners, caches, subprocesses, paths, native dependencies, or platform branches.
- Renderer-only scope means local, SSH, relay, folder-workspace, mobile, and mixed-version wire contracts are unchanged.

## Screenshots

No visual change.

## Testing

- [ ] `pnpm lint` — the monolithic command was not rerun; targeted oxlint, changed-code quality, React Doctor, max-lines ratchet, reliability gates, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`
- [ ] `pnpm test` — focused and adjacent suites were run instead:
  - 2 snapshot files / 14 tests
  - 27 automation-adjacent files / 172 tests
  - 3 remote snapshot/subscription files / 40 tests
  - 3 additional automation/settings/browser files / 7 tests
  - 6 lifecycle/service/persistence/buffer files / 502 tests
- [ ] `pnpm build` — Electron production build passed; the unrelated native release build was not rerun
- [x] Added high-quality exact-equivalence and boundary regression tests

## AI Review Report

Three independent final reviews found no P0/P1/P2 issues. They checked exact old-algorithm equivalence, source-backing ownership, retained/transient memory, CPU cost, UTF-16 and lone-surrogate behavior, ANSI/cap ordering, repeated/later appends, cleanup/resource bounds, and packaging of the new helper. The readiness review also checked macOS, Linux, and Windows behavior, SSH/relay/folder workspaces, mobile/backward compatibility, and remote wire compatibility. Its only pre-publication gate was including the new imported file; all four files are present in this commit.

Residual risk: source-backing ownership is verified with forced-GC process benchmarks rather than a timing-sensitive automated heap assertion.

## Security Audit

No new input authority, command execution, path handling, authentication, secrets, dependency, IPC, persistence, or network surface. The implementation copies already-received terminal string code units into bounded renderer memory. No follow-up is required.

## Notes

- Semantic performance scan item PSS-016.
- Headless automation reads stay below this threshold and were intentionally left unchanged.
- @nwparker_
