records.title: fix(computer-use): settle macOS permission checks
records.body:
## Summary

- Retry fresh-process Accessibility and Screen Recording trust checks while macOS TCC settles, preventing already-granted permissions from appearing denied.
- Apply settled trust to permission status, setup UI, snapshot gates, and delayed AX window availability.
- Warm Screen Recording trust with one cross-process capture probe, excluding Orca-owned windows so self-capture cannot produce a false grant.
- Probe Accessibility and Screen Recording concurrently, and coalesce setup-window refreshes on a background queue so AppKit never waits on the bounded retry loops.
- Show an immediate, honest checking state before rendering the settled permission result.

Fixes #9458.
Supersedes the combined intent of #10122 and #10373 while addressing the unresolved review findings on #10373.

## Visual proof

The helper now renders while permission probes are still settling:

![Pending permission check](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2b665e1d-d014-42f0-a1f6-ec899e141c28)

It then renders the settled missing-permission state:

![Settled permission result](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/299d63df-ee0e-4fe2-9834-4c6b91b01430)

Both screenshots use a temporary ad-hoc-signed helper with a unique bundle ID, giving it a deterministic ungranted TCC identity without resetting the developer's real Orca permissions.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`
- [ ] `pnpm test` — full repository suite not run locally; the complete native provider suite ran through `pnpm verify:computer-native`
- [ ] `pnpm build` — full application build not run; `pnpm build:computer-macos` built and signed the universal helper successfully
- [x] `pnpm verify:computer-native`
- [x] 71 XCTest cases and 11 Swift Testing cases pass
- [x] Added deterministic regression tests for immediate grants, transient denials, bounded persistent denials, Screen Recording fallback ordering, cross-process capture selection, concurrent permission snapshots, refresh coalescing, and later refreshes
- [x] Repeated the four new concurrency/coalescing tests 20 times without a failure
- [x] Earlier grant-path stress reproduction: 100 concurrent helper executions returned both permissions granted in all 100 results
- [x] Live ungranted helper status completed in 2.35 seconds, versus the previous ~3.5-second sequential ceiling
- [x] Live pending UI was accessible and captured 0.95 seconds after launch while both permission checks were still settling
- [x] A one-second process sample showed the main thread in the `NSApplication` event loop while both retry sleeps ran on the new permission-status queues

## AI Review Report

Reviewed the fresh-process TCC lifecycle, status/setup/runtime call sites, bounded wait behavior, genuine-denial path, refresh cadence, and Screen Recording fallback. The older Screen Recording PR could accept an Orca-owned window as proof of cross-app capture permission and did not test its fallback flow; this version excludes the current PID and adds direct fallback and selection tests. It also uses overflow-safe `Thread.sleep` instead of multiplying an unbounded interval for `usleep`.

The setup assistant can request a permission refresh every 350 ms while System Settings is visible. Those requests now coalesce behind one worker snapshot, preventing probe accumulation and repeated UI rebuilds. All window decisions consume the completed snapshot instead of calling TCC synchronously.

Cross-platform compatibility was checked explicitly. The implementation is confined to the macOS Swift provider and changes no shortcuts, paths, shell behavior, Electron IPC, remote wire formats, Linux behavior, or Windows behavior.

## Security Audit

No new external input, command execution, dependency, authentication, secret, path, or IPC surface is introduced. Retry loops remain bounded and the already-granted path performs no sleep. The capture fallback selects one normal window owned by another process, checks only whether CoreGraphics returns an image, and does not serialize, retain, or publish its pixels. Orca-owned windows are excluded to prevent a false-positive permission result.

Permission results cross only in-process Swift queues as a two-boolean `Sendable` snapshot. A lock protects concurrent result writes, and the UI handler returns to the main actor before touching AppKit.

## Notes

- macOS can answer a freshly launched helper with `preflight_unknown` / `do_not_cache` before the stable TCC grant becomes visible in that PID.
- A genuine denial can still add up to 1.5 seconds for Accessibility or 2 seconds for Screen Recording, but those checks now overlap. The setup window remains responsive and the CLI status ceiling is roughly 2 seconds instead of 3.5 seconds, excluding process launch overhead.
- Runtime requests that need only one permission retain their existing bounded settling behavior.
- The local helper is ad-hoc signed because this machine has no release signing identity. Universal build and signature verification passed; deterministic tests cover the transient TCC sequence independently of local signing identity.

records.title: fix(terminal): skip a too-wide alt frame on snapshot replay
records.body:
## Summary

Reopening a parked worktree could replay a full-screen TUI snapshot at its captured width and then fit xterm to a narrower pane. The alternate buffer does not reflow in our pinned xterm; instead, the fixed-grid frame stayed full-width and was clipped at the narrower viewport until the live application repainted, producing the filmed row fragments and mid-word cuts.

This change omits only a live alternate-screen frame when its captured grid is wider than the pending fit, or when a hidden pane has no trustworthy target grid yet. Normal-buffer scrollback, alternate-buffer activation/clearing, and frame-independent terminal state are restored, then the attached PTY owner receives repaint activity on the final grid.

## Root cause and implementation

The first renderer-only gate did not cover the filmed path. Instrumentation showed the parked reveal painted through `daemon-connectResult-snapshot`, where the daemon's composed snapshot bypassed the model-snapshot call sites.

The daemon now exposes additive optional strings for the normal-buffer/mode prefix and visual alt frame:

- `snapshotPrefixAnsi`
- `snapshotFrameAnsi`

The renderer preserves those fields through the transport projection. On a narrowing live restore it writes the prefix plus compact frame-independent restore state instead of the stale visual frame. Missing, empty, or partial split metadata falls back to the original merged snapshot, preserving compatibility without an escape-sequence boundary index that could drift.

The restore state covers alternate-buffer entry, SGR pen state, cursor/keypad/paste/insert/origin/wrap/focus/cursor/mouse modes, scroll region, and saved/current cursor positions. The unsupported SerializeAddon out-of-range-row SGR capture is documented and pinned by a direct test under our vendored xterm patch.

The width decision uses the same proposed pane-fit dimensions consumed by `safeFit`, including active fit overrides. Hidden or unmeasurable live restores conservatively omit the frame and carry the fit continuation through reveal. If the final reveal grid equals the snapshot grid, a one-column PTY size pulse still produces `SIGWINCH`; this prevents a skipped frame from leaving a permanently blank TUI when same-size resize calls would otherwise be ignored.

Equal-width and wider measurable restores keep their captured frame. The scope does not change `performSafeFit` behavior for unmeasurable override panes, preserving #12944's terminal-keyed metric deferral, settled gate, font-zoom folding, and retry invariants.

## Compatibility and deliberate boundaries

The split fields are additive and optional across local IPC/runtime contracts. Existing consumers ignore them, and producers without a complete split fall back to the merged snapshot.

- A cold restore with the owner gone drops a mismatched frame while retaining normal-buffer history and the existing restored-session/reset treatment. This polarity is unit-covered. The separate owner-death Electron lifecycle was not live-tested in the park/remount matrix.
- Offline/preconnect SSH retains its parked frame because no attached SSH process can repaint it yet.
- Paired remote-runtime snapshot recovery does not yet transport the optional split metadata and remains out of scope. Changing that independently updated mixed-version wire path would expand this defect fix; it continues to use the backward-compatible merged fallback.

The static TUI used for narrowing QA deliberately ignores `SIGWINCH`. It is a worst-case probe, not typical application behavior: a blank cleared alt screen proves the stale frame was omitted instead of being masked by a quick repaint.

## Verification

- Two final same-model review rounds returned CLEAN at exact post-rebase head `6ace57fd73`.
- Focused Vitest: 7 files, 949 passed; reviewer rerun: 7 files, 897 passed.
- `pnpm run typecheck`.
- `pnpm run audit:code-quality:native`.
- `pnpm run audit:code-quality:type-aware`.
- `git diff --check`.
- Exact-head GitHub CI: 50 checks completed with no failures or pending jobs; `verify`, Windows packaging, cross-version wire compatibility, and native smoke checks passed.
- Rebased onto `origin/main` at `2ee43bfc0d`; later main commits touch only README/ripgrep filesystem files, with no terminal/PTY/snapshot/pane-fit overlap.

### Electron/CDP matrix

All UI automation used `agent-browser` over Electron CDP with isolated profiles.

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| Narrow daemon remount, 135 to 9 cols | PASS: clean cleared alt screen from t0 through t5; no clipped stale-frame debris |
| Same-width daemon remount, 135 to 135 cols | PASS: complete captured frame remains intact |
| Wider daemon remount, narrow capture to 135 cols | PASS: captured frame remains intact at the left of the wider grid |
| Scrollback across all daemon cases | PASS: `SCROLLBACK-LINE` remains in the target main-buffer snapshot |
| Hidden same-grid reveal, 135×59 to 135×59 | PASS: skipped stale frame receives a two-step `SIGWINCH` repaint and shows `TOP_AFTER_SIGWINCH count=2` on the same PTY |

## Security audit

No new input, command execution, path, auth, secret, or dependency surface. The change adds optional terminal-snapshot metadata and replay choreography only.

records.title: fix(remote-workspace): stop stale snapshot applies from erasing freshly created terminal tabs
records.body:
## Problem

A terminal tab created around a direct-SSH remote-workspace snapshot apply can be permanently lost:

1. `createSessionWriteSubscriber` drops its pending write while an apply suppresses persistence (`pendingChangedFields.clear()`), so the tab never reaches the remote session store — the suppression window can last up to 30s of terminal reconnects plus a 1s trailing window.
2. The apply then replaces the worktree's tab list from the snapshot, which was fetched before the tab existed. `mergeDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSession` iterates only `remote.tabsByWorktree`, so a local-only tab cannot survive it.
3. Local state now matches the snapshot byte-for-byte, so the next push no-ops via `remoteWorkspaceSessionMatchesSnapshot` — the remote store never learns the tab existed.

The tab's pty keeps running unreachable on the host, and any sleeping-agent record for the tab is stranded against a tab id that no longer exists. Observed in production: an agent launched into a fresh tab moments before a `wake-refresh` apply; the tab was erased within seconds while its `claude` process kept running on the host.

## Fix

- **Hold suppressed writes instead of dropping them.** The subscriber's flush retries at the debounce cadence until suppression lifts, bounded by a 60s hold ceiling so back-to-back applies (or a misbehaving remote streaming new snapshot revisions) cannot starve local persistence indefinitely. Past the ceiling the write proceeds; the payload is rebuilt from the current store, which is always self-consistent.
- **Graft live local tabs into a stale snapshot before the merge.** A snapshot whose in-scope tab lists are missing a tab that is live locally — mid-reattach per the recovery ledger, or with an attached pty per `ptyIdsByTabId` — predates the session write that created that tab. The tab is appended to the snapshot's list for its worktree and added to the merge's preserve set, so its layout and session ids survive. Remote-only tabs from other clients still apply unchanged, and tabs without a live pty are still removed when the remote store says so — this cannot resurrect tabs deleted on another device.

## Tests

- Subscriber: held write lands after suppression lifts (suppressed at schedule time and mid-debounce); force-flush once the 60s ceiling passes.
- `staleDirectSshSnapshotTabIds` and `graftLocalTabsIntoRemoteSession` unit tests.
- Integration (target-sync): a live local tab omitted by an incoming snapshot survives the merge, with its layout, alongside the snapshot's remote-only tab.

records.title: fix(browser): gate the CDP proxy on Origin and loopback Host
records.body:
## Summary

Gate the agent-browser CDP proxy's WebSocket upgrade and HTTP discovery endpoints on two request checks, so only a local CDP client can reach them.

`CdpWsProxy` binds an HTTP + WebSocket server on an ephemeral loopback port and forwards CDP commands to a live browser tab's `webContents.debugger`. Today the server is constructed with no `verifyClient` and no path, and `handleHttpRequest` answers `/json/version` and `/json/list` unconditionally. Binding to `127.0.0.1` is not by itself an access check against a browser: WebSocket handshakes are not subject to the same-origin policy, `ws://127.0.0.1` is a potentially-trustworthy origin (so it is not blocked as mixed content), and DNS rebinding turns a remote origin into a same-origin reader of the HTTP endpoints. Chrome guards its own `--remote-debugging-port` endpoint the same two ways.

This adds `isAllowedCdpProxyRequest` in a small sibling module, applied on the upgrade (via `verifyClient`) and at the top of `handleHttpRequest`:

1. **Reject any request carrying an `Origin` header.** Browsers always send `Origin` on a WebSocket handshake and on cross-origin fetches; CDP clients (agent-browser, Playwright, chrome-remote-interface) never do.
2. **Require `Host` to name loopback at the port we actually bound.** A rebound page reaches `127.0.0.1` but still sends the attacker's hostname. This is also the check that has to carry the HTTP endpoints, since a same-origin fetch after rebinding sends no `Origin` at all.

I reported the underlying issue through the repository's private vulnerability reporting with the full analysis and reproduction, so this description stays at the level of what the code now does.

### Relationship to #5035 — please read this first

**#5035 (@nwparker, 2026-06-09) already identified this and proposed a broader fix**: a 144-bit token in the debugger URL path with a timing-safe compare, *plus* the same `Origin` rejection and loopback `Host` check, *plus* a cookie-import staging permissions fix. That design is strictly stronger than this PR — the path token also closes the local-process vector, which this PR explicitly does not.

I found this only after writing the change, and I want to be clear that the analysis there predates mine. The reason I'm still opening this: #5035 has been `CONFLICTING` / `DIRTY` with no reviews and no commits since 2026-06-09, and `cdp-ws-proxy.ts` has moved substantially since, so it does not currently apply. The endpoint is still unauthenticated on `main` today.

So please treat this as a **conflict-free minimal subset** that can land now, not as a replacement:

- If #5035 is going to be rebased, **close this one** — that is the better outcome and I'll say so. I'd be glad to do the rebase if that's useful.
- If it's stale, this closes the browser-reachable half immediately, and the path token can follow.

I deliberately did **not** port the path token here. #5035 states the bundled `agent-browser` was verified to follow the tokenized `webSocketDebuggerUrl` from `/json` discovery; I could not verify that myself, and shipping a token I hadn't confirmed the client honours risks silently breaking browser automation. `Origin` + `Host` need no client-side cooperation at all, which is why they are safe to land unverified against the binary.

### Compatibility

No change to the `--cdp <port>` contract with `agent-browser`. It receives a port, does its own `GET /json/version` discovery over Node's HTTP client (which always sets `Host` from the URL, so `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>` — both accepted) and connects with a Node WebSocket client, which does not set `Origin` unless explicitly asked to. `CdpWsProxy` has exactly one consumer, `agent-browser-bridge.ts`; nothing in the renderer or preload connects to it.

## Screenshots

No visual change.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint` — every gate that runs on this checkout passes; one pre-existing failure, see below
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` — full run (node + cli + web), clean
- [ ] `pnpm test` — ran the affected suites, not the full run; leaving this to CI. Details below.
- [ ] `pnpm build` — not run locally (Electron packaging). No build inputs changed; leaving this to CI.
- [x] Added or updated high-quality tests that would catch regressions

Lint detail: `oxlint`, `audit:code-quality:native`, `audit:code-quality:type-aware`, `check:reliability-gates` (69 gates), `check:max-lines-ratchet` (352 grandfathered, no new bypasses), `verify:bundled-skill-guides`, and `verify:localization-catalog` all pass. `verify:skill-bundle-manifest` fails — but it **fails identically on a clean `main` with zero changes** on my Windows checkout, reporting `resources\skills\current-manifest.json` and friends as stale. The backslashes point at path-separator or line-ending sensitivity in the generator on Windows. Nothing here touches `resources/skills/`, and I left those artifacts alone rather than regenerate them and add unrelated churn.

New file `src/main/browser/cdp-ws-proxy-access-guard.test.ts` (11 tests) drives the **real** `CdpWsProxy` over a real socket using the existing `cdp-ws-proxy-test-harness`, rather than unit-testing the predicate in isolation:

- upgrade carrying `Origin` → rejected, and `debugger.sendCommand` is never reached
- upgrade carrying an *empty* `Origin:` → rejected
- upgrade from an opaque origin (`Origin: null`, i.e. sandboxed iframe / `data:` URL) → rejected
- upgrade whose `Host` is a rebound hostname → rejected
- upgrade whose `Host` names a different port → rejected
- `/json/version` and `/json/list` carrying `Origin` → 403
- `/json/version` carrying an empty `Origin:` → 403
- `/json/version` from a rebound hostname → 403
- a local client sending no `Origin` still gets a full `Runtime.evaluate` round trip
- discovery still returns 200 for both `127.0.0.1:<port>` and `localhost:<port>`
- a rejected upgrade does **not** disturb the connected agent client

That last one is a deliberate pin: `wss.on('connection')` starts with `this.closeClient()`, so anything that reached the connection handler would evict the incumbent agent-browser client. The check has to run at the upgrade, before that handler.

All 8 rejection tests fail against an unguarded proxy — the upgrades are accepted (`Error: upgrade unexpectedly succeeded`) and reach `debugger.sendCommand`, and discovery returns 200 instead of 403.

The empty-`Origin` pair came out of @coderabbitai's review: `hasBrowserOrigin` originally rejected only a *nonempty* `Origin`, so a bare `Origin:` reached the debugger even though the doc comment claimed otherwise. Confirmed against the previous commit before fixing — both new tests failed — then fixed in 57ae7bd5d by testing presence rather than content, since the value is never inspected.

One test-only note worth flagging for review: `fetch()` silently drops a caller-supplied `Host` (it's a forbidden header name), which made the rebinding assertions pass vacuously at first. The helper uses `node:http` instead so the header is actually sent.

Existing coverage is unaffected — the pre-existing suites connect without an `Origin` and with a normal loopback `Host`, so they exercise the allowed path unchanged. `cdp-ws-proxy`, `cdp-ws-proxy-focus-replay`, `cdp-ws-proxy-access-guard`, `cdp-bridge-integration`, and `agent-browser-bridge` together: **5 files, 180 tests passed**.

## AI Review Report

Reviewed with an AI agent against the checklist. This change originated from an AI-assisted security audit of the loopback listener surface; the finding was then verified by hand against the full code path before writing any code.

- **Cross-platform.** Pure Node HTTP header handling — no filesystem path, shell, shortcut, label, or Electron platform branch. Node lowercases header names on all platforms, so `req.headers.origin` / `req.headers.host` are stable. Behaves identically on macOS, Linux, and Windows.
- **SSH / remote / local.** The proxy is always local to the machine running the Electron main process and is never exposed over the relay or an SSH channel. No RPC params, stream frames, or published content change, so there is no mixed-version wire concern.
- **Agent compatibility.** The consumer is the external `agent-browser` CLI. Verified it is invoked as `--cdp <port>` (`agent-browser-bridge.ts:2493`, `:2528`) and that neither the renderer nor the preload connects to the endpoint. `Host` accepts both loopback spellings so either discovery URL works.
- **Git provider / integration.** None touched.
- **Performance.** Two header comparisons per request on a connection that is established once per browser session. Not a hot path.
- **UI quality.** No UI.

Points it raised and how they were resolved: the initial version put the guard inline in `cdp-ws-proxy.ts`, which already carries an `eslint-disable max-lines` — moved to a sibling module instead of growing that file. It also asked whether `Host` with no port (`127.0.0.1`, implying :80) should pass; it should not, and it does not, since the bound port is never 80. `[::1]:<port>` is accepted for completeness even though the server binds v4 only.

## Security Audit

- **Auth / access control.** This PR *is* the access control. Both checks are on headers a browser cannot suppress or forge from page JS: `Origin` is set by the user agent on every WebSocket handshake, and `Host` always reflects the name the client connected to. Neither is attacker-controllable in the browser threat model.
- **What this does not claim to stop.** A local process running as the user can still connect, since it can omit `Origin` and set a correct `Host`. That is a strictly weaker boundary than the browser vector and matches the trust model documented for the other local servers (`src/relay/context.ts:20-24`). Closing it needs the path token from #5035; see the note above for why I left it out here rather than porting it unverified.
- **Input handling.** Only two request headers are read, compared against a fixed set and an integer. No parsing of attacker-controlled structure, no allocation proportional to input.
- **Command execution / path handling / secrets / dependencies.** None. No new dependency, no lockfile change, no new IPC channel.
- **Follow-up.** A CDP method allowlist would reduce blast radius further, but it risks breaking agent-browser's Playwright traffic and belongs in its own change.

## Notes

- No platform-specific, agent-specific, or provider-specific behavior.
- Deliberately kept to the upgrade/discovery gate so it is easy to review and safe to backport; the token-based follow-up is noted above.
- X: n/a

records.title: Closing a terminal tab with a missing persisted session record resurrects the tab — close aborts on tab_not_found before PTY kill and snapshot prune
records.body:
## Summary

A terminal tab in the desync state described in stablyai/orca#10747 (present in runtime hot state, no persisted workspace-session record) is not only unclosable from the CLI — it **visibly resurrects after every close attempt in the UI**. The tab disappears for a moment (optimistic client removal), the close RPC fails with `tab_not_found`, the runtime republishes the unchanged hot-state snapshot, and the tab reappears. The failure is deterministic, so the tab is immortal until its PTY dies or the runtime restarts.

This report adds two things to stablyai/orca#10747:

1. The user-facing resurrection loop, with a trace-log timeline of one tab "closed" six times over three hours.
2. Evidence that the desync can also arise from a **partially completed close** (persisted record removed, then a later step failed), not only from a failed reveal at creation time.

## Observed behavior

Environment: Linux desktop client, Orca 1.4.x, local runtime plus SSH worktrees.

* Closing an affected tab in the UI: the tab closes for a moment, then returns within seconds.
* `~/.config/orca/logs/main.trace.ndjson` for one session (2026-08-06): 14 `runtime.session-tabs.close` spans across three bursts (11:26, 14:18, 14:22) all ended in failure. One tab id appears six times — the user kept re-closing the same resurrected tab. 40 other closes in the same window recorded `decision: allowed` and stuck.
* Every failing span carries the same exit:

  ```
  Error: tab_not_found
      at OrcaRuntimeService.removePersistedHeadlessTerminalTab (.../out/main/index.js)
      at OrcaRuntimeService.closeHeadlessMobileTerminalTab (.../out/main/index.js)
      at OrcaRuntimeService.closeMobileSessionTab (.../out/main/index.js)
  ```
* Handle-based `terminal.close` RPCs against the same tabs **also** fail with `tab_not_found`, but they kill the daemon PTY session before the handler throws (daemon log shows `session-killed` / `session-exited` in lockstep with the failing RPCs). The terminals then stay gone — close "works" by side effect while reporting an error. This is the only non-restart escape from the loop.

## Root cause

Same throw site as stablyai/orca#10747, but the ordering inside `closeHeadlessMobileTerminalTab` is what turns it into a resurrection loop (`src/main/runtime/orca-runtime.ts` @ f713739, lines ~8049-8108):

1. `removePersistedHeadlessTerminalTab(worktreeId, closedParentTabId, { allowMissing: options.allowMissingPersistedTab })` — throws `tab_not_found` when the persisted row is missing (line ~8057). Only one internal recovery caller passes `allowMissingPersistedTab: true`.
2. PTY kill (line ~8084) — never reached.
3. Hot-state snapshot prune + republish (line ~8088) — never reached.

So the close aborts with the PTY alive and the hot snapshot untouched. The client already removed the tab optimistically; the next snapshot publication re-adds it.

By the time `closeHeadlessMobileTerminalTab` runs, `closeMobileSessionTab` has already resolved the tab from the hot snapshot — the tab provably exists in hot state. A missing persisted row at that point can only mean the persisted and hot states have diverged, and refusing the close can never repair that divergence; it just makes the tab immortal.

## How the desync arises

Two origins observed/inferred:

* **Never persisted** — the failed-reveal path documented in stablyai/orca#10747.
* **Partially completed close** — a prior close removed the persisted row, then a later step in the same transaction failed (the daemon log shows `session-kill-failed` events), leaving the hot snapshot with a tab whose persisted row is already gone. Every subsequent close then hits `tab_not_found` before reaching the kill/prune steps.

## Suggested fix

Make the headless close idempotent: treat a missing persisted row as "already de-persisted" and continue with the PTY kill and hot-state prune (i.e., what `allowMissingPersistedTab: true` already does for the relay-recovery caller, applied unconditionally). This fixes both this resurrection loop and stablyai/orca#10747's unclosable CLI tabs, and makes the partial-close origin self-healing: the second close attempt completes the interrupted transaction instead of failing forever.

PR to follow.

records.title: fix(remote-workspace): retry snapshot tabs whose worktree paths resolve after apply
records.body:
Fixes #12902

## Problem

`applyDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSnapshot` imports a pulled snapshot through `importRemoteWorkspaceSession`, whose resolver is built from the worktree catalog at apply time. Any snapshot path the catalog cannot resolve yet is dropped from the import and never retried. Remote catalogs populate asynchronously — often only after the user activates the worktree — so on connect/reconnect the tabs under a late-resolving path (and the sleeping agent sessions bound to them) simply vanish: the worktree hydrates empty, Orca creates a fresh terminal tab, and the next export pushes the tabless state back to the host, making the loss durable.

## Change

A bounded deferred-hydration watch at the end of `applyDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSnapshot`:

- After the eager hydrate, snapshot paths that carry tabs but do not map to exactly one catalog worktree — absent, or ambiguous while the catalog's async sources still hold a momentary duplicate — are polled every second, bounded by a 10-minute deadline. The watch seeds from the pending set captured before the eager hydrate and processes departures before its first sleep, so a path the catalog resolves while the hydrate is still awaiting terminal reconnects — dropped at import time like any other deferred path — is late-hydrated immediately instead of falling between the import and the watch. A pending path departs the watch only by becoming uniquely resolvable, so every departure hydrates.
- When a pending path resolves, only that tick's newly-resolved worktrees are re-imported and hydrated (`buildDeferredWorktreeMerge` keeps the imported session a strict subset of the replace scope, so already-hydrated worktrees are never reset to snapshot state). Live-only tabs are unioned into the remote list and preserved, making the late pass purely additive; the active repo/worktree/workspace/tab are pinned so a background hydrate never moves focus.
- The watch ends when a newer arrival supersedes it or the connection's authority changes (`isArrivalCurrent` + `directSshAuthoritiesEqual(getCurrentAuthority(...), ...)`); preparation tokens are deliberately not part of the loop guard, since every routine catalog refresh rotates them — including the refresh that resolves the deferred path.
- Paths that never resolve surface an error sync status at deadline expiry, after every hydrate this watch will perform — a sibling path's `synced` write cannot mask a loss.

The hydrate/reconnect/finalize sequence shared by the eager and deferred passes is extracted into `hydrateAndReconnectWorktrees`; the catalog-scope helpers live in a new `remote-workspace-deferred-hydration.ts` module. `RemoteWorkspaceSnapshotApplyInput` gains a `getCurrentAuthority` input, wired from the existing dep at both call sites in `remote-workspace-target-sync.ts`.

## Testing

New `remote-workspace-snapshot-deferred-hydration.test.ts` (fake timers): late-resolving worktree hydrates additively without moving focus or resetting eagerly-hydrated worktrees; deadline expiry reports an error; an ambiguously-mapped path defers and hydrates once the catalog dedupes it; a path that stays ambiguous errors at the deadline, and that error lands after a sibling path's successful hydrate; a plain disconnect exits the watch without writing status. A regression test covers a path that resolves during the eager hydrate's reconnect wait (fails without the first-pass processing). Pre-existing suites (`remote-workspace-snapshot-duplicate-tab-repair`, `remote-workspace-target-sync`) pass — 29/29 across the three files. `typecheck:web`, repo-wide `oxlint`, and the localization gates are clean.

Ambiguity handling: the main import still fails closed on an ambiguously-mapped path, but the path stays in the deferred watch — transient duplicates (catalog sources filling in asynchronously) dedupe within a few ticks and hydrate; permanent duplicates surface the deadline error instead of a silent drop.

## Deferred initial-terminal creation

Activating a remote worktree before its snapshot tabs arrive auto-created a terminal into the still-empty worktree — from the activation fallback and from the Terminal auto-create effect — burying the restored tabs behind a junk tab. The ssh slice now tracks the snapshot worktree paths still awaiting deferred hydration per target (registered before the eager hydrate so the gate never sees "hydrated, nothing pending" during the reconnect wait; re-synced each watch tick, after the tick's late hydrate has landed its tabs in the store; cleared on deadline expiry and on target removal). `shouldDeferInitialTerminalCreation` gates both creation sites for payloadless activations only — an explicit launch payload (creation templates, setup scripts, agent startup) always creates immediately. Both gate inputs are dependencies of the Terminal auto-create effect, so the initial terminal is created once the snapshot lands and the worktree still renders no tabs.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

records.title: Direct-SSH snapshot tabs are silently dropped when the worktree catalog resolves their paths late
records.body:
### Summary

When a direct-SSH remote workspace snapshot is applied, any snapshot worktree path the local worktree catalog cannot resolve **yet** is silently dropped and never retried. The tabs under that path — and any sleeping agent sessions bound to them — stay missing until the next full reconnect. To the user this looks like their remote agent session vanishing: activating the worktree shows a brand-new empty terminal instead of the restored session.

### Environment

- Orca 1.4.174 (also reproduced on 1.4.171), macOS (darwin arm64)
- Direct SSH workspace to a Linux host, claude agent running in a remote worktree tab

### What happens

`applyDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSnapshot` (`src/renderer/src/hooks/remote-workspace-snapshot-apply.ts`) imports the pulled snapshot through `importRemoteWorkspaceSession` with `resolveWorktreeId: uniqueWorktreeIdByPath(worktreeIds)`. In `importRemoteWorkspaceSession` (`src/shared/remote-workspace-session-projection.ts`):

```ts
for (const [worktreePath, tabs] of Object.entries(remote.tabsByWorktreePath ?? {})) {
  const worktreeId = resolvePath(worktreePath)
  if (!worktreeId) {
    continue          // <-- tabs for this path are dropped, no retry ever happens
  }
  ...
}
```

The resolver is built from the worktree catalog at apply time. For remote hosts the catalog populates asynchronously — in practice a remote worktree often only resolves after the user activates it in the sidebar. The snapshot apply, however, runs once on connect/reconnect. So the ordering is:

1. SSH connects, snapshot is pulled and applied. The catalog does not know the remote worktree path yet → its tabs are dropped from the import.
2. The sleeping-agent wake sweep finds its resume record but logs `tab <id> ... not present in any worktree (likely pre-hydration); skipping` forever — the tab never appears.
3. The user clicks the worktree. The catalog now resolves the path, but nothing re-runs the import. The worktree hydrates with no tabs, Orca creates a fresh empty terminal tab.
4. A subsequent workspace export pushes that tabless state back to the host, so the snapshot itself loses the tabs — the session loss becomes durable.

### Reproduction

1. On a direct-SSH workspace, run an agent (e.g. `claude`) in a terminal tab of a remote worktree; let the workspace snapshot sync.
2. Quit Orca. Kill the remote relay daemon on the host (simulates relay restart/update — same thing happens after an app update deploys a new relay).
3. Relaunch Orca and, before activating anything, let SSH reconnect and the snapshot apply run (catalog is still cold).
4. Activate the worktree: it comes up with a new empty terminal; the snapshot tabs and the agent resume record never fire.

### Expected

Snapshot tabs whose worktree path resolves *later* should still be hydrated — the import should be retried (bounded) as the catalog fills in, so restored sessions attach to their original tabs instead of being lost.

### Fix

PR incoming from this account: it appends a bounded deferred-hydration watcher to `applyDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSnapshot` that re-imports late-resolving paths scoped to just those worktrees, additively (never removing live tabs) and without moving user focus. Running patched locally; recovers the exact scenario above.

Related: #12722, #12704, #12751 (adjacent restore/merge issues in the same flow).

records.title: fix(browser): present Firefox UA on Google auth hosts to end ~1h sign-in staleness
records.body:
## Summary

Fixes Google sign-in sessions going stale after ~1 hour in the embedded browser (#11518).

Google binds a signed-in session to the browser identity that created it. Cookies sent under Orca's Electron/Chrome-shaped UA — which doesn't match a real first-party browser — get flagged by anti-fraud on `accounts.google.com` and expire within ~1h, and re-copying cookies from the desktop browser only resets the same losing clock. This PR stops relying on a UA/cookie shape Google rejects: it presents a **Firefox identity scoped to the Google/YouTube sign-in hosts** (`accounts.google.com`, `accounts.youtube.com`) so the user signs in *inside* the embedded browser and Google issues cookies bound to **this** browser that self-refresh.

The switch is applied at every layer Google probes:
- **Request headers** (`onBeforeSendHeaders`): sets the Firefox UA and strips `sec-ch-ua*` client hints (real Firefox sends none; Chromium hints under a Firefox UA are a sharper tell than either alone).
- **Per-`WebContents` UA** (`did-start-navigation`): the `navigator.userAgent` that Google's auth JS reads reflects the WebContents UA, not the request header — so both layers must agree or the mismatch is itself a bot signal.
- **CDP viewport-preset UA** (`Emulation.setUserAgentOverride`): the responsive-viewport presets install a *third* UA layer that outranks the other two. See *Third UA layer* below.

Scope is the auth hosts only. Post-auth app surfaces (Gmail, `myaccount.google.com`, Drive, etc.) keep the profile's real Chrome-shaped identity, so nothing else about the session shifts. Native-UA profiles (the `userAgentMode: 'native'` escape hatch introduced in #12608) opt out of the whole clean-UA path and are unchanged.

## Third UA layer: the viewport-preset CDP override

Reviewing this branch surfaced a real defect in the interaction between the auth-host switch and the responsive-viewport presets, now fixed in this PR.

`setViewportOverride` sends `Emulation.setUserAgentOverride` with a Chrome-shaped UA. Measured against real Electron 43.1.0 / Chromium 150 (standalone harness: local echo server, `webContents.setUserAgent` + `webRequest.onBeforeSendHeaders` + CDP, all three layers observed directly):

1. **A CDP override outranks `WebContents.setUserAgent`** for *both* `navigator.userAgent` and the outgoing request header. `webContents.getUserAgent()` still reports the WebContents value, so the disagreement is invisible from the Electron API.
2. **It is set once and stands** across every subsequent navigation — including to a different host — until explicitly cleared (`userAgent: ''`) or the debugger detaches. It is *not* re-applied per navigation.
3. **`onBeforeSendHeaders` still wins for the outgoing header**, so the wire-level Firefox switch was never at risk.

That combination produced a genuine mismatch: apply a desktop/mobile preset **first**, then navigate to `accounts.google.com`, and the request header says Firefox while `navigator.userAgent` — read by Google's auth JS — stays pinned to the Chrome-shaped preset UA. Exactly the two-layer disagreement this PR exists to remove.

The reverse order was benign, as suspected, and this was verified rather than assumed: `cleanElectronUserAgent()` finds no `Electron/` token and no `Chrome/` token in a Firefox UA, so it passes it through unchanged (asserted in tests). But it left a stale Firefox override standing on every later non-auth navigation.

**Fix:** the override payload moved to `buildViewportUserAgentOverride()` (`browser-viewport-user-agent.ts`), which reuses `isGoogleAuthUrl` and returns the Firefox UA — with no `userAgentMetadata`, since real Firefox emits no client hints — whenever the target URL is an auth host. `did-start-navigation` re-issues the standing override against the URL being navigated to, so all three layers move together. Native-UA profiles remain untouched. The async re-issue is safe: page JS reads `navigator.userAgent` after commit, and the header layer already forces Firefox on the wire independently.

### Host resolution across the navigation boundary

A follow-up review flagged the two CDP user-agent writers as an ordering race. That framing turned
out to be wrong and is worth recording so it is not re-raised: `debugger.sendCommand` dispatches in
call order over a single channel, so the later-issued write always wins and the two could not land
out of order.

The real defect was post-await staleness. Measured against real Electron 43.1.0,
`did-start-navigation` fires while an awaited `sendCommand` is still pending, and
`webContents.getURL()` keeps reporting the page being *left* until the navigation commits. So
`setViewportOverride`, resuming after its first `await`, resolved the **wrong host** — and then won
with the wrong value. Both predicted symptoms were reachable that way: the Firefox UA stranded after
leaving an auth host, and a Chrome-shaped UA standing on one (mobile presets only — the desktop
branch is masked, because `cleanElectronUserAgent` passes the already-switched Firefox UA through
unchanged).

Fixed by giving both writers one source of truth for the host: a per-tab pending-navigation target,
set at `did-start-navigation` and cleared on commit or failure, resolved in preference to
`getURL()`. No queue required.

Two further defects were found and fixed while re-examining this code:

- **Popup child windows bypassed the native-UA opt-out.** Popups get `attachGuestPolicies` but are
  never entered into `tabIdByWebContentsId`, so the mode read as `undefined` and the guard missed.
  That was worse than doing nothing: native profiles skip `setupClientHintsOverride` entirely, so
  such a popup would have sent the raw Electron UA on the wire while `navigator.userAgent` claimed
  Firefox 140 — the sharpest form of the mismatch this PR removes. Now resolved through the popup's
  owner tab.
- **The clear path dropped its tracking entry before the CDP clear succeeded**, stranding a
  still-standing override that the navigation path could never correct. Both branches now mutate
  tracking only after the writes land.

### Known follow-up: device emulation is not URL-aware

The UA stack is URL-aware; the device-emulation stack is not. `setDeviceMetricsOverride(mobile: true)`
and `setTouchEmulationEnabled(maxTouchPoints: 5)` are issued only from `setViewportOverride` and are
never revisited on navigation, so a mobile viewport preset on an auth host produces desktop Firefox
with `navigator.maxTouchPoints === 5`, where real desktop Firefox reports 0. Same class of internal
contradiction, different signal pair. Making device metrics URL-aware is a scope increase and is
deliberately left out of this PR.

Note the tempting alternative is wrong: emitting a mobile-Firefox UA on auth hosts would reintroduce
the bug this PR fixes, because `setupClientHintsOverride` is session-scoped and preset-blind and can
only ever emit the desktop `googleAuthUserAgent()`. The CDP layer would then disagree with the header
layer again. Desktop Firefox on auth hosts regardless of the preset is the only choice that keeps the
two UA layers in agreement.

## Live E2E validation — real account, 8h+ and still self-refreshing (2026-08-07)

Ran the patched build in the real Orca app (dev build of this branch, isolated browser profile) and signed into a **real Google account** inside the embedded browser. All cookie reads below are **metadata only** (name / host / timestamps), read-only — no cookie values.

**UA scoping (live in-app):**

| Surface | `navigator.userAgent` **and** WebContents UA |
| --- | --- |
| `accounts.google.com/v3/signin/identifier` | `…rv:140.0 … Firefox/140.0` ✅ Firefox override applied |
| `example.com` (off-host) | `…Chrome/150 … Safari/537.36` ✅ reverts to base identity |

Google served the genuine sign-in form (no bounce to `/v3/signin/rejected`), login succeeded, and `myaccount.google.com` rendered signed-in.

**Durability — the exact #11518 failure mode. Pre-fix behavior was death at ~1h; this session is past 8 hours and still rotating.**

Auth cookies issued at **2026-08-06 22:20:02 UTC**. Cookie DB re-read at **2026-08-07 06:34:58 UTC** — **8h 15m post-login**:

| Cookie | Host | Last rotated (UTC) | Age at measurement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `__Secure-1PSIDTS` | `.google.com` | 06:31:41 | 3m ago |
| `__Secure-3PSIDTS` | `.google.com` | 06:31:41 | 3m ago |
| `__Secure-1PSIDCC` | `.google.com` | 06:32:35 | 2m ago |
| `__Secure-3PSIDCC` | `.google.com` | 06:32:35 | 2m ago |
| `SIDCC` | `.google.com` | 06:32:35 | 2m ago |

The rotating freshness cookies are not merely alive at 8h — they were refreshed **minutes before the measurement**, i.e. the session is still actively self-renewing, not coasting on a long expiry. Earlier in the same session `__Secure-1PSIDTS` rotated on a clean ~10-min cadence (`22:20 → 22:30 → … → 23:20` UTC) and forced revalidation (hard reload of `myaccount.google.com`) at 1h4m returned the signed-in account page rather than a bounce to sign-in. Against a pre-fix baseline of ~1h, this is roughly **8x** and still climbing.

For contrast, the pre-fix signature captured as the live repro was a week-old release-app session in which `__Secure-1PSIDTS` / `__Secure-3PSIDTS` were **absent entirely** and every auth cookie was frozen at creation time.

**One asymmetry, stated plainly:** the `.youtube.com` copies of `__Secure-1PSIDTS` / `__Secure-3PSIDTS` are still frozen at the 22:20:02 login time and have never rotated. This is *not* a partial failure — it is explained by traffic, and the cookie DB confirms it rather than leaving it to inference. Grouping every cookie by host and taking the newest `last_access_utc`:

| Host | Cookies | Newest access (UTC) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.google.com` | 15 | 2026-08-07 06:32:35 |
| `myaccount.google.com` | 3 | 2026-08-07 06:32:34 |
| `ogs.google.com` | 1 | 2026-08-07 06:31:42 |
| `accounts.google.com` | 7 | 2026-08-07 06:31:41 |
| `.youtube.com` | 11 | **2026-08-06 22:20:02** |

No `youtube.com` host was contacted at any point after login. All 11 `.youtube.com` cookies were written by the cross-domain propagation during sign-in itself and have a `last_access_utc` still pinned to that instant — meaning they were never once attached to an outgoing request in the following 8 hours. No requests means no refresh responses, so there is nothing that *could* have rotated them. (Chromium's `last_access_utc` update is throttled to roughly hourly, which only strengthens this: 8 hours of no movement cannot be a throttling artifact.)

## The Electron bump is exonerated

A reviewer's first instinct here is to blame the Electron 43 upgrade, so this was tested directly and ruled out.

A **dual-engine A/B** ran the two engine versions in parallel — **Electron 42.3.3 / Chromium 148** vs **Electron 43.1.0 / Chromium 150** — against the same real cookies and the same laundered UA. Both arms went stale **identically**. The staleness is a property of the cookie/identity binding, not of the Chromium version, and the Electron 43 upgrade is not the cause of #11518.

## Methodology caveat: transplanted sessions cannot be A/B'd on one account

Worth recording, because it constrains how any future work in this area can be validated.

A transplanted Google session **cannot** be A/B tested against a single account. The **first** transplant of an account's cookies into a fresh partition works; **every subsequent transplant of that same account is rejected**, regardless of UA identity. The rejection tracks the re-import, not the browser fingerprint, so a second arm can never be a clean control — a valid transplant A/B would need **separate Google accounts per arm**.

Two consequences:

1. **Direct evidence against the periodic cookie re-import approach in #4748.** A 5-minute cookie re-import timer re-transplants the same account on a loop; the observed behavior is that every re-import after the first is rejected. That mechanism is fighting the binding this PR works with.
2. **It is why this PR's own validation is trustworthy.** The 8h+ result above is a **fresh in-Orca login**, not a transplant — so it is not subject to the first-transplant-only artifact and measures the real bound-cookie lifetime.

## Screenshots

End-to-end Electron QA in the real Orca app — the embedded browser reaching Google's genuine sign-in form under the scoped Firefox identity — is posted in [this comment](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/pull/12884#issuecomment-5202396647), with the `navigator.userAgent` proof and screenshots. (The post-login account page is intentionally not attached — it contains account PII; the sign-in-form capture demonstrates the UA mechanics without it.)

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` (all three projects clean)
- [x] `pnpm test` (`src/main/browser/` suite: 33 files, 586/586 passing — new `browser-google-auth-ua` and `browser-viewport-user-agent` suites, updated `setupClientHintsOverride` suite, `browser-manager` suite 67/67)
- [x] `pnpm build`
- [x] Added unit tests: host-matching (exact host, subdomain/lookalike rejection), Firefox UA shape, client-hint stripping, header overwrite, `setupClientHintsOverride` behavior on/off the auth hosts, per-`WebContents` UA apply-on-auth-host / restore-off-host / native-profile-untouched.
- [x] Added regression tests for the viewport-preset UA layer: Firefox UA for a preset applied on an auth host (desktop **and** mobile), re-issue of a standing override when navigating onto and back off an auth host, no re-issue when no preset is standing or after the preset is cleared, and native-UA profiles left untouched on navigation. Verified non-vacuous — all four positive assertions fail when the fix is reverted.

## AI Review Report

Codex (gpt-5.6-sol, high) ran the review-until-clean gate in its own worktree at the PR head, using four internal same-model adversarial passes. It found and fixed three defects, all introduced by this PR rather than pre-existing, and its final pass came back clean (`2363c3a04`).

All three are the same underlying class: **a UA writer that resolves the tab's identity from state the auth-host switch does not reach.**

1. **Navigation and redirect races.** The pending-navigation target was keyed by tab id and only recorded on `did-start-navigation`. Google's sign-in flow is redirect-heavy, so a redirect *into* an auth host mid-chain never triggered the switch, and a navigation that failed after being superseded could leave the auth identity standing on the document that remained. Now keyed per guest with an explicit superseded-URL set, applied on `will-redirect`, and restored on `did-fail-load` only when the failed navigation was the current one.
2. **Native profiles bypassed the opt-out after a cookie import.** `browser-session-registry` skips `setupClientHintsOverride` entirely for `userAgentMode: 'native'`, but `browser-cookie-import` re-installed it unconditionally after a browser-native import. Because this PR moved the Google-auth switch inside that function, a native profile that imported cookies silently acquired the Firefox header switch it had opted out of — while its `navigator.userAgent` stayed native, producing exactly the two-layer disagreement this PR exists to remove. Session-scoped mode state now gates it.
3. **Popup child windows bypassed the same opt-out.** Popups receive guest policies but are never registered in the tab-id map, so the direct lookup missed the native guard. Resolution now goes through the popup's owner tab, while the viewport reapply stays on the direct page id so a popup cannot inherit a preset UA it has no viewport for.

Earlier rounds in this PR also closed a viewport-preset CDP override that outranked the WebContents UA, a tracking-order bug where the override map was cleared before the CDP write was known to have landed, and a degenerate-root guard. One reported finding was **rejected after investigation**: an automated reviewer claimed the navigation reapply and the viewport chain could interleave out of order. Tracing showed `debugger.sendCommand` dispatches in call order, so the later write always wins; the speculative serialization queue added for it was removed rather than kept.

Reference comparison against embedded-browser implementations in comparable tools found **no architectural objection**. The closest equivalent independently arrived at the same design — the same two auth hosts, the same Firefox template, the same two layers — and does *not* strip `sec-ch-ua*`, so it ships Chromium client hints under a Firefox UA. This PR's `stripClientHints` is ahead of it. Two items were recorded as out of scope: device emulation is not URL-aware (already noted above as a known follow-up), and `navigator.userAgentData.brands` still reports Chromium under the Firefox UA — measured, tolerated by Google, and documented in the E2E comment.

Browser suite at the reviewed head: **33 files, 592 tests, all passing.** New coverage was mutation-checked rather than assumed — removing the redirect-time UA apply fails its specific test.

## Security Audit

No new input-handling, command-execution, path, or IPC surface. The change only rewrites outgoing request headers, the per-WebContents UA, and the CDP UA override for two exact-matched hostnames; hostname matching is exact (`URL.hostname` equality, lowercased) so lookalikes like `accounts.google.com.evil.test` do not match. No cookie transplant, no secret handling, no new dependencies. All cookie inspection during validation was read-only and metadata-only (name / host / timestamps); no cookie values were read or logged.

## Notes

- Cross-platform: the Firefox UA's platform token is derived from `process.platform` (macOS/Windows/Linux); no platform-specific shell/path/shortcut behavior touched.
- The persistence claim is **verified live** against a real account and now stands at **8h 15m as of 2026-08-07 06:34:58 UTC**, with freshness cookies rotated 2–3 minutes before that measurement — see *Live E2E validation* above.
- Builds on #12608, which introduced the native-UA session profiles this change deliberately opts out of.
- Closes #11518.

records.title: [Bug]: Embedded browser advertises FedCM but the flow never completes — breaks Google Sign-In
records.body:
### Operating system

macOS

### Orca version

1.4.173

### Details

**Summary**

Google Workspace SSO fails in the embedded browser with `NetworkError: Error retrieving a token.` The same account signs in fine in Chrome and in Safari.

The relying party uses the legacy `gapi.auth2` library. Its auth iframe runs with `supportBlocked3PCookies=1`, so it takes the FedCM path whenever the browser advertises FedCM. Orca exposes `IdentityCredential` and `IdentityProvider`, so feature detection selects FedCM — and that path never completes. No popup is ever opened, so the library never falls back to the popup flow that works elsewhere.

**Why Safari succeeds and Orca does not**

| Browser | FedCM API | 3P cookies | Path taken | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chrome | yes | allowed | FedCM | works |
| Safari | **no** | blocked by default | popup | works |
| Orca | yes | — | FedCM | **fails** |

Safari proves that neither FedCM nor third-party cookies are required for this flow — the popup path alone is sufficient. Orca fails specifically because it advertises FedCM support that does not complete.

**Reproduction**

1. In an embedded browser tab, confirm a signed-in Google session (`https://myaccount.google.com` shows the account).
2. Open a site that uses legacy `gapi.auth2` Google Sign-In.
3. Click the sign-in button.
4. No popup appears. The app surfaces `NetworkError: Error retrieving a token.`

A direct call from any https page reproduces the same rejection:

```js
await navigator.credentials.get({
  identity: {
    providers: [{
      configURL: 'https://accounts.google.com/gsi/fedcm.json',
      clientId: '<client-id>',
    }],
  },
  mediation: 'optional',
});
// → NetworkError: Error retrieving a token.
```

**What I ruled out**

- Google session — `myaccount.google.com` shows the signed-in account inside the embedded browser.
- Network — `accounts.google.com` is reachable and every request returns HTTP 200.
- Cookies — `.google.com` third-party cookies are present in the jar and unpartitioned.
- Popups — user-gesture `window.open()` works correctly in 1.4.173. Verified by hand with a local page whose buttons open a Google OAuth authorize URL and a plain URL: both returned a live `Window`, actually navigated (cross-origin `location.href` access threw, as expected), and were visible on screen. This is therefore not a regression of #7374 — the failing flow never attempts a popup at all.

**Not verified**

Whether Orca's FedCM is unimplemented or failing for some other reason. FedCM returns deliberately generic errors, so the two cannot be distinguished from the page side.

**Suggested direction**

If FedCM is not fully implemented, consider not exposing `IdentityCredential` / `IdentityProvider`. Feature detection would then fall back to the popup flow — which already works since #7392 and #8343, as verified above — and Google Sign-In would succeed the same way it does in Safari.

**Related but distinct**

- #7374 — OAuth popup denial (closed, fixed). Popups verified working here.
- #12718 — popups not addressable by the agent browser CLI.
- #6268 — embedded-browser cookie/session limitation (Auth0).

records.title: fix(browser): stop impersonating the source browser's UA on cookie import (STA-3514)
records.body:
## Summary

Cookie imports no longer impersonate the source browser's User-Agent. The embedded browser always presents its own engine-derived UA (cleaned, or native for opt-out profiles), whether or not cookies were imported. This is a net deletion (**+83/−429**): the import-time UA synthesis, the persisted per-partition UA state, and the #12811 version gate that existed only to catch the synthesis's bad output all go.

**User-visible fix:** an Arc import no longer brands the whole browser as `Chrome/1.x` (Arc's marketing version read as a Chromium version), which made sites reject the browser as ancient — permanently, since the UA was persisted and re-applied every launch. Post-fix the session presents the real engine UA (`Chrome/150.x`), and previously-poisoned persisted state is simply never read again.

**Why deletion rather than better version detection:**
- The synthesis's stated purpose — keeping Google-bound auth cookies valid — has been handled since #736 by `isGoogleSourceBoundCookie`, which excludes those cookies from import entirely. That mechanism stays.
- #12884 measured that Google rejects cookie re-transplants **regardless of UA identity**; the UA was never the binding variable.
- #12608 measured the synthesized Chrome-shaped UA reaching `/v3/signin/rejected` while the engine UA reached normal account lookup.
- Surveyed cookie-import tooling and Electron apps: none derive a UA from an installed browser's version; the convention is to present the running engine's real UA.

## Screenshots

No visual change.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint` (oxlint + oxfmt clean on touched files)
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` (all three projects, from clean — tsbuildinfo cleared first)
- [x] `pnpm test` — `src/main/browser/` suite: 33 files, 588/588 passing
- [x] Added or updated high-quality tests that would catch regressions

New/updated regression tests, all mutation-checked (re-introducing the old behavior flips them red):
- import never calls `setUserAgent` (`browser-cookie-import.test.ts`)
- legacy persisted UAs — valid Chrome-shaped **and** broken `Chrome/1.x` — are ignored on restore and the engine UA applies (`browser-session-registry.persistence.test.ts`)
- native-mode profiles get no `setUserAgent` at all, even with a legacy persisted UA

**Live Electron QA (real Electron 43 / Chromium 150 engine):** bundled the actual production `browser-session-ua.ts` from this branch into a standalone Electron harness with a local HTTPS echo server; `accounts.google.com` DNS-mapped to it to observe real wire headers. All checks pass:
- wire UA = `Chrome/150.0.7871.47` (real engine version), no `Electron`/app tokens, not `Chrome/1.x`
- `navigator.userAgent` byte-identical to the wire UA
- Google auth host: wire UA is Firefox with **no** `sec-ch-ua` headers — the #12884 switch survives intact
- Ran the identical harness against **main's** `browser-session-ua.ts`: every observed surface (wire UA, navigator UA, hints, auth-host behavior) is **byte-identical** between main and this branch. The deletion changes which code produces the session identity, not the identity itself.

## AI Review Report

Reviewed the full lifecycle of the deleted state: every reader/writer of `userAgent`/`userAgentByPartition` meta (import write, restore read, profile-delete cleanup, clear-cookies cleanup) is removed together, so no orphaned reader remains. Verified `persistMeta` naturally drops legacy keys on the next write since the loader no longer carries them — no migration code needed. Confirmed the native-UA opt-out (#12608) and the Google auth-host Firefox switch (#12884) are untouched: the registry still sets mode state before the native early-return, and `setupClientHintsOverride` still installs the auth-host handler for both clean sessions and (unchanged) native opt-outs. Checked the one behavior change beyond bug scope: Chrome/Edge imports previously presented the source browser's exact version and now present the engine version — one major apart, both real; the engine-UA path is the one all fork imports already land on in production today.

Cross-platform: this PR only deletes macOS-only synthesis code (`getUserAgentForBrowser` returned `null` off-darwin, so non-macOS behavior is unchanged by construction). No shortcuts, labels, paths, or shell behavior touched; no Windows/Linux-specific code in the deleted region.

## Security Audit

Removes an `execFileSync('defaults', …)` subprocess call and a persisted free-text value that was replayed into session state on every launch — both a net reduction in surface. No new input handling, IPC, path handling, or dependencies. The Google-bound cookie exclusion (`isGoogleSourceBoundCookie`) and partition allowlisting are unchanged.

## Notes

- Supersedes the earlier synthesis-hardening approach on this branch (preserved at tag `sta3514-synth-approach`).
- What cannot be verified without a real account: long-run Google sign-in longevity. Per #12884's methodology, transplant behavior can't be A/B'd on one account. Risk is bounded: the auth-host path is byte-identical to main (measured), and the engine-UA fallback is what every fork import on main already uses.
- Known residual (pre-existing, unchanged): with `session.setUserAgent()` active, Chromium emits no `sec-ch-ua` headers at all; identical on main, recorded in the harness diff.

records.title: fix(browser): recover browser tab when guest WebContents is destroyed (STA-3448)
records.body:
## Summary

Fixes [STA-3448](https://linear.app/stably/issue/STA-3448) / #12629 (P0, macOS): a browser tab renders solid black forever when its `<webview>` element outlives its guest WebContents.

**Root cause.** The renderer's recovery machinery only reacted to `render-process-gone`, system resume, a tab becoming visible, or an effect re-run. A guest WebContents destroyed *without* a renderer crash (detach/reattach race, guest-side close) while the tab stays visible fires none of those — Electron's `<webview>` `destroyed` event was not listened to anywhere in the codebase. The element stays registered (`browserWebviews`) while the guest registration is gone (`registeredBrowserGuests`), producing exactly the persistent off-by-one from the issue's trace-log table. Reload on the dead guest throws uncaught (`The WebView must be attached to the DOM…`, 15 breadcrumbs) and `webview.focus()` throws `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'focus')` (10 breadcrumbs), so Cmd+R could never recover the tab.

**Fix** (mirrors the existing `render-process-gone` handling at both layers):
- `webview-registry.ts`: listen for `destroyed`; if the element is still connected to the DOM (i.e. not an intentional `webview.remove()`), mark renderer recovery pending so a currently-unmounted pane recovers on remount.
- `BrowserPane.tsx`: wire `destroyed` → `guestRecovery.recoverRenderer()` for mounted panes — reload throws on a destroyed guest, so recovery falls into `replaceGuest()`, which tears down the dead element and rebuilds the webview in place.
- `browser-reload-action.ts` + all five reload entry points (toolbar, Cmd+R renderer path, Cmd+R IPC path, hard-reload IPC path, context menu): `reloadBrowserPageWebview()` distinguishes a dead guest (`getWebContentsId()` throws → route into guest recovery, per the issue's ask "make reload recreate it") from a live pre-dom-ready guest (a load is already in flight → no-op) instead of throwing uncaught.
- `focusWebviewNow`: guard `webview.focus()` against Electron's null-internals throw on a guestless webview.

## Reproduction / evidence

There are no deterministic user-level steps (the guest teardown is a race; destroying a guest without a renderer crash requires `webContents.destroy()` from the main process, which is not reachable from outside the app). Evidence chain, per the issue's "cheap to assert internally" pointer:

1. **Field signature** (from the reporter's `main.trace.ndjson`): `browserWebviews`/`registeredBrowserGuests` off-by-one appears at 08-05 00:08 and persists ~11.5h across unrelated tab churn; 25 `renderer_error` breadcrumbs (15× WebView-must-be-attached, 10× null-focus TypeError). These counters are `webviewRegistry.size` and `registeredWebContentsIds.size` — element alive, guest gone.
2. **Grep proof**: before this PR, no `destroyed` listener existed anywhere under `src/renderer` — the only guest-death signal handled was `render-process-gone`.
3. **Encoded repro (RED before fix)**: `webview-registry.test.ts` "flags renderer recovery when the guest is destroyed under a still-attached webview" fails on main (`isBrowserPageRendererRecoveryPending` stays `false`); passes with the fix. The reload-guard tests encode the two uncaught-throw modes from the breadcrumbs.

## Screenshots

No visual change. Recovery reuses the existing guest-recovery flow and existing failure overlay ("The browser page stopped unexpectedly. Retry to restore it.") when replacement fails.

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint` — `oxlint` clean on changed files; `config/scripts/check-changed-code-quality.mjs` (native + type-aware + React Doctor changed-lines gates): 0 new findings across 5 changed files; `oxfmt` clean
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` — all three tsconfigs pass (renderer covered by `tsconfig.tc.web.json`)
- [x] `pnpm test` — scoped run: all 40 test files / 320 tests under `browser-pane`, `crash-diagnostics`, and `store/slices/browser` pass; full suite left to CI (this host false-reds the full suite under Node 26)
- [ ] `pnpm build` — **not run locally**: host disk hit ENOSPC mid-run (machine-wide, unrelated to this change); relying on CI build
- [x] Added or updated high-quality tests that would catch regressions: 3 new registry lifecycle tests (destroyed-under-attached flags recovery / intentional removal ignored / listener removed on unregistration) and 3 new `reloadBrowserPageWebview` tests (live reload honors cache flag / dead guest reported without touching reload / pre-dom-ready live guest reported not-ready)

## AI Review Report

Reviewed the change for: (1) **intentional-teardown false positives** — `removePersistentWebview` calls `webview.remove()` then synchronously unregisters listeners, and both new handlers additionally check `webview.isConnected`, so close/replace paths never trigger spurious recovery; (2) **convergence** — `destroyed` → `recoverRenderer` → `reload()` throws → `replaceGuest()` → generation bump rebuilds the webview; replacement failure lands on the existing recovery-failed overlay with Retry, never a silent black tab; (3) **double-fire** with `render-process-gone` is absorbed by the existing `recoveryStarted` guard; (4) **pre-dom-ready discrimination** — `getWebContentsId()` requires only an attached guest, so a live loading guest is never replaced by a Cmd+R during initial load; (5) **hidden panes** — the registry-level pending flag survives pane unmount and is consumed by the existing remount path.

Cross-platform: renderer-only change; no keyboard shortcuts, labels, file paths, or shell behavior touched; the `destroyed` webview event and `getWebContentsId()` throw semantics are platform-independent Electron behavior (verified against `electron.d.ts` 43.x typings), so macOS/Linux/Windows behave identically. SSH and folder workspaces: the browser pane runs entirely in the local client renderer regardless of workspace type; no RPC params, stream frames, or host-published content changed, so there is no remote wire-compatibility impact.

## Security Audit

No input handling, command execution, path handling, auth, secrets, or dependency changes. No new IPC surface: recovery reuses the existing `registerGuest`/`isGuestRegistered`/`repairGuestRegistration` bridge calls with unchanged payloads. The new try/catch guards are scoped to two known DOM-API throw sites (`getWebContentsId`/`reload`/`focus` on a guestless webview) and cannot mask other failures; the guest-recovery path still surfaces errors through the existing failure overlay. No follow-up needed.

## Notes

- The issue's asks #3 (`orca tab list` not enumerating secondary-sidebar browser tabs) and #4 (per-tab trace spans) are diagnostics improvements intentionally left out of this tightly-scoped P0 fix — they deserve their own tickets.
- Limitation stated explicitly: no live macOS reproduction was possible because triggering guest destruction without a renderer crash requires main-process `webContents.destroy()`; the reproduction is encoded as the RED-before-fix registry test plus the field trace-log signature above.

records.title: fix(browser-pane): reschedule remote stream restart with bounded backoff (STA-3483)
records.body:
Fixes STA-3483.

## Summary

Remote browser panes currently make one restart attempt 500ms after a dropped screencast. If that attempt fails, the pane retains a frozen frame with no live callbacks and no recovery path until the tab is reactivated or Orca restarts.

This PR replaces that dead end with one serialized, bounded recovery lifecycle:

- Retry at `500ms`, `1s`, `2s`, `4s`, and `8s`.
- Keep at most one timer, one in-flight attempt, and one queued handoff per pane.
- Stop stale, superseded, missing-page, and permanent-failure work through pane/runtime/page/operation/stream generation guards.
- Treat a subscription that never reports `ready` within 30s as dropped.
- Refill the budget only after a stream stays healthy for 10s, preventing `ready`/`end` flapping from retrying forever.
- After exhaustion—or any path that will not retry—show an actionable **Reconnect** control.
- Reconnect runs the full open flow, so it also recovers a pane whose first stream never opened.

The lifecycle is extracted from `BrowserPane.tsx` into injectable page-session, subscription, token, liveness, status, restart-attempt, and scheduler modules. Stream UI state is one tagged value (`idle | opening | live | retrying | stopped`), so the spinner, notice, and Reconnect control cannot contradict one another.

## Root cause

On current `main`, `scheduleRemoteStreamRestart` arms one `setTimeout`. A transient failure in that callback reaches the terminal `catch`, reports an error, and never schedules another attempt. The original subscription has already been released, so no later event can restart the stream.

The authoritative failure boundary is the desktop renderer's remote-browser subscription lifecycle. The runtime host, screencast RPC, and wire format are unchanged.

## End-user behavior

- Short disconnects recover automatically within the bounded budget.
- While automatic recovery is active, the pane does not compete with it by showing a manual control.
- Once recovery stops, the pane shows user-facing connection copy and **Reconnect** rather than raw runtime/RPC text.
- A successful reconnect must paint a new frame; retaining only the frozen pre-drop frame does not count as recovery.

## Screenshots

Intentional visual change: the existing remote-stream error toast includes a **Reconnect** button after automatic recovery stops. The paired-runtime E2E captures both the dropped-stream and cold-open states as test artifacts.

## Verification

### Deterministic red/green

The same fake-clock scheduler oracle was run with only the post-failure reschedule disabled:

- Disabled: 7 targeted failures; the headline assertion received 1 attempt instead of 4.
- Restored: 12/12 scheduler tests passed with a clean tree.

Current `main` also structurally contains the original one-shot timer and terminal catch.

### Focused contracts

```text
pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts \
  src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane/remote-browser-stream-errors.test.ts \
  src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane/remote-browser-stream-lifecycle.test.ts \
  src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane/remote-browser-stream-restart-scheduler.test.ts \
  src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane/remote-browser-stream-status.test.ts
```

Result: 4 files, 64/64 tests passed. Coverage includes StrictMode cleanup/remount lifecycle reuse, malformed success-payload tolerance, counted backoff, exhaustion, cancellation during an await, serialized close handoff, stale rejection, missing/permanent failures, viewport supersession, no-close transport errors, never-ready subscriptions, flapping streams, cleanup, and manual reopen.

### Paired-runtime journey

```text
pnpm exec playwright test \
  tests/e2e/paired-remote-browser-stream-reconnect.spec.ts \
  --config tests/playwright.config.ts \
  --project electron-headless \
  --workers=1
```

Result on the final head: 2/2 passed locally on macOS in 45s. The same changed-E2E passed on Linux CI.

The journey uses an isolated headless Orca host and separate paired Electron client. It proves two paths:

1. A live stream paints a frame, the owning runtime disconnects, recovery exhausts, Reconnect remains actionable, the runtime reconnects, and a different frame object URL arrives.
2. The runtime disconnects before the pane mounts; Reconnect reruns the full open flow and establishes the first stream.

### CI

- [x] 46/46 checks green
- [x] Static analysis and typecheck
- [x] Node 24 and Node 26 test shards
- [x] macOS and Windows packaging
- [x] Cross-version wire compatibility
- [x] Changed paired-runtime E2E

## Performance and cleanup

Automatic recovery makes at most five attempts per pane. It adds no polling, subprocess, provider-wide scan, or cross-pane fanout. Cancellation retires pending and in-flight generations; exhaustion stops background work until explicit user action.

## Risk and compatibility

- Desktop remote-browser panes: intentional lifecycle and error-state change.
- Local browser panes: unaffected.
- Remote host and wire protocol: unchanged; mixed client/host versions remain compatible.
- SSH, relay, and paired transports: no transport-specific branch added.
- Folder workspaces and git worktrees: both continue through the existing runtime selector.
- Mobile/web browser surfaces: unaffected by this desktop-renderer component.

## Known gaps

- The live journey covers headless `orca serve`, not a headed desktop-server host.
- The live fault is an explicit runtime disconnect, not OS sleep/wake or a real network partition.
- Live behavior is covered on macOS and Linux; physical Windows paired-server evidence is not collected.
- The E2E proves UI convergence and new-frame identity but does not count subscribe attempts; exact attempt count and ordering are covered by fake-clock contracts.
- After a transport error with no close, a resize can temporarily re-enter the recovery budget before Reconnect returns. Current `main` has no recovery path for that failure shape, so this is an improvement rather than a regression, but it remains follow-up work.
- A host that reports `ready` and then goes silent without close or error remains a separate pre-existing liveness class.

The durable reliability gate is registered as experimental/partial until headed, Windows, network-loss, and soak evidence are collected.

## AI Review Report

Adversarial review findings drove the lifecycle extraction, generation ownership, serialized recovery, bounded budget, never-ready deadline, health threshold, tagged UI state, stale-error suppression, and Reconnect stacking fix. All existing actionable review threads are resolved. A fresh CodeRabbit review is requested on the final head before merge.

## Security Audit

No new permissions, credential handling, filesystem access, navigation policy, RPC methods, wire fields, or host-side inputs are introduced. Raw transport errors remain available to developer logs but are replaced with user-facing copy in the pane.

## Notes

The PR intentionally prefers bounded automatic recovery plus explicit user control over either a single attempt or an unbounded background retry loop.
