## Summary

- carry the host snapshot's optional `cols` / `rows` through the paired-runtime multiplexer and transport
- replay authoritative ANSI at the source grid, then fit to the destination viewport and report the resulting PTY size before releasing live output
- preserve snapshot geometry and escape-tail metadata if a pending shutdown is rolled back
- keep reattach host-authoritative: no client-side cached viewport replay and no delayed/offline input

## User impact

Before this change, a paired terminal snapshot created at one grid size could be parsed at the client's current grid size. Wrapped lines, cursor placement, and scrollback could therefore be reconstructed incorrectly after parking, reconnecting, resizing, sleep, or shutdown rollback.

After this change, users get the host's actual terminal state reconstructed at the grid where it was produced, then fitted to the visible pane. The practical benefit is a correctly restored, interactive terminal without mangled wrapping, displaced cursor state, or stale rollback output. If the host is unreachable, Orca still waits for the authoritative reconnect; it does not show a non-interactive cached image.

## Expected performance

- **Steady-state typing and output:** no expected difference. This code is not on the live-output hot path.
- **Reattach/reconnect:** no intended time-to-first-content speedup. The client still waits for the authoritative snapshot. When its grid differs, replay adds one temporary xterm resize before parsing and one destination fit/PTY resize before live output resumes; this is bounded to the replay transaction and expected to be marginal relative to parsing the snapshot.
- **Network:** two optional small integers (`cols` and `rows`) per snapshot; effectively negligible compared with the ANSI snapshot payload.
- **Memory:** no client-side screenshot or ANSI viewport cache, so there is no additional retained terminal-frame memory.
- **Compared with the removed cache experiment:** the final PR intentionally gives up cosmetic instant paint while disconnected. The earlier 72 ms macOS and 544 ms Windows cached-paint measurements do not apply; the user-visible content arrival time is now governed by authoritative reconnect/snapshot latency.

## Reproduced evidence

A paired two-client Electron A/B reproduced the pre-fix failure and verified the fix. The source terminal was 30 columns, the destination was 119 columns, and a later live `!` exposed whether the restored cursor stayed attached to the wrapped line.

- **Before:** restored text and subsequent live output detach across the grid change.
- **After:** rows remain `ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcd` / `efghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz!`, with the cursor immediately after `!`.

[View the before/after screenshots and exact fixture results](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/pull/12768#issuecomment-5208424746). The screenshots were captured from Electron through `agent-browser`; they are PR attachments, not repository files.

## Testing

- [ ] `pnpm lint` — full repository lint not run; standard and type-aware focused lint passed on changed code
- [x] `pnpm run typecheck:web`
- [ ] `pnpm test` — full repository suite not run; 799 final-review focused tests passed, including 4 cross-version wire tests
- [x] Electron E2E app build and paired-runtime regression
- [x] Added or updated regression coverage for source-grid metadata and shutdown rollback
- [x] Formatting, max-lines ratchet, and `git diff --check`

Electron paired-runtime QA passed hidden-mounted, cold-parked, and reconnect-parked scenarios. Each restored the authoritative buffer, delivered input to the host, painted live, and ended with matching client and PTY grids.

## AI Review Report

A same-model senior review loop checked replay ordering, stale PTY/generation races, mixed-version wire behavior, macOS/Linux/Windows compatibility, SSH/folder workspaces, and performance. It found one meaningful issue: shutdown rollback dropped snapshot dimensions and escape-tail metadata. That path was fixed and covered with focused tests; a fresh post-fix review returned clean.

The final implementation follows the common authoritative-state pattern used by terminal systems: restore the terminal model/stream from the owner, rather than displaying a non-interactive cached image. The new work is snapshot-only and does not add live-output hot-path work.

## Security Audit

No new command execution, paths, authentication, secrets, dependencies, or IPC surfaces. Snapshot dimensions remain optional for mixed-version peers, are validated as positive terminal dimensions before resize, and all asynchronous replay/fit work remains guarded by PTY identity and stream generation. Removing cached viewport replay also avoids retaining extra terminal content client-side. No follow-up required.

## Notes

- Optional metadata preserves client/server update independence; older peers continue without source-grid correction.
- The path is shared across local, paired, SSH-hosted, and folder workspaces without assuming a git worktree or platform-specific shell/path behavior.
- Reconnect/connecting UI and warm transport lifetime are intentionally owned by the adjacent remote-server work and are out of scope here.

records.title: fix(remote-workspace): keep local tabs when a pulled snapshot reports none for a populated worktree
records.body:
Fixes #12748

A pulled direct-SSH workspace snapshot that carries zero tabs for a worktree the renderer is showing tabs in leaves those tabs in place.

`narrowDirectSshReplaceWorktreeIds` removes such worktrees from the replace scope: local state wins until the remote reports at least one tab for the worktree. The snapshot carries no tombstones, so "no tabs" is indistinguishable from a regressed or corrupted snapshot — honoring it deletes terminal surfaces the user can see, unrecoverably, while keeping local state leaves surfaces the user can still close.

The narrowed scope drives every step of the apply: the merge (remote per-worktree records are filtered to the scope, so a spread cannot undo the narrowing), `replaceWorkspaceKeys` for `hydrateWorkspaceSession`/`hydrateTabsSession`, and `reconnectPersistedTerminals` — a protected worktree left in the hydration scope would still get its live tabs reset and swept into PTY reconnect.

`mergeDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSession` applies the narrowing itself rather than relying on the caller to have done it. The narrowing predicate depends only on the worktree id and the three session inputs, never on the input set, so applying it twice is a no-op: the caller — which still needs the narrowed set as a value for `replaceWorkspaceKeys` — pays nothing, and no caller can delete a populated worktree's tabs by handing the merge a wider scope.

Worktrees with tabs on both sides are unaffected; the remote stays authoritative for them.

## Bounded regression, not convergence

Single-client this converges: the next push re-exports the protected worktree, and a genuinely emptied worktree replaces once the remote reports any tab for it.

Multi-client it does not. Two clients against one SSH box is the point of a shared snapshot: if client B closes every tab in worktree W while client A still holds them, A protects, A pushes, and B's tabs come back. That repeats until the tabs are closed on the holding client too.

The trade is deliberate — resurrected tabs are visible and one click to close, deleted tabs are silent and permanent — but it is a bounded regression, not convergence. Real convergence needs tombstones plus a monotonic per-scope revision, tracked in #12447.

## Testing

`pnpm run typecheck:web` and `npx oxlint` are clean; the renderer hook, store, and lib vitest suites pass.

Coverage runs at two levels. `remote-workspace-session-merge.test.ts` pins the merge, including that it narrows a replace scope handed to it un-narrowed. `remote-workspace-snapshot-empty-worktree-guard.test.ts` drives `applyDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSnapshot` against a real store and asserts on post-apply state — live PTY bindings, `pendingReconnectWorktreeIds`, and the workspace keys handed to `reconnectPersistedTerminals` — so the hydration scope is pinned and not only the merge.

records.title: A pulled remote workspace snapshot with zero tabs for a populated worktree permanently deletes the local tabs
records.body:
## Symptom

After a remote (direct-SSH) workspace snapshot pull, all terminal tabs of a worktree disappear locally, permanently — including tabs bound to live remote PTYs. Any snapshot regression (revision race during a reconnect flap, corrupted write, or an export bug like stablyai/orca#12721) becomes irreversible local data loss on the next pull.

## Cause

`mergeDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSession` is remote-authoritative for every worktree in the target scope: `omitTargetWorktrees(current.tabsByWorktree)` drops all target-scope worktrees from local state before spreading the remote's `tabsByWorktree`. A worktree that is absent from the snapshot — or present with `[]` — loses all local tabs, layouts and per-worktree records. The snapshot carries no tombstones, so "no tabs" from the remote is indistinguishable from a regressed snapshot, yet it is honored as an authoritative delete.

## Fix direction

A worktree with live local tabs and zero remote tabs leaves the replace scope: local state wins until the remote reports at least one tab for it. Deletion by absence stays impossible; a genuinely emptied worktree converges as soon as the remote carries any tab for it again. The narrowed scope must drive the hydration steps (`replaceWorkspaceKeys`) too, or the hydration pipeline still resets the protected tabs.

records.title: Bug: Arc cookie import persists User-Agent Chrome/1.x (product version) — sites mark browser incompatible
[Feature]: Add Chrome-style Local Network Access permissions to embedded browser profiles
records.body:
## Problem or use case

Modern Chromium applies a web-origin permission boundary when a public website accesses loopback or private-network resources. This Local Network Access (previously Private Network Access) permission is separate from the macOS application-level Local Network/TCC/NECP permission.

Orca already declares `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` and Bonjour services, and it has dedicated support for local development URLs. Its embedded browser session policy is deny-by-default, but there is no explicit per-origin Local Network Access permission flow or diagnostic state for Chromium requests.

The result is that browser-based administration and authentication flows which legitimately need to reach `localhost`, RFC1918 addresses, or `.local` services can fail without the Chrome-style decision surface the user expects.

This is separate from:

- #12711, which concerns macOS 27 beta denying LAN access to the Orca process tree through NECP/TCC;
- #5260/#5303, which concern SSH reachability and fallback;
- #8454/#9104, which concern local HTTPS URL/certificate handling.

## Proposed outcome

Add explicit Chrome-style Local Network Access permission handling to embedded browser profiles, with clear separation between Chromium origin permission and macOS process permission.

## Acceptance criteria

- When Chromium requests Local Network Access, Orca shows a trusted prompt identifying the requesting origin and target address class.
- The user can allow once, always allow for this browser profile/origin, or deny.
- Grants are scoped by browser profile and origin, persisted deliberately, visible in Settings, and revocable.
- Public-origin to loopback, public-origin to RFC1918/private address, and public-origin to `.local` are covered.
- Same-origin/local-origin behavior follows the Chromium specification rather than a blanket allow.
- Workers/iframes cannot silently inherit broader permission than the top-level origin policy allows.
- The browser CLI exposes a typed `permission-requested` / `awaiting-user` / `granted` / `denied` state so an agent can explain the blocker, but cannot silently grant it.
- Diagnostics distinguish Chromium LNA denial, macOS TCC/NECP denial, certificate failure, DNS failure, and ordinary network failure.
- Tests cover allow once, persistent grant, denial, revoke, profile isolation, iframe/worker requests, and macOS-denied behavior.

## Security considerations

This permission can expose internal services to public web origins and must not be auto-granted merely because Orca itself has macOS Local Network access. Existing browser profile isolation and audit expectations should apply.

## References

- Chrome Local Network Access: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access
- macOS process-level issue: #12711
- Local HTTPS handling: #8454 and #9104

records.title: [Feature]: Support user-approved external app protocol handoff from the embedded browser
records.body:
## Problem or use case

Embedded login flows sometimes hand off from the browser to a registered local application through a custom URL scheme. Okta Verify is one example: an authentication flow may navigate to a scheme such as `oktaverify://...` so the installed app can complete device binding or verification.

Orca's embedded browser currently accepts navigation to `http:`, `https:`, and `file:` URLs, while its external-open normalization is intentionally restricted to web URLs. There is no user-approved path for a web origin to invoke a registered local application. The navigation is therefore blocked even when the same flow works in Chrome.

Orca's Computer Use capability can operate supported local app windows after launch, but it does not solve the browser-to-app handoff.

I found no existing issue or discussion covering Okta Verify or general outbound custom schemes from the embedded browser. The `orca://focus` work in #4384/#7930 is Orca's own inbound deep link and is a different trust boundary.

## Proposed outcome

Provide a Chrome-style, explicitly user-approved handoff from an embedded browser origin to an OS-registered external application protocol.

## Security requirements

- Only process attempts caused by a recent, trusted user gesture.
- Resolve through the operating system's registered protocol handler; never execute a command supplied by page content.
- Show a trusted Orca prompt containing the requesting origin, scheme, and resolved application identity when available.
- Offer cancel, allow once, and optionally remember per browser profile + origin + scheme.
- Provide a settings surface to inspect and revoke remembered grants.
- Never allow dangerous or internal schemes such as `javascript:`, `data:`, unrestricted `file:`, shell commands, or executable paths.
- Keep navigation and external-app grants separate from ordinary HTTP link handling.
- Record requested, approved, denied, opened, failed, and no-handler outcomes without logging sensitive URL parameters.

## Agent behavior

Agents should be able to trigger the page action and observe a typed `external-app-requested` / `awaiting-user-approval` state. Approval of launching the local app must remain a user decision unless Orca already has an explicit remembered grant for that origin and scheme.

## Acceptance criteria

- A test custom protocol registered with the OS can be invoked from a trusted user-gesture click in an embedded page after explicit approval.
- The same navigation without a user gesture is blocked.
- Denial, missing handler, malformed URL, and forbidden scheme produce visible, actionable errors.
- Remembered permission is scoped to browser profile, origin, and scheme and can be revoked.
- Sensitive query/fragment data is excluded from telemetry and audit logs.
- Popup and top-level embedded browser contexts behave consistently.
- An Okta Verify handoff can reach the installed app without weakening existing browser navigation validation.

## Related work

- #4384
- #7930

records.title: [Feature]: Make embedded browser popups addressable through the agent browser CLI
records.body:
## Problem or use case

OAuth/SSO popups in the embedded browser now work for a human: stablyai/orca#7392 and [#8343](<https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/8343>) preserve a real child `WebContents`, session, `window.opener`, `postMessage`, and `window.close()`. However, the child popup is not exposed as an addressable browser target to agents using the Orca CLI.

This leaves an automation gap in login and consent flows. The user can see the popup, but an agent cannot inspect or operate it using the same snapshot/click/type/eval workflow available for a normal embedded browser tab.

## Reproduction

Tested with Orca 1.4.171:

1. Serve a page containing a user-gesture button that calls `window.open('/popup.html', 'probe', 'width=520,height=320')`.
2. Open the page through `orca tab create`.
3. Take a snapshot and click the button through the browser CLI.
4. The native Orca popup appears and loads its content.
5. Run `orca tab list --json` and snapshot the opener again.

## Actual behavior

* The popup is visible to the user.
* `orca tab list` lists only the opener.
* The popup receives no discoverable `browserPageId`.
* Snapshot/click/type/eval cannot target the popup.

This matches the current architecture: the popup is a separate `BaseWindow`/`WebContentsView` with inherited security context, but it is not registered as a managed browser page target.

## Expected behavior

A popup should preserve its native opener semantics while also becoming a discoverable, switchable target for the agent browser API.

## Acceptance criteria

* A newly created popup emits a typed event containing a stable target/page identifier and its opener identifier.
* It appears in `orca tab list` or a dedicated `orca popup list` command.
* `snapshot`, `screenshot`, `click`, `type/fill`, `keypress`, `eval`, console, and network inspection can explicitly target it.
* The popup remains a real child browsing context with the same session, `window.opener`, `postMessage`, and `window.close()` behavior.
* The controlled origin bar and existing popup security policy remain intact.
* Closing either side updates target state deterministically; stale popup IDs return a clear error.
* Nested popups, OAuth process swaps, Cmd/Ctrl-click handling, and ordinary `target=_blank` links do not regress.
* Tests cover popup creation, discovery, operation, navigation/process swap, self-close, opener close, and blocked popup policy.

## Related work

* stablyai/orca#7374
* stablyai/orca#7392
* [#8343](<https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/8343>)
* [#8659](<https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/8659>)
* stablyai/orca#8718
* stablyai/orca#8416 (process-swap lifetime, not agent addressability)

records.title: fix(browser): wake display on demand for remote screencast
records.body:
Fixes #11492

Supersedes the approach in #11491 (closed): that PR only held `prevent-display-sleep` after a screencast was already running. Maintainer feedback asked for an explicit **wake-on-demand** path that recovers when the host display/compositor is **already asleep** before remote browsing starts.

## Summary

- On the first live `browser.screencast`, **wake** the host display (macOS: `caffeinate -u`; Linux: best-effort `xset dpms force on` when `DISPLAY` is set), then hold Electron `prevent-display-sleep` + the same macOS/Linux sleep assertions agent-awake uses until the last stream ends.
- Temporarily disable main-window background throttling while streaming; restore the default when idle.
- Document lock-screen / lid / Windows caveats in `docs/reference/remote-browser-display-wake.md`.

## Why this is different from #11491

| | #11491 | This PR |
|--|--|--|
| Already-asleep display | Not addressed (`prevent-display-sleep` does not turn the panel on) | Explicit wake pulse before hold |
| Complexity | Stale TTL + live-token reconciliation lease model | Simple per-page token set + wake on 0→1 + hold while live |
| Docs | PR notes only | Checked-in reference doc for caveats |

## Screenshots

No visual change.

## Testing

- [x] Targeted vitest: screencast awake, display-wake helpers, platform-assertion isolation, runtime screencast lifecycle
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`
- [x] `pnpm run check:code-quality:changed -- upstream/main`
- [ ] Manual: pair mobile → turn host display off (session still running) → open browser pane → page should update; close pane → host may sleep again
- [ ] Manual: confirm lock screen may light up but unlock is not required for CDP streaming

## AI Review Report

- Cross-platform: macOS wake is the primary path; Linux is best-effort; Windows holds `prevent-display-sleep` only (documented).
- Remote/mobile: triggered from runtime `browser.screencast` start/teardown; no wire protocol change.
- Performance: cost only while a screencast is live (display/compositor + stream); idle releases assertions.

## Security Audit

No new IPC, auth, or secrets. Spawns existing OS tools (`caffeinate` / `xset`) with fixed args. Quit-time dispose releases blockers.

## Notes

- Unlock is usually unnecessary because screencast streams WebContents pixels, not the desktop framebuffer; waking may still illuminate the lock UI (privacy in shared spaces).
- Lid-closed / clamshell / full system sleep limitations are documented rather than papered over.
- Please approve fork workflows so CI can run.

records.title: fix(agents): defer the sleeping-agent sweep until a direct-SSH workspace merges its snapshot
records.body:
## Summary

Fixes #12701.

For direct-SSH workspaces the worktree tab lists arrive with the remote snapshot merge, after connect; the sleeping-agent sweep runs earlier (its only gate, `workspaceSessionReady`, means local hydration) and judges every record against tab lists that don't exist yet — cold-resuming live remote sessions and letting the background wake's canonical-record dedupe delete records permanently. This PR sequences the sweep behind the merge:

- `sleeping-agent-remote-hydration-gate.ts` — `shouldDeferSleepingAgentResumeForRemoteHydration`: defer only when the worktree's resolved execution host is an SSH target that is connected/connecting, not in `remoteWorkspaceHydratedTargetIds`, and whose first pull hasn't concluded (sync phase absent or `pulling`). Local worktrees, disconnected targets, and settled pulls pass through unchanged, so offline sessions keep today's behavior.
- Both sweep entry points check the gate: `resumeSleepingAgentSessionsForWorktree` (covers all worktree-activation callers) and `wakeSleepingAgentsForWorktreeInBackground` (whose canonical-record dedupe is destructive and must not run against a pre-merge tab list). Deferred background wakes are buffered, not dropped.
- Every pull conclusion settles the deferral: the snapshot apply re-runs the sweep for the visible worktree and replays buffered wakes; `concludePullWithoutApply` (shared by the previously silent no-apply-token exits of both `syncAfterConnect` and `applyUnsolicitedSnapshot`), the offline branch, the revision-0 branch, and both workspace-hydration-timeout branches all reach a terminal phase and flush the wake buffer. A buffered wake never outlives the deferral that parked it; replayed wakes whose target is still mid-pull re-buffer without looping.

## Validation

- `pnpm exec vitest run --config config/vitest.config.ts src/renderer/src/lib/resume-sleeping-agent-session-ssh-hydration-gate.test.ts src/renderer/src/lib/wake-sleeping-agents-remote-hydration.test.ts src/renderer/src/lib/wake-sleeping-agents-in-background.test.ts src/renderer/src/hooks/remote-workspace-target-sync.test.ts`
- `pnpm run typecheck:web`

New tests cover: deferral while a connected target is mid-pull; sweep proceeds when hydrated / disconnected / pull concluded offline; local worktrees never deferred; buffered wakes replay once on flush and re-buffer while still deferred; no-apply-token and hydration-timeout pulls conclude with a terminal error phase.

records.title: SSH: sleeping-agent sweep races the remote workspace snapshot merge — every restart cold-resumes live remote sessions and destroys their records
records.body:
## Summary

For direct-SSH workspaces, the worktree tab lists live in the remote workspace snapshot (`~/.orca/sessions/<ns>.json` on the host) and only land in the renderer store after connect, via `remoteWorkspace.get` → `mergeDirectSshRemoteWorkspaceSession` (`remote-workspace-target-sync.ts` → `remote-workspace-snapshot-apply.ts`). That pull is a network round trip.

The sleeping-agent wake sweep does not wait for it. Its only readiness gate is `workspaceSessionReady`, which means "the LOCAL orca-data session hydrated" (`terminals.ts`) and is already true before the remote pull even starts — `syncAfterConnect` itself awaits `waitForWorkspaceSessionReady()` before fetching. So on every app start + SSH connect, worktree activation runs `resumeSleepingAgentSessionsForWorktree` against a `tabsByWorktree` that contains none of the target's tabs yet.

Consequences, observed in production logs (~2s after connect, before the merge):

- `recordPaneIsOwnedByPreservedPane` misses for every record (its tab exists in no worktree yet) → `launchSleepingAgentSession` creates a fresh tab typing `claude --resume <id>` for sessions still running on the remote → duplicate writers, one orphan tab + relay PTY per session per restart.
- The launch destroys the record (`clearSleepingAgentSession`), and `wakeSleepingAgentsForWorktreeInBackground`'s canonical-record dedupe (`getCanonicalPassiveWakeRecords`) deletes records judged against the empty tab list — permanently, so even the later merge can't restore correct behavior for this run.

## Proposed fix (sequencing, not symptom-patching)

Defer the sweep for a worktree whose resolved execution host is a direct-SSH target that is connected/connecting but whose first snapshot pull has not concluded — consuming the existing `remoteWorkspaceHydratedTargetIds` latch (`ssh.ts`) plus `remoteWorkspaceSyncStatusByTargetId` phases. Offline / disconnected targets and local worktrees must pass through unchanged, and every pull-conclusion path (success, offline, empty snapshot, error, no-apply-token) must (a) settle on a terminal phase and (b) replay any background wakes the deferral parked — otherwise the gate would trade duplicate launches for dropped mobile wakes or a wedged deferral. After the merge applies, re-run the sweep for the visible worktree so deferred auto-resume still happens, now judged against real state.

PR to follow.

records.title: fix(ssh): snapshot detached SSH leases on quit and bound the teardown
records.body:
Implements the design in #12425 (STA-3366). **Stacked on #12673 (STA-3365)** — the base branch is that PR, so review it first; the diff shown here is this ticket only.

## The problem

Quit already started SSH teardown before `store.flushAsync()`, but per-target teardown awaits port-forward removal *before* anything marks the session's recovery lease detached:

```ts
await portForwardManager?.removeAllForwards(targetId)   // slow
await teardown(session)                                 // ← only here does the lease become 'detached'
```

So a slow forward close let the final store flush latch and snapshot while leases still said `attached`. The per-session durable write that arrived afterwards was rejected, because persistence had already been finalized. The next launch then believed it was still attached to PTYs the app had let go of.

Separately, the SSH shutdown bound applied only to the in-flight join *between* the two drains. Either drain could consume the whole global quit deadline. And `waitForSystemSshForwardStop` had no timer after `SIGKILL`, so a child that never reported exit left the promise pending forever and could hold quit open.

## What changed

**One shutdown entry point.** `beginSshShutdown()` performs every in-memory transition synchronously before it returns — invalidating connect and reset authorities, transitioning each active session, and marking its recovery lease detached in memory — then returns the asynchronous transport drain. The quit path calls it immediately before `store.flushAsync()` with no await in between, so the flush that succeeds is the one that persists the detached state. It is idempotent: a second call joins the same drain and repeats no transition.

**Durability split, not weakened.** `detachAndPersist()` keeps its required durable write and still reports a failed one to its caller. Only the shutdown transition delegates durability to the immediately following final flush, via a new in-memory-only `Store.markSshRemotePtyLeasesForShutdown`. Because the in-memory update lands first, the drain's later `markSshRemotePtyLeasesAsync` finds nothing changed and attempts no flush at all — which is also what stops async drain code from mutating recovery state after the snapshot.

The guarantee is conditional and stated as such: *when the final store flush succeeds*, its snapshot contains detached SSH leases. Write failure and the outer process deadline remain visible residual risk.

**One deadline for the whole drain.** The drain/join/drain sequence shares a single absolute budget instead of bounding only the join, so no single phase can consume the global quit deadline. On expiry it stops awaiting later phases and returns unfinished work as `{ targetId, phase }` entries with one aggregate log line.

**A post-`SIGKILL` bound.** `waitForSystemSshForwardStop` arms a short timer when `SIGKILL` is sent, because `SIGKILL` is never acknowledged and a reparented child or lost handle would otherwise leave the promise pending. A child that has already exited is detected before any signal, so teardown never signals a pid the OS may have reassigned.

## Why nothing here destroys a session

This is the part the ticket most needed to get right, given #12642 (STA-3376) established that an abandoned SSH PTY is **not** proven dead.

- `detached` means *this app let go of the lease*, not that the remote shell died. It is the same state an ordinary user-initiated disconnect writes.
- Every PTY those leases name is left running for the next attach. Nothing on this path terminates, tombstones, or reaps anything, and no recovery identity is removed.
- The pre-pass is the opposite of a reaper: it exists so that still-running remote PTYs are correctly recorded as detached-but-alive rather than being lost to a snapshot that says `attached`.
- The shared deadline is used strictly for *reporting* unfinished phases. Expiry changes no lease state, removes no recovery record, and draws no conclusion about liveness — the test asserts exactly that.
- The post-`SIGKILL` timer bounds teardown; it does not claim the child is gone and drops no state that assumed it was alive.

## Acceptance criteria

| Criterion | Status |
| --- | --- |
| A successful final flush contains detached state for every session at the pre-pass | Met |
| No SSH connect/reset continuation publishes after the pre-pass | Met (pre-existing publication fence, covered by the retained connect-fence test) |
| The whole SSH shutdown path returns within its local budget | Met |
| A never-exiting forward child cannot hold quit open | Met |
| Ordinary detach durability behavior is unchanged | Met |
| Platform/topology impact documented | Met, below |

## Verification

Each production behavior was proven covered by breaking it and watching a named test fail, then restoring the edit:

| Mutation | Tests red |
| --- | --- |
| Pre-pass deferred past one await (the original defect) | 1 |
| Shutdown transition does a per-session durable write instead | 4 |
| Shutdown idempotency removed | 1 |
| Each phase gets its own full budget | 1 |
| Post-`SIGKILL` timer removed | 1 |
| Already-exited child is still signalled | 1 |

The headline ordering test asserts, with no `await` between, that every lease is already detached in memory while forward removal is still pending — the exact instant the quit path starts the final flush. Two of these tests were initially not sensitive to their mutation (one polluted by a shared mock, one that hung rather than failed); both were rewritten until the mutation produced a clean, fast failure.

Negative coverage that live sessions survive: leases are marked `detached` and never `terminated`; recovery records are never removed, including when the budget expires with work unfinished; and ordinary non-quit detach still surfaces a failed durable write to its caller.

Suites `src/main/ssh`, `src/relay`, `src/shared`, `src/main/ipc`, `src/main/persistence.test.ts`: 9692 passed, 2 failed. Both failures (`agent-exec-handler`) reproduce identically on `origin/main` in a clean worktree and are unrelated. `pnpm run typecheck`, `oxlint`, and `oxfmt --check` are clean.

## Platform and topology impact

- **SSH:** the changed path. Covered by the tests above.
- **Local, daemon, WSL, folder workspaces, mobile/relay, Git providers:** unaffected. `beginSshShutdown()` replaces `detachAllSshSessionsForShutdown()` one-for-one at the same point in the quit sequence, and the new store method is only called from the SSH shutdown transition.
- **macOS/Linux/Windows:** the forward-stop change is signal handling on a `ChildProcess`, already guarded by an exit check on all platforms; no new platform-conditional behavior.

Refs STA-3366.

records.title: fix(browser): stop an over-limit screencast frame from killing the paired runtime socket (STA-2970)
records.body: Fixes STA-2970. ## Symptom A Mac client paired to another Mac over LAN. Opening any webpage in the remote browser drops the runtime connection, and the client then retries forever and never recovers until the whole client app is restarted. ## Why it happens Host -> client screencast frames are admitted up to **8 MiB** (`REMOTE_RUNTIME_MAX_OUTBOUND_BINARY_FRAME_BYTES`, `src/shared/remote-runtime-memory-limits.ts:19`). The host's E2EE channel refuses anything larger and answers by closing the **entire runtime socket** with close code **1013 "Outbound reply buffer overflow"** (`src/main/runtime/rpc/e2ee-channel.ts:300-306`) — taking terminals and agent streams down with the browser view, not just the screencast. The screencast producer reads a `false` return from its `onFrame` sink as **backpressure** and re-queues the *identical* frame every 50 ms (`schedulePendingFrameRetry`, `src/main/browser/browser-screencast-stream.ts:285-303`). An over-limit frame can never become smaller, so the retry can never succeed: every attempt trips 1013 again. That single confusion explains both halves of the report — the connection dying on page load, and never coming back. This is a **permanent condition being treated as transient** — the mirror image of the hidden-output bug fixed in #12655, where a transient condition was treated as permanent. ## What makes an 8 MiB frame reachable at all Live frames are hard-bounded: `maxWidth`/`maxHeight` go straight to `Page.startScreencast` and Chromium scales to fit. The **navigation snapshot** path does not. `emitSnapshotFrame` fires on `Page.frameNavigated` / `Page.loadEventFired` — i.e. exactly "opening a webpage" — and passed `webContents.capturePage(...)` straight into `toJPEG()`/`toPNG()`. `capturePage`'s rect is CSS pixels but the returned bitmap is *device* pixels, so with `deviceScaleFactor` up to 2 (desktop) the snapshot could be **4x the pixel area the live path is allowed to send**, and `maxWidth`/`maxHeight` were never applied there. That is the path that produces the over-limit frame on an ordinary page load. ## The fix Two parts, both small: 1. **`src/main/runtime/remote-browser-screencast-frame-admission.ts` (new)** — an over-limit frame is reported as *handled*, so the producer advances to the next frame instead of retrying a doomed one, and it never reaches the transport that would close the socket. Genuine backpressure still round-trips: a `false` from the transport is still returned as `false`. 2. **`scaleSnapshotToFit`** in `browser-screencast-stream.ts` — apply the caller's own `maxWidth`/`maxHeight` to the snapshot capture, using the `scaleToFit` helper already in that file. This removes the asymmetry above, so the drop guard becomes a backstop rather than the primary mitigation. It can only ever make a frame smaller, and only when the capture already exceeds bounds the live path enforces anyway. ### Why the guard sits at the paired-runtime boundary, not in the generic producer The 8 MiB ceiling is a property of the *paired-runtime transport*, not of screencasting. Putting the check in `startBrowserScreencast` would bake a remote-transport constant into the generic Chromium producer. Wrapping at `orca-runtime-browser.ts` keeps it where the limit actually applies. Ordering matters here and is deliberate: `stream.sendBinary` is already wrapped by `sendBinaryAfterReady` (`orca-runtime.ts:34257`), which legitimately returns `false` for frames arriving before the JSON `ready` event. The size check runs **before** delegating, so an over-limit first snapshot is dropped immediately rather than spinning in the 50 ms retry loop until `ready`, while the pre-`ready` transient backpressure is preserved untouched. ## Behavior questions a reviewer should ask **Does dropping a frame leave the view stuck?** Frames are complete standalone JPEG/PNG images, not deltas — each one replaces the `` wholesale on the client. A dropped frame is self-healing by construction: the next frame fully repaints. In the transient case (one heavy frame mid-load) the user sees nothing at all. The honest caveat: if *every* frame for a given page and viewport were over the limit, the pane would sit on its last good image with no error shown, because Chromium stops producing frames once a static page settles. Part 2 is what closes that gap for the realistic trigger. It is not fully closed for one residual path — the mobile web-view mode sends no viewport, so its snapshot takes the `Page.captureScreenshot` branch with no clip and no clamp; there the drop guard is still the only protection. Even then the outcome is strictly better than today: a quiet skipped frame instead of a 1013 that kills every subscription on the connection. **Is "never reconnects without an app restart" fixed?** Partly, and I want to be precise. The doomed-retry loop is gone, so the specific failure in the report no longer strands anyone. But there is an **independent client-side recovery defect** that this PR does not touch: `scheduleRemoteStreamRestart`'s terminal `.catch` in `BrowserPane.tsx:1621-1633` arms exactly one 500 ms retry and never reschedules. If that single attempt fails — host still unreachable, RPC queue overloaded — the pane holds a null subscription with no live callbacks, so nothing can re-arm it short of tab reactivation or an app restart. Any cause of connection loss triggers it, not just this one. It is a renderer-side concern with a different trigger surface and needs its own renderer test setup, so it belongs in a separate ticket rather than mixed into a main-process transport fix. Not yet filed — flagging it here so it gets an owner. ## Validation - Red re-proven before green, by reverting each production change in place: - admission guard reverted -> **3 failed / 20 passed**; the integration oracle failed with the real `[1013, "Outbound reply buffer overflow"]` from the actual `E2EEChannel`, and the call-site wiring test failed independently. - snapshot clamp reverted -> **1 failed / 1 passed** in the snapshot suite. - `src/main/browser` + `src/main/runtime` + `src/preload`: **278 files, 4239 passed, 6 skipped**. - `pnpm run typecheck` clean; `oxlint` (default + code-quality-native) clean; `oxfmt --check` clean; `check:max-lines-ratchet` OK (new snapshot tests went in their own file rather than pushing an existing one past the 800-line cap).

records.title: [Bug]: Browser tab renders solid black — <webview> element outlives its guest WebContents
records.body:
### Operating system

macOS

### Orca version

`Orca.app` `CFBundleShortVersionString` 1.4.161 — status bar reported 2.1.221, updated to 2.1.222 during the observation window. macOS / Darwin 25.5.0, Apple Silicon.

### Details

**Short summary**

An embedded browser tab turns solid black and never repaints again. The `<webview>` element stays attached to the DOM after its guest WebContents is gone, so the tab paints only the element's own dark background while the tab title and URL bar still show the old page.

**What happened?**

A browser tab that had been open for a while went fully black. Cmd+R does nothing — there is no guest left to reload. Closing the tab and reopening the URL is the only recovery.

It preferentially hits long-lived tabs pointing at self-hosted / internal dev apps — pages that redirect, re-authenticate, or whose dev server restarts underneath them. Static pages (e.g. Claude artifacts) are rarely affected. I could not recover the affected URL from the logs (see request 4 below), so that correlation is observational, not proven.

**How can we reproduce it?**

I do not have deterministic steps — it appears when a guest gets torn down and re-created while the element is detached/reattached. What I do have is a signature in the trace log that pins the state exactly, and it should be cheap to assert against internally:

`~/Library/Application Support/orca/logs/main.trace.ndjson`

1. `renderer_memory` crash-breadcrumb shows a persistent off-by-one between `browserWebviews` and `registeredBrowserGuests`. It appears the moment the tab goes black and never recovers:

```
08-04 21:14  browserWebviews 20  registeredBrowserGuests 20
08-04 23:34                  16                          16
08-05 00:08                  11                          10   <-- mismatch appears
08-05 01:18                  15                          14   (black tab confirmed on screen at 01:20)
08-05 11:46                  17                          16   (same tab still black at 11:46)
```

The delta stayed exactly 1 for ~11.5 h, across many unrelated tab open/close events.

2. `renderer_error` crash-breadcrumbs — 25 occurrences between 08-03 17:29 and 08-05 01:10, all webview lifecycle:

```
15x  Uncaught Error: The WebView must be attached to the DOM and the dom-ready event
     emitted before this method can be called.
10x  Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'focus')
     at WebViewElement.focus (node:electron/...)
```

They occur in pairs 5–10 s apart, consistent with a tab switch / detach-reattach.

3. Not an OOM: `usedHeapMB` stayed around 80 with `heapLimitMB` 4192 across the whole window.

Ruled out along the way: it is not a Cloudflare Access session expiry rendering problem — a separate tab whose Access session had expired rendered the sign-in page correctly (white, `document.readyState` `complete`, 34 KB of DOM).

**Anything else that might help**

1. Detect element-without-guest and recreate the guest — or make reload recreate it — instead of leaving a permanently black tab.
2. Guard the `focus()` and pre-`dom-ready` call sites so a dead guest does not throw into the renderer.
3. `orca tab list` does not enumerate tabs living in the secondary sidebar browser pane. The log showed 17 webviews while the CLI listed 11 tabs, and the affected tab was among the invisible ones — so the tab could not be inspected with `orca eval` / `orca screenshot` at all. Exposing those tabs would make this class of bug diagnosable from the CLI.
4. Consider emitting a per-tab span (URL, navigation, guest lifecycle) in the trace log. Today `main.trace.ndjson` carries only `git.exec`, `renderer.breadcrumb` and `crash.breadcrumb`, so the affected URL cannot be recovered after the fact.

records.title: fix(browser): add native-UA session profiles
records.body:
## Summary

- let users create an isolated browser profile that keeps Electron's unmodified user agent
- keep Orca's cleaned Chrome-shaped UA as the default for Cloudflare compatibility
- preserve a single, stable UA identity for the profile across redirects and subresources
- expose the opt-out in Settings, the browser toolbar, runtime RPC, and `orca tab profile create --no-ua-spoof`
- add a repeatable Google sign-in UA probe for future regression investigation

Google sign-in testing consistently reached `/v3/signin/rejected` with Orca's cleaned Chrome-shaped UA and reached normal account lookup with the untouched Electron UA. A fresh sign-in under the untouched UA also completed and remained usable for 92 minutes. This PR therefore adds a narrow opt-out rather than changing the default or switching identity by destination host.

Closes #11518

## Screenshots

Profile creation option:

![New browser profile dialog with Use unmodified user agent option](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/39c53cca-d461-467c-ab46-23fe65189a69)

Persisted profile label:

![Browser settings showing an Unmodified user agent profile](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8882d101-25a4-49b7-936c-0a21fbcca310)

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm lint`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck`
- [ ] `pnpm test` — 9 focused files / 166 tests passed instead
- [ ] `pnpm build` — no dependency or packaging changes
- [x] Added or updated high-quality tests that would catch regressions

Additional validation:

- Google UA probe: cleaned UA rejected; untouched Electron UA reached account lookup
- probe syntax: `node --check tests/tools/google-signin-ua-probe.cjs`
- Electron QA: option defaults off, toggles, resets after creation, persists `userAgentMode: "native"`, and appears on the profile row

## AI Review Report

Reviewed the user-agent precedence and lifecycle end to end: persisted imported-browser UA first, then the profile's native/clean fallback choice before first navigation. Checked metadata hydration and validation, profile creation through trusted local IPC and remote runtime RPC, CLI parsing, deletion cleanup, UI state reset, and client-hint behavior. The review rejected destination-host UA switching because it would create one session under inconsistent request and JavaScript-visible identities.

Cross-platform review: production changes add no OS-specific paths, shell commands, shortcuts, or labels. The profile option flows through local IPC and runtime RPC, so it applies to local, SSH, and folder-workspace use without assuming a git worktree. Behavior is the same on macOS, Linux, and Windows; the live Google measurement and Electron screenshot QA were run on macOS.

## Security Audit

The new mode is a closed enum validated at RPC and registry boundaries, and persisted profiles still pass the owned-partition allowlist before hydration. Local profile creation remains restricted to the trusted browser renderer. No cookies, auth tokens, or secrets are logged; no dependency, command-execution, or new filesystem-path input is introduced in production code. The diagnostic probe accepts a test account identifier and records navigation/request metadata, but does not accept or store passwords.

## Notes

- Existing profiles and newly created profiles keep today's cleaned UA unless the user explicitly opts out.
- A UA persisted by native browser import still wins over the fallback mode, preserving source-browser fidelity.
- Native mode also avoids Orca's client-hint override, keeping the request headers consistent with Electron's UA.
- Google embedded-browser policy and detection behavior are external and undocumented; this is a compatibility option, not a guarantee.

records.title: fix(browser): align cookie import safeguards
records.body:
## Summary

- apply the Google source-bound cookie filter to file, Firefox, and Safari imports as well as native Chromium imports
- replace existing cookies only for domains represented by the incoming snapshot, preserving unrelated signed-in sites
- count filtered integrity cookies consistently in import summaries

Closes #12601

## Screenshots

## Testing

Focused result: 3 files passed, 34 tests passed.

## AI Review Report

Reviewed the shared import policy, native Chromium path, and the file/Firefox/Safari setter path together. The review checked domain-bound filtering, replacement-before-set ordering, unrelated-cookie preservation, skip accounting, failure behavior, and suffix-confusion cases such as `google.com.evil.example`.

Cross-platform review: the new policy uses Electron's cookie API and URL/domain normalization with no OS branches, paths, shells, shortcuts, or platform labels. The existing native browser discovery/version behavior remains unchanged on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

records.title: fix(computer-use): probe EditableText iface on Linux set-value
records.body:
## Summary

`computer set-value` fails on every Linux desktop with `'Accessible' object has no attribute 'is_editable_text'` — the feature is completely broken, not degraded.

- `Atspi.Accessible.is_editable_text` is not exposed through Python GObject Introspection, so the attribute access raised before `attempt()` could catch it.
- Use `get_editable_text_iface()` and fall back to the Value interface.
- Unit test stubs ATSPI and covers editable / value / no-iface paths.

Root cause independently confirmed by @nwparker on issue #10569 (2026-07-27):

> `set_value()` uses `node.is_editable_text`, which is **not** present on the Python GObject Introspection `Atspi.Accessible` binding (`gir1.2-atspi-2.0`).

> Use `node.get_editable_text_iface() is not None` (GIR-exposed) instead of `node.is_editable_text`.

Fixes #10569

## Test plan
- [x] `python3 native/computer-use-linux/set_value_test.py`

records.title: feat(browser): browser action recorder with agent-ready session logs
records.body:
## What this does

Adds a **browser action recorder** to the browser pane that captures every user interaction, network request, console message, WebSocket frame, clipboard operation, and storage write into a structured, compact markdown log an LLM agent can reason about in a single pass.

### What's new in this update

While recording, the element picker, annotator, and screenshot markup tools now feed the same session log — one unified timeline of what the user did and why:

- **Element picker selections are logged in both flows** (copy and annotate), each with a compact selector suffix: `selected input "Kullanıcı Adınızı Giriniz" (#kadi)`
- **Annotations carry their intent** (`[change]` / `[question]`) and deletion is logged too: `annotated input "Şifre" (#sifre) [question]: "burada şifre girerken **** çıkıyor değil mi?"`
- **Screenshot markup is logged as a shape tree** — geometry, drawn text, and the DOM element each shape points at (resolved via `elementFromPoint`), with selectors:
  ```
  6. markup (3 shapes) @ webticari.net/main.php
     └ arrow (687,782)→(744,722) → div "Recep TEST" (.col-xs-24)
     └ rect (542,423 → 1095,558) → form "Giriş" (#form_giris)
  ```
- **Record mode changes tool behavior**: grab and markup log instead of copying to the clipboard, the annotations tray stays closed (a toast confirms the add), and the toolbar icons (grab / annotate / draw) turn destructive while recording to signal the log-instead-of-copy mode. Everything returns to normal when recording stops.
- **Storage capture fixed**: guest script sent `key/value` while the parser read `storageKey/storageValue` — storage lines always printed empty. Now they show the real pair, debounced 30s per key+value (value changes still report immediately).
- **Recorder's own injected UI filtered out** — clicks/hovers on the grab overlay host (`#__orca-grab-host`) no longer pollute the log as fake user interactions.
- **Collapsed tray expand affordance is clickable** (previously only the log text expanded it).

### How it works
1. An in-page script listens to user events (click, type, hover, scroll, selection, clipboard) + hooks into fetch/XHR send + wraps WebSocket and Storage prototypes
2. Events are reported via tagged `console.debug` lines picked up by the main-process observer
3. The recorder coalesces repeats, deduplicates requests, schematizes HTML responses, and streams structured steps to the renderer
4. The renderer groups steps (lead interaction → member requests/console), renders them in a collapsible tray, and formats a copyable markdown log

### What the agent sees
- **Every interaction** with selector, coordinates, element props — click, type, key, scroll, hover (dwell-based, only when the pointer pauses)
- **Every network request** with method, URL (redacted secrets), status, duration, caller origin (`fn@file:line`), POST body, and response
- **HTML responses schematized** into structure spine + table rows + controls with event handler attributes — not raw 148KB HTML
- **Console errors with stack traces** (`@ fillDiv@otoban.js:317`) — agent knows the throwing function
- **New event kinds agents need**: `change` (form values), `clipboard` (copy/paste with password masking), `ws` (WebSocket push payloads), `storage` (localStorage writes), `select_text` (user text selection)
- **Session summary**: `**Session:** 39s · 27 requests · 3 slow >1s` at log end
- **Step gap labels** (`+5s`, `+1m10s`) between steps — agent knows user wait/think time
- **Slow request markers** (`⚠`) for requests ≥ 500ms

### Architecture
| Layer | Files | Role |
|-------|-------|------|
| In-page script | `browser-interaction-capture-preamble.ts`, `-network.ts` | Event listeners + fetch/XHR/WS/Storage hooks |
| Main process | `browser-recorder-observer.ts`, `-event-recorder.ts`, `-message-parsing.ts`, `-console-streak.ts` | Parse tagged console lines, coalesce repeats, dedupe, cap, stream to renderer |
| Renderer | `browser-recorder-types.ts`, `-output.ts`, `-stream-output.ts`, `-grouping.ts`, `BrowserRecorderTray.tsx` | Step grouping, markdown formatting, collapsible tray with copy/clear |
| Shared | `browser-recorder-automation.ts` | Type unions, budgets, IPC channel contract |

### Noise reduction
- Cloudflare Turnstile challenge requests + two-part token console logs filtered
- requestKey `decodeURIComponent` normalization (page-hook vs webRequest dedupe)
- `markRequestKey` TTL 350ms — follow-up data requests no longer swallowed
- WebSocket empty keep-alive frames skipped
- Storage empty writes skipped, same key+value debounced 2s
- Step cap 200→1000 — long sessions do not silently drop steps

### UX in the browser pane
- Collapsible tray bar (collapsed: recording dot + last event + step counter + copy/clear buttons)
- Auto-copy on recording stop: markdown log copied to clipboard + toast
- Step rows show inter-step gaps

## Demonstration

[browser-action-recorder.webm](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6884efb3-8df3-4cca-affa-0ba186f47feb)

Result: [record-log.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30706305/record-log.md)

## Testing

- [x] `pnpm typecheck` — clean
- [x] `pnpm lint` — 0 warnings, 0 errors
- [x] `pnpm test` — 790 tests (787 existing + 3 new)
- [x] `pnpm build`
- [x] Script syntax + runtime validation (node --check, happy-dom scenarios)
- [x] Added tests: grouping (155 lines), utils (71 lines)
- [x] Updated tests: observer (change/clipboard/gap), output (step gaps, summary, nesting)


---

## What's new in this update (`b1564aeef2`)

### Full annotation text in the log
- Annotations (and removed-annotation lines) previously showed only the first 80 chars of the comment in the recorder log — a 2000-char annotation was cut mid-sentence. The log now carries the complete comment (whitespace still collapses to one line).

### Record options menu (right-click the record button)
- Right-clicking the record button opens a checkbox list: **Console messages**, **Network requests**, **Request details** (postData + response bodies), **Storage writes**, **WebSocket messages**.
- Toggles apply live mid-session via a new `browser:setRecorderOptions` IPC channel; the recording keeps running while options change.
- Filtering happens in the main process (`BrowserRecorderEventRecorder`), not the renderer — disabled streams do not consume per-session caps (console 400 / request 300) and do not waste IPC bandwidth.
- Details:
  - "Request details" off → request lines keep method/url/status, bodies are dropped.
  - "Network requests" off → requests AND the stop-time network summary are suppressed; "Request details" cascades off.
  - "Console messages" off → the pending streak buffer is drained first so messages captured while it was on are not lost.
  - Options are passed at enable time (fail-closed toggle unchanged) and normalized at the IPC boundary (`normalizeRecorderOptions`) so malformed payloads cannot break the session.
- The menu stays open while toggling checkboxes (Radix item select is prevented from closing it); it closes on outside click or Esc.
- i18n: 7 new keys synced via `sync:localization-catalog`.
- Tests: observer (5 new option-filtering cases), hook (options state + IPC + requests→details cascade), output (full annotation text).

### Verification
- [x] `pnpm run typecheck` — clean
- [x] `pnpm exec oxlint` (recorder stack) — 0 warnings, 0 errors
- [x] `pnpm run verify:localization-catalog` — passed
- [x] Vitest: 891 tests in `src/main/browser` + `src/renderer/src/components/browser-pane`, 2784 in preload/shared/ipc — all passing
- [x] `oxfmt --check` on touched files — clean

records.title: feat(browser): add hard reload option and shortcut hints to reload button
records.body: ## Summary Add a tooltip to the browser reload button showing the reload shortcut, and a right-click context menu with "Reload" and "Hard Reload" options, each displaying its shortcut. When iterating on frontend changes (local dev server, Design Mode), the reload button performs a normal reload that serves cached assets. Updated styles or scripts do not appear until the cache expires or the user discovers the `Ctrl+Shift+R` shortcut — which exists but has no visible entry point in the UI. Every major browser exposes hard reload visibly (Chrome long-press on reload, Firefox/Edge context menu). Orca's embedded browser lacked this discoverability. ## What changed - **Reload button** (`BrowserPane.tsx`): wrapped in `Tooltip` + `DropdownMenu` in both `RemoteBrowserPagePane` and `BrowserPagePane`. Left-click still performs a normal reload (existing behavior). Right-click opens a dropdown with two options. - **Hard Reload**: local browser calls `webview.reloadIgnoringCache()` — the same method already wired to the `Ctrl+Shift+R` keybinding. Remote browsers degrade to normal reload (no ignore-cache RPC exists). - **Shortcuts**: displayed via `DropdownMenuShortcut` in the menu and appended to the tooltip text, sourced from the existing `browser.reload` and `browser.hardReload` keybinding definitions (platform-aware labels, no hardcoded `metaKey`). - **i18n**: new `a1f3c2e4b5` key ("Hard Reload") added to all 5 locale files (EN, ZH, JA, KO, ES). ## Screenshots ## Testing - [x] Dev server builds and HMR applies cleanly. - [x] Hover on reload button shows tooltip "Reload · Ctrl+R" (Windows) / "Reload · ⌘R" (Mac). - [x] Right-click reload button opens dropdown with "Reload" + "Hard Reload". - [x] Left-click reload button still performs normal reload (no menu opens). - [x] "Hard Reload" menu item triggers `reloadIgnoringCache()`. - [x] `pnpm lint` - [x] `pnpm typecheck` ## AI Review Report AI agent reviewed the full diff before submission. Checks performed: - **Event handling**: `onPointerDown` prevents default only for left-click so the click reaches the reload action while `DropdownMenuTrigger` stays closed; `onContextMenu` prevents the native menu and opens the dropdown. Verified left-click path preserves the existing stop / error-retry / guest-recovery logic unchanged. - **Shortcut correctness**: menu and tooltip labels come from the existing keybinding registry via `useShortcutLabel`, so `Ctrl+R`/`Ctrl+Shift+R` on Windows/Linux and `⌘R`/`⇧⌘R` on macOS render correctly without hardcoding `e.metaKey` — cross-platform display confirmed. - **i18n completeness**: new key added to all 5 locale files; no missing-key fallback risk. - **Remote path**: confirmed remote panes have no ignore-cache RPC, so Hard Reload intentionally degrades to `browser.reload` there rather than inventing a new IPC surface. No blockers found. Left-click behavior and loading/error branches are byte-identical to the previous implementation. ## Security Audit Low-risk, mostly-presentational change. Nothing new reaches across the trust boundary: - **Input handling**: none new — no new user-input fields or URL parsing. - **Command execution**: none — only calls existing `webview.reload()` / `webview.reloadIgnoringCache()` (local renderer API) and the existing `browser.reload` RPC for remote panes. - **IPC**: no new channels or payloads introduced; remote menu reuses the already-audited `runRemoteNavigation('browser.reload')` path. - **Path / auth / secrets / dependencies**: untouched. No follow-up needed. ## Notes - Remote browser Hard Reload degrades to a normal reload because no ignore-cache RPC exists for remote panes — documented in the menu label context (still labeled "Hard Reload" for consistency). - `pnpm lint` and `pnpm typecheck` pass locally.

records.title: fix(mobile): stop host snapshots yanking the phone off its current tab
records.body:
The phone re-derived its active tab from every incoming host snapshot. Any republication — an agent turn, a desktop focus change, or the browser-activation bootstrap that a mobile browser tap itself triggers — moved the user away. It was permanent, because the host also persisted that fallback to disk.

## Fix

One resolver owns the precedence: pending local activation → explicit `follow` intent → the device's own pick if still present → snapshot `isActive` → `tabs[0]`. Plus stop `ClientSessionTabSelectionStore.project()` writing a topology fallback over the device's explicit pick.

> Both issues are one root cause and one resolver, so they share a PR.

**Behaviour change to note:** the phone no longer mirrors the desktop's active tab on ordinary republications. Explicit navigation (`navigation: 'clients' | 'all'` → `navigationIntent: 'follow'`) still moves it.

## Verification

- `pnpm typecheck` clean on this branch
- This branch's own tests pass; the new cases fail before the change and pass after
- Split out of the original combined branch; the union of all 12 split branches was diffed back against it to prove nothing was lost

Fixes #8364
Fixes #8700

## Summary

Follow-up to #12232. The merged interrupted-download fix updated only module-local veto state, so the Terminal guest-budget effect did not rerun when a download, automation lease, or mobile driver released its veto. An over-budget live guest could therefore remain retained until an unrelated worktree, surface, or setting change.

This change:

- invalidates the guest-retention pass when download activity crosses active/inactive
- subscribes the same pass to automation visibility and mobile-driver changes
- deduplicates duplicate progressing/null/unknown download events, avoiding work per progress tick
- removes download, automation, and mobile subscriptions with the Terminal host

The sanctioned eviction path is unchanged: selected worktrees still fully destroy their guests through destroyWorktreeBrowserGuests; no live guest is unmount-detached.
